# Question Threshold Evidence If NO
1 Does the Month 2 technical audit show that no more than 35% of carriers lack a credible path to the p95 <2 s / 99.5% SLA by their tier date, and that shared adapters cover at least 60% of observed legacy patterns? At most 35% of carriers unable to meet the SLA by tier date; shared adapter patterns cover at least 60% of legacy systems (A2 / FM2 tripwires, proposed thresholds). The audit must also cover carriers on all four priority corridors. Technical audit of all carriers with synthetic three-leg queries, due Month 2; per-operator tier assignment published Month 6. Downsize or split. Re-tier with a Tier 1.5 cohort, rely on the distributed cache, and restrict the first wave to corridors whose carriers all meet the SLA. Treat the EUR 240M adapter line and the 8-15 at-risk operators as a re-baselining item; FM2 stop rule applies if fewer than 15 operators are conformant by Month 36.
2 Is there written confirmation of a Regulation timetable that keeps adoption at about Month 18, with no adoption later than Month 24, and do regulators on the four priority corridors accept the data-sharing and clearing design? Written timetable from the Commission legislative affairs unit showing adoption no later than Month 24 (A6 trigger, proposed threshold; target about Month 18); no national regulator on a priority corridor signalling it will not enforce API exposure; DG COMP pre-notification filed by Month 2. Legislative timetable confirmation and regulator impact assessments, due Month 3; DG COMP pre-notification filed Month 2. Delay or downsize. Launch the shadow-standards workstream and pilot authority, issue a voluntary conformance profile, and plan on the 15-30% planning range (estimate). If adoption is still not in sight, the FM5 fallback is a voluntary corridor-pilot model; the stop date needs to be set (see contradictions).
3 Have at least 8 major carriers and CER signed non-binding letters of intent to expose inventory under the interim liability parameters? At least 8 major carriers plus CER sign by Month 4, against the Month 3 interim parameters (indicative cap EUR 500-1,000 per stranded passenger; co-insurance above EUR 50M annual pool draw; both proposed thresholds). Loss data supplied by at least 3 major carriers (FM3 tripwire). Actuarial interim results and draft model at Month 3; signed letters of intent at Month 4; mediation at Month 5 if short. Delay and redesign. Escalate to Commission mediation at Month 5 and pause dependent procurement. Offer a two-tier pool with reinsurance for smaller operators and use the Month 12 deferral. Stop rule: pivot to the Prudent Consolidator model if fewer than 6 major carriers commit by Month 12.
4 Does the Month 6 gate pass: the liability model is signed within the agreed band of the final actuarial study, steering votes on Decisions 1-5 reach the 75% supermajority, and the audit and tier assignment are published? At least 75% (7 of 9 core members) on Decisions 1, 2, 3 and 12; final study within the agreed band of the interim parameters; tiers published at Month 6; unresolved at Month 9 means deferral to Month 12. Binding steering votes, final actuarial study and tier assignment at Month 6; mediation outcome at Month 5. Delay. Defer the gate to Month 12 under the pre-agreed rule and compress Phase 1. Month 18 binding standards remains the user constraint, so every month of deferral is a schedule risk to be reported, not absorbed. Prepare pilot authority and shadow standards.
5 Does the concession market test support a bounded last-resort service: at least 3 credible bidders, subsidy within EUR 60M over five years, volume at least 60% of forecast, and a decided split of the EUR 300M envelope? At least 3 credible bidders; subsidy at or below EUR 60M over five years; forecast volume at least 60% of plan; envelope split between set-up and service payments decided (proposed thresholds). Market sounding with 5-8 concessionaires, business case and 75% steering approval at Month 9; tender issued Month 12; award about Month 18. Downsize. Hold the tender, re-scope to a lean last-resort service or direct public operation (EUR 30-50M, estimate), and re-baseline under the variance triggers. Stop rule: withdraw the concession and run a minimal public service if no compliant bid is within the cap by Month 18.
6 Has DG COMP issued guidance confirming that the federated clearing and data-sharing design is compatible with Article 101, with the clean-team protocol approved, before the clearing contract becomes unconditional? Guidance letter by Month 12; clean-team protocol approved by Month 14 and no later than Month 18; cumulative rework variance below EUR 50M; at least 6 carriers confirming feed commitments by Month 15 (FM1 tripwires). DG COMP guidance letter (Month 12), clean-team approval (Month 14), interim feedback requested by Month 9. Stop or downsize the clearing layer. Freeze clearing commitments, pivot to bilateral clearing with a neutral dispute layer, and re-baseline the EUR 220M line. Stop rule: cancel the shared clearing layer if no compliant design is approved by Month 18.

8 open decisions: 3 high and 5 medium severity. The earliest decisions are the force-majeure reserve rule (before the Month 4 = 2027-02-12 liability sign-off), the variance trigger basis and the regulation-slip tolerance (by Month 3 = 2027-01-12), then the headroom funding order and concession envelope split (Months 6-8 = 2027-04-12 to 2027-06-12). Until they are made, the plan can safely run the Month 2 (2026-12-12) audit, DG COMP pre-notification, actuarial study commissioning and steering set-up, but cannot lock budget lines, tranches or the concession tender.

1. Concession envelope split (🔴 High)

Decision: How is the EUR 300M concession envelope split between platform set-up, operating subsidy and public service-level payments, and is any unallocated part returned to headroom?

Why it is open: Canonical: EUR 300M envelope, subsidy capped at EUR 60M. Review 11.1 calls EUR 250-270M 'operating subsidy'; Review 3.3 says the business case 'locks' the envelope on only about EUR 110M of defined use. About EUR 190-210M has no stated use.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Fix set-up EUR 30-50M (proposed), subsidy EUR 60M, and quantify service-level payments for the remainder. Keeps EUR 300M line; business case at Month 9 (2027-07-12) can lock a full split; tender at Month 12 (2027-10-12) proceeds on a defined payment basis. budget_line_concession_eur_m; Reviews 11.1, 1.3, 3.3; concession_controls.
B. Reduce the envelope to the defined uses and return the difference to headroom. Headroom rises above EUR 85M by up to about EUR 190-210M; eases C3 claims and variance triggers; EUR 200M trigger 'cut 20% (EUR 60M)' must be redefined. budget_line_concession_eur_m; budget_unallocated_headroom_eur_m; budget_variance_triggers.
C. Defer the split until the Month 9 (2027-07-12) market sounding. Tender at Month 12 (2027-10-12) stays feasible but the envelope remains partly unallocated for 9 months; headroom claims cannot be capped. open_decisions; Review 3.3 wording.
  • If nobody decides: Envelope stays at EUR 300M with an unallocated remainder; the Month 9 (2027-07-12) business case cannot be approved by the 75% steering vote.
  • Owner: Programme Steering Committee (75% supermajority for concession business case)
  • Decide by: Month 8 (2027-06-12), so the Month 9 (2027-07-12) business case and Month 12 (2027-10-12) tender have a defined payment basis.
  • Blocks: Month 9 (2027-07-12) concession business case and Month 12 (2027-10-12) tender issue; the concession market-test gate.

2. Headroom claims and validation hardware financing (🔴 High)

Why it is open: Named claims on headroom total roughly EUR 130-205M against EUR 85M. The EUR 50M reserve has no canonical line. Review 11.2 funds validation hardware (EUR 30-80M) from headroom; Premortem A8 says it must not draw on headroom.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Carve the reserve from headroom and make carriers finance validation hardware. C. Drop the reserve and rely on variance triggers. Headroom stays EUR 85M, but adapter slips of EUR 150-250M (estimate) hit triggers earlier. Exec Summary Risks; Reviews 1.2, 2.2, 3.2.

4. Variance trigger basis (🟡 Medium)

Decision: Are the EUR 100M / 200M / 300M variance triggers measured gross against committed lines or net of the EUR 85M headroom?

Why it is open: Review 2.2 uses a net-of-headroom basis; Reviews 1.2, 3.2 use gross exposures. Self-Audit 18 lists EUR 50M/100M/200M. A hard cap of EUR 1,500M with EUR 85M headroom means a net basis lets spend exceed the cap before the first trigger.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Gross cost growth against committed lines (EUR 1,415M). First trigger fires at EUR 100M, above headroom; a gap of EUR 15M needs a cut or reserve use before it fires. budget_variance_triggers; Self-Audit 18; Reviews 1.2, 2.2, 3.2.
B. Net of headroom, so triggers fire only after headroom is exhausted. Triggers fire at EUR 185M/285M/385M gross; cap likely breached before action. budget_variance_triggers; public_budget_cap_eur_m interpretation.
C. Lower first trigger to at or below headroom (e.g. EUR 50M, proposed threshold). Earlier TEN-T deferral; protects cap; changes canonical values. budget_variance_triggers; negative consequences in escalation matrix.
  • If nobody decides: Triggers stay ambiguous; PSC cannot apply them consistently at quarterly review.
  • Owner: Programme Steering Committee, with Commission Financial Controller
  • Decide by: Month 3 (2027-01-12), before first quarterly variance tracking.
  • Blocks: First quarterly variance review; Self-Audit and budget governance baseline.

Focus and Context

Across the EU, cross-border rail journeys require separate bookings, liability splits and distributor friction that leaves passengers unprotected and rail uncompetitive against short-haul air. This programme delivers a federated EU backbone—OSDM-compatible APIs, shared real-time data, carrier-funded liability pools and unified clearing—layered over legacy systems to enable 40% of cross-border journeys to be sold as single through-tickets within five years, halving distributor complaints and catalysing EUR 1.5–3.0 billion in private carrier IT investment.

Purpose and Goals

Enable 40% of cross-border EU rail journeys to be sold as single through-tickets with unified passenger-rights protection and automatic rerouting if a connection fails, by Month 60 (2031-10-12), within a EUR 1,500M public budget cap. Deliver binding OSDM standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12), mandatory API exposure for all Tier 1 carriers (Month 30 = 2029-04-12; Tier 1 count fixed by the Month 6 = 2027-04-12 tier assignment), four-corridor go-live (Month 48 = 2030-10-12) and full TEN-T extension (Month 60 = 2031-10-12). Halve distributor complaints. Air-to-rail modal shift of 5–10% on benchmarked routes is reported as an indicative observation (estimate), not a success metric.

Key Deliverables and Outcomes

OSDM binding standards with liability backstop, clearing rulebook and SLA requirements (Month 18 = 2028-04-12). Tier 1–3 carrier API exposure (Months 30/36/42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12). Four-corridor through-ticketing go-live by Month 48 (2030-10-12), with 40% through-ticket share by Month 60 (2031-10-12). Federated EUR 220M clearing infrastructure with 5-business-day settlement, <0.5% reconciliation error. Public reference distributor concession with EUR 60M subsidy cap. Shared adapter modules (EUR 30M) for legacy systems. Real-time availability layer and disruption rerouting. Accessibility compliance (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours' notice). Passenger-rights compliance manual and complaints handling (halved complaints by Month 60 = 2031-10-12).

Timeline and Budget

Five-year horizon: Phase 1 (Months 0–18 = 2026-10-12 to 2028-04-12) governance, decisions, standards, pilots; Phase 2 (Months 18–48 = 2028-04-12 to 2030-10-12) API exposure and four-corridor go-live; Phase 3 (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) TEN-T extension. EUR 1,500M public cap: standards EUR 80M, real-time layer EUR 50M (distributed cache EUR 15–25M, SLA proxy, event feed), clearing EUR 220M, adapters EUR 240M, concession EUR 300M, capacity-building EUR 200M, consumer-rollout EUR 100M, programme-management EUR 75M, force-majeure reserve EUR 150M. Unallocated headroom EUR 85M (5.7% of cap). Private carrier IT investment EUR 1.5–3.0B (estimate), outside public budget.

Risks and Mitigations

Carrier refusal if liability model remains unpriced: Commission actuarial study (Month 1 = 2026-11-12), publish interim parameters at Month 3 (2027-01-12), secure carrier sign-off from 8+ carriers by Month 4 (2027-02-12) against those interim parameters (final Month 6 = 2027-04-12 study adjustable only within an agreed band), mediation Month 5 (2027-03-12), binding vote Month 6 (2027-04-12). Thin EUR 85M headroom threatened by fallback exposures (adapters EUR 65–165M over headroom; concession up to EUR 65M over; Article 101 up to EUR 15M over) (adapter slip, concession overrun, Article 101 rework): fix price ceilings and framework terms with conditions precedent for about EUR 330M (23% of committed lines; standards, clearing and shared adapter modules) by Month 6 (2027-04-12), with contracts conditional on DG COMP guidance (Month 12 = 2027-10-12) and clean-team approval (Month 14 = 2027-12-12); establish EUR 50M adapter-acceleration reserve; monthly cash-flow variance tracking starting Month 1 (2026-11-12) with automatic scope-cut triggers (EUR 100M defers TEN-T; EUR 200M cuts concession; EUR 300M restricts to four corridors). Regulation adoption slip and DG COMP guidance delay compound standards risk: File DG COMP pre-notification Month 2 (2026-12-12), request interim feedback by Month 9 (2027-07-12), guidance letter expected Month 12 (2027-10-12); prepare shadow-standards workstream by Month 6 (2027-04-12).

Audience Tailoring

Programme stakeholders (DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways, 25+ national rail operators, distributors, member states, regulators): a formal executive summary in institutional tone, balancing accessibility for transport policymakers with technical precision for carrier CIOs and clearing engineers. Avoids jargon but assumes familiarity with EU transport regulation and rail industry structure.

Action Orientation

Month 1 (2026-11-12): Establish steering governance (75% supermajority voting rule) and commission actuarial study. Month 2 (2026-12-12): File DG COMP pre-notification and conduct technical audit. Month 3 (2027-01-12): Publish actuarial interim findings and conduct regulator impact assessments. Month 4 (2027-02-12): Obtain non-binding letters of intent from at least 8 major carriers and CER on the liability model, against interim parameters. Month 6 (2027-04-12): Publish technical audit tier assignment, execute steering votes on Decisions 1–5, finalize clearing rulebook, request DG COMP interim feedback (by Month 9 = 2027-07-12). Month 9 (2027-07-12): Publish concession business case and obtain steering approval. Month 12 (2027-10-12): Tender concession, procure shared adapters, deploy SLA monitoring. Month 18 (2028-04-12): Obtain binding standards adoption and complete live pilots (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12; before Month 14 = 2027-12-12 on non-contested data flows only). Month 30 (2029-04-12): Tier 1 API exposure and concession launch. Month 48 (2030-10-12): Four-corridor through-ticketing go-live. Month 60 (2031-10-12): Full TEN-T extension and programme close.

Overall Takeaway

This programme delivers transformational through-ticketing at scale (40% cross-border share) and cuts regulatory and operational friction by layering federated standards over existing carriers, using milestone-gated funding to drive compliance without central control. Risk is real (carrier participation, budget headroom, legislative uncertainty), but mitigation pathways are documented with clear trigger points (Month 6 = 2027-04-12 readiness gate, Month 9 = 2027-07-12 deferral escalation, EUR 100/200/300M variance cuts). Early action on actuarial validation, technical audit and steering governance (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-04-12) unblocks Phase 1 and secures non-binding carrier letters of intent on the liability model by Month 4 (2027-02-12), with the binding vote at Month 6 (2027-04-12), towards 25+ carriers in the network by Month 42 (2030-04-12). Success hinges on transparent decision-making, tight budget discipline and fallback contingency authority.

Feedback

Version 2 significantly strengthens the plan by quantifying risks (20-risk taxonomy with per-item fallback exceedances vs. EUR 85M headroom), adding expert reviews (8 domain specialists with mitigation protocols), defining binding governance rules (75% supermajority, mediation escalation, scope-cut triggers at EUR 100/200/300M variance), and specifying Phase 1 readiness gates (Month 6 = 2027-04-12 with precise carrier sign-off thresholds). Recommend: (1) Lock DG COMP pre-notification filing by Month 2 (2026-12-12), not Month 2 (2026-12-12), to recover 4–6 week schedule buffer; (2) Publish monthly cash-flow forecasts and variance dashboard by Month 3 (2027-01-12) for real-time budget visibility; (3) Establish independent audit function (external firm retained Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12) to verify SLA performance and milestone gate readiness, removing Programme Office self-certification risk; (4) Define post-Month 60 (2031-10-12) cost-recovery and governance transition model by Month 36 (2029-10-12) to signal long-term infrastructure permanence and sustain carrier IT investment commitment.

Unoptimized waterfall. Parallel work not modelled here.

Part 2: Supporting analysis

Persuasive elevator pitch.

EU Cross-Border Rail Ticketing and Passenger Protection Programme

Project Overview

Imagine boarding a train in Paris and seamlessly transferring across three carriers to reach Vienna with a single ticket, unified passenger protection, and automatic rerouting if a connection fails. Today, that journey requires separate bookings, separate liability, and no recourse if one carrier's delay strands you.

This programme delivers that vision: a federated EU cross-border rail ticketing system that turns fragmented national rail networks into one integrated market. By layering shared real-time data, carrier-funded liability protection and universal booking access over existing carrier systems, the programme enables 40% of cross-border journeys to be sold as single through-tickets within five years—halving distributor complaints. It does so on a fixed EUR 1.5 billion public budget, with carriers funding their own connection liability and a private last-resort distributor handling the rest. Subject to adoption of the Regulation (not verified) and DG COMP guidance, this is regulation-backed, pragmatically federated, and delivers transformational passenger value without centralised control risk.

Target Audience

Primary stakeholders: EU institutions (DG MOVE, the Agency for Railways, the Commission); national rail operators and CER; independent distributors (Trainline, Omio); member-state governments.

Secondary stakeholders: National railway regulators, disability-rights and consumer bodies, and DG COMP.

The pitch aligns institutional interests (member states and the Commission want digital integration), industry interests (carriers want network effects and regulatory certainty for investment; distributors want fair access), and passenger interests (seamless cross-border travel). The language avoids jargon but assumes familiarity with EU transport regulation and rail industry structure.

Risks and Mitigation Strategies

  • Carrier refusal over unpriceable connection liability: Mitigated by an actuarial study (Month 6 = 2027-04-12) and a carrier-signed guarantee pool with per-incident caps, coinsurance thresholds and trailing-performance incentives.

  • Legacy IT delays: Tiers spread mandatory API exposure across Months 30/36/42 (2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12), with EUR 240M adapter budget line for legacy modernisation (EUR 30M shared adapter modules tendered by Month 12 (2027-10-12); EUR 210M tiered carrier funding released on verified conformance).

  • Regulation adoption slip: Parallel shadow-standards workstream prepared, with pilot authority, by Month 6 (2027-04-12), to be launched if the regulation slips past Month 9 (2027-07-12).

  • Competition-law challenge: Pre-notification to DG COMP at Month 2 (2026-12-12), guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12), clean-team protocol for Article 101 safe-harbour by Month 14 (2027-12-12).

  • Budget overrun: EUR 150M force-majeure reserve and variance triggers at EUR 100M (defer TEN-T extension), EUR 200M (cut concession funding 20%, i.e. EUR 60M of the EUR 300M envelope, and extend term from 5 to 7 years) and EUR 300M (restrict to four corridors).

Metrics for Success

Outcome metrics:

  • 40% of cross-border journeys sold as single through-tickets by Month 60 (2031-10-12)
  • Distributor complaints halved

Delivery metrics:

  • Binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12)
  • Tier 1 API exposure achieved by all Tier 1 carriers (count fixed by the Month 6 (2027-04-12) tier assignment) by Month 30 (2029-04-12); 25+ carriers network-wide by Month 42 (2030-04-12)
  • Four corridors live by Month 48 (2030-10-12)
  • Full TEN-T network by Month 60 (2031-10-12)

Operational metrics:

  • p95 latency below 2 seconds, availability 99.5%, stale-seat failures below 1%
  • Settlement cycle 5 business days, reconciliation error below 0.5%
  • SLA misses trigger 5% tranche penalties

Budget metric:

  • Public spend within EUR 1,500M cap; concession operating subsidy capped at EUR 60M over five years

Stakeholder Benefits

Passengers: Unified cross-border tickets with automatic rerouting if a connection fails, halved complaints and reduced distributor friction.

National operators: Network effects from through-ticketing drive passenger volumes; carrier-funded liability pool shares connection risk fairly; mandatory API access is intended to be regulation-backed, subject to adoption of the Regulation (not verified), not ad-hoc.

Member states: EU decarbonisation targets supported (indicative 5–10% air-to-rail shift on benchmarked routes, estimate); digital integration strengthens European competitiveness; coordinated funding leverages EUR 1.5 billion alongside EUR 1.5–3.0 billion (estimate) of carrier-financed IT investment.

Independent distributors: Level playing field enforced by the conformance gate and commission band (2.5–4.5%, indicative); non-discriminatory OSDM API access; public last-resort distributor is a concessionaire (private), not a competitor.

DG COMP: Data-sharing and clearing structures are targeted for legal comfort via DG COMP pre-notification at Month 2 (2026-12-12) and guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12) (not verified); clean-team protocol limits commercial data visibility.

Ethical Considerations

Passenger protection: Existing EU rail passenger-rights regulation is the floor; independent legal review by Month 6 (2027-04-12) ensures through-ticket liability rules are accessible and enforceable.

Accessibility: Persons with reduced mobility and bicycle reservations are bookable through-components; 80% wheelchair access and 90% assistance within 4 hours' notice (proposed threshold) on corridors by Month 40 (2030-02-12).

Fair competition: Commission-supervised commission band (identical for all distributors); non-discriminatory API access; public last-resort channel is tendered to a private concessionaire, not operated by the state.

Data governance: Clean-team protocol ensures carriers' commercial data is held only by a neutral trustee; no data pooling for purposes beyond clearing and settlement.

Inclusivity: Biweekly steering group includes disability-rights and consumer bodies as observers; usability testing by Month 18 (2028-04-12).

Collaboration Opportunities

Carriers (CER, national operators):

  • Design and sign off the liability model (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-04-12)
  • Commit Tier 1 API readiness (by Month 30 = 2029-04-12)
  • Shape commission band and SLA standards through the steering group

Distributors (Trainline, Omio, CRS):

  • Contribute conformance test scenarios
  • Serve on the API design working group
  • Bid on the EUR 300M concession or backend integration contracts

Member states and regulators:

  • Receive national carrier support and training, delivered to member states from the EUR 200M capacity-building envelope financed from the public cap
  • Co-host the Technical Secretariat (Agency at Valenciennes)
  • Conduct local regulator impact assessments by Month 3 (2027-01-12)

Technology and fintech partners:

  • Develop shared adapter modules (EUR 30M), real-time cache and event-feed infrastructure (EUR 50M), federated clearing platform (EUR 220M)

International railways (SBB, DB, ÖBB, SNCF):

  • Lead by example on Tier 1 API exposure
  • Pilot disruption re-accommodation choreography at Months 12–18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12)

Long-term Vision

By Month 60 (2031-10-12), the programme establishes cross-border rail as seamlessly bookable and reliably protected as domestic rail today—. This is sustained beyond the programme by transferring governance to the EU Agency for Railways (custodian of the OSDM standard and conformance test suite), a permanent carrier steering committee and national regulators as observers.

The federated architecture (streamed availability shadow, carrier-funded liability, distributed clearing) scales to multimodal integration with bus, ferry and short-haul air under the same OSDM and liability frameworks. The EUR 1.5 billion public investment catalyses EUR 1.5–3.0 billion in carrier IT, creating a permanent digital infrastructure layer that supports not just through-ticketing but real-time disruption management, carbon-intensity signalling and demand-responsive services.

The 40% through-ticket target and halved complaints reduce regulator burden and distributor friction for decades, making European rail a model for other continents.

Call to Action

Member-state governments and national operators: Commit now to the steering group and liability model sign-off by Month 4 (2027-02-12); early commitment unlocks EUR 80M in conformance support.

Independent distributors: Join the Month 1 (2026-11-12) governance launch to shape the commission band and API access rules before binding standards.

Investors and technology partners: Contact DG MOVE to bid on the EUR 50M real-time layer, EUR 220M clearing infrastructure and EUR 30M shared adapter modules—all to be tendered by Month 12 (2027-10-12); the remaining EUR 210M of the adapter line is tiered carrier funding released on verified conformance.

The Commission: Adopt the Digital Booking and Ticketing Regulation by Month 18 (2028-04-12) with OSDM pinned, and secure DG COMP competition-law guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12).

Goal Statement: Deliver a federated EU cross-border rail through-ticketing programme, aligned with the proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail, so that 40% of cross-border journeys are sold as single through-tickets and distributor complaints are halved by Month 60 (2031-10-12), within a EUR 1,500M public budget cap.

SMART Criteria

  • Specific: Establish shared standards, a real-time availability layer, federated clearing, a carrier-funded rights backstop and a last-resort distributor so any compliant distributor can sell through-tickets across participating carriers on four priority corridors, then the TEN-T network.
  • Measurable: 40% of cross-border journeys sold as single through-tickets, distributor complaints halved, binding standards at Month 18 (2028-04-12), Tier 1 API exposure at Month 30 (2029-04-12), four corridors live by Month 48 (2030-10-12), public spend within EUR 1,500M.
  • Achievable: Builds on OSDM and existing clearing arrangements, layering over legacy carrier systems. Carrier-funded liability pool and milestone tranches protect the budget. Risks: carrier participation, legislative slip; planning range if prerequisites slip is 15-30% (estimate).
  • Relevant: Removes fragmentation that blocks single-ticket cross-border rail travel, improves passenger rights continuity, distributor access and the competitiveness of rail against short-haul air.
  • Time-bound: Five years from project start: governance at Month 1 (2026-11-12), binding standards Month 18 (2028-04-12), Tier 1 API exposure Month 30 (2029-04-12), four corridors live Month 48 (2030-10-12), target full network and 40% share by Month 60 (2031-10-12).

Dependencies

  • Adoption of the Regulation, with binding standards and OSDM pinned by Month 18 (2028-04-12)
  • Competition-law comfort from DG COMP on shared data and clearing, before standards bind
  • Carrier-signed liability model (guarantee pool, caps, co-insurance) before inventory exposure
  • Technical audit of carrier booking systems and tier assignment to set conformance timelines
  • Steering governance with binding votes on liability, clearing, public distributor and commission band

Resources Required

  • Public coordination budget of EUR 1,500M (user constraint)
  • Programme Office (about 80 staff, estimate) and Technical Secretariat (about 50 staff, estimate)
  • Carrier IT integration teams, financed privately at EUR 1.5-3.0 billion (estimate)
  • Actuarial, competition-law and passenger-rights legal specialists
  • Conformance test environments, reconciliation platform and SLA monitoring proxy

Related Goals

  • Air-to-rail modal shift on competitive short-haul corridors (5-10% planning value, estimate)
  • Accessible assistance and bicycle reservation across carriers
  • Multimodal integration with bus, ferry and short-haul air
  • Full TEN-T network through-ticketing

Tags

  • rail
  • through-ticketing
  • OSDM
  • EU regulation
  • clearing and settlement

Risk Assessment and Mitigation Strategies

Key Risks

  • Carriers refuse to expose inventory because connection liability cannot be priced
  • Legacy booking systems miss Month 30 (2029-04-12) API exposure; 8-15 smaller operators at risk (estimate)
  • Regulation adoption slips 6-12 months beyond Month 18 (2028-04-12) (estimate, not verified)
  • Article 101 TFEU challenge forces clearing rework of EUR 50-100M (estimate)
  • Pool or concession overruns exceed the EUR 85M free headroom

Diverse Risks

  • Steering deadlock delays binding standards by 2-4 months (estimate)
  • Latency and availability shortfalls across multi-leg queries reduce through-ticket success
  • Reconciliation errors lengthen settlement cycles and deter distributors
  • Ticket validation gaps on corridor vehicles reduce passenger trust
  • Low-fare airline response limits modal shift

Mitigation Plans

  • Actuarial study and carrier-signed liability model with caps and co-insurance by Month 4 (2027-02-12); Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate, deferring to Month 12 (2027-10-12) if unresolved
  • Technical audit by Month 2 (2026-12-12), tiered conformance (Months 30/36/42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12) and EUR 240M adapter funding released on verified performance
  • DG COMP pre-notification at Month 2 (2026-12-12), guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12), clean-team protocol by Month 14 (2027-12-12); shadow standards workstream for legislative slip
  • EUR 150M force-majeure reserve, no pool draw-downs after Month 36 (2029-10-12), variance triggers at EUR 100M/200M/300M and concession subsidy cap of EUR 60M
  • 75% supermajority steering rule with Commission mediation, SLA scorecards tied to tranches, and live pilots at Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12)
