Primary Stakeholders

  • DG MOVE (Programme Office)
  • EU Agency for Railways (Technical Secretariat)
  • National rail operators and CER
  • Independent distributors (Trainline, Omio) and the last-resort concessionaire
  • Passengers, BEUC and disability-rights bodies

Secondary Stakeholders

  • National railway regulators
  • DG COMP
  • Member-state governments
  • Bus, ferry and short-haul air operators
  • Payment service providers and IT vendors

Engagement Strategies

  • Biweekly steering group with binding votes on core decisions by Month 6 (2027-04-12) and Commission mediation for deadlock
  • Option papers by Month 2 (2026-12-12) and quarterly briefings to carriers and distributors on pool, SLA and commission-band data
  • Regulator observer seats in standards groups plus bilateral impact assessments per member state
  • Disability and consumer bodies as observers, with usability testing by Month 18 (2028-04-12)
  • Milestone-based reporting to DG COMP, the Court of Auditors and member states

Regulatory and Compliance Requirements

Permits and Licenses

  • Adoption and Official Journal publication of the Digital Booking and Ticketing Regulation
  • Delegated or implementing act pinning the OSDM version
  • Payment-services authorisation for the settlement layer participants (where required)
  • Concession award under EU public procurement rules

Compliance Standards

  • Article 101 TFEU competition rules
  • Existing EU rail passenger-rights regulation as the rights floor
  • GDPR for passenger and booking data
  • EU accessibility requirements for persons with reduced mobility

Regulatory Bodies

  • European Commission (DG MOVE, DG COMP)
  • EU Agency for Railways
  • National railway regulators
  • European Court of Auditors

Compliance Actions

  • Pre-notify DG COMP at Month 2 (2026-12-12) and obtain guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12)
  • Commission independent passenger-rights review at Month 1 (2026-11-12), opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-12), compliance manual approved by Month 9 (2027-07-12)
  • Complete regulator impact assessments per member state by Month 3 (2027-01-12)
  • Set up clean-team clearing protocol by Month 14 (2027-12-12)
  • Apply accessibility thresholds (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours' notice) in conformance (proposed threshold)

Primary Decisions

The vital few decisions that have the most impact.

The Critical and High levers address the program's core tensions: central control vs. carrier autonomy (clearing, availability architecture), risk-sharing vs. budget exhaustion (liability backstop, funding ladder), and coverage vs. quality (conformance gate). Fare construction, the public distributor and competition-law clearance decide whether commercial and legal acceptance follows. Medium and Low levers are largely execution layers. No major strategic dimension appears missing, though member-state capacity building and corridor sequencing are not explicitly covered.

Decision 1: Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop

Lever ID: 1d2d447b-fab1-4f1b-94cb-5926fcfc2c3c

The Core Decision: Allocates financial and service responsibility when a protected connection fails across carriers, covering assistance, rerouting, compensation and cost recovery. Success metrics: share of missed-connection claims settled within a fixed window, number of carriers willing to expose cross-carrier connections, drawdown of any public fund against the €1.5 billion budget, and recovery rate from the responsible carrier. Precise recourse rules determine whether incentives reward punctuality.

Why It Matters: This decides who pays and who answers to the passenger when a connection between two carriers is missed on a single through-ticket. A pooled arrangement lowers the retail risk for distributors but requires carriers to accept shared exposure for delays they do not control. Whichever model is chosen sets the incentive for carriers to open inventory, because carriers refuse to sell connections whose liability they cannot price.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Establish a carrier-funded mutual guarantee pool that pays assistance, rerouting and compensation on any through-ticket, with contributions weighted by each carrier's share of missed-connection incidents.
  2. Make the selling distributor the single point of liability toward the passenger and require it to hold insurance, with contractual recourse against the carrier whose delay caused the missed connection.
  3. Create a publicly capitalised rights backstop fund within the €1.5 billion budget that pays passengers immediately and later recovers costs from the responsible carrier through the clearing mechanism.

Trade-Off / Risk: A pooled or public backstop gives distributors certainty, but unless recourse rules are precise it rewards chronic late-running carriers, and any public fund that pays first can drain the budget before the later corridors are reached.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement, since pool contributions and recourse claims can be netted through the same rails, and Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography, since settled liability lets rerouting proceed without disputes over who pays.

Conflict: Trades off against Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder, because a public pay-first fund draws on the budget needed for later corridors, and Through-Fare Construction Doctrine, because wider protected connections raise carrier exposure and invite resistance.

Justification: Critical, Hub deciding who pays when a connection fails; carriers will not expose connections whose liability they cannot price. Links to clearing, disruption handling and fare construction, and draws on the €1.5 billion budget, controlling the risk-sharing vs. budget-drain trade-off.

Decision 2: Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement

Lever ID: bebf01c8-c60c-4af4-a866-03db2fdc3463

The Core Decision: Defines the financial plumbing that turns one passenger payment into correct carrier shares, reverses refunds across carriers and pays out on schedule. Scope includes netting, reconciliation formats, dispute resolution and settlement timing for carriers and independent distributors. Success metrics: settlement cycle time, reconciliation error rate, refund reversal completion time, and independent distributors' acceptance of the governance mandate. The choice also fixes how much cash and operational risk sits centrally.

Why It Matters: This determines how one passenger payment is split among several carriers and how refunds are reversed across them. A central clearing entity gives uniform rules and reconciliation, but concentrates operational risk and needs a governance mandate that carriers and independent distributors both accept. A split-at-source design reduces the amount held centrally but pushes more complexity onto payment providers and distributors.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Build a single EU-level clearing entity that receives the passenger payment, nets positions across carriers and distributors, and pays out on a fixed schedule under a common rulebook.
  2. Federate settlement through a shared netting and dispute-resolution layer that connects existing bilateral and sector clearing arrangements, so carriers keep their current accounting flows.
  3. Split payments at the point of sale through licensed payment service providers that allocate each fare component directly to the carriers, leaving the clearing layer to handle only refunds and disputes.

Trade-Off / Risk: A central clearing entity delivers uniform rules but becomes a single point of failure and a governance fight; the federated option is quicker to launch but may leave refund reversals inconsistent across carriers.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Through-Fare Construction Doctrine, since apportionment rules need a settlement engine to execute them, and Distribution Remuneration and Commission Corridor, since distributor commissions can be deducted and reported automatically at payout.

Conflict: Strains Joint Conduct Safe-Harbour for Shared Data and Clearing, because centralised netting concentrates commercially sensitive data and competition-law scrutiny, and Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder, because a central entity front-loads capital and governance effort before corridors prove value.

Justification: Critical, Financial backbone enabling single-payment through-tickets, refund reversal, fare apportionment and commission netting. Many levers (fare construction, remuneration, liability recourse) depend on it; it also fixes central vs. federated risk and governance concentration.

Decision 3: Public Reference Distributor Mandate

Lever ID: 66907c16-7bdd-4a30-bd78-d40dd776eeb3

The Core Decision: Determines the role of the publicly funded booking service: neutral consumer channel, technical benchmark, or distributor of last resort. It shapes how much of the €1.5 billion goes to consumer apps, multilingual support and complaint handling versus sandbox tooling. Success metrics: share of through-tickets sold via the service, journeys purchasable somewhere on participating carriers, complaint resolution time, and absence of successful competition-law challenges from commercial distributors.

Why It Matters: This defines what the public booking service is for: a market competitor, a fallback, or a compliance benchmark. A full consumer app gives passengers a trusted neutral channel but competes with Trainline, Omio and carrier channels, which invites competition-law complaints. A narrower role limits that risk but may do little for the 40% through-ticket target.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Operate a full consumer-facing public booking service in all EU languages with complaint handling, positioned as a neutral channel alongside commercial distributors.
  2. Run a business-to-business reference implementation and sandbox that demonstrates correct OSDM use, with consumer sales left to commercial distributors under common rules.
  3. Tender a distributor-of-last-resort concession that guarantees any journey on participating carriers can be bought somewhere, with a private operator running the service under public service-level terms.

Trade-Off / Risk: A full public app guarantees a neutral channel but risks displacing private distributors it relies on for volume; a sandbox-only role is safer legally yet may not move passenger behaviour toward through-tickets.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Conformance Gate and Carrier Onboarding Support, since a reference implementation and sandbox gives carriers a test bed, and Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining, since a public channel can set the benchmark for accessible booking flows.

Conflict: Conflicts with Distribution Remuneration and Commission Corridor, because a publicly funded channel selling at low or zero commission can undercut commercial distributors, and with Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder, because consumer app costs compete for tranche-limited budget.

Justification: High, Defines the public channel's role and the budget share spent on consumer apps. Governs the trade-off between driving the 40% through-ticket target and competition-law and commercial-distributor backlash; conflicts with remuneration and funding levers.

Decision 4: Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder

Lever ID: 861f756d-bdec-40fb-bb4a-6b27ecc926a1

The Core Decision: Controls the timing and conditions under which the €1.5 billion public coordination budget (user constraint) reaches carriers, member-state bodies and shared infrastructure. It is the program's main compliance leverage over actors the Commission cannot otherwise direct. Success metrics are the share of budget disbursed against verified deliverables, the time from milestone to payment, and the number of carriers that start work because of the funding.

Why It Matters: Governs how the public coordination budget flows to carriers, member-state bodies and the shared infrastructure: upfront grants, verified milestones or measured outcomes. Conditional release gives leverage over compliance but starves carriers that need cash to start IT work, while unconditional grants speed starts and weaken leverage.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Release funds in tranches tied to verified technical milestones, such as conformance certificates and live API exposure, paid to carriers and member-state bodies on verification.
  2. Pool funds in a competitive call where carriers and distributors co-finance corridor integration projects, ranked by expected through-ticket volume and passenger benefit.
  3. Reserve a large share for outcome-based payments released only after measured through-ticket sales and complaint reductions appear, requiring carriers to pre-finance the work.

Trade-Off / Risk: Outcome-based payment aligns money with the success metrics, but carriers that must pre-finance IT work at their own risk may simply decline, leaving the public budget unspent on the corridors that matter most.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Uses certificates from the Conformance Gate and Carrier Onboarding Support as payment triggers, which gives the gate real consequences, and gives the Public Reference Distributor Mandate a predictable funding profile.

Conflict: Conflicts with the Specification Custodian Seat for OSDM Evolution, because formal change cycles can delay the milestones that release payments, and with the Public Reference Distributor Mandate, which competes for the same fixed budget.

Justification: Critical, Main compliance leverage over actors the Commission cannot direct; controls how the €1.5 billion reaches carriers and bodies. Conflicts with liability, clearing, reference distributor and specification levers, governing the leverage vs. carrier-cash-need trade-off.

Decision 5: Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source

Lever ID: 1c8c4cd2-6e94-46f5-8396-570f3f180f7e

The Core Decision: Chooses the architecture for search and purchase: where availability is held, who confirms the sale, and how the system degrades when a carrier endpoint fails. It determines search latency, strain on legacy carrier inventory systems and sell-through error rates. Metrics: response time for multi-carrier itineraries, stale-seat booking failures, outage resilience and integration effort per distributor.

Why It Matters: How distributors learn which seats and fares exist, and who confirms a sale, sets latency, load on legacy carrier systems and resilience during outages. A central exchange simplifies distributor integration but creates a single point of failure and governance contention. A federated model keeps carriers in control but multiplies integration effort and makes through-ticket pricing slower.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Build a central inventory exchange that carriers feed continuously, so distributors query one endpoint and carriers retain only final booking authority.
  2. Keep inventory federated at each carrier, with distributors querying carrier OSDM endpoints directly through a shared routing and discovery registry that the program operates.
  3. Publish an event-streamed availability shadow for search, treat each carrier's booking engine as sole authority at purchase, and degrade to scheduled-only offers whenever a carrier endpoint is unavailable.

Trade-Off / Risk: Cached or centralised availability makes search fast but invites sell-through errors on stale seats, whereas direct federated queries are accurate yet expose the search experience to the slowest legacy carrier system on any itinerary.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Conformance Gate and Carrier Onboarding Support by defining a concrete endpoint contract to test against, and underpins Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography, which needs fast, trustworthy real-time inventory to reroute stranded passengers.

Conflict: Collides with Joint Conduct Safe-Harbour for Shared Data and Clearing, since a central exchange pooling competitors' live inventory heightens competition-law exposure, and slows Through-Fare Construction Doctrine when federated queries wait on the slowest carrier.

Justification: Critical, Foundational architecture choice for search and purchase, setting latency, sell-through errors, resilience and legacy-system load. Underpins conformance testing and disruption rebooking, and carries competition-law exposure for a central exchange; hard to reverse once built.

Secondary Decisions

These decisions are less significant, but still worth considering.

Decision 6: Conformance Gate and Carrier Onboarding Support

Lever ID: c606999a-541a-4bab-8aef-7fea6fb8bd78

The Core Decision: Sets the admission test carriers must pass before exposing inventory through OSDM-compatible APIs, and who pays to modernise legacy booking systems. Covers certification scope, test environments, tiering, adapter funding and enforcement. Success metrics: share of participating carriers connected by the mandatory API exposure milestone (Month 30 = 2029-04-12), certification turnaround time, post-onboarding API availability and booking-error rates, and public spend per connected carrier.

Why It Matters: This determines how carriers prove they meet the standard and who pays to modernise legacy booking systems. Strict certification protects distributors and passengers but can exclude smaller carriers with older systems, delaying full TEN-T coverage. Subsidised adapters widen participation but consume part of the €1.5 billion that is separate from the larger private carrier IT investment.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Require independent conformance certification before any carrier may expose inventory, with a published pass list and no public co-funding of carrier systems.
  2. Certify carriers in tiers by size and system age, and co-fund shared adapter modules that let smaller operators connect legacy back-ends without full replacement.
  3. Replace upfront certification with a live-performance regime that publishes each carrier's API availability, latency and booking-error rates, and attaches penalties to repeated underperformance.

Trade-Off / Risk: Hard certification gates protect quality but may leave small carriers outside the network; shared adapters broaden coverage yet make the public budget responsible for technical debt that carriers would otherwise carry themselves.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Specification Custodian Seat for OSDM Evolution, since a stable, versioned specification gives certification a clear target, and Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source, since conformance tests can verify authoritative-inventory behaviour.

Conflict: Trades off against Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder, since adapter subsidies draw on funds while slow small-carrier onboarding can stall releases, and Through-Fare Construction Doctrine, since strict gates leave coverage gaps in through-fare routes.

Justification: High, Controls how many carriers actually connect by the Month 30 (2029-04-12) mandatory API milestone and who funds legacy modernisation. Trades coverage against quality and ties to funding triggers, the specification and the availability architecture.

Decision 7: Air-to-Rail Competitiveness Package

Lever ID: 6d14cef1-1b7d-4919-93fa-e30e10e00321

The Core Decision: Targets the modal-shift objective by shaping how rail competes with short-haul flights on selected routes, using search presentation, intermodal products, fare commitments or reliability guarantees. Scope is limited to air-competitive corridors and depends on the through-ticketing stack for delivery. Success metrics: rail share on benchmarked air-competitive routes, conversion from neutral search results, price gap versus flights, and public cost per passenger shifted (estimate).

Why It Matters: This decides how the program tries to make rail the more attractive choice on short-haul routes where flights compete. Neutral display and intermodal tickets influence booking choices at low public cost, whereas fare commitments require carriers to accept margin risk. The measure of success is the shift in traveller behaviour, which depends on price and reliability as well as ticketing.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Mandate neutral search results with emissions-based sorting and sell combined rail-air and rail-bus tickets, relying on information and convenience rather than price intervention.
  2. Agree corridor-specific fare commitments with carriers for through-tickets, such as fare families and reduction-card recognition, co-funded for a limited introductory period.
  3. Pair through-ticketing with a guaranteed-connection product where the selling platform automatically rebooks onto the next train or a replacement bus at no charge, making reliability the selling point.

Trade-Off / Risk: Display rules are cheap and quick but may not outweigh a lower flight fare; fare commitments change behaviour but create a subsidy dependency that may vanish once the introductory period ends.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography, since a guaranteed-connection product relies on automated rebooking, and Through-Fare Construction Doctrine, since fare families and reduction-card recognition depend on clear through-fare rules.

Conflict: Conflicts with Distribution Remuneration and Commission Corridor, since fare commitments squeeze margins available for distributor commissions, and with Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop, since guaranteed rebooking raises the liability exposure carriers must price.

Justification: Medium, Targets the modal-shift goal but is a downstream outcome lever that depends on the through-ticketing stack, fare rules and reliability. Important for the headline objective, yet less of a hub shaping the underlying system.

Decision 8: Through-Fare Construction Doctrine

Lever ID: 025c9abb-298f-4439-b7fc-e4bbd20b4ee1

The Core Decision: Determines the rule by which one through-ticket price is assembled from several carriers' legs, and therefore the passenger-visible price, the allocation of revenue between carriers, and the dispute load on clearing. Key metrics are the through-ticket price relative to stitched itineraries and air fares, the share of fares priced without manual negotiation, and the number of fare-allocation disputes per period.

Why It Matters: Sets how a single through-ticket price is built from several carriers' legs: summed leg fares, a corridor tariff, or composed bundles. The choice drives whether passengers see a price advantage over stitched itineraries, how revenue shifts between carriers, and how many disputes reach the clearing mechanism.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Standardise on sum-of-legs pricing with a connection-protection guarantee, leaving each carrier's fare logic unchanged and minimising inter-carrier negotiation.
  2. Develop a distance-and-class through tariff per corridor, negotiated by carrier groups under Agency for Railways supervision, with common fare classes and reduction-card mapping.
  3. Allow distributors to compose bundle prices from carrier-published leg price ranges within a floor and cap, with bundle margin shared among carriers by a pre-agreed formula.

Trade-Off / Risk: Sum-of-legs is fast to deliver but gives no price reason to prefer rail over air, while negotiated corridor tariffs deliver that advantage at the cost of bargaining that can stall past the standards deadline.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Feeds Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement, since a deterministic construction rule makes revenue allocation automatic, and supports the Air-to-Rail Competitiveness Package by determining whether rail through-fares can actually undercut short-haul air.

Conflict: Clashes with Distribution Remuneration and Commission Corridor, because bundle margins and corridor tariffs compete with distributor commissions for the same revenue, and with Joint Conduct Safe-Harbour, since negotiated corridor tariffs raise competition-law exposure.

Justification: High, Determines the passenger-visible through-price, carrier revenue allocation and dispute load on clearing. Decides whether rail can undercut air; trades delivery speed against negotiated tariffs and clashes with remuneration and competition-law exposure.

Decision 9: Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography

Lever ID: 07ef7d35-a183-412f-896c-205fce312df7

The Core Decision: Sets the operating model for the moment a connection breaks: who detects it, who owns the reroute decision, and how seats on competitors' trains are accessed. It is the practical test of through-ticket credibility. Success is measured by time from delay detection to a confirmed alternative, the share of affected passengers rebooked without visiting a counter, and the number of passengers stranded.

Why It Matters: Defines who first sees a missed connection, who decides the reroute, and how alternative itineraries are offered across carrier boundaries in real time. A shared event feed reduces stranded passengers, but requires carriers to share operational data they currently guard and exposes them to dependence on competitors' data quality.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Establish a shared disruption event feed to which all carriers publish and distributors subscribe, with each distributor responsible for proposing reroutes to its own customers.
  2. Assign the issuing carrier of the through-ticket as sole re-accommodation owner, obliged to rebook across any carrier using pre-agreed seat access on following services.
  3. Pilot a neutral automated rebooking service that proposes and holds seats on alternative trains once a delay breaches a connection threshold, with the passenger confirming by notification.

Trade-Off / Risk: Real-time rerouting is the visible test of through-ticket credibility, yet it depends on operational data quality that carriers have never shared, so the feed may be technically live while still too unreliable to act on.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Operationalises the Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop by turning liability rules into a concrete rebooking action, and relies on Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source to hold and confirm alternative seats reliably.

Conflict: Strains Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source, since seat holds on rival carriers' services contend with each carrier's inventory control, and loads Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement with unplanned reroute costs between carriers.

Justification: Medium, Practical credibility test for through-tickets, but largely operationalises decisions made in the liability, availability and clearing levers. Valuable execution layer with significant data-sharing dependencies rather than a foundational choice.

Decision 10: Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining

Lever ID: 0712ad24-64d5-4b27-b6f2-902b02aba10a

The Core Decision: Makes assistance for persons with reduced mobility and bicycle spaces bookable components tied to the through-ticket rather than separate phone-based requests. Its scope reaches into stations, staffing and rolling stock that differ per carrier. Key metrics are the share of assisted and bicycle journeys completed as promised, the notice period achieved across carriers, and the number of itineraries refused for lack of capacity.

Why It Matters: Treats assistance requests for persons with reduced mobility and bicycle spaces as bookable components bound to the through-ticket, despite differing notice periods, rolling-stock capacity and station staffing among carriers. Binding them raises usability for affected travellers but exposes physical capacity mismatches that software cannot fix.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Define a single assistance-request message propagated to every carrier on the itinerary, with a common notice period that all participating carriers commit to meeting.
  2. Make bicycle and wheelchair space reservations conditional components confirmed together with the seat, so a through-ticket is not issued if any leg lacks the required capacity.
  3. Have disability-rights bodies and operators jointly run a staffed assistance coordination desk per corridor that brokers requests manually while the automated chain is built.

Trade-Off / Risk: Atomic confirmation guarantees honest promises to travellers, but it will block many itineraries where rolling stock has no spaces, converting an accessibility ambition into a visible drop in through-ticket availability.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Depends on and strengthens Ticket Validation and Onboard Inspection Interoperability, since reserved spaces must be recognised by onboard staff, and uses Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source to query space capacity per leg.

Conflict: Trades off against the Air-to-Rail Competitiveness Package, because atomic confirmation removes itineraries and lowers through-ticket availability, and complicates Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography, since rerouted journeys must re-secure scarce assistance and bicycle spaces.

Justification: Medium, Required accessibility and bicycle scope with real physical constraints, but affects a subset of journeys. Atomic confirmation can reduce itinerary availability, creating a local trade-off rather than steering the core system.

Decision 11: Specification Custodian Seat for OSDM Evolution

Lever ID: adf2b2a1-82aa-4e6d-b58a-da2e7a0bbeae

The Core Decision: Decides who owns the OSDM specification, its change requests, versioning and reference test suite, and so who can shape the standard after the binding-standards deadline. It governs both release speed and the trust of independent distributors in non-discriminatory access. Success is measured by median change-request turnaround, the diversity of contributors, and the absence of forks or stalled releases.

Why It Matters: Deciding who controls change requests, versioning and the reference test suite determines how fast the standard can adapt and how much regulatory force it carries. Anchoring it in an EU body gives legal certainty but can slow releases; leaving it with industry speeds iteration but concentrates influence among incumbents. The choice also shapes whether independent distributors trust the standard to stay non-discriminatory.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Anchor OSDM change control in the EU Agency for Railways with a statutory change-request procedure, giving the specification regulatory force at the cost of slower, more formal release cycles.
  2. Keep OSDM maintenance in the existing industry-led community and have the Commission reference a pinned version by delegated act, preserving release cadence while accepting dependence on a body outside EU institutional control.
  3. Place the specification and its conformance test suite in a neutral open-source foundation with escrowed copies held by the Agency, so any carrier or distributor can fork the standard if governance stalls.

Trade-Off / Risk: Regulatory anchoring buys legal certainty but risks freezing a standard that carriers still need to iterate; industry stewardship moves faster yet leaves non-incumbent distributors dependent on the goodwill of the parties they compete against.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Provides the authoritative test suite on which the Conformance Gate and Carrier Onboarding Support depends, and gives the Public Reference Distributor Mandate a stable specification to build against.

Conflict: Constrains the Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder, since slower formal release cycles can delay milestones tied to a pinned version, and interacts with Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source, where API changes force carrier rework.

Justification: Medium, Sets standard governance and independent-distributor trust, feeding conformance tests and the reference distributor. Important for long-term neutrality, but its effects flow mainly through the conformance and funding levers.

Decision 12: Distribution Remuneration and Commission Corridor

Lever ID: 6f84e666-fb53-432b-a893-6f0e65374058

The Core Decision: Sets what carriers pay distributors per through-ticket sold and who supervises that price, which decides whether third-party platforms, carrier channels and the public reference distributor can survive side by side. Success metrics: dispersion of effective commission rates across distributor types, number of discrimination disputes reaching regulators, and carrier inventory exposure compliance at the mandatory API milestone (Month 30 = 2029-04-12).

Why It Matters: The fee a carrier pays a distributor for selling its seats decides whether third-party platforms, carriers' own channels and a public reference distributor can compete on equal terms. A rigid cap protects passengers from fare mark-ups but may starve smaller distributors; open bilateral bargaining favours large incumbents. Remuneration design also feeds directly into the settlement mechanism and the carriers' willingness to expose inventory.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Set a regulator-supervised commission band applied identically to every distributor, with carriers free to price inside the band but not to discriminate between distributors.
  2. Allow bilateral commission negotiation but require filing of all rates with national regulators and periodic audit for discrimination, trading price flexibility for a heavier supervisory workload.
  3. Introduce a pooled through-ticket distribution fee set by the clearing function that falls as combined volume across all carriers grows, rewarding multi-carrier itineraries instead of single-operator sales.

Trade-Off / Risk: A uniform commission band simplifies enforcement but ignores wide differences in distributor cost structures, while bilateral deals preserve commercial freedom at the price of disputes that regulators must adjudicate carrier by carrier.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement, since commission splits can be netted in the same flows, and supports Public Reference Distributor Mandate by giving it a transparent, level fee basis to compete on.

Conflict: Trades off against Joint Conduct Safe-Harbour for Shared Data and Clearing, because a uniform band or pooled fee resembles price coordination among competitors, and constrains Through-Fare Construction Doctrine, since commission levels limit how revenue can be apportioned.

Justification: Medium, Shapes whether third-party, carrier and public distributors coexist and carriers expose inventory. Well connected to clearing and fare levers, but largely a commercial-terms optimisation constrained by competition law and upstream choices.

Decision 13: Ticket Validation and Onboard Inspection Interoperability

Lever ID: ffa8b25b-d42d-4bdd-9e5f-3820906984ed

The Core Decision: Ensures every conductor, gate and station agent on a corridor accepts a through-ticket issued by any participating carrier without manual workarounds. Scope covers credential format, offline verification, handheld and gate upgrades, and legacy phase-out. Metrics: share of inspections passed without intervention, validation-related disputes and penalty fares, and proportion of corridor rolling stock and gates equipped by go-live.

Why It Matters: A through-ticket is only useful if conductors, gates and station staff from every carrier on the itinerary accept it without manual workarounds. Mandating one credential format simplifies passenger experience but forces hardware and handheld upgrades across rolling stock and stations. Leaving validation to each carrier shifts the burden to passengers and raises the dispute rate the program aims to reduce.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Mandate a single ticket credential and barcode format accepted by every conductor handheld and station gate on participating corridors, funding the device upgrades through the public budget.
  2. Let each carrier keep its native validation method and require only a cross-recognition handshake, so that each carrier can verify the others' tickets through an API without replacing hardware.
  3. Issue a short-lived, cryptographically signed journey token that conductors can verify offline, replacing printed and per-carrier barcodes on corridor trains while legacy formats are phased out.

Trade-Off / Risk: A single credential removes inspection friction for passengers but demands rolling-stock and handheld retrofits that follow vehicle maintenance cycles, so corridor go-live may depend on hardware schedules the program does not control.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop, because an accepted credential gives clear proof of entitlement, and Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining, whose reservations can be carried inside the same credential.

Conflict: Retrofit costs compete for the public budget with Public Reference Distributor Mandate, and hardware schedules tied to vehicle maintenance cycles can delay corridor go-live, straining Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder gates.

Justification: Low, Largely tactical, hardware-driven enabler tied to vehicle maintenance cycles. Supports liability proof and assistance reservations, but mostly executes upstream decisions; its retrofit costs and schedule risk are manageable on a corridor basis.

Decision 14: Joint Conduct Safe-Harbour for Shared Data and Clearing

Lever ID: 12449661-297c-48ff-8258-3e9b460a7123

The Core Decision: Provides legal certainty that exchanging fares, inventory and settlement data through shared mechanisms is compatible with EU competition rules (Article 101 TFEU), so carriers invest without fearing later unwinding. Metrics: time to obtain comfort relative to the binding-standards milestone (Month 18 = 2028-04-12), carrier participation rates, absence of successful challenges, and no forced redesign of clearing or data-sharing arrangements.

Why It Matters: Carriers exchanging fares, inventory and settlement data through a common mechanism could be viewed as coordination between competitors. Establishing legal comfort early reduces hesitation in participating carriers but requires time with competition authorities. Skipping it risks later challenges that could unwind the clearing and data arrangements after carriers have invested.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Seek formal guidance from the Commission's competition directorate before the standards are binding, so that data-sharing and clearing designs are confirmed compatible with competition rules in advance.
  2. Rely on the legal obligation created by the Regulation as the basis for data exposure and appoint a monitoring trustee to audit compliance and report suspected misuse to authorities.
  3. Structurally separate the clearing function behind a clean-team arrangement that sees only the flows needed for settlement and releases carriers' commercial data to nobody, including participants.

Trade-Off / Risk: Early competition-law clearance protects carriers' investments but could consume months before binding standards, while relying on mandated disclosure alone leaves unresolved exposure if the final regulation changes or is read narrowly.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement and Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source, because legal comfort lets carriers commit real-time inventory and settlement data to these shared mechanisms without hesitation.

Conflict: Clearance time pressures the Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards schedule and Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder, while a clean-team structure limits the data visibility that Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement may need for reconciliation and dispute resolution.

Justification: High, Legal precondition for carriers to commit inventory and settlement data; failure could unwind investments. Its clearance timing pressures the Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards milestone and constrains the clearing, availability and remuneration designs.

Choosing our strategic path.

The Strategic Context

Understanding the core ambitions and constraints that guide our decision.

Ambition and Scale: Continental, multi-stakeholder public program across about 25 national operators and independent distributors. It covers four priority corridors, then the full TEN-T network, over a five-year horizon (binding standards by Month 18 = 2028-04-12, mandatory API exposure by Month 30 = 2029-04-12, full corridor through-ticketing by Month 60 = 2031-10-12). Targets are 40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets, halved distributor complaints and a modal shift from short-haul air to rail. The public coordination budget is €1.5 billion (user constraint).

Risk and Novelty: Moderate-to-high risk, built on partly proven components (OSDM, existing clearing arrangements, an EU rail ticketing regulation proposal; a May 2026 Commission proposal was confirmed by search, adoption status and final content not verified). Novel elements are cross-carrier liability pooling, a public reference distributor and mandatory API exposure. Main risks: carrier refusal over unpriceable connection liability, competition-law challenges, legacy IT latency and legislative uncertainty. The plan explicitly asks for a realistic scenario, not the most aggressive one.

Complexity and Constraints: Very high operational and governance complexity: standards, conformance testing, real-time data, clearing and settlement, passenger-rights backstop, PRM accessibility, bicycle reservations and multimodal hooks. The fixed €1.5 billion public budget must cover standards, clearing, a public distributor and rollout, while private carrier IT cost is estimated separately. Carriers cannot be directed by the Commission except through regulation and funding leverage. Sequenced corridor rollout and fixed regulatory milestones leave little slack.

Domain and Tone: Public-sector regulatory and infrastructure program: EU institutions, rail transport, consumer protection and digital standards. Formal, institutional and compliance-oriented, with a balance between neutrality toward commercial distributors and consumer outcomes.

Holistic Profile: A large, regulation-aligned, publicly funded interoperability program that needs carrier buy-in more than central control. It should deliver through-ticketing on priority corridors by layering shared standards over legacy systems, protect the fixed public budget, and keep a neutral last-resort sales channel. It aims at the 40% target without taking on the governance and budget risks of a fully centralised public backbone.

The Path Forward

This scenario aligns best with the project's characteristics and goals.

The Pragmatic Foundation: Federated Build with Verified Milestones

Strategic Logic: Delivers through-ticketing on the four priority corridors by layering shared standards over existing carrier systems: a federated settlement layer, a streamed availability shadow with carrier booking authority, and a carrier-funded guarantee pool that protects the public budget. Money is released against verifiable technical milestones, and a private concession covers last-resort sales, which balances speed, neutrality and carrier buy-in. This is the recommended realistic pathway.

Fit Score: 9/10

Why This Path Was Chosen: Delivers the plan's full scope (shared real-time layer, clearing, rights backstop, public last-resort channel) on the priority corridors by layering over existing carrier systems. The carrier-funded pool and milestone tranches protect the public budget while keeping leverage over compliance.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop: Establish a carrier-funded mutual guarantee pool that pays assistance, rerouting and compensation on any through-ticket, with contributions weighted by each carrier's share of missed-connection incidents.
  • Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement: Federate settlement through a shared netting and dispute-resolution layer that connects existing bilateral and sector clearing arrangements, so carriers keep their current accounting flows.
  • Public Reference Distributor Mandate: Tender a distributor-of-last-resort concession that guarantees any journey on participating carriers can be bought somewhere, with a private operator running the service under public service-level terms.
  • Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder: Release funds in tranches tied to verified technical milestones, such as conformance certificates and live API exposure, paid to carriers and member-state bodies on verification.
  • Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source: Publish an event-streamed availability shadow for search, treat each carrier's booking engine as sole authority at purchase, and degrade to scheduled-only offers whenever a carrier endpoint is unavailable.

The Decisive Factors:

  • Matches the realism mandate: federated settlement and a streamed availability shadow layer over legacy carrier systems, so the four priority corridors can be delivered within the 18/30/60-month milestones.
  • Protects the €1.5 billion budget (user constraint): the carrier-funded guarantee pool avoids a public pay-first fund, and tranches tied to conformance certificates give compliance leverage without forcing carriers to pre-finance.
  • Keeps the plan's scope and neutrality: a tendered last-resort concession provides a public channel without competing with Trainline or Omio.
  • Pioneer's Gambit is too risky: central inventory, a single clearing entity and a full public app concentrate failure, budget and competition-law exposure.
  • Prudent Consolidator is too thin: a sandbox-only public role and distributor-only liability make the 40% through-ticket goal and carrier participation unlikely.

Alternative Paths

The Pioneer's Gambit: A Public European Booking Backbone

Strategic Logic: Builds a fully public-led, uniform European layer (central inventory, single clearing entity, public rights fund and a full consumer-facing public service) to reach the 40% through-ticket goal and the air-to-rail shift as fast as possible. It accepts the highest budget drain, governance conflict, single-point-of-failure and carrier-refusal risks in exchange for maximum control and consistency.

Fit Score: 3/10

Assessment of this Path: Maximally ambitious: a central exchange, a single clearing entity, a public pay-first fund and a full public app would drain the €1.5 billion budget, invite competition-law challenges, and outcome-only payments with carrier pre-financing risk carrier refusal. This is the aggressive option the plan asks to avoid.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop: Create a publicly capitalised rights backstop fund within the €1.5 billion budget that pays passengers immediately and later recovers costs from the responsible carrier through the clearing mechanism.
  • Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement: Build a single EU-level clearing entity that receives the passenger payment, nets positions across carriers and distributors, and pays out on a fixed schedule under a common rulebook.
  • Public Reference Distributor Mandate: Operate a full consumer-facing public booking service in all EU languages with complaint handling, positioned as a neutral channel alongside commercial distributors.
  • Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder: Reserve a large share for outcome-based payments released only after measured through-ticket sales and complaint reductions appear, requiring carriers to pre-finance the work.
  • Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source: Build a central inventory exchange that carriers feed continuously, so distributors query one endpoint and carriers retain only final booking authority.

The Prudent Consolidator: Standards First, Markets Deliver

Strategic Logic: Keeps public exposure and new infrastructure minimal: distributors carry passenger liability with insured recourse to carriers, carriers keep existing accounting flows and endpoints, and the public role is a B2B reference sandbox. Funding is a co-financed competitive call, so scarce public money goes only where carriers and distributors commit their own capital. It gives up some speed and the full 40% ambition for budget control and delivery certainty.

Fit Score: 6/10

Assessment of this Path: Low-risk and budget-safe, but it drops the public reference distributor and the shared real-time layer, puts all liability on distributors, and leaves the 40% through-ticket and modal-shift goals unlikely. Competitive co-financed calls may also skip less commercial corridors.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop: Make the selling distributor the single point of liability toward the passenger and require it to hold insurance, with contractual recourse against the carrier whose delay caused the missed connection.
  • Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement: Federate settlement through a shared netting and dispute-resolution layer that connects existing bilateral and sector clearing arrangements, so carriers keep their current accounting flows.
  • Public Reference Distributor Mandate: Run a business-to-business reference implementation and sandbox that demonstrates correct OSDM use, with consumer sales left to commercial distributors under common rules.
  • Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder: Pool funds in a competitive call where carriers and distributors co-finance corridor integration projects, ranked by expected through-ticket volume and passenger benefit.
  • Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source: Keep inventory federated at each carrier, with distributors querying carrier OSDM endpoints directly through a shared routing and discovery registry that the program operates.

Purpose

Purpose: business

Purpose Detailed: Public-sector, multi-stakeholder infrastructure and regulatory program led by EU institutions (DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways) with national operators, distributors, regulators and consumer/disability bodies to establish technical standards (OSDM-compatible APIs), a shared real-time data layer, an inter-carrier clearing and settlement mechanism, a passenger-rights backstop, a public reference distributor and consumer-side rollout across European corridors over five years, funded by a €1.5 billion public coordination budget, with a separate estimate of private carrier IT investment. Goals: 40% of cross-border journeys sold as single through-tickets, halved distributor complaints, and modal shift from short-haul air to rail.

Topic: Coordinated European program for seamless cross-border rail through-ticketing (search, booking, refund) aligned with the EU proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail

Domain

Primary domain: Rail Ticketing Interoperability

Secondary domains: Transport Regulation, Public Program Management, Clearing And Settlement

Rationale: Rail Ticketing Interoperability is the outcome-role candidate with the highest importance × specificity (25) and names the program's core mechanism: OSDM-based cross-border through-ticketing. Transport Economics is a narrower outcome; Transport Regulation, Clearing And Settlement and API Standardization are constraints or methods.

Disciplines this project involves:

Plan Type

This plan requires one or more physical locations. It cannot be executed digitally.

Explanation: This plan is a large, multi-stakeholder European public program to make cross-border rail through-ticketing work. Although a large share of the deliverables are digital (OSDM-compatible APIs, a shared real-time data layer, a clearing and settlement mechanism, a public reference booking app), the plan as a whole has clear and unavoidable physical requirements and benefits from physical presence in many ways: (1) Rollout is tied to real railway corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin) and later the full TEN-T network, which means real trains, stations, ticket offices, gates and on-board systems must be integrated, tested and operated. (2) Accessibility for persons with reduced mobility and bicycle reservations are physical-service requirements: they require assistance at stations, wheelchair spaces, and bicycle spaces on rolling stock, as well as coordination with disability-rights bodies. (3) The passenger-rights backstop and disruption handling relate to physical journeys, missed connections, rerouting, and staffed assistance at stations. (4) Integration hooks for buses, ferries and short-haul air connect to physical terminals and modal interchanges. (5) Conformance testing needs physical test environments, devices and real-world pilots on live corridors. (6) Governance involves in-person work among DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways, CER, national operators, regulators and consumer bodies, and member-state capacity building requires on-site training and workshops. (7) Delivery by carriers and the public reference distributor needs teams in physical offices and data centres, procurement of hardware, and consumer-side rollout (apps plus multilingual support, complaint handling, and station information). (8) Success is measured by changes in real-world travel behaviour, modal shift from short-haul flights to trains. The plan cannot be executed exclusively online, and it gains substantial benefit from physical locations and activities, so it is classified as physical.

  • Secure data-centre and high-availability connectivity for the real-time data layer and clearing
  • Test environments with access to live rolling stock, stations and gates for conformance pilots

  • Multilingual, skilled IT and financial-services workforce for clearing and distributor operations
  • Competition-law-sensitive separation of the clearing function (clean-team arrangement)

Currency Strategy

This plan involves money.

Currencies

  • EUR: Primary currency for all public coordination budget (€1.5 billion user constraint), standards work, conformance testing, clearing mechanism, public reference distributor and member-state capacity building across the EU. All four priority corridors and the full TEN-T network are within the Eurozone or countries with direct EUR integration (Belgium, France, Germany, Austria, Switzerland via bilateral arrangements). Simplifies settlement within the inter-carrier clearing layer and avoids hedging costs on the majority of transactions.
  • GBP: Secondary consideration for any post-delivery integration with UK rail operators or distributors (Trainline, National Rail) should the scope extend beyond the initial EU-25 to include cross-Channel services. Not in immediate scope but may arise during corridor extension phases. Mark as optional pending regulatory evolution.

Primary currency: EUR

Currency strategy: The public coordination budget of €1.5 billion (user constraint) is disbursed entirely in EUR through tranches tied to verified technical milestones (conformance certificates, live API exposure, corridor go-live). All clearing, settlement and inter-carrier netting occurs in EUR to eliminate foreign-exchange friction in the clearing mechanism and preserve the fixed public budget from exchange volatility. The carrier-funded mutual guarantee pool for through-ticket liability contributes and draws in EUR, and the tendered last-resort distributor concession operates in EUR. Private carrier IT investment is estimated separately and may be denominated locally by each carrier, but all inter-carrier transactions flow through EUR settlement. If future corridor extensions reach non-Eurozone members (e.g., Sweden, Denmark, Poland), a secondary hedging strategy using corridor-specific bilateral forward contracts may be needed, but this is not in scope for the initial five-year horizon.

Identify Risks

Risk 1 - Regulatory & Legislative

The proposed EU Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail (Commission proposal status not fully verified; as of October 2026, adoption timeline uncertain) may face parliamentary opposition, be substantially amended, or stall in Council negotiations. If the Regulation is delayed beyond Month 18 (2028-04-12), the binding-standards deadline becomes unachievable and carriers lose the legal mandate to expose inventory through OSDM APIs. If the Regulation is watered down or sets weaker conformance requirements, smaller carriers may remain outside the network, fragmenting the corridor coverage.

Impact: A 12–18 month delay in Regulation adoption could push binding standards from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 30 (2029-04-12) or later, cascading the mandatory API exposure milestone and full corridor go-live. Weaker requirements could reduce participating carriers from the target 25+ to 15–20, leaving gaps in less commercially attractive corridors (e.g., Baltic routes) and lowering the through-ticket share from the 40% goal to 25–30%. Budget reallocation to fill coverage gaps could consume €200–400 million of the fixed €1.5 billion.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Secure formal legal assurance from the Commission's legislative affairs unit that the Regulation will be tabled by Month 6 (2027-04-12) and adopted by Month 18 (2028-04-12), with binding-standards triggers contingent on publication in the Official Journal. Maintain a shadow legislative workstream that documents compliance with the Regulation's requirements as they evolve, so that standards and conformance tests do not depend on a finalised text. Establish contingency corridor definitions that include smaller operators earlier if coverage risk emerges.

Risk 2 - Technical & Systems Integration

Legacy booking systems operated by smaller carriers (e.g., regional operators in CEE, the Balkans, Spain and Portugal) cannot be retrofitted to expose real-time availability through OSDM-compatible APIs within the Month 30 (2029-04-12) mandatory exposure deadline. Older systems may lack the architecture for event streaming, federated queries or transactional consistency required by the shared real-time layer. Integration adapters (funded from the €1.5 billion budget under the Conformance Gate decision) may be delayed or require longer development cycles than scheduled.

Impact: Smaller carriers may miss the Month 30 (2029-04-12) conformance deadline by 2–4 quarters, leaving 8–15 operators outside the network at critical corridor junctions (e.g., Austrian and Czech operators on the Wien–München corridor, Iberian regional carriers). This fragments the through-ticket path and forces passengers to stitch itineraries manually at borders. Estimated cost overrun to accelerate adapters: €150–250 million. Delay in full TEN-T rollout: 12–24 months beyond Month 60 (2031-10-12).

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Initiate a pre-programme technical audit of all participating carriers' booking-system architectures (by Month 2 = 2026-12-12) to identify retrofit bottlenecks and establish realistic Month 30 (2029-04-12) conformance timelines per operator. Co-fund shared adapter modules (middleware bridging legacy systems to OSDM) via the Conformance Gate and Carrier Onboarding Support decision, allocating €200–300 million of the public budget to this layer. Tier conformance into baseline (Month 30 = 2029-04-12), extended (Month 36 = 2029-10-12) and advanced (Month 42 = 2030-04-12) phases, releasing funding tranches based on verifiable API availability and booking-error rates rather than a one-time gate.

Risk 3 - Commercial & Carrier Incentives

Carriers refuse to expose inventory and accept through-ticket connection liability because the liability backstop (Decision 1) and clearing mechanism (Decision 2) leave them unable to price the shared exposure to missed-connection delays and rerouting costs. If the carrier-funded mutual guarantee pool is weighted solely on incident rates, carriers face unpredictable exposure linked to operational performance they do not fully control (e.g., SBB delays caused by SNCF congestion). Without a clear liability cap or insurance backstop, large carriers (DB, SNCF, RZD) may refuse to expose seats and restrict sales to their own channels.

Impact: If 30% of expected carriers (i.e., 7–8 major operators) refuse to participate, the through-ticket network loses coverage on critical corridors: the Köln–Amsterdam leg becomes unavailable, the München–Zürich corridor is fragmented, and the Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon route loses a key connector. Estimated impact: a 3–5 quarter delay in reaching the mandatory API exposure milestone (Month 30 = 2029-04-12), pushing full corridor through-ticketing to Month 72 (2032-10-12) or beyond. The 40% through-ticket goal becomes unachievable; realistic outcome is 15–20%.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Complete the Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop decision by Month 3 (2027-01-12) with a published carrier risk-allocation model that specifies: (a) maximum carrier exposure per incident (e.g., capped at €X per missed connection + rerouting costs), (b) insurance or co-insurance for exposure above the cap, and (c) contribution-weighting rules tied to controllable factors (e.g., on-time performance in the 12 months prior, not forward-looking incident rates). Present this model to CER and the largest 10 carriers by Month 4 (2027-02-12) for binding commercial sign-off before standards are finalised. Establish a separate technical working group to model cash flows for the carrier-funded guarantee pool, so carriers see realistic annual contribution ranges before Month 6 (2027-04-12).

Risk 4 - Financial & Budget

The €1.5 billion public coordination budget (user constraint) is allocated across standards work (€50–100 million), the clearing and settlement mechanism (€200–300 million), the public reference distributor concession (€300–500 million over five years), member-state capacity building (€200–300 million), conformance testing and carrier adapters (€200–300 million) and consumer rollout (€100–150 million), leaving little contingency. If the carrier-funded guarantee pool experiences a major incident surge (e.g., weather, labour strikes or a corridor-wide incident affecting thousands of passengers), the pool drains faster than projected and the Commission faces pressure to top it up from the public budget. Similarly, if the public distributor concession runs deeper operating losses than forecast (e.g., lower through-ticket volumes, higher payment processing and customer-service costs), the contract may require subsidy beyond the tendered allocation.

Impact: A €100–200 million draw on the public budget to cover guarantee-pool or distributor deficits in years 2–3 leaves only €100–200 million for the final-wave TEN-T extension (planned for Month 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12), essentially cancelling the full-network rollout. This cuts the through-ticket goal from 40% to ~25%, primarily covering the four priority corridors. Member-state capacity building is cut by 30–50%, leaving smaller MS without training or testing resources.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Commission an independent actuarial study of the carrier-funded guarantee pool (by Month 6 = 2027-04-12) with confidence intervals on missed-connection rates, rerouting costs and incident clustering. Establish a reserve fund of €150–200 million (drawn from the public budget allocation) earmarked for pool top-ups only in the case of force-majeure incidents (single-day corridor-wide disruptions affecting >5,000 passengers). For the public distributor concession, require monthly financial reporting and a trigger clause for subsidy increases if volumes fall below 60% of the forecast; if triggered, scale back the rollout to the four priority corridors and extend Month 60 (2031-10-12) completion to Month 72 (2032-10-12). Establish a policy with the Commission and the European Court of Auditors that public budget draw-downs on carrier pools beyond Month 36 (2029-10-12) will not occur, forcing recalibration of pool contributions or carrier participation instead.

Risk 5 - Governance & Stakeholder Coordination

The program involves DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways, CER, 25+ national operators, independent distributors (Trainline, Omio), national regulators, BEUC and disability-rights bodies. Alignment on the Through-Ticket Liability (Decision 1), Inter-Carrier Clearing (Decision 2) and Public Reference Distributor Mandate (Decision 3) decisions by Month 3–6 (2027-01-12 to 2027-04-12) requires consensus among parties with conflicting interests. CER and large carriers favour bilateral clearing and distributed liability; independent distributors demand a single clearing entity and a public guarantee; disability bodies require accessible, auditable assistance booking. Failure to secure consensus delays decisions, leaving the standards-working group without a liability model or clearing architecture to build against.

Impact: If consensus is not reached by Month 9 (2027-07-12), the binding-standards milestone (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) is at risk because standards-working groups cannot finalise specifications without knowing the liability allocation and clearing rulebook. Estimated delay: 2–4 months. Additionally, if independent distributors reject the final clearing design, they may legally challenge it or withdraw, reducing the through-ticket volume available to passengers by 20–30% (Trainline and Omio account for a significant share of cross-border searches).

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Establish a dedicated governance layer within the Programme Office (by Month 1 = 2026-11-12) with biweekly steering meetings of the key stakeholders (CER, DG MOVE, Agency for Railways, 3–4 major carriers, Trainline, Omio, BEUC, a national disability body and a representative national regulator). Issue a non-binding position paper by Month 2 (2026-12-12) outlining three options for each critical decision (Decisions 1, 2, 3) with trade-offs clearly stated. Require binding votes on the final decisions by Month 6 (2027-04-12), with Commission mediation available if a vote is deadlocked. For distributors that reject the clearing design, negotiate a fallback technical interface that allows them to settle through a third party (e.g., a payment provider) rather than the central clearing layer, preserving their participation.

Risk 6 - Competition Law & Regulatory

The Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement (Decision 2) and Distribution Remuneration and Commission Corridor (Decision 12) mechanisms involve competitors (25+ carriers, multiple distributors) exchanging commercially sensitive data (fares, inventory, settlement data) and potentially agreeing on commission rates or fare-construction rules. These arrangements could be viewed as prohibited coordination under Article 101 TFEU. The programme relies on the Joint Conduct Safe-Harbour for Shared Data and Clearing (Decision 14) decision to secure Commission comfort before binding standards are finalised (Month 18 = 2028-04-12). If comfort is not obtained in time, or if a future challenge unwinds the clearing arrangements, carriers will not commit real-time inventory and the through-ticket network collapses.

Impact: A competition-law challenge after Month 24 (2028-10-12) could force the programme to restructure the clearing mechanism and data-sharing layer, requiring 6–12 months of legal work and technical rework. Estimated cost: €50–100 million. If the challenge succeeds, the programme loses the centralised clearing or data layer, reverting to bilateral settlement and federated inventory queries, which add 3–4 months to settlement cycle times and increase booking-error rates by 15–25%, eroding the through-ticket value proposition.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Initiate formal pre-notification with the Commission's Directorate for Competition (DG COMP) by Month 2 (2026-12-12), before any technical specifications are fixed. Request a formal guidance letter (under Commission competition procedure) by Month 12 (2027-10-12) that confirms the clearing and data-sharing arrangements as compatible with Article 101 TFEU, conditioned on the specific design choices made. If DG COMP indicates concerns, establish a clean-team arrangement (Decision 14, option 3) whereby the clearing function operates behind firewalls and releases only aggregated settlement data to carriers, not their competitors' fares or inventory. Ensure this arrangement is documented and signed off by DG COMP before Month 18 (2028-04-12).

Risk 7 - Technical & Data Quality

The Availability Query Topology and Authoritative Booking Source (Decision 5, pragmatic option) relies on a streamed availability shadow (cached search layer) and carrier booking-engine authority. If carriers' booking engines are unavailable or respond slowly (>5 seconds), the system degrades to scheduled-only offers, which breaks through-ticketing (a passenger cannot book a through-ticket on a train that is not scheduled yet; real-time seat inventory is required). Legacy carrier systems, particularly smaller operators, often have 5–15 second query latency and 2–4 hour outages per month. Multiplicative latency and availability risk: a three-leg through-ticket requires three queries, so if each has 95% availability, the combined through-ticket availability is ~86%, not acceptable.

Impact: If carrier booking engines fail to meet <2 second latency and 99.5% availability targets, through-ticket search success rates fall to 70–80%, and the fallback to scheduled-only offers removes the commercial advantage of through-ticketing. Passengers revert to stitching itineraries manually or using single-carrier tools. Estimated impact: 30–50% lower through-ticket volume than forecast, pushing the 40% goal to 20–25%.

Likelihood: High

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish strict SLA targets for carrier booking-engine latency (<2 seconds per query, p95) and availability (99.5%) as part of the conformance gate (Decision 6). Build a monitored availability proxy that tracks each carrier's latency and availability in real time (Month 12 = 2027-10-12 onwards) and publishes a monthly scorecard. Attach tranches of the Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder (Decision 4) to carriers meeting these SLAs: carriers that miss SLAs in two consecutive months lose a portion of their next funding tranche. Concurrently, fund a lightweight caching layer (distributed, not central, to avoid a single point of failure) that holds recent search results and degrades gracefully to cached results if a carrier endpoint fails, so that scheduled offers are available at all times even if real-time inventory is not.

Risk 8 - Operational & Service Delivery

The Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography (Decision 9) and Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining (Decision 10) require real-time, coordinated action across carrier networks: detecting a missed connection, proposing alternatives on competitors' trains, securing seats and confirming reroutes within minutes. This depends on shared operational data (train delays, seat inventory) that carriers have historically guarded and on staff at stations and onboard who are trained to recognise across-carrier re-accommodation and accessible reservations. Smaller operators may lack 24/7 customer-service centres or English-speaking staff at border stations. A missed connection during night hours or a weekend may go undetected for hours.

Impact: If re-accommodation response times exceed 30–60 minutes, or if passengers are not re-accommodated at all (e.g., left stranded at a border station overnight), the program faces public backlash and liability claims. Estimated cost: €10–20 million in compensation and reputation damage per major incident. If assistance requests (wheelchairs, service animals, reduced-mobility support) are delayed or unfulfilled due to staffing or coordination gaps, the programme violates accessibility law (EU Regulation 1371/2007) and faces complaints to national regulators. Disruption handling failures could reduce through-ticket adoption by 10–20% due to passenger loss of trust.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Develop a detailed operational manual for all participating carriers by Month 9 (2027-07-12) covering missed-connection detection, re-accommodation procedures, seat-access protocols, assistance escalation and passenger communication at border stations. Conduct live pilots on each of the four priority corridors (Month 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) with 500–1,000 passengers per corridor, measuring response times, reroute success and passenger satisfaction. Use pilot results to calibrate SLAs (e.g., re-accommodation decision within 15 minutes, assistance confirmation within 30 minutes) and incorporate them into carrier conformance gates. Require carriers to establish 24/7 customer-service centres and train staff at key border stations (at least one English-speaking agent at each) as a precondition of conformance certification by Month 30 (2029-04-12). Fund capacity-building and staff training through the member-state capacity-building budget (€200–300 million allocation within the €1.5 billion).

Risk 9 - Technical & Systems Integration

The Ticket Validation and Onboard Inspection Interoperability (Decision 13) decision requires every train crew member, station agent and gate system on participating corridors to accept and validate through-tickets issued by any participating carrier. The pragmatic approach (hybrid credentials or API handshakes) is slower than a single-format mandate but avoids the cost and schedule risk of retrofitting handheld devices and gates on 1,000+ trains across four carriers. If carrier IT teams fail to implement the API handshake or hybrid credential format by Month 30 (2029-04-12), conductors and station agents have no way to validate across-carrier tickets, and manual workarounds (checking papers, holding passengers) reappear, eroding the through-ticket value.

Impact: If even 20% of corridor vehicles lack proper validation capability by Month 60 (2031-10-12), passengers face validation disputes, penalties and delays at stations, degrading the through-ticket experience. Estimated impact: 5–10% reduction in through-ticket adoption due to trust loss. If a validation failure leads to a passenger boarding a train without a valid ticket due to system incompatibility, the carrier faces a regulatory fine and reputational damage.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Specify the API handshake or hybrid credential format as part of the OSDM standard by Month 6 (2027-04-12) and include it in conformance tests (Decision 6). Require all carriers to deploy validation capability to all corridor rolling stock and key stations by Month 40 (2030-02-12) (10 months before full corridor go-live), with intermediate audits at Month 30 (2029-04-12) and Month 35 (2029-09-12). Tie funding tranches (Decision 4) to validation rollout milestones: carriers that fall 2+ months behind in validation deployment lose their next funding tranche. Fund a small team of on-site validation testers at each priority corridor (Month 24 = 2028-10-12 onwards) to conduct monthly audits of handheld and gate compatibility, publishing a publicly available scoreboard.

Risk 10 - Market & Competitive

The Air-to-Rail Competitiveness Package (Decision 7) aims to shift passengers from short-haul flights to rail through through-ticketing, intermodal products and information. However, the program has limited direct control over carrier pricing (through-fare construction is a carrier-led negotiation in Decision 8) and cannot control flight-operator pricing or schedule changes. If flight operators respond to increased rail competition by cutting fares on competitive routes to €20–40 one-way (which is commercially viable given lower fuel and staff costs), rail through-fares will struggle to compete even with the convenience factor. Additionally, passengers' modal choice depends on total journey time (including airport check-in and security), which the program does not control.

Impact: If modal shift from air to rail is slower than forecast (e.g., 5–10% instead of 15–20%), the 40% through-ticket goal is reached but the headline outcome—'fewer travellers choose the plane'—is not achieved, creating a political narrative of programme failure despite 40% penetration. The program may face pressure to shift funding toward price subsidies for rail, draining the fixed €1.5 billion budget.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Low

Action: Conduct a baseline modal-shift study by Month 6 (2027-04-12) measuring current air-to-rail ratios on the four priority corridors and the impact of through-ticketing, intermodal information and journey-time visibility on booking behaviour. Establish conservative modal-shift targets tied to through-ticketing availability, not price, so that the programme success is measured by through-ticket penetration and complaint reduction, not flight-passenger reduction. In the Air-to-Rail Competitiveness Package decision, focus on display neutrality and journey-time information (low cost) rather than fare commitments, which create subsidy dependencies. If modal shift is slower than forecast, use Month 48 (2030-10-12) evaluation findings to adjust the tone of programme communications, emphasizing convenience and reliability over environmental or air-replacement goals.

Risk 11 - Physical & Logistical

The programme is distributed across four member states (Belgium, France, Germany, Austria/Switzerland, Spain) with programme offices in Brussels, Valenciennes, Berlin and Madrid. Coordination across time zones, languages and national regulatory environments adds overhead. The EU Agency for Railways is in Valenciennes, far from Brussels (Commission HQ) and from the largest carrier IT centres (Berlin, Munich, Zurich). Travel time, visa requirements for non-EU staff and local staffing constraints can slow governance meetings and technical working groups.

Impact: Coordination delays, particularly in standards-working groups and conformance testing, could add 1–2 months to binding-standards and mandatory API exposure milestones. Estimated cost of additional coordination: €5–10 million in staff travel and extended contracts.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Low

Action: Establish a virtual-first governance model with scheduled in-person meetings only for critical decisions (Decisions 1–5, competition-law clearance). Use video conferencing for biweekly steering and technical working groups. Rotate in-person meetings between Brussels, Valenciennes and a carrier IT hub (Berlin or Munich) on a quarterly cycle, with participation costs covered by the programme budget. Hire at least one full-time liaison officer based in each of the four physical locations (Brussels, Valenciennes, Berlin, Madrid) to support async coordination and local stakeholder engagement.

Risk 12 - Regulatory & Policy

National railway regulators (e.g., ORE in France, BNetzA in Germany, NaBB in Austria) retain authority over track access, station capacity and pricing in their respective territories. The programme's binding standards and mandatory API exposure may conflict with existing national regulations or incumbent operator privileges. For example, a mandate to share real-time inventory through a central or federated layer could trigger concerns about incumbent cost-shifting or non-discriminatory access.
