If a national regulator blocks the programme's data-sharing or clearing arrangements on competition or incumbent-protection grounds, the programme cannot proceed in that member state.

Impact: If one major corridor (e.g., the Wien–München–Zürich or the Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln route) loses a national regulator's approval, the through-ticket network is fragmented and the corridor is blocked for 12–24 months while regulatory issues are resolved. Estimated impact: delay in mandatory API exposure milestone of 6–12 months and a reduction in through-ticket reach of 20–30%.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: By Month 3 (2027-01-12), the DG MOVE and the EU Agency for Railways must conduct bilateral engagement with each national regulator on the programme's scope, data-sharing arrangements and competition-law compliance. Prepare a regulatory-impact assessment for each member state that identifies potential conflicts with national law. If conflicts are identified, work with national regulators to adapt the programme design or secure regulatory waivers by Month 12 (2027-10-12). Include national regulators as observers in the standards-working groups so they can flag regulatory constraints early. If a regulator's concerns cannot be resolved by Month 12 (2027-10-12), consider deferring that member state's participation to a Phase 2 rollout (Month 60 = 2031-10-12 onwards) rather than the four priority corridors.

Risk 13 - Accessibility & Inclusivity

The Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining (Decision 10) aims to make through-tickets accessible for persons with reduced mobility (PRM) and cyclists. However, compliance depends on carriers to provide wheelchair spaces, assistance at stations and onboard staff training. Rolling stock ages and accessibility standards vary widely across operators (e.g., older trainsets on regional routes may have no wheelchair spaces). Atomic confirmation of assistance and bicycle reservations as part of the through-ticket booking means that itineraries without available spaces are refused, reducing the volume of through-tickets available to these passenger groups and potentially creating legal exposure under EU Regulation 1371/2007 (railway passengers' rights) and the Accessibility Directive.

Impact: If participating carriers cannot guarantee assistance or bicycle space on 50%+ of through-ticket itineraries, the programme risks legal complaints to national regulators and the European Court of Justice. Alternatively, if atomic confirmation is dropped in favour of 'best-effort' booking, passengers are left uncertain whether they will have access at journey time, eroding trust. Estimated reputational and legal cost: €20–50 million.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: By Month 6 (2027-04-12), require all participating carriers to publish their rolling-stock accessibility inventory (wheelchair spaces, assistance availability, onboard staff language skills) for each service on the priority corridors. Establish minimum accessibility levels (e.g., wheelchair access on ≥80% of services, assistance availability with ≤4 hours' notice on ≥90% of services) as a precondition of conformance (Decision 6). For carriers unable to meet these levels by Month 40 (2030-02-12), allow a fallback to 'best-effort' booking with transparent communication to passengers (e.g., 'wheelchair space availability uncertain; you will receive confirmation 48 hours before departure'). Engage disability-rights bodies (e.g., EBU) as observers in the Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining working group and conduct usability testing with PRM passengers by Month 18 (2028-04-12). Fund accessibility infrastructure improvements (rolling-stock retrofits, station accessibility) through member-state capacity-building budget if carriers cannot self-fund.

Risk 14 - Financial & Budget

The Public Reference Distributor Mandate (Decision 3, pragmatic option: tendered last-resort concession) requires the Commission to contract a private operator to run a last-resort sales channel. The concession contract must specify service levels (availability, booking success, complaint resolution time), volume targets and subsidy triggers. If the concessionaire overstates their cost efficiency, the contract runs into operating losses within 18–24 months and requests subsidy increases from the €1.5 billion budget. Alternatively, if volume forecast is too optimistic, the concessionaire operates at a loss and may withdraw, leaving the Commission without a last-resort channel.

Impact: If the concessionaire withdraws by Month 36 (2029-10-12) or requests a subsidy increase >€50 million, the Commission must either operate the distributor directly (consuming staff and overhead) or leave the last-resort role unfilled, which undermines the programme's claim to provide a neutral channel. Estimated risk: €75–150 million in subsidy overrun or €30–50 million in government operating costs to take over directly.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: By Month 9 (2027-07-12), the Commission must develop a detailed business case for the public distributor concession, including volume forecasts, cost benchmarks (from Trainline, Omio and carrier apps) and margin assumptions. Issue a competitive tender for the concession by Month 12 (2027-10-12) with a two-stage evaluation: (a) technical requirements (system architecture, compliance with OSDM, accessibility, multilingual support) and (b) financial viability (total cost of ownership, subsidy threshold). Cap the initial subsidy at €60 million over five years and include a clawback clause: if through-ticket volumes exceed forecast by >20%, the concessionaire must rebate surplus fees to the Commission. Require the concessionaire to publish quarterly financial reports and trigger a contract review if operating costs exceed budget by >15% in any quarter.

Risk 15 - Technical & Data Quality

The Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement (Decision 2, pragmatic option: federated layer) depends on carriers submitting consistent, timely settlement data (fares, refunds, reroute costs, commission splits). If carriers' financial systems use different formats, currencies or accounting methods, reconciliation is slow and error-prone. A 2–3% reconciliation error rate (which is typical in financial services) translates to thousands of disputed transactions per month, overwhelming dispute-resolution capacity and delaying payouts to distributors.

Impact: If reconciliation error rates exceed 2%, settlement cycle times lengthen from the targeted 5 business days to 10–15 days, cash flow friction increases for distributors, and distributor complaints about delayed payouts rise. Estimated impact: 15–20% of distributors may reduce their participation in through-ticket sales due to cash-flow concerns, lowering through-ticket volume by 10–15%.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a detailed data-format standard for settlement feeds (fares, refunds, reroute costs, commission) as part of the OSDM specification by Month 6 (2027-04-12). Require all carriers to submit settlement data in the standard format via a validated API by Month 24 (2028-10-12), with test environments available from Month 12 (2027-10-12) onwards. Fund a shared reconciliation platform (part of the clearing mechanism budget) that automates basic matching and flags mismatches for manual review. Set a target reconciliation error rate of <0.5% by Month 30 (2029-04-12), with automatic penalties for carriers exceeding 1% error rates in any month (e.g., 0.1% reduction in their next funding tranche).

Risk 16 - Operational & Service Delivery

Member-state capacity building (€200–300 million allocation within the €1.5 billion budget) is required to train national railway operators, regulators and consumer bodies on the new standards, systems and passenger-rights procedures. Smaller member states (e.g., Baltic countries, Luxembourg, Cyprus) may lack in-country expertise and depend on external training from the EU Agency for Railways or contractors. If capacity building is delayed or under-resourced, local operators and regulators may not meet the mandatory API exposure or conformance milestones, delaying the full TEN-T rollout.

Impact: A 6–9 month delay in capacity building for smaller member states could push their participation in the full TEN-T rollout from Month 60 (2031-10-12) to Month 72 (2032-10-12) or later. This fragments the pan-European through-ticket coverage and reduces the overall through-ticket share from 40% to 30–35%.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Medium

Action: Allocate €30–50 million of the capacity-building budget specifically for external training programs, delivered by the EU Agency for Railways or contracted trainers, targeting smaller member states and less-resourced operators. Establish regional training hubs in Brussels, Valenciennes, Berlin and one southern hub (e.g., Madrid or Rome) so that training is accessible without extensive travel. Conduct a skills audit by Month 6 (2027-04-12) to identify member states with capacity gaps and tailor training curricula. Schedule intensive training programs (2–3 weeks per operator) at Month 18–24 (2028-04-12 to 2028-10-12) to coincide with the binding-standards deadline, so operators can begin implementation planning immediately after training.

Risk 17 - Regulatory & Policy

The programme's success relies on attracting independent distributors (Trainline, Omio and smaller platforms) to integrate with the shared real-time data layer and clearing mechanism. The Distribution Remuneration and Commission Corridor (Decision 12) sets the terms under which carriers pay distributors per through-ticket sold. If the negotiated commission rates are too low, distributors reduce their investment in through-ticket search and promotions; if too high, carriers view through-distribution as unprofitable and restrict inventory access. A misstep in commission design can fracture the distributor ecosystem and lower through-ticket sales.

Impact: If commission rates are set below distributors' cost of acquisition and support (typically 3–5% of fare), large independents (Trainline, Omio) may deprioritise the programme's through-tickets in their search results and marketing, reducing through-ticket volume by 20–30%. Alternatively, if rates are set above 5%, smaller distributors and new entrants cannot sustain a business, and the market consolidates to incumbents, reducing competition and innovation. Estimated impact: 15–20% reduction in through-ticket share if either scenario occurs.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Commission an industry survey by Month 3 (2027-01-12) of Trainline, Omio and 5–10 smaller distributors to establish their cost of acquisition, customer support and payment processing for cross-border through-tickets. Use this data to establish a commission-rate band (e.g., 2.5–4.5% of through-fare) that covers distributors' costs while allowing carriers margins. Include the band in the Distribution Remuneration and Commission Corridor decision (Decision 12) by Month 9 (2027-07-12). Require the clearing function to publish monthly commission-rate data by distributor type and check for discrimination; publish results quarterly. If a distributor claims discrimination, require a mediated review with the Agency for Railways before Month 30 (2029-04-12).

Risk 18 - Technical & Systems Integration

The Specification Custodian Seat for OSDM Evolution (Decision 11, pragmatic option: Agency for Railways anchoring with an escrowed open-source reference implementation) requires a formal, published change-control process for the OSDM specification. If the process is too slow (e.g., change requests take 3–6 months to be reviewed and approved), carriers and distributors may fork the specification or apply proprietary extensions, fragmenting the ecosystem. If the process is too fast (e.g., changes approved in weeks), carriers with legacy systems struggle to keep pace and integration failures emerge.

Impact: If the specification forks or diverges significantly from carriers' implementations by Month 42 (2030-04-12), conformance testing becomes ambiguous and the mandatory API exposure milestone is delayed or fails. Estimated delay: 3–6 months. A slow change process (>2 month review cycles) could delay critical bug fixes or security updates by 6–9 months, creating vulnerability windows.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish the OSDM change-control process as part of the Agency for Railways mandate by Month 3 (2027-01-12), with published criteria for change request severity (critical: security/safety; major: functional gaps; minor: optimisations), review timelines (critical: 2 weeks; major: 6 weeks; minor: 8 weeks) and approval gates (technical review by at least 3 independent carriers, competition-law check for sensitive changes). Publish a quarterly release cadence so carriers can plan integration work. Archive all historical versions in an open-source repository with escrowed backups, so carriers can fork if needed. Establish a change-request dashboard showing pending and approved changes, helping carriers plan their implementation roadmaps.

Risk 19 - Compliance & Legal

Passenger rights on cross-border rail journeys are governed by EU Regulation 1371/2007 (railway passengers' rights), which covers compensation, assistance and liability for operators. The Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop (Decision 1) and Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography (Decision 9) must ensure that a through-ticket passenger has equivalent rights regardless of the number of carriers involved. If the programme's rights backstop and liability rules are less generous than Regulation 1371/2007 or create gaps, passengers may lose rights and the programme faces regulatory complaints.

Impact: If passengers lose rights (e.g., compensation for delays due to an unclear liability allocation), the EU Agency for Railways or national regulators may issue enforcement notices, forcing the programme to redesign the liability and disruption-handling rules, delaying implementation by 3–6 months. Estimated cost: €10–20 million in legal work and programme redesign.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Medium

Action: By Month 3 (2027-01-12), commission an independent legal review of the Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop (Decision 1) design against EU Regulation 1371/2007, ensuring that through-ticket passengers have equivalent or better rights than single-carrier passengers. Publish the legal opinion and any required design adjustments by Month 6 (2027-04-12). Ensure that the Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography (Decision 9) operating manual includes step-by-step procedures for compensation claims, assistance and liability that comply with Regulation 1371/2007. Submit the manual to the EU Agency for Railways for formal review and approval by Month 9 (2027-07-12) before carrier pilots begin.

Risk 20 - Organizational & Governance

The programme requires a Programme Office (within DG MOVE) and a Technical Secretariat (within or supporting the EU Agency for Railways) to coordinate standards work, conformance testing, funding releases and stakeholder engagement across five years and four locations. Programme staff turnover, particularly in leadership roles, can disrupt continuity and delay decision-making. Additionally, if the Programme Office lacks clear authority over budget releases or standards-working groups, carrier and distributor consensus becomes harder to achieve.

Impact: A change in Programme Director or Technical Lead at critical junctures (e.g., Month 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12 for binding standards, Month 24–30 = 2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12 for API exposure) could add 2–3 months of ramp-up time and defer milestones. If the Programme Office cannot enforce milestone conditions (e.g., conformance certificates before funding release), compliance will drop and the schedule will slip. Estimated cost: €5–10 million in extended programme management and consultant engagement.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Low

Action: By Month 1 (2026-11-12), the Commission must formally establish the Programme Office and Technical Secretariat with clear governance (reporting lines, decision authority), a multi-year budget (€50–100 million for programme management) and retention incentives for key staff (e.g., 3–5 year appointments with continuity clauses). Define success milestones and annual review cycles so that leadership changes are planned at low-risk points (e.g., after month 12 = 2027-10-12, month 36 = 2029-10-12 reports). Establish an advisory board of external experts (from carriers, distributors and academics) to provide independent oversight and escalation paths if the Programme Office is blocked by stakeholders.

Risk summary

This is a large, multi-stakeholder public infrastructure program spanning five years, four priority corridors and the full TEN-T network. It layers shared standards (OSDM-compatible APIs, clearing, rights backstop) over existing national carrier systems to enable seamless cross-border rail through-ticketing. The program operates under a fixed €1.5 billion public coordination budget (user constraint) and faces three interconnected critical risks: (1) Carrier unwillingness to expose inventory and accept connection liability unless the backstop design and clearing mechanism guarantee they can price the risk fairly—blocking the binding-standards milestone if not resolved by Month 18 (2028-04-12); (2) Legacy IT integration delays and conformance failures on priority corridors, particularly with smaller operators' systems, which could push the mandatory API exposure milestone (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) into the later quarters and starve funding for subsequent corridors; (3) Budget exhaustion if the carrier-funded guarantee pool drains faster than projected or the public distributor concession runs deeper deficits, cutting funding for member-state capacity building and reducing the likelihood of the 40% through-ticket goal. The regulatory and competition-law pathway is complex, with a Regulation proposal in Commission hands (not fully verified) and Article 101 TFEU clearance needed before binding standards. Physical location dependencies (EU institutions in Brussels, Agency for Railways in Valenciennes, carrier IT in Berlin/Munich/Zürich, pilot corridors across four member states) add coordination overhead. The program also depends on passenger behaviour change, multimodal integration and disability-rights compliance that are largely outside the program's control. Most critical are the carrier liability and inventory-exposure decisions (Decision 1 and 5), which, if mishandled, could trigger carrier non-participation and unravel the entire through-ticketing stack.

Make Assumptions

Question 1 - How should the €1.5 billion public budget be split across standards, clearing, the last-resort concession, adapters, capacity building and contingency, and what reserve is held?

Assumptions: Assumption: Allocation follows the pragmatic path: standards €50-100M, clearing €200-300M, concession €300-500M, adapters €200-300M, capacity building €200-300M, consumer rollout €100-150M (all estimates), with a €150-200M reserve (proposed). Private carrier IT investment is estimated separately, roughly €1.5-3B (estimate).

Assessments: Title: Financial Feasibility Assessment Description: Tests whether the fixed budget covers scope with contingency. Details: Upper-range allocations sum above €1.5B, so contingency is thin. Risks: pool top-ups, concession losses (€75-150M overrun, estimate), adapter overruns (€150-250M, estimate). Mitigation: milestone tranches, a reserve for force-majeure only, a subsidy cap on the concession, and quarterly budget re-baselining. Opportunity: carrier co-financing of adapters lowers public draw.

Question 2 - What is the realistic sequence of milestones from Month 0 (2026-10-12) to Month 60 (2031-10-12), and how much slack exists if the Regulation's adoption slips?

Assumptions: Assumption: Governance set-up by Month 1 (2026-11-12); liability and clearing decisions by Month 6 (2027-04-12); binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12); mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-12); tiered conformance to Month 42 (2030-04-12); four-corridor through-ticketing by Month 48 (2030-10-12); full TEN-T by Month 60-72 (2031-10-12 to 2032-10-12) (realistic, not aggressive). A 6-12 month slip in the Regulation is plausible.

Assessments: Title: Schedule Realism Assessment Description: Evaluates milestone feasibility and dependencies. Details: Critical path: Regulation text, DG COMP comfort, liability model, then standards. A 12-18 month legislative delay moves Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 30 (2029-04-12) (estimate). Mitigation: shadow standards workstream, pilots at Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12), tiered conformance, and a pre-agreed Month 72 (2032-10-12) fallback for full TEN-T. Benefit: priority corridors deliver visible value by Month 48 (2030-10-12) even if the network completes later.

Question 3 - Which teams and expertise are required in the Programme Office, Technical Secretariat, conformance labs and corridor pilots, and who supplies them?

Assumptions: Assumption: Programme Office of about 60-100 staff in DG MOVE (estimate), technical secretariat of 40-60 at the Agency in Valenciennes (estimate), plus contracted test engineers, actuaries and legal specialists. Carriers supply their own integration teams; liaison officers sit in Brussels, Valenciennes, Berlin and Madrid.

Assessments: Title: Resource Capacity Assessment Description: Reviews availability of skilled personnel and leadership continuity. Details: OSDM and clearing expertise is scarce and concentrated at a few carriers and vendors. Risks: key-person turnover, competition with carriers for engineers, and capacity gaps in smaller member states. Mitigation: multi-year appointments, framework contracts with integrators, regional training hubs, and an external advisory board. Budget about €50-100M for programme management (estimate).

Question 4 - Which legal instruments and approvals underpin binding standards, competition-law comfort, passenger-rights equivalence and national regulator consent?

Assumptions: Assumption: The Regulation is adopted with amendments by about Month 18 (2028-04-12); OSDM is pinned via delegated or implementing act; DG COMP guidance on Article 101 is sought from Month 2 (2026-12-12); Regulation 1371/2007 rights remain the floor; national regulators join as observers. Adoption status of the proposal is not verified.

Assessments: Title: Regulatory Compliance Assessment Description: Maps legal preconditions to programme decisions. Details: Largest exposure is Article 101 challenge after investment (€50-100M rework, estimate). Mitigation: early pre-notification, clean-team clearing, independent legal review of the backstop by Month 3 (2027-01-12), and regulator impact assessments per member state. Gaps in rights versus Regulation 1371/2007 would force 3-6 month redesign. Benefit: legal certainty encourages carrier commitment of inventory.

Question 5 - How will liability for missed connections, platform outages, settlement errors and accessibility failures be capped, insured and monitored?

Assumptions: Assumption: A carrier-funded guarantee pool with per-incident caps, co-insurance above caps and contributions based on trailing on-time performance; reserve for force majeure only; availability SLAs of p95 latency under 2 seconds and 99.5% uptime (proposed thresholds); reconciliation error under 0.5% (proposed).

Assessments: Title: Risk Exposure Assessment Description: Evaluates liability, technical and operational hazards. Details: Highest risks: carrier refusal over unpriceable liability (high likelihood), compounded availability across three-leg queries (about 86% at 95% each, recomputed), and pool drain from disruption clusters. Mitigation: actuarial study by Month 6 (2027-04-12), caps, SLA scorecards linked to tranches, cached fallback. Residual risk stays medium until pilots validate loss rates.

Question 6 - What environmental outcomes are expected, and how will modal shift and the footprint of new IT and rolling-stock upgrades be measured?

Assumptions: Assumption: Programme-level impact is mainly indirect via air-to-rail shift on competitive corridors; baseline measured by Month 6 (2027-04-12); targets stated as through-ticket penetration and observed shift, with a conservative 5-10% shift on benchmarked routes (estimate). Hardware retrofits follow maintenance cycles, and data centres use existing carrier or cloud capacity.

Assessments: Title: Environmental Impact Assessment Description: Judges net climate benefit and measurement validity. Details: Rail emits far less CO2 per passenger-km than short-haul flights, so even modest shift gives net benefit. Risks: low-fare airline response, attribution difficulty, and added e-waste from device upgrades. Mitigation: baseline and control routes, emissions-sorted neutral display, device reuse and recycling clauses, and a Month 48 (2030-10-12) evaluation. Do not promise air-replacement as a success metric.

Question 7 - Which stakeholders hold decision or veto power, and how will consensus be reached among carriers, distributors, consumer and disability bodies?

Assumptions: Assumption: A steering group meets biweekly with DG MOVE, the Agency, CER, 3-4 major carriers, Trainline, Omio, BEUC, a disability body and a regulator; binding votes on core decisions by Month 6 (2027-04-12) with Commission mediation; independent distributors may settle via a third-party fallback interface.

Assessments: Title: Stakeholder Alignment Assessment Description: Assesses consensus risk and engagement structure. Details: Conflicts: carriers prefer bilateral clearing, distributors want neutral central rules, disability bodies need auditable assistance booking. Failure by Month 9 (2027-07-12) risks a 2-4 month standards delay (estimate) and 20-30% loss of distributor volume. Mitigation: option papers by Month 2 (2026-12-12), transparent commission band, observer seats, PRM usability testing by Month 18 (2028-04-12). Benefit: early buy-in lowers later legal challenge.

Question 8 - What operational systems and service processes are needed: availability layer, clearing platform, disruption handling, validation, support and monitoring?

Assumptions: Assumption: Streamed availability shadow with carrier booking authority; federated netting layer on EUR settlement with 5-business-day cycle (proposed); shared disruption event feed; API handshake or signed journey token for validation; 24/7 support and monitored SLA dashboard; live pilots of 500-1,000 passengers per corridor (proposed).

Assessments: Title: Operational Readiness Assessment Description: Evaluates whether systems and processes work end to end. Details: Legacy latency, data quality and unshared operational data are main constraints. Risks: stale-seat errors, reconciliation backlog, validation gaps on 20% of vehicles lowering adoption 5-10% (estimate). Mitigation: operational manual by Month 9 (2027-07-12), pilots Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12), validation deployment by Month 40 (2030-02-12), shared reconciliation platform. Benefit: staged tiers let strong carriers go live first.

Distill Assumptions

  • Public coordination budget is fixed at €1.5 billion (user constraint), covering standards, clearing, concession, adapters, capacity building and rollout.
  • Private carrier IT investment is estimated separately at roughly €1.5-3B (estimate).
  • Budget split (estimates): standards €50-100M, clearing €200-300M, concession €300-500M, adapters €200-300M, capacity building €200-300M.
  • Consumer rollout is €100-150M (estimate); reserve of €150-200M (proposed) is for force majeure only.
  • Upper-range allocations exceed €1.5B, so contingency is thin; quarterly budget re-baselining and a concession subsidy cap apply.
  • Governance is set up by Month 1 (2026-11-12); liability and clearing decisions are made by Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • Binding standards are due by Month 18 (2028-04-12); mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-12).
  • Tiered conformance runs to Month 42 (2030-04-12); four-corridor through-ticketing is delivered by Month 48 (2030-10-12).
  • Full TEN-T completes Months 60-72 (2031-10-12 to 2032-10-12), with Month 72 (2032-10-12) as pre-agreed fallback.
  • Regulation adoption is assumed with amendments by about Month 18 (2028-04-12); status is not verified; 6-12 month slip is plausible.
  • Pilots of 500-1,000 passengers per corridor run Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12); validation deployment completes by Month 40 (2030-02-12).
  • Pragmatic path chosen: federated settlement, streamed availability shadow, carrier booking authority, carrier-funded guarantee pool, tendered last-resort concession.
  • Funds are released in tranches against verified milestones such as conformance certificates and live API exposure.
  • Guarantee pool uses per-incident caps, co-insurance above caps, and contributions based on trailing on-time performance; actuarial study by Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • DG COMP Article 101 guidance is sought from Month 2 (2026-12-12); clean-team clearing and legal review of backstop by Month 3 (2027-01-12).
  • OSDM is pinned via delegated or implementing act; Regulation 1371/2007 rights remain the floor.
  • Stakeholders: DG MOVE, Agency, CER, 3-4 major carriers, Trainline, Omio, BEUC, disability body and regulator sit in a steering group.
  • Steering group meets biweekly; binding votes on core decisions by Month 6 (2027-04-12) with Commission mediation.
  • Programme Office has 60-100 staff at DG MOVE; Agency secretariat has 40-60 staff (estimates).
  • Carriers supply their own integration teams; OSDM and clearing expertise is scarce.
  • Settlement uses EUR with a 5-business-day cycle; reconciliation error stays under 0.5% (proposed).
  • Availability SLAs are p95 latency under 2 seconds and 99.5% uptime (proposed thresholds).
  • Targets: 40% of cross-border journeys as through-tickets, distributor complaints halved, within five years.
  • Modal shift is conservative at 5-10% on benchmarked routes (estimate); air replacement is not a success metric.
  • Key risks: carrier refusal over unpriceable liability, Article 101 challenge (€50-100M rework), legacy latency, legislative delay.
  • Stakeholder alignment failure by Month 9 (2027-07-12) risks a 2-4 month standards delay and 20-30% distributor volume loss (estimates).

Review Assumptions

Domain of the expert reviewer

Public infrastructure programme planning and multi-stakeholder governance, with focus on regulatory alignment, financial risk and operational integration at scale

Domain-specific considerations

  • Fixed public budget (€1.5 billion, user constraint) must cover five-year rollout across four corridors and full TEN-T; no contingency for cost overruns beyond force majeure
  • Carrier participation is voluntary and depends on predictable liability pricing; unpriceable risk exposure triggers non-participation and network fragmentation
  • Regulatory pathway uncertain: Regulation adoption status not verified; Article 101 TFEU comfort needed before binding standards; Regulation 1371/2007 rights must be preserved
  • Legacy systems integration: smaller operators' booking engines may not meet latency and availability targets, delaying mandatory API exposure milestone by 6–12 months
  • Multi-stakeholder consensus among 25+ carriers, independent distributors, national regulators and disability bodies is required by Month 6 (2027-04-12); failure cascades to standards
  • Through-ticket value depends on seamless operational coordination (disruption rebooking, validation, accessibility) across independent national operators with varying systems and cultures

Issue 1 - Critical Missing Assumption: Carrier Liability Pricing Model Not Defined

The programme assumes carriers will expose through-ticket connections and accept shared liability via a carrier-funded guarantee pool (Decision 1), but the liability-weighting formula, per-incident caps, co-insurance thresholds and risk-transfer mechanism are not yet specified. Carriers cannot price their participation or commit inventory without knowing their maximum exposure and contribution rules. Absence of a published liability model by Month 3 (2027-01-12) leaves the core commercial assumption untested and triggers carrier refusal.

Recommendation: By Month 2 (2026-12-12), commission an independent actuarial study to model missed-connection rates, rerouting costs and incident clustering using historical data from each participating carrier. Publish a draft liability-weighting formula by Month 3 (2027-01-12) that specifies: (a) maximum per-incident cap (e.g., €500–1,000 per stranded passenger), (b) co-insurance threshold (e.g., carriers self-insure up to €50M annual pool draw, above which public or reinsurance cover applies), and (c) contribution weights tied to controllable factors (on-time performance, booking-system availability) not forward-looking incident rates. Present this model to CER and the 10 largest carriers by Month 4 (2027-02-12) for binding commercial sign-off before standards are finalised. Establish a quarterly pool-monitoring process that publishes incident rates and contribution adjustments.

Sensitivity: If the liability model is not agreed by Month 6 (2027-04-12), carriers face unpriceable risk and 30–40% (estimate) may refuse to expose inventory. This delays mandatory API exposure from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 36 (2029-10-12) or later and reduces network coverage by 20–30%, pushing the 40% through-ticket goal to 15–25% (estimate). Cost impact: €100–150 million in lost programme value if the goal is unachievable. Budget impact: funding for later corridors (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) faces reallocation to cover smaller operator adapter overruns, compressing the full TEN-T rollout to Month 72–84 (2032-10-12 to 2033-10-12) instead of Month 60 (2031-10-12).

Issue 2 - Critical Missing Assumption: Legacy System Integration Timeline and Hidden Adapter Costs Not Validated

The plan allocates €200–300 million (estimate) for conformance testing and carrier adapters to retrofit legacy booking systems to OSDM standards. However, a pre-programme technical audit of all 25+ operators' systems and realistic integration timelines per operator tier (large, regional, small) has not been conducted. Smaller carriers' systems may require 9–15 months of development per operator, not the 18–24 months between Month 12 (2027-10-12) and Month 30 (2029-04-12) mandatory exposure. Risk: adapters miss the Month 30 (2029-04-12) milestone, leaving 8–15 operators outside the network and fragmenting the corridor coverage.

Recommendation: Conduct a detailed technical audit of all participating carriers' booking-system architectures by Month 2 (2026-12-12), assessing API readiness, event-streaming capability, transaction consistency and on-time/availability data quality. Establish a per-operator conformance timeline (baseline, extended, advanced tiers) and publish it by Month 6 (2027-04-12). Allocate adapter funding in tranches: Tier 1 (large carriers, Month 30 = 2029-04-12) receives €80–100M (estimate); Tier 2 (regional, Month 36 = 2029-10-12) receives €80–100M (estimate); Tier 3 (small, Month 42 = 2030-04-12) receives €50–80M (estimate). Require carriers in each tier to demonstrate API availability and booking-error rates (<1% stale-seat failures) before their tier release, not a one-time conformance gate.

Sensitivity: If tier-based funding is not adopted and all carriers are held to a single Month 30 (2029-04-12) gate, 40–50% (estimate) of smaller and regional carriers miss the deadline by 6–12 months. This creates a 12–18 month delay in reaching full-corridor through-ticketing (from Month 48 = 2030-10-12 to Month 60–66 = 2031-10-12 to 2032-04-12). Budget impact: adapter overruns of €150–250 million (estimate) due to emergency acceleration efforts, or alternatively, € 200–300 million in unused budget if the later corridors cannot launch. Network coverage drops from 25+ carriers to ~15 by Month 48 (2030-10-12), reducing the through-ticket share from 40% to 20–25% (estimate).

Issue 3 - Critical Missing Assumption: Stakeholder Consensus Mechanism and Fallback Governance for Deadlocked Decisions

The plan requires binding decisions on liability (Decision 1), clearing architecture (Decision 2), public distributor role (Decision 3) and remuneration (Decision 12) by Month 6 (2027-04-12), involving 25+ carriers, CER, Trainline, Omio, BEUC, disability bodies and national regulators with conflicting interests. No formal consensus mechanism, escalation path or fallback governance is defined if a vote is deadlocked or a stakeholder withdraws. Without this, a single veto (e.g., from a large carrier or an independent distributor) can block standards and push binding milestones from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12).

Recommendation: Establish a tiered governance structure by Month 1 (2026-11-12): (a) biweekly steering group of CER, DG MOVE, Agency, 3–4 major carriers (DB, SNCF, SBB, ÖBB or Renfe), Trainline, Omio, BEUC and one disability-rights body; (b) a voting rule requiring supermajority (75%) of steering members to approve Decisions 1, 2, 3, 12; (c) formal escalation to the Commission Transport Commissioner if a vote does not reach 75% by Month 5 (2027-03-12), with Commission mediation required by Month 6 (2027-04-12); (d) a fallback clause that if a major carrier (>5% of network) refuses a decision, the programme offers a technical fallback (e.g., bilateral clearing with netting, or a third-party settlement interface for distributors) rather than stalling the entire decision. Publish an option paper for each decision by Month 2 (2026-12-12) outlining three variants with trade-offs, so stakeholders see alternatives before voting.

Sensitivity: If consensus is not reached by Month 9 (2027-07-12), binding standards are delayed from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12), a 2–4 month slip (estimate). This cascades to mandatory API exposure (Month 30 = 2029-04-12 → Month 36 = 2029-10-12, estimate) and four-corridor go-live (Month 48 = 2030-10-12 → Month 54–60 = 2031-04-12 to 2031-10-12, estimate). If a major distributor (e.g., Trainline or Omio) rejects the clearing design, they withdraw from the programme, reducing available through-ticket volume by 15–25% (estimate), which lowers the 40% goal to 20–30%. Estimated cost to resolve deadlock through litigation or renegotiation: €10–20 million and 3–6 month delay.

Review conclusion

The programme's three most critical missing assumptions are: (1) a published, actuarially validated carrier liability-pricing model specifying caps, co-insurance and contribution weights, absent by Month 3 (2027-01-12), which triggers carrier refusal and threatens network participation; (2) a pre-programme technical audit and per-operator tier-based adapter funding plan, absent which 40–50% of smaller carriers miss the Month 30 (2029-04-12) API exposure deadline and compress later-wave funding; and (3) a formal multi-stakeholder consensus mechanism with escalation and fallback clauses, absent which deadlock on Decisions 1–3 delays binding standards by 2–4 months and cascades throughout the schedule. Each missing assumption poses a 15–25% risk to the 40% through-ticket goal and €100–250 million budget variance. Recommendation: complete liability modelling by Month 3 (2027-01-12), conduct a technical audit by Month 2 (2026-12-12) and establish steering governance with published options by Month 2 (2026-12-12). These three workstreams must run in parallel Months 0–6 (2026-10-12 to 2027-04-12) to unlock the binding-standards pathway.

Governance Audit

Audit - Corruption Risks

  • Collusion among major carriers to exclude smaller competitors from the shared real-time data layer or clearing mechanism by leveraging privileged access to the OSDM API or settlement data, circumventing the non-discriminatory access mandate and the Joint Conduct Safe-Harbour decision.
  • Bribery or corrupt influence by carriers or distributors on standards-working groups or conformance certification bodies to weaken accessibility requirements, latency SLAs or reconciliation accuracy thresholds, allowing non-compliant systems to access through-ticket corridors.
  • Nepotism or conflict-of-interest appointments within the Programme Office or Technical Secretariat, where staff members approve funding tranches (Month 30 = 2029-04-12, Month 36 = 2029-10-12) for carriers or adapter vendors that employ their relatives or former employers, bypassing competitive procurement.
  • Misuse of commercially sensitive carrier data (fares, inventory, settlement flows, on-time performance) shared within the clearing or data-sharing layer by staff members trading on the information or disclosing it to competitors outside the clean-team arrangement.
  • Kickbacks or side payments from the last-resort distributor concessionaire or payment-service providers to Commission procurement officials or steering-group members in exchange for favorable contract terms, subsidy increases above the EUR 60M cap, or relief from performance penalties.
  • Fraudulent conformance certification by carriers or test laboratories claiming OSDM API compliance and latency/availability SLAs (p95 <2 seconds, 99.5% uptime) without genuine technical validation, allowing non-compliant systems onto the priority corridors and triggering failures during Month 48 (2030-10-12) go-live.

Audit - Misallocation Risks

  • Budget drift: Adapter funding (EUR 240M allocation) overspends by EUR 150-250M due to emergency acceleration for missed Tier 1 timelines (Month 30 = 2029-04-12), consuming EUR 65-165M more than the EUR 85M headroom and forcing reallocation from capacity building or TEN-T extension to the reserve.
  • Double spending or uncoordinated invoicing across the Programme Office and Technical Secretariat, where both entities reimburse the same external legal counsel, actuaries or integration contractors, inflating programme management costs beyond the EUR 75M allocation.
  • Inefficient allocation of the EUR 150M force-majeure reserve: draw-downs after Month 36 (2029-10-12) to cover carrier-pool overruns or concession subsidy gaps that should instead trigger policy recalibration, depleting the reserve and leaving no contingency for genuine disruptions.
  • Misuse of the EUR 300M concession envelope by shifting subsidy payments to the last-resort distributor to cover cost overruns beyond the EUR 60M cap without triggering contract reviews or clawback clauses, reducing funding available for other programme functions.
  • Unauthorized or poorly documented use of the EUR 100M consumer-rollout budget (multilingual support, complaint handling, accessibility testing) for programme communications or marketing that benefits carriers or distributors rather than passengers, diverting funds from intended consumer services.
  • Incomplete or late reporting of settlement reconciliation errors, latency SLAs and conformance audit results to the steering group and Commission, obscuring milestone status and delaying trigger-based funding releases or variance corrections, allowing non-compliant systems to remain live past Month 30 (2029-04-12).

Audit - Procedures

  • Quarterly financial reconciliation audits (Month 3 = 2027-01-12 onwards) verifying that all budget lines (programme management, standards, clearing, adapters, concession, capacity building, consumer rollout, reserve) are allocated and spent against documented approvals, no double invoicing, and variance triggers at EUR 100M/200M/300M are tracked and reported to the Commission within 10 business days.
  • Independent actuarial audit of the carrier-funded guarantee pool at Month 6 (2027-04-12) and annually thereafter, confirming that missed-connection rates, rerouting costs and pool contributions are calculated according to the signed liability model, per-incident caps are enforced, and no draw-downs occur after Month 36 (2029-10-12) without force-majeure certification.
  • Conformance certification audit for each carrier at Months 24, 30, 36 and 42 (2028-10-12, 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12), verifying OSDM API compliance, latency (p95 <2 seconds), availability (99.5%), stale-seat failures (<1%), and booking-error rates via independent test laboratories; results published to the steering group and used to trigger funding tranches.
  • Settlement and reconciliation audit (monthly by Month 24 = 2028-10-12, then quarterly) confirming EUR settlement cycle time (5 business days), reconciliation error rate (<0.5%), and that carrier contributions to the clearing layer match their invoice-to-invoice settlement volumes and do not exceed agreed commercial terms; dispute-resolution cases sampled for proper authority.
  • Post-concession audit at Months 30, 48 and 60 (2029-04-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12), reviewing concessionaire operating costs against budget, through-ticket volumes against forecast, subsidy claims against the EUR 60M cap, clawback calculations and contract-review triggers; auditors must be independent of the procurement authority.
  • Biennial external audit (Month 24 = 2028-10-12 and Month 48 = 2030-10-12) by the European Court of Auditors or contracted firm covering programme governance, steering-group voting records, funding-tranche release conditions and adherence to the 75% supermajority rule, competition-law compliance (DG COMP guidance letter filing, clean-team data segregation), and passenger-rights legal review sign-offs.

Audit - Transparency Measures

  • Published monthly SLA dashboard accessible to steering group and regulators, displaying each carrier's OSDM API latency (p95), availability, stale-seat error rate and booking failures; carriers missing targets for two consecutive months identified with explanation and tranche-release impact.
  • Quarterly public financial report (Month 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-12, 2027-04-12, 2027-07-12, 2027-10-12, … = 2027-01-12 onwards) showing cumulative spend per budget line, variance against allocation, forecast-to-completion, reserve balance and any draw-downs approved; flagged thresholds (EUR 100M, EUR 200M, EUR 300M) trigger a published variance-mitigation explanation within 10 business days.
  • Steering group meeting minutes published within 15 days (redacting competition-sensitive data), including voting records, dissents, escalation decisions and Commission mediation outcomes; binding votes on core decisions (liability, clearing, concession, commission) recorded with each member's position.
  • Conformance certification results published per carrier on a public registry maintained by the EU Agency for Railways, showing pass/fail status, test-report summary, any remediation required and certification expiry date; carriers must disclose any failed audit attempts before receiving a pass certificate.
  • Carrier-funded guarantee pool actuarial reports published annually, showing missed-connection incident rates by carrier, pool contributions, claim payouts, co-insurance thresholds triggered and reserve balance; individual carrier data redacted to comply with commercial confidentiality, but aggregate statistics disclosed.
  • Public concession performance dashboard updated monthly, displaying through-ticket volumes sold via the last-resort distributor against forecast, operating costs against budget, subsidy drawn against the EUR 60M cap, clawback calculations if volumes exceed forecast by >20%, and any contract-review triggers if costs exceed budget by >15% in a quarter.

Internal Governance Bodies

1. Programme Steering Committee (PSC)

Rationale for Inclusion: This is a large, multi-stakeholder, regulation-dependent public infrastructure program with a fixed €1.5B budget, distributed execution across four corridors, and critical dependencies on carrier participation, legislative adoption, and competition-law clearance. The programme has multiple high-impact strategic decisions (liability backstop, clearing architecture, public distributor role, funding release conditions) that require binding votes by Month 6 (2027-04-12) to unblock standards work and maintain the Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards milestone. Strategic oversight must operate above operational delivery and hold explicit decision authority over funding tranches, milestone conditions and escalation to the Commission.

Responsibilities:

  • Approve and enforce critical strategic decisions (Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop, Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement, Public Reference Distributor Mandate, Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder, Availability Query Topology) by binding votes at Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • Set and approve annual programme budgets and funding-tranche release conditions; trigger variance-mitigation actions when cumulative spend reaches thresholds (EUR 100M, EUR 200M, EUR 300M).
  • Approve conformance-gate and carrier-tier assignments; escalate conformance failures or missed SLA targets (latency, availability, reconciliation error) to the Programme Office for remedial action or funding tranche withholding.
  • Oversee and approve the binding Commission guidance letter from DG COMP on Article 101 TFEU and passenger-rights legal compliance by Month 14 (2027-12-12); escalate unresolved legal or regulatory conflicts to Commission Transport Commissioner.
  • Monitor and approve quarterly SLA and financial reports; authorize policy recalibrations (e.g., reserve draws, concession subsidy increases above the EUR 60M cap, TEN-T extension deferrals) if contingencies are triggered.
  • Resolve deadlocked steering votes or stakeholder disputes via a formal escalation and mediation process; record all votes and dissents; publish meeting minutes within 15 days (redacting sensitive data).

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Formally establish the Committee by Commission decision at Month 1 (2026-11-12) with explicit charter, voting rules (75% supermajority for core decisions), and escalation authority to the Transport Commissioner.
  • Appoint Chair (DG MOVE Director or equivalent) and Secretary (Technical Secretariat lead) by Month 1 (2026-11-12).
  • Confirm membership and secure binding commitment letters from all nine core members (DG MOVE, Agency, CER, 3-4 major carriers, Trainline, Omio, BEUC, disability body) by Month 2 (2026-12-12).
  • Publish the option-papers document outlining three variants for each of Decisions 1-5 with explicit trade-offs by Month 2 (2026-12-12) to inform stakeholder positions.
  • Establish a published voting and decision-recording process, including dissent documentation and tie-breaker rules, by Month 1 (2026-11-12).
  • Schedule biweekly meetings (rotating virtual and in-person) for Months 1-12 (2026-11-12 to 2027-10-12) to maintain momentum on the Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate and Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards milestone.

Membership:

  • Chair: DG MOVE (Director or Transport Commissioner designate)
  • Vice-Chair: EU Agency for Railways (Director)
  • CER (Chief Executive)
  • Deutsche Bahn (or ÖBB/SBB if DB unavailable)
  • SNCF (Chief Commercial Officer)
  • Renfe or SJ (second major carrier)
  • Trainline (Head of Policy or Chief Executive)
  • Omio (Head of Regulatory Affairs or Chief Executive)
  • BEUC (Head of Transport Policy)
  • European Disability Forum (or equivalent disability-rights representative) (independent observer, non-voting)

Decision Rights: Binding strategic decisions over critical programme levers (liability backstop, clearing architecture, public distributor role, funding-tranche conditions, conformance gates, SLA thresholds, regulatory escalations). Decisions above EUR 100M cumulative variance or affecting programme schedule milestones must be approved by the Committee. Decisions below EUR 10M or operational (e.g., monthly reconciliation reviews, individual carrier SLA remediation) are delegated to the Programme Office without Committee approval.

Decision Mechanism: Supermajority voting (at least 7 of 9 core members, 75%) required for approval of Decisions 1-5 and for any variance triggers above EUR 100M. Simple majority (5 of 9) for procedural matters (meeting schedule, charter updates) and quarterly financial reports. In the event of a deadlock (vote below 75%), the issue is escalated to the Commission Transport Commissioner with a formal briefing by Month 5 (2027-03-12); mediation is completed by Month 6 (2027-04-12) or the decision defers to a fallback governance path (e.g., bilateral clearing interface for distributors, tiered conformance with mixed gates). Tie-breaker: the Chair (DG MOVE) casts the deciding vote only if the vote is 4.5-4.5 or a member abstains; otherwise, deadlock triggers escalation. All votes and dissents are recorded in minutes published within 15 days.

Meeting Cadence: Biweekly during Phase 1 (Months 1-18 = 2026-11-12 to 2028-04-12) to maintain momentum on standards-setting and stakeholder consensus; monthly during Phase 2 (Months 18-48 = 2028-04-12 to 2030-10-12) to oversee API exposure, conformance audits and funding tranches; quarterly during Phase 3 (Months 48-60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) for TEN-T extension and final evaluation. Emergency sessions convoked within five business days if a funding variance trigger is hit or a regulatory escalation occurs.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Voting on critical decisions (liability model sign-off, clearing architecture, public distributor concession award, funding tranche conditions) by Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • Quarterly SLA and financial reports: conformance-certification results, latency/availability scorecards, settlement reconciliation error rates, pool-contribution and clawback calculations, concession operating costs vs. budget.
  • Regulatory and legal updates: DG COMP guidance-letter status, passenger-rights legal-review findings, national regulator impact assessments, clean-team protocol approval.
  • Variance-trigger management: review of cumulative spend against budget lines, authorization of contingency draws (reserve, concession subsidy cap), policy recalibrations if thresholds (EUR 100M, EUR 200M, EUR 300M) are crossed.
  • Stakeholder escalations: resolution of deadlocked votes, discrimination complaints from distributors, carrier non-participation signals, national regulator conflicts.
  • Schedule and milestone tracking: binding-standards progress, API exposure tier readiness, corridor go-live date confirmation, TEN-T extension planning.

Escalation Path: Unresolved deadlocks on core decisions (Decisions 1-5) at the Committee escalate to the Commission Transport Commissioner with a formal briefing and mediation request by Month 5 (2027-03-12); mediation completes by Month 6 (2027-04-12) or a fallback governance path is invoked. Funding variances above EUR 300M or programme-scope reductions (deferral of TEN-T extension beyond Month 72 = 2032-10-12, restriction to four corridors only) escalate to the Commission's Financial Controller and the Court of Auditors. Regulatory or competition-law conflicts that block standards adoption escalate to DG COMP and DG MOVE's legal service for resolution by Month 12 (2027-10-12) or standards are deferred. Carrier or distributor disputes unresolved by the Committee after 30 days escalate to the Commission for independent mediation or binding arbitration.

2. Programme Office and Operational Management Board (OMB)

Rationale for Inclusion: The programme spans four physical locations, 25+ carriers, independent distributors, and five-year delivery horizons with fixed regulatory milestones (Month 18 = 2028-04-12, Month 30 = 2029-04-12, Month 60 = 2031-10-12). Day-to-day programme management, budget execution, milestone tracking, carrier engagement, and operational risk management require a dedicated operational governance body with clear authority below the Steering Committee's strategic thresholds. The OMB must manage EUR 1.5B budget execution, oversee the Programme Office's 80+ staff, coordinate standards-working groups, conduct conformance testing and audits, manage funding tranches, and escalate blockers to the Steering Committee. Separating operational from strategic governance prevents agenda congestion at the Committee level and gives clear accountability for delivery.

Responsibilities:

  • Execute the Programme Office mandate: manage the 80-person team across DG MOVE, coordinate the Technical Secretariat (50 staff) at the Agency, deploy liaison officers in Brussels, Valenciennes, Berlin and Madrid, and maintain the shared reconciliation platform and SLA proxy.
  • Manage EUR 1.5B public budget execution: prepare quarterly financial reports showing cumulative spend per line (standards EUR 80M, clearing EUR 220M, adapters EUR 240M, concession EUR 300M, capacity building EUR 200M, consumer rollout EUR 100M, reserve EUR 150M), track variances against allocations, and recommend contingency triggers (EUR 100M, EUR 200M, EUR 300M) to the Steering Committee.
  • Own technical audit and tier assignment: conduct the full audit of all 25+ carriers' booking systems by Month 2 (2026-12-12), assign carriers to tiers (Tier 1: Month 30 = 2029-04-12; Tier 2: Month 36 = 2029-10-12; Tier 3: Month 42 = 2030-04-12), and publish per-operator integration timelines and adapter funding allocations.
  • Manage conformance testing and certification: operate test environments, conduct independent audits for OSDM API compliance, latency (p95 <2 seconds), availability (99.5%), stale-seat failures (<1%), and booking-error rates; publish monthly SLA scorecards by carrier; recommend funding tranche withholding for carriers missing SLAs for two consecutive months.
  • Manage funding-tranche releases: verify milestone conditions (API exposure, conformance certificates, SLA targets) before authorizing each tranche; track clawback and subsidy-cap conditions for the concession; escalate funding-release delays or remediation needs to the Steering Committee.
  • Coordinate standards-working groups: chair the technical working group on OSDM, liability model, clearing architecture, fare construction, disruption re-accommodation and ticket validation; prepare option papers and steering-group briefings; track standards progress against Month 18 (2028-04-12) deadline.
  • Manage carrier and distributor engagement: conduct bilateral briefings with carriers on liability model, conformance requirements and funding tranches; mediate commission-rate disputes and discrimination complaints; manage fallback interfaces for distributors rejecting the clearing design.
  • Oversee pilots and live validation: conduct live pilots of 500-1,000 passengers per corridor at Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12); track reroute response times, passenger satisfaction and re-accommodation success; manage validation deployment to corridor rolling stock and station gates by Month 40 (2030-02-12).
  • Manage risk and issues: maintain a register of top risks and issues; track mitigation actions (e.g., DG COMP guidance letter, passenger-rights legal review, national regulator impact assessments); escalate risks reaching their trigger conditions (e.g., legislation delay, carrier participation drop) to the Steering Committee within five business days.

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Appoint Programme Director and Operations Manager by Month 1 (2026-11-12); establish the Operational Management Board as a sub-committee of the Steering Committee with Chair (Programme Director), Secretary (Operations Manager), and representatives from Programme Office, Technical Secretariat, carrier leads and distributor lead.
  • Commission the technical audit of all carriers' booking systems by Month 1 (2026-11-12); complete by Month 2 (2026-12-12).
  • Establish the Programme Office (80 staff) and Technical Secretariat (50 staff) by Month 1 (2026-11-12); hire core staff for standards, conformance, clearing, adapters, capacity building and consumer rollout by Month 3 (2027-01-12).
  • Procure shared reconciliation platform, SLA proxy and test-environment infrastructure by Month 3 (2027-01-12); deploy by Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • Commission carrier-liability actuarial study and competition-law pre-notification to DG COMP by Month 1 (2026-11-12).
  • Establish and publish the quarterly financial reporting and variance-tracking process by Month 2 (2026-12-12).

Membership:

  • Chair: Programme Director (DG MOVE, appointed by Month 1 = 2026-11-12)
  • Secretary: Operations Manager (Programme Office, appointed by Month 1 = 2026-11-12)
  • Head of Standards and Conformance (Technical Secretariat lead)
  • Head of Clearing and Settlement (Programme Office, clearing function lead)
  • Head of Carrier Engagement (Programme Office, liaison to CER and major carriers)
  • Head of Distributor and Consumer Affairs (Programme Office, liaison to Trainline, Omio and last-resort concessionaire)
  • Head of Compliance and Risk (Programme Office, legal, competition-law and passenger-rights lead)
  • Representative from Financial Planning and Control (DG MOVE Finance)

Decision Rights: Operational decisions on budget execution below EUR 10M per line, milestone tracking, conformance-certification results, SLA scorecards, funding-tranche conditions (verification of milestone achievement), carrier tier assignment and adapter funding allocation, and pilot results. Decisions on funding tranches up to EUR 50M are delegated to the OMB; larger releases (EUR 80M Tier 1, EUR 80M Tier 2, EUR 50M Tier 3) require Steering Committee approval. Decisions on variance responses below EUR 50M (e.g., accelerating adapter schedules within existing budget, reallocating between standards and testing) are delegated; responses exceeding EUR 50M escalate to the Committee. Conformance-gate remediation (requiring carriers to retest, withholding tranches) is delegated; deferral of entire tiers or carriers from the programme escalates to the Steering Committee.

Decision Mechanism: Simple majority (at least 4 of 7 OMB members) for operational decisions. Consensus preferred for budget execution and milestone tracking to maintain transparency; if consensus is not reached, the Chair (Programme Director) decides, with written record to the Steering Committee within five business days. Any decision affecting the Steering Committee's strategic milestones (Month 18 = 2028-04-12, Month 30 = 2029-04-12, Month 48 = 2030-10-12) requires Steering Committee approval, not OMB-only decision. Tie-breaker: Programme Director casts deciding vote.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly during Phase 1 (Months 1-18 = 2026-11-12 to 2028-04-12) to maintain momentum on standards and readiness-gate prep; biweekly during Phase 2 (Months 18-48 = 2028-04-12 to 2030-10-12) to track API exposure, conformance and funding tranches; monthly during Phase 3 (Months 48-60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) for TEN-T extension. Emergency sessions within two business days if a conformance audit fails, a carrier signals non-participation, or a funding variance reaches a trigger threshold.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Technical audit findings and carrier tier assignment (Month 2 = 2026-12-12).
  • Standards-working group progress: OSDM specification, liability model, clearing architecture, fare construction, disruption choreography, ticket validation.
  • Quarterly financial reports: cumulative spend per budget line, variance tracking, reserve balance, concession operating-cost and subsidy tracking, clawback calculations.
  • Conformance audit results: monthly SLA scorecards by carrier, latency/availability/error-rate trends, remediation tracking for carriers missing targets, tranche-withholding recommendations.
  • Funding-tranche verification: milestone-completion evidence (API exposure certificates, conformance certificates), conditions for next tranche release.
  • Carrier and distributor engagement: feedback from bilateral briefings, commission-rate disputes, discrimination complaints, fallback-interface adoption.
  • Pilot results: passenger satisfaction, reroute response times, accessibility issues, validation acceptance rates (by Month 18 = 2028-04-12).
  • Risk and issue tracking: top 10 risks, mitigation status, trigger-condition monitoring, escalation flags.

Escalation Path: Funding variances above EUR 50M, conformance failures affecting entire tiers, carrier non-participation affecting corridor connectivity, or delays to Month 18/30/48/60 (2028-04-12, 2029-04-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12) milestones escalate to the Steering Committee within two business days. Regulatory or competition-law blockers escalate to the Steering Committee's legal-escalation path (DG COMP, passenger-rights review). Unresolved carrier or distributor disputes escalate to the Steering Committee after 30 days. Budget variances reaching thresholds (EUR 100M, EUR 200M, EUR 300M) trigger automatic escalation to the Committee and a published variance-mitigation plan within ten business days.

3. Compliance, Competition Law and Passenger Rights Committee (CCPR)

Rationale for Inclusion: This is a regulation-aligned public infrastructure programme operating at the intersection of EU transport regulation (Digital Booking and Ticketing Regulation, passenger-rights regulation 1371/2007), competition law (Article 101 TFEU, data-sharing and clearing arrangements) and accessibility law (Regulation 1371/2007, EU Accessibility Directive). The programme creates several competition-law exposures: shared data exchange through a clearing layer, potential rate-fixing on commissions, and exclusive access to real-time inventory could trigger Article 101 scrutiny. Passenger-rights continuity across carriers, liability allocation, and assistance/bicycle-reservation guarantees must comply with existing law. Accessibility for persons with reduced mobility is a legal requirement with reputational and liability risk. A dedicated specialized body ensures systematic compliance monitoring, early escalation of legal risks, and documented due diligence that protects both the programme and participating carriers. This committee reports to the Steering Committee and the Commission's legal services.

Responsibilities:

  • Secure and maintain DG COMP Article 101 guidance: manage pre-notification to DG COMP at Month 2 (2026-12-12), obtain formal guidance letter by Month 12 (2027-10-12), establish clean-team protocol for the clearing function by Month 14 (2027-12-12), and publish a compliance certificate by Month 18 (2028-04-12) confirming that data-sharing and clearing arrangements are compatible with competition rules.
  • Monitor and ensure passenger-rights compliance: commission independent legal review of the Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop design against EU Regulation 1371/2007 by Month 1 (2026-11-12), obtain opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-12), approve a detailed compliance manual by Month 9 (2027-07-12) covering assistance, rerouting, compensation and refund procedures that meet or exceed existing passenger-rights protections.
  • Oversee accessibility compliance: establish accessibility thresholds (wheelchair access on ≥80% of services, assistance within ≤4 hours' notice on ≥90% of services) as a precondition of conformance; conduct usability testing with persons with reduced mobility by Month 18 (2028-04-12); publish annual accessibility audit results; establish fallback procedures for carriers unable to meet thresholds.
  • Manage data governance and GDPR compliance: establish rules for handling commercially sensitive data (fares, inventory, settlement flows) within the clearing and data-sharing layers; ensure the shared reconciliation platform and disruption event feed comply with GDPR; publish a data-governance policy by Month 6 (2027-04-12); conduct annual GDPR impact assessments.
  • Monitor national regulatory alignment: conduct bilateral regulatory-impact assessments per member state by Month 3 (2027-01-12) to identify conflicts between the programme's design and national railway regulations; escalate conflicts to the Steering Committee and national regulators for resolution by Month 12 (2027-10-12) or defer that member state's participation.
  • Oversee discrimination and fair-access monitoring: audit commission-rate data published by the clearing function monthly to detect discrimination between distributor types; investigate complaints from distributors claiming unfair access or pricing; publish a discrimination-monitoring report quarterly; escalate substantive discrimination findings to national regulators.
  • Document and audit compliance: maintain a compliance register tracking Article 101 guidance, passenger-rights legal opinions, accessibility certifications, GDPR assessments and discrimination audits; publish a biennial external audit by the Court of Auditors or contracted firm; produce quarterly compliance reports to the Steering Committee.

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish the Committee and appoint Chair (external legal expert with EU competition and transport-law experience) by Month 1 (2026-11-12).
  • Commission independent legal reviews: (1) Article 101 TFEU compatibility of data-sharing and clearing by Month 1 (2026-11-12); (2) Passenger-rights compliance against Regulation 1371/2007 by Month 1 (2026-11-12); (3) GDPR and data-governance assessment by Month 2 (2026-12-12); (4) Accessibility and EU Accessibility Directive compliance by Month 2 (2026-12-12).
  • File Article 101 pre-notification with DG COMP by Month 2 (2026-12-12); request guidance letter by Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • Publish the compliance roadmap and quarterly compliance reporting schedule by Month 3 (2027-01-12).
  • Conduct bilateral regulatory-impact assessments per member state (25+ operators across 5-6 member states) by Month 3 (2027-01-12).
  • Establish a discrimination-monitoring protocol and data-audit schedule by Month 6 (2027-04-12) to track commission-rate data from the clearing function.

Membership:

  • Chair: External EU competition and transport-law expert (appointed by Month 1 = 2026-11-12), independent of DG MOVE and DG COMP
  • Legal Counsel from DG MOVE
  • Legal Counsel from DG COMP (observer seat)
  • Head of Passenger-Rights Compliance (commissioned external specialist)
  • Head of Data Governance and GDPR (Programme Office or external specialist)
  • Representative from the EU Agency for Railways (regulatory liaison)
  • Observer: BEUC (consumer representative) (non-voting)

Decision Rights: Authority to approve compliance certifications (Article 101 guidance letter, passenger-rights legal opinion, accessibility audit results, GDPR assessments) before they are released to the Steering Committee and public. Authority to issue compliance warnings to the Steering Committee if Article 101 guidance is not obtained by Month 12 (2027-10-12) or passenger-rights review is not approved by Month 9 (2027-07-12). Authority to block the release of any programme milestone (binding standards, API exposure, corridor go-live) if a material compliance gap is not addressed. Authority to recommend discrimination investigations and escalations to national regulators. Authority to recommend Member-State participation deferrals if regulatory conflicts cannot be resolved by Month 12 (2027-10-12). Decisions on compliance policy (thresholds, audit schedules, reporting formats) are made by simple majority; escalations to the Steering Committee require Committee approval.

Decision Mechanism: Consensus preferred on compliance certifications to ensure rigorous review; if consensus is not reached within 10 business days, the Chair (external legal expert) makes the decision and documents dissenting views. Compliance warnings and block decisions require Chair approval only, issued immediately to the Steering Committee. All formal compliance opinions (Article 101, passenger-rights, accessibility, GDPR) must be signed off by the Chair and at least one other member before publication.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly during Phase 1 (Months 1-18 = 2026-11-12 to 2028-04-12) to track Article 101 guidance, passenger-rights review and accessibility compliance; quarterly during Phase 2 (Months 18-48 = 2028-04-12 to 2030-10-12) to monitor discrimination audits and national-regulator alignment; biannually during Phase 3 (Months 48-60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) for final compliance audit. Emergency sessions within three business days if a compliance gap blocks a milestone or a discrimination complaint is escalated.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Article 101 guidance letter status and clean-team protocol approval (Months 2-18 = 2026-12-12 to 2028-04-12).
  • Passenger-rights legal review findings and compliance-manual approval (Months 1-9 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-07-12).
  • Accessibility audit results and thresholds enforcement (ongoing from Month 6 = 2027-04-12).
  • GDPR and data-governance compliance for clearing and disruption event feed.
  • National regulator impact assessments and conflict resolution (Months 3-12 = 2027-01-12 to 2027-10-12).
  • Quarterly discrimination audits: commission-rate data analysis by distributor type, complaint investigation results, escalations to regulators.
  • Compliance register and audit tracking: biennial external audit status, quarterly reporting to Steering Committee.

Escalation Path: Unresolved compliance gaps or failed Article 101 guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12) escalate to the Commission Transport Commissioner and DG COMP for resolution; if unresolved by Month 18 (2028-04-12), binding standards are deferred. Material discrimination findings or national-regulator conflicts unresolved by Month 12 (2027-10-12) escalate to the Steering Committee; the Committee decides whether to defer that Member State or require programme redesign. Any compliance gap that would block a Steering Committee milestone decision (binding standards, API exposure, corridor go-live) is escalated to the Committee with a recommended remediation plan within five business days. Passenger-rights gaps discovered post-deployment (after Month 30 = 2029-04-12) escalate immediately to the Commission and the EU Agency for Railways for emergency remediation and passenger notification.

4. Technical Standards and Interoperability Working Group (TSWG)

Rationale for Inclusion: The programme depends on binding technical standards (OSDM-compatible APIs, real-time data formats, clearing settlement feeds, ticket validation credentials) by Month 18 (2028-04-12) and mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-12). The TSWG must own specification development, conformance test design, reference implementation, carrier-integration support and change-control governance. This is a specialized operational and advisory body that reports to the Operational Management Board and the Steering Committee. Unlike the Steering Committee (which makes binding strategic decisions on liability and clearing architectures), the TSWG makes technical decisions on how those architectures are specified, tested and evolved. Without a dedicated technical body with clear authority over standards and conformance, the programme risks specification drift, inconsistent testing, and missed binding-standards deadlines.

Responsibilities:

  • Develop and publish the binding OSDM specification: establish a formal change-control process (critical: 2-week review, major: 6-week review, minor: 8-week review) and quarterly release cadence; anchor specification custodianship in the EU Agency for Railways with an escrowed open-source copy; pin the version via delegated or implementing act by Month 18 (2028-04-12).
  • Design and operate conformance testing: develop test cases for OSDM API compliance, latency (p95 <2 seconds), availability (99.5%), stale-seat failures (<1%), booking-error rates; establish independent test laboratories; conduct conformance audits for all carriers by Months 24, 30, 36, 42 (2028-10-12, 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12); publish certification results on a public registry.
  • Maintain and evolve the reference implementation: develop a reference OSDM implementation as a sandbox and technical benchmark; publish it under open-source terms; use it to validate carrier integrations and test distributor client implementations; make it available to carriers for testing by Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • Coordinate carrier-integration support: chair technical working sessions with carrier integration teams monthly; provide guidance on OSDM adoption, API design patterns, and legacy system adaptation; identify common adapter bottlenecks and escalate to the Programme Office for shared-adapter development.
  • Define and enforce SLA thresholds: establish and publish SLA targets for API latency, availability, error rates, and settlement-reconciliation accuracy; monitor monthly SLA scorecards; recommend funding-tranche withholding for carriers missing SLAs for two consecutive months.
  • Specify ticket validation and credential formats: define the API handshake, barcode, or cryptographic token format for cross-carrier ticket validation; coordinate with conductor handheld and station-gate system upgrades; ensure validation works offline and across all participating carriers by Month 40 (2030-02-12).
  • Coordinate disruption and real-time data specs: develop specifications for the shared disruption event feed, availability shadow architecture, and settlement data formats; ensure all are compatible with carrier billing systems and independent distributor platforms.
  • Support accessibility and bicycle-reservation integration: work with disability-rights bodies to specify assistance and bicycle-space reservation schemas; ensure these are auditable and cannot be bypassed; validate via usability testing by Month 18 (2028-04-12).

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish the Working Group and appoint Chair (senior OSDM expert) by Month 1 (2026-11-12).
  • Publish the formal OSDM change-control process and quarterly release schedule by Month 3 (2027-01-12).
  • Develop conformance test cases for OSDM API, latency, availability, error rates by Month 6 (2027-04-12); release test environments to carriers by Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • Commission or develop a reference OSDM implementation (sandbox) by Month 9 (2027-07-12); publish under open-source licence by Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • Establish public conformance-certification registry by Month 12 (2027-10-12); publish first carrier audit results by Month 24 (2028-10-12).
  • Coordinate with carrier integration teams to identify and resolve common technical bottlenecks by Month 12 (2027-10-12); recommend shared-adapter development for legacy systems by Month 3 (2027-01-12).

Membership:

  • Chair: Senior OSDM or rail-API technical expert (appointed by Month 1 = 2026-11-12), from the Technical Secretariat or external contractor
  • OSDM specification custodian (EU Agency for Railways or delegated external body)
  • Head of Conformance Testing (independent test laboratory or Programme Office)
  • Representative from carrier IT (rotating among Tier 1 carriers: DB, SNCF, SBB, ÖBB, Renfe)
  • Representative from independent distributor IT (Trainline or Omio)
  • Reference-implementation lead (open-source steward or Programme Office)
  • Accessibility specialist (disability-rights body or accessibility consultant) (non-voting observer)
  • EU Agency for Railways technical liaison (regulatory perspective)
