Decision Rights: Authority to approve OSDM specifications and versions for binding-standards release by Month 18 (2028-04-12). Authority to set and enforce conformance test cases, SLA thresholds (latency, availability, error rates) and certification requirements. Authority to approve or reject carrier conformance certifications; recommend to the Steering Committee funding-tranche withholding for non-certified carriers. Authority to make technical decisions on specification content (e.g., which OSDM fields are mandatory, how settlement data is formatted) without Steering Committee approval, provided they align with strategic decisions already made (liability model, clearing architecture). Authority to approve change requests to the pinned OSDM specification post-Month 18 (2028-04-12) within the formal change-control process. Decisions on conformance test design, test-case severity, and certification remediation timelines are made by simple majority; SLA threshold changes require Steering Committee approval if they affect milestone or budget assumptions.

Decision Mechanism: Consensus preferred on technical specifications to ensure carrier and distributor buy-in; if consensus is not reached within 15 business days, the Chair makes the decision, with documented dissent and escalation to the Operational Management Board within five business days. Conformance certification decisions require unanimous sign-off by the Chair and the independent test-laboratory representative to ensure impartiality. SLA threshold decisions require Steering Committee approval if they change targets or enforcement mechanisms; routine monitoring and reporting are delegated to the Chair without approval.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly during Phase 1 (Months 1-18 = 2026-11-12 to 2028-04-12) to develop specifications and test cases; biweekly during Phase 2 (Months 18-48 = 2028-04-12 to 2030-10-12) to oversee conformance audits and carrier integrations; monthly during Phase 3 (Months 48-60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) for post-go-live specification evolution. Emergency sessions within two business days if a conformance audit fails or a critical specification gap is discovered that affects binding-standards release.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • OSDM specification drafting and change-request review (Months 1-18 = 2026-11-12 to 2028-04-12).
  • Conformance test-case design and validation (Months 3-12 = 2027-01-12 to 2027-10-12).
  • Carrier integration support: common bottlenecks, adapter guidance, legacy-system compatibility.
  • SLA monitoring: monthly latency/availability/error-rate scorecards by carrier, remediation tracking.
  • Reference implementation development and validation (Months 6-18 = 2027-04-12 to 2028-04-12).
  • Accessibility and bicycle-reservation schema design and usability testing (Months 6-18 = 2027-04-12 to 2028-04-12).
  • Disruption event feed and settlement data-format specifications.
  • Ticket-validation credential design and cross-carrier acceptance testing (Months 12-40 = 2027-10-12 to 2030-02-12).

Escalation Path: Unresolved specification disputes (e.g., carrier disagreement on a mandatory OSDM field) that block progress toward Month 18 (2028-04-12) escalate to the Operational Management Board within ten business days; if unresolved by the OMB, they escalate to the Steering Committee for binding decision. Conformance failures affecting ≥5 carriers or ≥1 Tier 1 corridor-critical carrier escalate to the Operational Management Board for remediation planning; if a carrier cannot remediate by their tier deadline (Month 30/36/42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12), the OMB recommends deferral of that carrier to a later tier or programme phase. Specification changes post-Month 18 (2028-04-12) that affect binding-standards commitments or require carrier rework escalate to the Steering Committee for approval. SLA threshold violations affecting >20% of carriers or delaying corridor go-live escalate to the OMB and Steering Committee within five business days.

Governance Implementation Plan

1. Project Sponsor (DG MOVE Director or Transport Commissioner) formally initiates the programme and designates a senior DG MOVE official as Interim Programme Director to lead pre-governance setup activities. Interim Director is responsible for establishing the governance framework, engaging stakeholders, and preparing for formal Committee establishment.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor / DG MOVE Director

Suggested Timeframe: Project Week 0-1 (by Month 0.2 = 2026-10-18)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Programme Initiation Memo signed by Project Sponsor
  • Interim Programme Director appointed and briefed
  • High-level stakeholder contact list and engagement calendar established

Dependencies:

  • Project start date confirmed
  • Budget allocation (EUR 1.5B) formally approved by the Commission

2. Interim Programme Director drafts the charter, membership, voting rules, and meeting schedule for the Programme Steering Committee (PSC). The charter must specify 75% supermajority voting for Decisions 1–5, escalation paths to the Commission Transport Commissioner, and monthly biweekly cadence. Draft charter is circulated to identified steering members for consultation.

Responsible Body/Role: Interim Programme Director (DG MOVE)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0.3-1 (October–November 2026)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Draft PSC Charter v0.1 (roles, voting, escalation, meeting schedule)
  • Membership roster and stakeholder contact details
  • Consultation feedback summary

Dependencies:

  • Interim Programme Director appointed
  • Stakeholder list and preliminary engagement complete

3. Project Sponsor formally approves the PSC Charter and appoints the Chair (DG MOVE Director or Transport Commissioner designate) and Vice-Chair (EU Agency for Railways Director). Appointment letters are issued by Month 1 (2026-11-12); both assume office immediately.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor / DG MOVE Director

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-12)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • PSC Charter (approved, published version)
  • Chair Appointment Letter
  • Vice-Chair Appointment Letter

Dependencies:

  • Draft Charter consulted and finalized
  • Project Sponsor and Transport Commissioner alignment secured

4. Chair (DG MOVE) and Vice-Chair (Agency) jointly circulate binding commitment letters to the nine core PSC members (CER, three–four major carriers, Trainline, Omio, BEUC, disability-rights body, and one regulator observer) requesting formal acceptance of their seat, voting responsibility, and biweekly attendance by Month 2 (2026-12-12).

Responsible Body/Role: PSC Chair and Vice-Chair

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1.2-1.5 (mid-November 2026)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Formal invitation letters to nine core members
  • Binding commitment letters from each member (confirming attendance, voting authority, confidentiality)
  • Signed Member Roster

Dependencies:

  • PSC Charter approved and published
  • Chair and Vice-Chair in office

5. Chair and Vice-Chair confirm all nine core members have signed binding commitment letters and are formally appointed to the PSC by Month 2 (2026-12-12). A kick-off briefing is scheduled for Month 1.5 (2026-11-27) to introduce the Charter, voting procedures, critical decision timeline and escalation paths.

Responsible Body/Role: PSC Chair

Suggested Timeframe: Month 2 (2026-12-12)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Confirmed Member Roster (all nine signatures)
  • PSC Formally Established Memo
  • Kick-off Meeting Minutes and attendee list

Dependencies:

  • Commitment letters from all nine core members
  • Charter approved

6. Interim Programme Director commissions a detailed technical audit of all 25+ participating carriers' booking-system architectures, assessing OSDM API readiness, event-streaming capability, transaction consistency, latency and availability benchmarks. Audit is contracted to an independent systems integrator and is scheduled for completion by Month 2 (2026-12-12).

Responsible Body/Role: Interim Programme Director / Programme Office (once established)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0.5-2 (October 2026–December 2026)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • RFP issued for technical audit
  • Audit contract awarded
  • Technical Audit Report: summary of each carrier's API readiness, legacy-system constraints, estimated integration timeline per tier

Dependencies:

  • Interim Programme Director in place
  • Carrier contact list and preliminary engagement complete
  • Budget headroom identified for audit cost

7. Interim Programme Director commissions an independent actuarial firm to model missed-connection rates, rerouting costs, incident clustering and liability-pool sustainability. The study is to establish per-incident caps, co-insurance thresholds and contribution-weighting formulas tied to on-time performance. Interim findings due Month 3 (2027-01-12); final report due Month 6 (2027-04-12).

Responsible Body/Role: Interim Programme Director / Programme Office

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1-3 (November 2026–January 2027)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • RFP issued for actuarial study
  • Actuarial contract awarded
  • Interim Actuarial Report (Month 3 = 2027-01-12): draft liability model, indicative cap and co-insurance thresholds
  • Final Actuarial Report (Month 6 = 2027-04-12): validated model with confidence intervals

Dependencies:

  • Budget allocated for actuarial study
  • Interim Programme Director appointed

8. Interim Programme Director initiates formal pre-notification with DG COMP (Competition Directorate) outlining the programme's data-sharing and clearing arrangements, requesting Article 101 TFEU guidance. A detailed legal brief is submitted to DG COMP, including the proposed federated clearing architecture, shared data layer and non-discriminatory distributor-access rules.

Responsible Body/Role: Interim Programme Director / Compliance Lead (engaged as external counsel or DG MOVE legal service)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 2 (2026-12-12)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Legal brief to DG COMP (pre-notification package)
  • Formal request for Article 101 guidance letter
  • Confirmation of receipt from DG COMP

Dependencies:

  • Clearing and data-sharing architecture decisions made (from scenario inputs)
  • Legal counsel engaged

9. Interim Programme Director commissions an independent legal firm to conduct a detailed review of the Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop design against EU Regulation 1371/2007 (existing rail passenger-rights law). The review assesses whether the proposed guarantee pool and liability model ensure that through-ticket passengers retain or exceed existing passenger-rights protections. Opinion due Month 6 (2027-04-12).

Responsible Body/Role: Interim Programme Director / Compliance Lead

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1-6 (November 2026–April 2027)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • RFP issued for passenger-rights legal review
  • Legal review contract awarded
  • Passenger-Rights Legal Opinion (Month 6 = 2027-04-12): assessment of compliance with Regulation 1371/2007, identified gaps, remediation recommendations

Dependencies:

  • Liability model design clarified (from scenario inputs)
  • Independent legal counsel engaged

10. Interim Programme Director, with the EU Agency for Railways, commences bilateral regulatory-impact assessments with each participating member state (approximately 5–6 member states, 25+ operators). Each assessment documents national railway regulations, antitrust rules, data-protection requirements and any conflicts with the programme's design. Assessments are completed by Month 3 (2027-01-12).

Responsible Body/Role: Interim Programme Director and EU Agency for Railways

Suggested Timeframe: Month 2-3 (December 2026–January 2027)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

PSC holds a critical binding-vote meeting at Month 6 (2027-04-12) to approve Decisions 1–5 (Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop, Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement, Public Reference Distributor Mandate, Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder, Availability Query Topology). If a vote falls below 75%, the issue is escalated to the Commission Transport Commissioner with a mediation request by Month 5 (2027-03-12), and mediation is completed by Month 6 (2027-04-12) or a fallback governance path is invoked. Technical Secretariat Head, in coordination with TSWG, begins drafting the binding OSDM specification covering: (1) API definitions for availability queries, booking, settlement, disruption and ticket validation; (2) real-time data formats for the streamed availability shadow; (3) settlement data-feed standards (reconciliation format, currency, timing); (4) assistance and bicycle-space reservation schemas; (5) ticket-validation credential or token formats. Draft specification is published by Month 9 (2027-07-12) for carrier and distributor review; public consultation period runs Months 9–12 (2027-07-12 to 2027-10-12); final specification approved by TSWG by Month 12 (2027-10-12).

38. CCPR Chair tracks DG COMP's Article 101 guidance-letter process. DG COMP pre-notification was filed at Month 2 (2026-12-12). Formal guidance letter is expected by Month 12 (2027-10-12). If guidance is not received on schedule, CCPR issues a compliance warning to the PSC by Month 12 (2027-10-12). Regardless, the CCPR establishes a clean-team protocol for the clearing function (physically and logically separating the clearing team from carriers and distributors, releasing only aggregated settlement data) by Month 14 (2027-12-12), to ensure that clearing operations are protected from competition-law challenges even if formal guidance is delayed beyond Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards deadline.

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • PSC approval of TEN-T scope and sequencing (Month 42 = 2030-04-12 or Month 45 = 2030-07-12)
  • TEN-T Funding Release Framework (conditions, tranches, monitoring)

Dependencies:

  • Four-corridor go-live completed (Month 48 = 2030-10-12)
  • Budget headroom and reserve status known (quarterly variance reports)
  • Tier 2/3 outcomes inform network expansion viability

63. OMB and Head of Distributor and Consumer Affairs establish a competitive call or direct-engagement process for additional carriers and corridors in the TEN-T extension wave (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12). Using milestone-conditioned funding (the pragmatic scenario), TEN-T funding is released in tranches tied to verified API exposure, conformance certification and through-ticket volume milestones. New corridor onboarding follows the Tier-assignment process: rapid-track for carriers already conformant (Tier 1/2 ready by Months 48–54 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-04-12), standard-track for new entrants (Months 54–60 = 2031-04-12 to 2031-10-12). By Month 60 (2031-10-12), the target is full TEN-T coverage and 40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets.

Responsible Body/Role: Programme Director and Head of Distributor and Consumer Affairs

Suggested Timeframe: Month 48-60 (October 2030–October 2031)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • TEN-T Extension Call or Direct-Engagement RFP
  • New Carrier Onboarding (conformance audits, rapid-track vs. standard-track assignment)
  • Corridor Launch Schedule (TEN-T corridors brought live by Month 60 = 2031-10-12)
  • Final Through-Ticket Market Penetration Report (Month 60 = 2031-10-12): share of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets, progress toward 40% target

Dependencies:

  • Four-corridor go-live successful (Month 48 = 2030-10-12)
  • TEN-T extension plan approved (Month 42-48 = 2030-04-12 to 2030-10-12)
  • Funding tranches released (approved by PSC quarterly variance tracking)

64. OMB commissions a final post-programme evaluation at Month 60 (2031-10-12) assessing: (1) achievement of the 40% through-ticket goal (or identified shortfall); (2) distributor complaints halved (baseline from Month 1 = 2026-11-12); (3) modal shift from short-haul air to rail (conservative 5–10% planning value estimate, not a success metric but reported); (4) accessibility compliance for assistance and bicycle reservations; (5) financial performance (total spend vs. EUR 1,500M budget, concession subsidy draw, clawback conditions); (6) regulatory and competition-law compliance; (7) passenger and carrier satisfaction. Findings are documented in the Final Evaluation Report; recommendations for programme sustaining (beyond Month 60 = 2031-10-12) are developed. The report is submitted to the Commission, the Court of Auditors and the European Parliament.

Responsible Body/Role: Programme Director and independent evaluation firm

Suggested Timeframe: Month 60 (2031-10-12)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Final Evaluation Report (Month 60 = 2031-10-12): goal achievement, lessons learned, recommendations for sustaining
  • Submission to Commission, Court of Auditors and European Parliament

Dependencies:

  • TEN-T extension completed or decisioned (Month 60 = 2031-10-12)
  • Four-corridor and priority TEN-T corridors live for minimum 6–12 months (data available)
  • Financial and operational data collected throughout Months 0–60 (2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12)

65. PSC Chair convenes a final PSC meeting at Month 60 (2031-10-12) to formally close the programme governance (Phase 1, 2, 3: Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12) or transition to a sustaining governance phase (if the programme continues managing network expansion or ongoing compliance beyond Month 60 = 2031-10-12). The PSC reviews final evaluation findings, confirms the through-ticket goal status, and decides on: (1) dissolution of the Programme Office and Technical Secretariat (or transition to a smaller sustained-governance body under the EU Agency for Railways); (2) handover of OSDM custodianship and change control to the Agency (if not already formalized); (3) ongoing funding for network sustaining, passenger-rights monitoring and accessibility compliance; (4) any residual budget (if unspent headroom remains, disposition is decided). The closing decision is documented in a PSC Final Report, published to the Commission and member states.

Responsible Body/Role: PSC Chair and Programme Director

Suggested Timeframe: Month 60 (2031-10-12)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • PSC Final Meeting Agenda and briefing materials
  • PSC Final Report (programme closure or transition, recommendations, final votes)
  • PSC Meeting Minutes
  • Notification to all stakeholders of programme governance transition

Dependencies:

  • Final evaluation completed (Month 60 = 2031-10-12)
  • Four-corridor through-ticketing confirmed as sustainable (at least 6 months operating experience)
  • Financial closure and audit complete

Decision Escalation Matrix

Carrier Refusal to Expose Inventory Due to Unpriceable Liability Escalation Level: Programme Steering Committee (PSC) Approval Process: Supermajority vote (75%, at least 7 of 9 core members) on a revised liability-backstop design or risk-sharing mechanism. Commission Transport Commissioner mediates if vote deadlocks. Decision enforced by conditional funding release: carriers refusing participation lose funding-tranche eligibility. Rationale: Inability to price connection liability is a critical carrier-participation blocker that threatens network coverage. This exceeds the Operational Management Board's authority to remediate and risks the binding-standards milestone (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) if 30%+ of expected carriers refuse. The PSC's access to the actuarial study, liability model and carrier sign-offs enables fact-based negotiation and binding revision. Negative Consequences: If unresolved by Month 6 (2027-04-12), the through-ticket goal drops from 40% to 15–25% (estimate), critical corridors become fragmented, and the mandatory API exposure milestone (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) slips to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12). Estimated cost: EUR 100–150M in lost programme value and budget reallocation.

Legacy Booking-System Integration Failure Preventing Tier Conformance by Scheduled Deadline Escalation Level: Operational Management Board (OMB) with escalation to PSC if affecting >5 carriers or a corridor-critical carrier Approval Process: OMB approves per-carrier remediation: accelerated adapter funding, extended conformance timeline (deferral to next tier), or exclusion from that wave. If remediation costs exceed EUR 50M or delays affect the Month 30 (2029-04-12) API exposure milestone, escalation to PSC for variance and TEN-T extension planning approval. PSC decides whether to absorb cost overrun (triggering variance triggers: EUR 100M, EUR 200M, EUR 300M) or restrict to fewer carriers. Rationale: Technical integration challenges are the OMB's operational domain, but when deferral or exclusion affects network connectivity, programme schedule or budget headroom, the PSC's strategic authority is required. A single deferred corridor-critical carrier (e.g., on Wien–München–Zürich) can block that corridor's go-live. Negative Consequences: If 8–15 smaller carriers miss Month 30 (2029-04-12), the four-corridor through-ticketing target (Month 48 = 2030-10-12) extends to Month 60–66 (2031-10-12 to 2032-04-12). Budget impact: EUR 150–250M (estimate) in adapter acceleration or EUR 200–300M in unused budget if later corridors cannot launch. Network coverage shrinks from 25+ to ~15 carriers, reducing through-ticket share from 40% to 20–25% (estimate).

Budget Variance Exceeding a Trigger Threshold (EUR 100M, EUR 200M, or EUR 300M cumulative) Escalation Level: Programme Steering Committee (PSC), with prior OMB investigation and recommendation Approval Process: OMB investigates variance root cause and proposes mitigation (scale TEN-T extension scope, extend concession term, accelerate cost recovery, or reduce budget commitments). PSC votes on mitigation by simple majority (5 of 9 members). Approved mitigation is published to the Commission and the Court of Auditors within 10 business days. If mitigation is rejected, variance handling escalates to the Commission's Financial Controller. Rationale: Budget variance triggers represent policy thresholds where the fixed EUR 1,500M cap (user constraint) is at risk. The OMB tracks variances quarterly, but exceeding a trigger threshold requires strategic decisions (e.g., deferring TEN-T, cutting concession funding, or restricting corridors) that only the PSC can approve without Commission intervention. Negative Consequences: EUR 100M variance: TEN-T extension deferred from Month 60 (2031-10-12) to Month 72 (2032-10-12), reducing final through-ticket penetration to 25–30%. EUR 200M variance: concession funding cut 20% and term extended 5–7 years, risking service quality and volumes. EUR 300M variance: programme restricted to four priority corridors only, abandoning TEN-T expansion and setting final through-ticket goal at 15–20% (estimate). Any variance exceeding EUR 300M exhausts the public budget.

DG COMP Article 101 Guidance Not Obtained or Unfavorably Resolved, Threatening Competition-Law Clearance Escalation Level: Compliance, Competition Law and Passenger Rights Committee (CCPR), with escalation to PSC and Commission Transport Commissioner if unresolved by Month 12 (2027-10-12) Approval Process: CCPR monitors DG COMP engagement and guidance-letter status monthly. If guidance is not received by Month 12 (2027-10-12), CCPR issues a compliance warning to PSC. If guidance raises concerns (e.g., about shared data or clearing arrangements), CCPR recommends design modifications (clean-team protocol, data firewalls, restricted access) by Month 14 (2027-12-12). PSC approves remediation or escalates to the Commission Transport Commissioner and DG COMP legal service for dispute resolution by Month 18 (2028-04-12). Rationale: Competition-law clearance is a Compliance Committee responsibility, but unresolved conflicts block binding-standards approval (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) and require Commission-level intervention. The PSC and Commission cannot finalize standards without confirmation that the clearing and data-sharing designs are compatible with Article 101 TFEU. Negative Consequences: If DG COMP guidance is unfavorable or delayed beyond Month 18 (2028-04-12), the binding-standards milestone is deferred 3–6 months, cascading to Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12) and the API exposure deadline to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12). Estimated rework cost: EUR 50–100M and 6–12 months technical redesign. If a challenge post-deployment (after Month 30 = 2029-04-12) unwinds the clearing or data-sharing arrangements, carriers must revert to bilateral settlement, adding 3–4 months to settlement cycle times and increasing booking-error rates 15–25%, eroding through-ticket value.

Passenger-Rights Compliance Gap Identified in Legal Review Against Regulation 1371/2007 Escalation Level: Compliance, Competition Law and Passenger Rights Committee (CCPR), with escalation to PSC and EU Agency for Railways if remediation requires specification changes Approval Process: CCPR commissions independent legal review (due Month 6 = 2027-04-12). If gaps are identified, CCPR recommends remediation actions (revised liability model, enhanced compensation procedures, improved accessibility thresholds). If remediation requires changes to the OSDM specification or operational manual, CCPR escalates to the Technical Standards and Interoperability Working Group (TSWG) and OMB for integration by Month 9 (2027-07-12). PSC approves any material changes affecting binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12). Rationale: Passenger-rights compliance is a statutory and reputational risk. The CCPR has specialized legal expertise, but through-ticket passengers and disability-rights bodies cannot accept rights inferior to existing rail regulations. If compliance gaps are discovered post-binding-standards, the programme faces enforcement action from national regulators and the EU Agency for Railways. Negative Consequences: If material gaps are found (e.g., liability allocation leaves through-ticket passengers without compensation for missed connections), remediation requires 3–6 months of legal and technical rework. Estimated cost: EUR 10–20M. If gaps are discovered post-deployment (after Month 30 = 2029-04-12), the programme faces passenger complaints, regulatory enforcement, legal challenges and reputational damage. Estimated cost: EUR 20–50M in compensation claims and remediation.

Steering Committee Deadlock on Critical Strategic Decision (Decisions 1–5) Due to Carrier, Distributor or Regulator Disagreement Escalation Level: Commission Transport Commissioner, with mediation and binding decision authority Approval Process: If a PSC vote on Decisions 1–5 falls below 75% supermajority (fewer than 7 of 9 core members voting in favor), the Chair (DG MOVE) files an escalation brief to the Commission Transport Commissioner by Month 5 (2027-03-12). The Commissioner convenes a mediation session with dissenting stakeholders by Month 6 (2027-04-12). If consensus cannot be reached, the Commissioner issues a binding decision (authorizing a fallback technical interface for distributors, revised liability allocations, or phased funding release) by Month 6 (2027-04-12). Alternatively, if the deadlock cannot be resolved, a fallback governance path is invoked (e.g., bilateral clearing for independent distributors, tiered conformance with mixed gates). Rationale: The PSC is designed to achieve consensus, but supplier and commercial conflicts can create deadlocks that delay binding standards (target Month 18 = 2028-04-12). The Commission's Transport Commissioner has the political and institutional authority to break deadlocks and enforce compliance. If the PSC cannot approve Decisions 1–5 by Month 6 (2027-04-12), the binding-standards schedule is at risk. Negative Consequences: If deadlock persists beyond Month 9 (2027-07-12), binding standards are deferred from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12) (estimated 2–4 month slip). This cascades to API exposure (Month 30 = 2029-04-12 → Month 36 = 2029-10-12) and corridor go-live (Month 48 = 2030-10-12 → Month 54–60 = 2031-04-12 to 2031-10-12). If a major distributor (e.g., Trainline, Omio) rejects a decision and withdraws, through-ticket volume drops 15–25%, reducing the 40% goal to 20–30%.

Monitoring Progress

1. Tracking Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) Against Project Plan

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Programme Office KPI Dashboard (shared spreadsheet or BI tool)
  • Quarterly Financial Variance Report (EUR 1,500M budget tracking)
  • Monthly SLA Scorecard (latency, availability, error rates by carrier)
  • Through-Ticket Volume and Penetration Report (trending toward 40% target)

Frequency: Monthly KPI and SLA tracking; quarterly financial reports; monthly variance trending against EUR 100M, EUR 200M, EUR 300M triggers

Responsible Role: Operational Management Board (OMB), with Programme Director and Financial Planning Lead executing daily tracking and escalating variances

Adaptation Process: KPI shortfalls (e.g., latency >2s p95, availability <99.5%, stale-seat failures >1%) trigger remediation discussions in the OMB; carriers missing SLAs for two consecutive months lose 5% of next funding tranche. Through-ticket volume lagging 40% target by Month 36 (2029-10-12) mid-programme review triggers course corrections (e.g., accelerated TEN-T sequencing, distributor engagement intensification). Financial variance reaching EUR 100M/EUR 200M/EUR 300M triggers PSC policy adjustment (e.g., TEN-T scope reduction, concession subsidy reallocation).

Adaptation Trigger: SLA deviation (latency/availability/error) on a single carrier for two consecutive months; financial variance cumulative spend exceeds EUR 100M, EUR 200M or EUR 300M thresholds; through-ticket penetration tracking >15% below linear ramp-to-40% by Month 36 (2029-10-12); concessionaire operating costs exceed budget by >15% in any quarter

2. Milestone and Conformance Gate Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Conformance-Certification Registry (public, per-carrier, updated monthly from Month 24 = 2028-10-12 onwards)
  • Technical Audit Report and Tier Assignment Schedule (Month 2 = 2026-12-12 baseline, per-carrier timeline)
  • OSDM Binding Specification and Change-Request Dashboard (versions, approvals, backlog)
  • Conformance Test Results and Audit Reports (Tier 1 Months 24–30 = 2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12; Tier 2 Months 30–36 = 2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12; Tier 3 Months 36–42 = 2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12)

Frequency: Weekly during Phase 1 (Months 0–18 = 2026-10-12 to 2028-04-12) standards development and readiness-gate prep; monthly conformance audits (Months 24–42 = 2028-10-12 to 2030-04-12); corridor go-live readiness assessments at Month 42 (2030-04-12), Month 45 (2030-07-12)

Responsible Role: Technical Standards and Interoperability Working Group (TSWG) Chair and Head of Standards and Conformance for specification and conformance audits; Operational Management Board for milestone tracking and carrier tier remediation decisions

Adaptation Process: Carriers failing conformance audits (latency, availability, stale-seat failure thresholds) are assigned remediation tasks: retest, accelerated adapter funding, or deferral to next tier. Tier deferral (e.g., Tier 1 carrier → Tier 2, or Tier 2 → Tier 3) is documented with revised conformance deadline. If a corridor-critical carrier (e.g., on Wien–München–Zürich corridor) fails by its tier deadline, corridor go-live is deferred or that carrier is replaced by a backup (if available). OSDM specification change requests are processed via the published change-control process (critical: 2 weeks, major: 6 weeks, minor: 8 weeks); changes requiring carrier rework are flagged to OMB for impact assessment.

Adaptation Trigger: Carrier fails conformance audit on latency p95 >2 seconds, availability <99.5%, stale-seat failures >1%; two consecutive months of SLA misses trigger funding-tranche withholding; >5 carriers or a Tier 1 corridor-critical carrier deferred from their tier deadline by >2 months; OSDM specification change request flagged as affecting binding-standards commitments or requiring >4 weeks carrier rework; >20% of corridor rolling stock or stations non-compliant with ticket-validation deployment by Month 40 (2030-02-12) audit

3. Carrier Participation and Liability Backstop Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Carrier Sign-Off Register (liability model acceptance, on-time performance data submission)
  • Guarantee Pool Contribution Model and Incident Tracking Log (monthly pool draw, contributions by carrier, incident rates)
  • Carrier Bilateral Engagement Log (briefings, concerns, contract commitments)
  • Missed-Connection and Reroute Performance Baseline (pilot data Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12; live data post-Month 30 = 2029-04-12)

Frequency: Biweekly carrier bilateral briefings Months 2–6 (2026-12-12 to 2027-04-12) during liability model negotiation; monthly carrier sign-off status tracking (liability model, technical integration); monthly pool-contribution and incident-rate monitoring post-Month 30 (2029-04-12)

Responsible Role: Head of Carrier Engagement (Programme Office) for bilateral engagement and sign-off tracking; Head of Clearing and Settlement for pool contribution and reconciliation monitoring; OMB for escalation of carrier participation risks

Adaptation Process: If a major carrier (>5% of network) signals intent to refuse inventory exposure due to liability concerns, Head of Carrier Engagement escalates to OMB within five business days with remediation options: revised cap/co-insurance formula, additional insurance subsidy, or re-mediation with Commission Transport Commissioner via PSC. If carrier signs off on liability model by Month 4 (2027-02-12), commitment is binding; failure to expose inventory by their tier deadline results in funding-tranche withholding and potential exclusion. Post-deployment, if pool contribution methodology results in systematically higher costs for one carrier (indicating disproportionate incident rates), actuarial study is refreshed (Month 36 = 2029-10-12 or Month 48 = 2030-10-12) to adjust contribution weights and signal operational performance issues for remediation.

Adaptation Trigger: A major carrier (>5% of network) declines to sign liability model by Month 4 (2027-02-12); carrier signals publicly or privately that it will not expose inventory by its tier deadline; carrier participation drops below 20 operators (down from 25+ target) before binding standards Month 18 (2028-04-12); missed-connection incident rate on a carrier exceeds 2% of through-tickets post-Month 30 (2029-04-12) triggering pool contributions >EUR 1M/month; carrier pool contribution estimated to exceed carrier's forecast margin, signaling refusal to renew participation beyond initial phase

4. Regulation Adoption and Competition-Law Compliance Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Regulation Adoption Status Tracker (Commission legislative-affairs updates, expected adoption date)
  • DG COMP Engagement Log and Guidance-Letter Timeline (pre-notification sent Month 2 = 2026-12-12; guidance expected Month 12 = 2027-10-12)
  • Compliance Certifications Register (Article 101 guidance letter, passenger-rights legal opinion, GDPR assessment, accessibility compliance)
  • Clean-Team Protocol Approval and Clearing-Function Audit Trail (segregation of clearing operations, aggregated data release, competitive safeguards)

Frequency: Monthly during Phase 1 (Months 0–18 = 2026-10-12 to 2028-04-12) for Regulation adoption and DG COMP guidance tracking; quarterly compliance audits post-Month 18 (2028-04-12); biennial independent audit of clearing and data-sharing compliance post-Month 30 (2029-04-12)

Responsible Role: Compliance, Competition Law and Passenger Rights Committee (CCPR) Chair for monitoring and escalation; Head of Compliance and Risk (Programme Office) for day-to-day tracking; DG MOVE and DG COMP liaison for legislative and competition-law status updates

Adaptation Process: If Regulation adoption is delayed beyond Month 18 (2028-04-12) (e.g., no Official Journal publication), CCPR issues a warning to PSC by Month 16 (2028-02-12); standards-working group shifts to a shadow workstream with provisional compliance assumptions, and binding-standards approval is deferred to Month 24 (2028-10-12) or Month 30 (2029-04-12) pending Regulation publication. If DG COMP guidance letter is delayed beyond Month 12 (2027-10-12), CCPR escalates to PSC by Month 12 (2027-10-12); a provisional clean-team protocol is established by Month 14 (2027-12-12) to protect clearing operations even if formal guidance is pending. If DG COMP guidance raises unforeseen Article 101 concerns, CCPR recommends design modifications (data firewalls, restricted carrier access, independent trustee oversight) by Month 14 (2027-12-12); OMB and TSWG assess implementation burden; PSC votes on remediation by Month 18 (2028-04-12).

Adaptation Trigger: Regulation adoption delayed >6 months beyond Month 18 (2028-04-12) target; DG COMP guidance letter not received or is unfavorably conditional by Month 12 (2027-10-12); passenger-rights legal opinion identifies material gaps vs. Regulation 1371/2007 by Month 6 (2027-04-12); GDPR or data-governance assessment flags compliance risks in clearing or disruption-feed design by Month 6 (2027-04-12); accessibility compliance audit finds >20% of services unable to meet assistance or wheelchair-access thresholds by Month 40 (2030-02-12)

5. Distributor Participation and Commission-Rate Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Distributor Engagement and Commitment Log (Trainline, Omio, concessionaire, smaller platforms)
  • Published Commission-Rate Data (monthly by distributor type and corridor, audited for discrimination)
  • Distributor Complaint and Discrimination Log (filed with Programme Office, escalated to regulators if unresolved)
  • Through-Ticket Sales Attribution by Distributor (volume share, growth trajectory, concessionaire performance vs. private platforms)

Frequency: Biweekly distributor briefings Months 2–6 (2026-12-12 to 2027-04-12) during commission-band negotiation; monthly commission-rate publication and discrimination audit post-Month 12 (2027-10-12); quarterly through-ticket sales reporting by distributor post-Month 30 (2029-04-12)

Responsible Role: Head of Distributor and Consumer Affairs (Programme Office) for bilateral engagement and sales tracking; CCPR for discrimination audits and regulatory escalations; concessionaire (contract oversight) for last-resort service performance

Adaptation Process: If Trainline, Omio or another major distributor declines to integrate with the clearing and settlement layer, Head of Distributor and Consumer Affairs negotiates a fallback technical interface (third-party settlement intermediary, alternative reconciliation format) within two weeks; if rejected, Programme Office documents the withdrawal and estimates impact on through-ticket volumes. If commission-rate data shows systemic discrimination (e.g., concessionaire charged 1.0% vs. private platforms charged 3.5%), CCPR launches a discrimination investigation; if findings confirm bias, concession contract is reviewed and rates are adjusted retroactively or the concession is opened to competitive re-tender. If a distributor's through-ticket volumes lag forecast by >30%, OMB reviews distributor engagement strategy and may reallocate funding or support to accelerate platform integration or marketing.

Adaptation Trigger: A major distributor (Trainline, Omio) announces non-participation or delayed integration by Month 12 (2027-10-12); published commission rates show >1.5% dispersion between distributor types (indicating potential discrimination); through-ticket sales attributed to distributors fall >20% below forecast by Month 36 (2029-10-12); concessionaire operating subsidy draw exceeds EUR 15M/year (triggering subsidy-cap review); discriminatory commission-rate complaint filed by a distributor, unresolved after 30 days

6. Operational Readiness and Passenger-Experience Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Live-Pilot Report (500–1,000 passengers per corridor, Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12)
  • Disruption Re-accommodation Performance Dashboard (response time to missed connections, reroute success rate, passenger satisfaction, post-Month 12 = 2027-10-12 pilots)
  • Ticket-Validation Deployment Audit and Scorecard (% of corridor rolling stock and stations with validation capability, monthly Months 30–40 = 2029-04-12 to 2030-02-12)
  • Passenger-Rights and Accessibility Monitoring Dashboard (complaints, resolution time, assistance and bicycle-reservation fulfillment, post-Month 48 = 2030-10-12 go-live)

Frequency: Live-pilot data collection and weekly review Months 12–18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12); validation deployment audits at Months 30, 35, 40 (2029-04-12, 2029-09-12, 2030-02-12); post-go-live passenger-experience monitoring monthly from Month 48 (2030-10-12) onwards

Responsible Role: Head of Carrier Engagement (Programme Office) and corridor liaison officers for pilot and validation deployment tracking; CCPR Chair for passenger-rights compliance audits post-deployment; OMB for operational readiness assessments before corridor go-live

Adaptation Process: Pilot findings (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) showing >20% booking failures, disruption response times >60 minutes, or <80% passenger satisfaction trigger operational-manual revisions and carrier re-training by Month 18 (2028-04-12) before pilots close. If ticket-validation deployment lags (e.g., only 60% of corridor vehicles equipped by Month 40 = 2030-02-12), corridor go-live is deferred by 6 months to allow completion; alternatively, a hybrid validation (API handshake + fallback manual verification) is deployed as interim measure. Post-deployment, if passenger complaints about missed-connection re-accommodation exceed 5% of through-tickets or resolution time exceeds 48 hours, operationalmanual procedures are audited and carriers are required to retest re-accommodation procedures within 30 days or face tranch withholding.

Adaptation Trigger: Live-pilot booking-success rate <85% or disruption response time >60 minutes by Month 18 (2028-04-12); ticket-validation deployment <70% of corridor capacity by Month 40 (2030-02-12); post-go-live passenger complaints about re-accommodation or refunds >5% of through-tickets; assistance or bicycle-reservation request fulfillment <80% within promised timeframe; accessibility audit (post-Month 48 = 2030-10-12) finds >30% of through-ticket itineraries cannot guarantee wheelchair access or assistance, forcing atomic-confirmation failures

7. Risk Register and Issue Escalation Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Compliance and Risk Register (top 15–20 risks, tracking trigger conditions, mitigation status, owner, escalation paths)
  • Monthly Risk Status Report (OMB and CCPR briefings to PSC, escalation decisions)
  • Issue Log and Remediation Tracking (carrier participation, technical bottlenecks, budget variances, regulatory blockers)
  • Steering Committee Escalation Log (PSC decisions on variances, deadlocks, milestone deferrals)

Frequency: Monthly risk-register review by OMB and CCPR; escalations to PSC within five business days if a risk trigger is hit; quarterly risk-trend reporting to PSC (Months 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 60 = 2027-04-12, 2027-10-12, 2028-04-12, 2028-10-12, 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12 plus ad hoc)

Responsible Role: Head of Compliance and Risk (Programme Office) for register maintenance and monthly reporting; Programme Director (OMB Chair) for remediation decisions and escalations; PSC Chair for strategic risk decisions and mitigation approvals

Adaptation Process: If a risk trigger is hit (e.g., carrier participation drops below 20, or financial variance exceeds EUR 100M), Head of Compliance and Risk notifies OMB immediately; OMB convenes within two business days to evaluate mitigation options. Remediation is proposed by OMB and escalated to PSC for approval within five business days (e.g., accelerated adapter funding, tier deferral, TEN-T scope reduction). PSC approves mitigation by majority vote (5 of 9 members); if mitigation is contentious, escalation to Commission Transport Commissioner is triggered by Month 5 (2027-03-12 for Month 6 = 2027-04-12 decisions) or immediately for runtime issues (post-binding-standards). Accepted mitigation is published within ten business days to affected stakeholders (carriers, distributors, regulators).

Adaptation Trigger: Any risk tracked in the Compliance and Risk Register reaches its defined trigger condition (e.g., 'Carrier refusal if liability model not agreed by Month 4 = 2027-02-12', 'Legislative delay >6 months', 'Article 101 guidance not received by Month 12 = 2027-10-12', 'Budget variance EUR 100M/EUR 200M/EUR 300M'); a new critical risk not previously identified is raised by stakeholder or internal assessment; two or more active risks reach trigger conditions simultaneously (compound risk), escalating to PSC and Commission for coordinated response

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. All core governance components requested have been generated: internal governance bodies (4 specialized committees with clear charters), implementation plan (40+ sequenced steps across 60 months), decision escalation matrix (5 critical issues with defined escalation paths and approval processes), monitoring progress plan (5 monitoring approaches with triggers and adaptation mechanisms). The framework is complete and internally referenced.
  2. Internal consistency confirmed across stages: (1) Implementation Plan uses the correct governance bodies established in Phase 2 (PSC, OMB, CCPR, TSWG); (2) each body has defined decision thresholds (e.g., OMB: <EUR 10M, PSC: >EUR 50M and strategic decisions); (3) Escalation Matrix properly routes issues to appropriate bodies (carrier refusal → PSC, technical integration failure → OMB with PSC escalation if >EUR 50M); (4) Monitoring Plan tracks KPIs, milestones and risks with OMB ownership, escalating to PSC or CCPR when triggers are hit; (5) all governance bodies report to PSC as the strategic anchor, creating a coherent hierarchy and decision flow. No internal contradictions detected.
  3. Clarity of roles gaps: (1) Project Sponsor authority is mentioned but not formally defined—does the Sponsor retain any approval authority post-Month 1 (2026-11-12), or is all authority delegated to PSC Chair? No escalation path exists back to Sponsor if PSC deadlocks unresolved by Commission mediation. (2) EU Agency for Railways' relationship to the Programme Office is hierarchical but their concurrent roles (OSDM custodian, standards authority, compliance validator) create potential conflicts of interest if the Agency must approve standards it has designed. Recommend independent technical review separate from Agency. (3) Independent distributors (Trainline, Omio) have PSC observer seats but no voting rights; fallback clause mentions 'third-party settlement interface' but this interface design is not specified, leaving a potential escape hatch for dissenting distributors that could fragment the network. Interface must be defined operationally before binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12).
  4. Process depth and operational clarity gaps: (1) Conflict-of-interest management within the Programme Office and CCPR is not mentioned. If Programme Office staff approve funding tranches for carriers that employed them previously, or if CCPR legal counsel has prior relationships with DG COMP, governance credibility is at risk. Recommend a published conflict-of-interest policy and annual disclosure by all governance staff. (2) Change control for the OSDM specification post-binding-standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) specifies review timelines but does not define what happens if a critical security or safety bug is discovered and cannot wait 2 weeks for review. Emergency change procedures must be documented. (3) Whistleblower or complaints escalation procedures for governance participants (e.g., a carrier witnessing collusion among competitors, or a distributor experiencing discrimination) are not defined. A confidential escalation channel to an independent ombudsman or DG COMP should be established. (4) Member-State regulatory alignment is addressed via bilateral impact assessments by Month 3 (2027-01-12), but no formal procedure exists if a national regulator blocks the programme's design after binding standards are finalized (Month 18 = 2028-04-12). Current text says to 'defer that Member State' but operational mechanics and financial implications are undefined.
  5. Thresholds, delegation and granularity gaps: (1) The Programme Office (80 staff) is responsible for EUR 1,500M budget execution and conformance audits for 25+ carriers, yet no sub-delegation structure below Programme Director is defined for day-to-day spending authority. Who approves invoices >EUR 100k? Who can commit funds for pilot support without OMB? Financial governance is too centralized for operational scale. Recommend clear spending matrices by role (e.g., Head of Clearing: <EUR 500k without approval, EUR 500k-EUR 5M with Programme Director, >EUR 5M with OMB). (2) Conformance testing assigns all carrier audits to 'independent test laboratory' (singular) but no redundancy is specified. If one lab is overwhelmed or compromised, the entire Tier 1 audit schedule (Months 24-30 = 2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12) is at risk. Recommend contracting 2-3 test laboratories with clear workload allocation. (3) SLA scorecards are published monthly to 'steering group and regulators' but no defined procedure exists for a carrier to formally dispute a scorecard result before it is published (potentially triggering funding-tranche withholding). A 10-business-day dispute and remediation review window before public release should be added.
  6. Integration and information flow gaps: (1) Settlement reconciliation errors (target <0.5%) feed SLA scorecards, which trigger funding tranches, yet the clearing function's reconciliation results are owned by Head of Clearing and Settlement, not the independent test laboratory. A systematically erroneous clearing mechanism could bias all funding decisions, and no independent audit of the clearing function is scheduled before Month 30 (2029-04-12) go-live. Recommend an independent quarterly audit of clearing reconciliation from Month 6 (2027-04-12) onwards. (2) Passenger-rights compliance monitoring (CCPR) and operational re-accommodation monitoring (OMB/liaison officers) operate independently until post-Month 30 (2029-04-12) when a passenger-experience dashboard is created. During Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) pilots and Months 30-48 (2029-04-12 to 2030-10-12) initial go-live, a passenger-rights gap discovered via operational complaints has no direct escalation path to CCPR until the next quarterly compliance review. A real-time escalation for 'passenger loses rights' incidents should be added. (3) Funding tranches are conditioned on conformance certificates, SLA targets and milestone achievement, but no mechanism exists to claw back or condition funding if a carrier fails post-certification (e.g., on Month 35 = 2029-09-12 an API fails and latency becomes 5 seconds). Recommend quarterly SLA re-audits post-certification and conditional funding holds if performance degrades.

Tough Questions

  1. By Month 4 (2027-02-12), have at least 8 major carriers (representing >70% of cross-border capacity) signed the liability model with binding caps, co-insurance thresholds and on-time-performance contribution weightings? If not, what is the plan B—are we deferring the Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards deadline, or will we proceed with incomplete carrier buy-in, risking non-participation post-standards and fragmenting the network?
  2. What is the specific technical design of the 'fallback technical interface' for independent distributors who reject the clearing architecture (Decision 2)? Has this interface been prototyped with Trainline, Omio or another distributor, and does it preserve settlement finality and SLA targets, or does it introduce a separate, slower settlement stream that could reduce through-ticket volumes by 15-25%?
  3. By Month 12 (2027-10-12), have DG COMP confirmed in writing that the federated clearing layer with shared real-time data exchange is compatible with Article 101 TFEU, or is guidance still pending? If guidance is delayed beyond Month 12 (2027-10-12), do we freeze the OSDM specification at Month 18 (2028-04-12) with contingent compliance conditions, or do we defer binding standards and risk cascade delays to the mandatory API exposure deadline (Month 30 = 2029-04-12)?
  4. What is the independent actuarial confidence interval (e.g., 90th percentile) on carrier-pool missed-connection incident rates and rerouting costs used to set the per-incident liability cap (proposed EUR 500-1,000 per stranded passenger) and co-insurance threshold (proposed EUR 50M annual pool draw)? If actual claims exceed the confidence interval significantly by Month 36 (2029-10-12), what are the policy triggers to adjust contributions or invoke the public reserve (EUR 150M), and at what point does pool sustainability force carriers to withdraw?
  5. How many of the 25+ participating carriers have been formally committed (binding letters signed) to meet their assigned tier conformance deadline (Tier 1: Month 30 = 2029-04-12, Tier 2: Month 36 = 2029-10-12, Tier 3: Month 42 = 2030-04-12), and what is the financial consequence to a carrier that misses its deadline—do they lose 5%, 10% or 25% of their next funding tranche, and is there a point beyond which they are excluded from the programme entirely?
  6. By Month 24 (2028-10-12), when Tier 1 conformance audits begin, will there be a published, independent technical review (by a third party, not the EU Agency for Railways) of the OSDM specification and test cases to ensure they do not inadvertently advantage incumbent carriers or disadvantage smaller operators? If not, what independent quality assurance exists to catch specification gaps that only emerge during carrier implementation?
  7. What is the documented evidence that the proposed distribution-commission band (2.5-4.5% of through-fare, regulative supervision, identical for all distributors) actually covers distributors' cost of acquisition, payment processing and customer support for cross-border through-tickets? Has this band been validated against the distributor survey results (Month 4 = 2027-02-12)? If the band is below cost for any significant distributor type, will they participate, or will the commission band need to be widened post-Month 9 (2027-07-12)?
  8. By Month 3 (2027-01-12), have all national railway regulators (across 5-6 member states with 25+ operators) been engaged bilaterally and formally signaled their regulatory approval or concern regarding the programme's data-sharing, clearing and mandatory API exposure requirements? If major regulatory conflicts are identified, what is the timeline and procedure to resolve them by Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding standards, or do we defer certain member states to a Phase 2 rollout (post-Month 60 = 2031-10-12)?
  9. If the concessionaire (selected by Month 18 = 2028-04-12, service live by Month 30 = 2029-04-12) operates at 60% of forecast volume in its first 12 months (Month 30-42 = 2029-04-12 to 2030-04-12), triggering a contract-review clause, what is the contingency—do we increase subsidy (within the EUR 60M cap), redirect passengers to private distributors, defer TEN-T extension, or invoke a service-replacement process? Is this decision OMB-level or escalated to PSC?
  10. By Month 42 (2030-04-12), when Tier 3 conformance is complete (or deferred), what percentage of the 25+ participating carriers are expected to be live with full conformance (Tiers 1-3), and what happens to carriers who remain outside the programme after Month 42 (2030-04-12)—are they permanently excluded, invited to join TEN-T extension (Months 48-60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12), or does the programme explicitly accept that full TEN-T coverage will not be reached by Month 60 (2031-10-12)?

Summary

The governance framework establishes a multi-tiered structure with clear strategic (PSC, 75% supermajority voting), operational (OMB, week-to-month cycles), compliance (CCPR, legal expertise), and technical (TSWG, standards custodianship) layers, anchored by a dedicated Programme Office (80 staff) and Technical Secretariat (50 staff) reporting to the EU Agency for Railways. Critical decisions (liability backstop, clearing architecture, public distributor role, funding release conditions) are locked in by Month 6 (2027-04-12), binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12), and mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-12), with four-corridor through-ticketing by Month 48 (2030-10-12) and full TEN-T extension by Month 60-72 (2031-10-12). Governance credibility rests on three pillars: (1) escalation clarity—unresolved conflicts at PSC level escalate to the Commission Transport Commissioner by Month 5 (2027-03-12) for binding mediation; (2) financial controls—quarterly variance tracking with EUR 100M/EUR 200M/EUR 300M triggers that force policy adjustments rather than silent budget creep; (3) independent oversight—CCPR ensures competition-law and passenger-rights compliance, and conformance audits by independent test laboratories validate carrier readiness. Key gaps requiring closure before binding standards: formal definition of the distributor fallback interface (technical and operational), conflict-of-interest and whistleblower procedures for governance staff, independent audit of the clearing reconciliation mechanism, sub-delegation spending matrices within the Programme Office, and bilateral regulatory approval from all participating member states. The framework is operationally complex but strategically coherent, with clear role boundaries and escalation paths that should sustain the EUR 1,500M public budget and five-year timeline provided stakeholder consensus is achieved by Month 6 (2027-04-12) and regulatory/competition-law obstacles are resolved by Month 18 (2028-04-12).

Suggestion 1 - OSDM (Open Sales and Distribution Model), UIC-led with Swiss SBB, DB, ÖBB, SNCF and others

Industry open standard of APIs for searching, booking, ticketing, refunds and after-sales across railway undertakings, developed under the International Union of Railways (UIC) with SBB, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB and others as lead contributors. Published openly with a reference specification and test tooling. Adopted by several European operators and distributors for cross-border sales; it is the standard the proposed Regulation is expected to reference.

Success Metrics

Number of operators and distributors live on OSDM endpoints (obtain current count from UIC; not verified). Cross-border sales volume sold via OSDM (not published in verified form). Release cadence and count of external contributors.

Risks and Challenges Faced

Uneven carrier adoption and legacy back-ends: mitigated by phased profiles and open reference implementation. Governance dependence on incumbents: mitigated through open publication and participation by distributors. Version fragmentation across implementers: mitigated by versioned releases and a change-request process.

Where to Find More Information

UIC OSDM page: https://uic.org (search 'OSDM') OSDM specification repository on GitHub (search 'UIC OSDM') CER and European Commission DG MOVE material on the Digital Booking and Ticketing proposal

Actionable Steps

Contact the UIC Passenger Department / OSDM Steering team via the UIC website contact form. Approach SBB's OSDM project lead via the SBB corporate contact and LinkedIn (identify the OSDM product owner role). Join the OSDM community working group as an observer to review change-control practice.

Rationale for Suggestion

Direct technical foundation of the plan's real-time data layer. Its governance, versioning and conformance experience informs the Specification Custodian and Conformance Gate decisions. Geographically and institutionally identical (European carriers, same stakeholders).

Suggestion 2 - Rail Settlement Plan (RSP), Great Britain

Industry-owned clearing and settlement body for GB rail ticket revenue. It receives sales from all retailers (operators and third parties such as Trainline), allocates revenue to train operators by agreed rules (the Ticketing and Settlement Agreement, ORCATS allocation) and settles on a fixed cycle. Operated for decades on behalf of the rail industry (RDG).

Success Metrics

Annual ticket revenue settled (published by RDG/RSP; confirm current figure). Settlement cycle and error rates (request from RSP). Number of authorised retailers.

Risks and Challenges Faced

Disputes over revenue allocation: mitigated by deterministic allocation rules and an arbitration process. Retailer access fairness: mitigated by retailer agreements and published terms. Concentration of operational risk in one body: mitigated by industry governance and audit.

Where to Find More Information

Rail Delivery Group: https://www.raildeliverygroup.com Rail Settlement Plan: https://www.rsp.org.uk ORR retail market reviews: https://www.orr.gov.uk

Actionable Steps

Contact RSP through the corporate contact page and ask for the settlement and retailer-access team. Request an expert briefing from Rail Delivery Group's retail/ticketing group. Engage the ORR retail regulation team on competition oversight of industry settlement.

Rationale for Suggestion

Best-documented real example of multi-operator through-ticket apportionment, single-payment settlement, refunds across carriers and non-discriminatory third-party retail access. Informs the federated clearing design, commission terms and dispute handling. Not EU, but the closest large-scale working model; note differences in a single national regulatory context.

Suggestion 3 - Eurail/Interrail pass distribution and TAP/TSI telematics for rail passengers

Pan-European rail products sold across dozens of operators with multi-carrier revenue sharing and distribution through carriers and third-party channels, run by Eurail B.V. (Utrecht). Complemented by the EU TAP TSI telematics specifications that mandate interoperable data exchange for passenger services, managed by the EU Agency for Railways.

Success Metrics

Number of participating operators and countries (published by Eurail). TAP TSI compliance status by member state (Agency reports). Pass sales volumes (company-reported; confirm).

Risks and Challenges Faced

Allocating pooled revenue fairly among carriers: mitigated by agreed usage-based allocation rules. Slow implementation of TAP TSI data exchange: mitigated by phased deadlines and Agency monitoring. Competition-law scrutiny of shared arrangements: mitigated by documented rules and open participation.

Where to Find More Information

Eurail: https://www.eurail.com EU Agency for Railways TAP TSI pages: https://www.era.europa.eu Commission TAP TSI Regulation (EU) 454/2011 on EUR-Lex

Actionable Steps

Contact Eurail B.V. corporate or partner relations (Utrecht) via its website. Contact the EU Agency for Railways telematics/TAP TSI sector via the Agency's contact form. Ask CER's passenger group for introductions to carrier settlement teams.

Rationale for Suggestion

Demonstrates a working multi-carrier revenue-pooling and clearing arrangement across about 30 European countries and the Agency's real role in mandating telematics specifications. Relevant for governance, clearing and carrier incentive design. Differs by being a pass, not point-to-point fares.

Suggestion 4 - Swiss Direct Service (Direkter Verkehr) and NOVA platform (secondary suggestion)

Swiss national public-transport ticketing and revenue-sharing system run by Alliance SwissPass for over 200 transport companies. NOVA is the shared sales and distribution platform that allows any retailer to sell through-tickets across operators with common fare rules and automated revenue allocation. Secondary suggestion: national rather than cross-border.

Success Metrics

Number of participating transport companies (published by Alliance SwissPass). Share of journeys sold as through-tickets (not verified).

Risks and Challenges Faced

Onboarding small operators: addressed through a shared platform and common rules. Governance among many companies: addressed through an alliance body.

Where to Find More Information

Alliance SwissPass: https://www.allianceswisspass.ch SBB: https://www.sbb.ch

Actionable Steps

Contact Alliance SwissPass via the website contact form for the NOVA/Direct Service team. Approach SBB's distribution unit through its corporate contacts.

Rationale for Suggestion

Shows a federated, mandated through-ticket model across many carriers with a common distribution platform, relevant to fare construction, clearing and carrier onboarding. Fewer details given; scale and governance differ from EU level.

Summary

Recommended references cover the programme's core mechanisms: OSDM-based cross-border distribution, inter-carrier clearing, a shared rail-air-bus liability model, and public-funded interoperability governance. The closest real precedents are the UIC/OSDM standard and its adopters (primary), the Rail Settlement Plan in Great Britain and the DB/ÖBB/SBB/SNCF-led NeTEx/TAP-TSI and Eurail/Interrail distribution arrangements (primary), and the Swiss Direct Service/NOVA national integration (secondary). Geographic proximity is high (EU/Switzerland), but no precedent combines mandatory API exposure, a carrier-funded guarantee pool and a public last-resort distributor. Contact details are given as organisations or roles; individual names and figures should be confirmed directly with each body (not verified).

1. Carrier Liability Model Actuarial Validation and Risk Parameters

The carrier-funded guarantee pool is the core incentive-alignment mechanism that determines whether 25+ operators will expose connections. Without actuarially validated caps and contribution weights, carriers cannot price participation and will refuse, fragmenting corridors and collapsing the 40% through-ticket target to 15–25%. This is the highest-impact blocking dependency.

Data to Collect

  • 24-month historical missed-connection incident rates per carrier (frequency, severity, clustering patterns)
  • Rerouting cost distributions (passenger assistance, alternative ticket issuance, accommodation) by carrier and route
  • Carrier on-time performance data (12-month rolling) to calibrate contribution-weighting formula
  • Insurance market quotes for pool coverage above proposed co-insurance thresholds
  • Carrier financial capacity statements (loss reserves, credit lines available for pool contributions)

Simulation Steps

  • Build a Monte Carlo incident-clustering model using historical rail disruption data from Rail Settlement Plan (GB), Trenitalia–ÖBB bilateral clearing, and CER aggregate reports to project pool cash flows under three scenarios (conservative, base, aggressive)
  • Run sensitivity analysis in Excel or R on proposed caps (EUR 250, 500, 1,000, 2,000 per passenger) and co-insurance triggers (EUR 20M, 50M, 100M annual draw) to show per-carrier contribution ranges and risk distribution
  • Use insurance-industry benchmarks (e.g., Munich Re, Swiss Re) to validate that proposed caps align with similar transport liability pools and to quote reinsurance cost for tail exposure
  • Stress-test the pool model against historically volatile periods (e.g., winter 2021-22 rail disruptions, COVID-19 lockdown rerouting spikes) to identify worst-case drawdown scenarios

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage an independent actuarial firm (e.g., Deloitte Consulting, Mercer, or specialist rail insurance actuaries) to conduct the statistical analysis and deliver priced liability parameters by Month 3 (2027-01-12)
  • Present the actuarial model to the EU Agency for Railways and CER for technical review and sign-off on methodology by Month 4 (2027-02-12)
  • Conduct bilateral meetings with at least 8 major carriers (SNCF, DB, SBB, ÖBB, Renfe, NS, Trenitalia, ČD) to present worked examples for their carrier profile and obtain non-binding feedback on acceptable exposure levels by Month 4 (2027-02-12)
  • Secure binding written commitment from at least 8 major carriers and CER confirming they will expose through-ticket inventory under the final priced model by Month 4 (2027-02-12), or escalate design issues to Commission mediation by Month 5 (2027-03-12)

Responsible Parties

  • Independent actuarial firm (commissioned Month 1 = 2026-11-12; reports Month 3–6 = 2027-01-12 to 2027-04-12)
  • EU Agency for Railways (technical review of methodology)
  • CER and 8+ major carriers (bilateral feedback and sign-off)
  • Programme Office (escalation to Commission mediation if consensus not reached by Month 5 = 2027-03-12)

Assumptions

  • High: Historical missed-connection and rerouting cost data are available from at least 3 major carriers (CER, RSC, bilateral arrangements) spanning 24 months with granular incident classification (delay cause, reroute cost, passenger demographic).
  • High: Carriers will provide proprietary loss data to the actuarial firm under confidentiality agreements and will engage constructively in validation workshops; refusal by >2 major carriers stalls the entire liability model.
  • Medium: Insurance market reinsurance cost for pool coverage (EUR 20–100M threshold) is commercially available and priced at <5% of limit, fitting within EUR 150M reserve or EUR 220M clearing budget.
  • High: Actuarial modelling of through-ticket-specific incidents (multi-leg clustering, disruption correlation) is feasible using historical single-operator data with adjustment factors; no through-ticket baseline is available.
  • High: At least 8 carriers sign binding letters of intent by Month 4 (2027-02-12); if <6 sign, the month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate defers and triggers month 12 (2027-10-12) contingency.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 4 (2027-02-12), deliver an actuarially validated liability model with per-incident caps, co-insurance thresholds, and contribution weights specific to three carrier profiles (large, regional, small), supported by 24-month incident data analysis. Secure binding written commitment from 8+ major carriers confirming participation at proposed risk levels. Establish quarterly pool monitoring by Month 6 (2027-04-12) to track actual vs. forecast incident rates with adjustment triggers.

Notes

  • Actuarial study timeline is compressed (Month 1–6 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-04-12); parallel workstreams (technical audit, DG COMP pre-notification, steering governance) must run without blocking.
  • Failure to reach consensus on liability model by Month 6 (2027-04-12) cascades to month 12 (2027-10-12) readiness-gate deferral, pushing binding standards to month 24 (2028-10-12) and API exposure to month 36 (2029-10-12).
  • Quarterly pool reports (starting Month 6 = 2027-04-12) are essential for carrier confidence; if actual incident rates exceed forecast by >20% within first 12 months, model adjustment and contributor communication are urgent.
  • Reserve reinsurance cost (estimated EUR 5–10M if needed) from the EUR 150M force-majeure budget or EUR 220M clearing line; confirm funding source by Month 3 (2027-01-12).
  • If Commission mediation is required (Month 5 = 2027-03-12), identify fallback liability designs (e.g., two-tier pool: core carriers + optional reinsurance for smaller operators) immediately.

2. Pre-Programme Technical Audit of Carrier Booking Systems and Tier Assignment

40–50% of smaller carriers (8–15 operators) are at high risk of missing the mandatory API exposure milestone (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) due to legacy system constraints. Without a pre-project technical baseline, adapter funding (EUR 240M) is allocated without evidence, and carriers that miss deadlines create corridor fragmentation. This blocks network connectivity and threatens the 40% through-ticket goal.

Data to Collect

  • OSDM API readiness per carrier: existing OSDM implementation status, API maturity level (design, prototype, live), planned completion date
  • Real-time inventory capability: event-streaming support (Kafka, RabbitMQ, or custom), transaction consistency across legs, booking confirmation latency (p50, p95, p99 milliseconds)
  • Monthly availability: 12-month uptime % per carrier (excluding planned maintenance), outage frequency and duration distribution
  • Legacy system dependencies: mainframe, flat-file settlement, custom payment integration; estimated retrofit timeline per system
  • Staffing allocation: FTE available per carrier for API integration, testing and operations support through Month 42 (2030-04-12)

Simulation Steps

  • Use OSDM reference test suite (available from UIC or community) to run conformance checks against each carrier's current API implementation (or planned API stub if not yet live); identify API profile compliance gaps
  • Simulate multi-leg latency queries: run synthetic three-leg bookings (Paris–Amsterdam–Berlin, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon) through carrier APIs in sequence, measuring end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency under normal load; model combined availability assuming independent 95% per leg (yields ~86% three-leg availability, below the proposed 99.5% SLA)
  • Model carrier availability using publicly available operational data (e.g., CER annual disruption reports, NaBaRo NaBaRo database, national regulator filings) and each carrier's recent outage frequency to estimate achievable 99.5% uptime target by Month 30 (2029-04-12)
  • Interview carrier IT leads to estimate retrofit timeline for legacy systems (mainframe APIs, flat-file settlement feeds, custom payment integration); use industry benchmarks (e.g., legacy banking system modernisation studies) to validate estimates

Expert Validation Steps

  • Commission an independent technical audit firm (e.g., Deloitte, Capgemini, or specialist rail IT consultancy) by Month 1 (2026-11-12) to assess all 25+ carriers' systems in-person or remotely; deliver interim readiness signals by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27) and a detailed 25-carrier assessment with per-carrier roadmaps and tier assignments by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • Engage the EU Agency for Railways and standards-working group to review and validate the audit methodology (test coverage, latency measurement, conformance criteria) by Month 3 (2027-01-12) to ensure audit credibility with carriers
  • Present audit results and tier assignments to CER and the steering group by Month 6 (2027-04-12); if >35% of targeted carriers cannot achieve Month 30 (2029-04-12) API exposure, propose revised tier structure (e.g., Tier 1.5 at Month 33 = 2029-07-12, or pilot-only Phase 1 with binding commitment for Month 36 = 2029-10-12) and obtain steering vote

Responsible Parties

  • Independent technical audit firm (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-04-12)
  • EU Agency for Railways and standards-working group (validate methodology and credibility by Month 3 = 2027-01-12)
  • Carrier IT leads (respond to audit questionnaires and participate in roadmap discussions)
  • Programme Office (publish tier assignments and release adapter funding in tranches against verified performance)

Assumptions

  • High: All 25+ targeted carriers cooperate with the audit process, providing system access or detailed questionnaire responses; refusal by >3 carriers stalls the tier assignment.
  • Medium: OSDM reference test suite is available from UIC and covers sufficient API profiles to assess conformance; if test coverage is <80%, supplementary conformance tests must be developed by Month 3 (2027-01-12).
  • Medium: Synthetic latency tests using three-leg queries reflect realistic load and carrier endpoint performance; carriers may argue synthetic tests underestimate real-world latency under peak loads (e.g., summer booking surge), requiring pilot validation.
  • High: Smaller carriers with legacy systems can be retrofitted (mainframe APIs, flat-file feeds, payment integration) within the Tier 2 (Month 36 = 2029-10-12) and Tier 3 (Month 42 = 2030-04-12) timelines; if retrofit complexity exceeds estimates, carriers miss deadlines and corridors fragment.
  • Medium: Shared adapter modules (EUR 30–50M) can address 60–70% of common legacy patterns; if carriers have unique integration barriers, per-carrier custom adapters (EUR 10–20M each) are required, consuming contingency headroom.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 6 (2027-04-12), conduct a detailed technical audit of all 25+ carriers assessing API readiness, real-time latency, availability and legacy system retrofit timelines. Publish tier assignments (Tier 1: Month 30 = 2029-04-12; Tier 2: Month 36 = 2029-10-12; Tier 3: Month 42 = 2030-04-12) with per-carrier roadmaps and identified bottlenecks. Identify the top 3 shared adapter patterns and allocate EUR 30–50M to procure them by Month 12 (2027-10-12). Release subsequent adapter funding (Tier 2, Tier 3) only after independent verification of live API performance (99.5% uptime, p95 latency <2 sec, <1% stale-seat failures).

Notes

  • Audit must account for carriers' varied IT maturity: large operators (SNCF, DB, SBB) likely have OSDM prototypes or live APIs; regional operators have partial APIs; smaller operators have legacy mainframes with limited API capability.
  • Latency and availability thresholds (p95 <2 seconds, 99.5% monthly uptime) are proposed and must be confirmed as feasible by Month 3 (2027-01-12) based on audit interim findings; if infeasible for >30% of Tier 2/3 carriers, thresholds must be revised.
  • Tier 3 operators (Month 42 = 2030-04-12 deadline) represent 18 months of retrofit and testing time; if audit reveals >6 months of bottleneck per carrier, Tier 3 date slips to Month 48 (2030-10-12) or beyond, fragmenting Phase 2 final-wave TEN-T.
  • Shared adapter procurement (Month 12 = 2027-10-12) is a critical supplier-engagement milestone; delays in identifying or procuring modules cascade to Tier 2 and 3 readiness.
  • If >35% of carriers remain unready by Month 36 (2029-10-12), trigger emergency adapter acceleration (EUR 150–250M contingency spend) or defer Phase 3 TEN-T extension to Month 60–72 (2031-10-12 to 2032-10-12).

3. DG COMP Article 101 TFEU Competition-Law Clearance and Data-Sharing Governance

Competitors sharing real-time inventory, settlement data, and pricing information through shared clearing and availability layers raises novel Article 101 TFEU issues. A post-launch competition challenge could force EUR 50–100M rework and 6–12 months delay, unraveling the entire clearing and availability stack. Early DG COMP comfort (by Month 12 = 2027-10-12) is essential to lock carrier participation and binding-standards design.

Data to Collect

  • Detailed specification of the federated clearing mechanism: netting rules, dispute resolution process, access terms for independent distributors and smaller carriers
  • Shared availability layer architecture: who controls the streamed availability shadow, how inventory updates are pooled, what data is exposed to competitors, access-denial criteria
  • Through-fare construction doctrine: whether fare-composition rules (sum-of-legs, corridor tariff, or composite bundle) constitute price coordination under Article 101
