  • Distribution remuneration and commission band: proposed commission rate range, how rates are set and enforced, whether there are mechanisms for discrimination or margin squeezing against independent distributors
  • Carrier-funded guarantee pool governance: who controls the pool rules, dispute adjudication, and reserve investment; whether pool governance creates cartel-like coordination on liability pricing

Simulation Steps

  • Document the clearing and data-sharing arrangements as implemented in competing transport sectors (e.g., air-transport IATA clearing, bus-industry bilateral arrangements, electricity market clearing) to identify Article 101 precedents and safe-harbour patterns; use CJEU and General Court case law (e.g., Wouters, Pechstein, Comb. Practices cases) to stress-test the programme's design against known blocking issues
  • Build a data-flow diagram showing what commercially sensitive information (fares, inventory, rerouting decisions, settlement positions, on-time performance, contribution weights) passes through each shared layer (availability shadow, clearing, disruption feed, pool monitoring); identify which flows are unavoidable and which could be redesigned to reduce exposure
  • Model two alternative governance structures for the shared layers: (A) centralized (one entity controls rules and data access), (B) federated (bilateral arrangements with a netting overlay); compare each against Article 101 Regulation 1/2003 exemption criteria (restrictions are proportionate, not harmful to consumers, do not allow competitors to eliminate competition in a substantial part of the market) and identify which design carries lower legal risk
  • Simulate a post-launch Article 101 challenge: if a distributor or smaller carrier claims exclusion or discrimination, what evidence in the governance charter and access logs would defend the programme? Model the cost and timeline of a redesign forced by DG COMP or EU court judgment (estimated EUR 50–100M and 6–12 months)

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage an external EU competition law specialist (e.g., major law firm with Brussels office: Cleary Gottlieb, Jones Day, White & Case; or specialist rail transport counsel) by Month 1 (2026-11-12) to draft a detailed DG COMP pre-notification memorandum (estimated EUR 300–500K); submit to DG COMP by Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Engage in formal dialogue with DG COMP directorate (DG COMP/B or /C sector desk) starting Month 2 (2026-12-12); request expedited review and interim guidance by Month 9 (2027-07-12), final guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12)
  • If DG COMP raises Article 101 concerns, work with external counsel to design a clean-team arrangement (independent compliance officer with sole access to sensitive data, firewalls between clearing and competitive functions) and obtain DG COMP approval by Month 14 (2027-12-12), no later than Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding standards
  • Retain competition counsel for ongoing monitoring (Months 18–60 = 2028-04-12 to 2031-10-12) to detect early signals of post-launch challenges; prepare contingency redesign documentation (options for bilateral clearing, third-party settlement, or other alternatives) by Month 24 (2028-10-12)

Responsible Parties

  • External EU competition law firm (pre-notification memorandum, dialogue with DG COMP, clean-team protocol design)
  • DG COMP (issuance of guidance letter by Month 12 = 2027-10-12)
  • Standards-working group (integrate Article 101 safe-harbour conditions into OSDM binding text by Month 18 = 2028-04-12)
  • Programme Office and carriers (implement agreed clean-team and data-governance protocols by Month 24 = 2028-10-12)

Assumptions

  • High: DG COMP will engage constructively and provide guidance within 9–12 months; if review extends beyond Month 12 (2027-10-12), binding standards slip and Programme timeline compresses by 3–6 months.
  • High: The federated clearing and shared availability designs can be modified to satisfy Article 101 without material loss of efficiency or carrier participation; if fundamental redesign is required (e.g., abandoning the shared availability shadow in favor of federated-only queries), latency and through-ticket success rates degrade by 10–20% (estimate).
  • Medium: A clean-team arrangement (independent compliance officer, IT firewalls, data-access logs) is legally and operationally feasible and will satisfy DG COMP; if DG COMP judges the clean-team insufficient, more drastic separation (e.g., separate legal entities for clearing and data layers) may be required.
  • High: No third-party distributor or smaller carrier launches a post-launch Article 101 challenge; if one does before the programme is commercially proven (Month 36–48 = 2029-10-12 to 2030-10-12), the challenge could succeed, forcing design rework during the critical four-corridor go-live phase.
  • Medium: The clean-team protocol (if required) can be implemented by Month 14 (2027-12-12) without delaying binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12); if implementation requires >4 months, standards slip by 2–3 months.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 12 (2027-10-12), obtain a written guidance letter from DG COMP confirming that the inter-carrier clearing, shared availability layer, through-fare construction and carrier-funded pool design are compatible with Article 101 TFEU, or identifying specific conditions (e.g., clean-team protocol, governance safeguards, access-denial appeal process) required for compatibility. Publish a binding Governance Charter by Month 6 (2027-04-12) specifying non-discriminatory access rules, composition of decision-making bodies, and appeal procedures. Implement agreed clean-team protocol and data-governance safeguards by Month 14 (2027-12-12). Integrate DG COMP guidance into OSDM binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12).

Notes

  • Article 101 risk is highest for the shared availability layer and inter-carrier clearing; through-fare construction and commission band face moderate risk depending on negotiation and enforcement mechanisms.
  • DG COMP's guidance letter is not binding, but formal comfort provided before standards bind significantly reduces post-launch challenge risk (probability reduction estimated 50–70%).
  • If DG COMP's interim feedback (expected Month 9 = 2027-07-12) indicates fundamental concerns, the standards-working group must pivot to alternative designs immediately; delaying redesign past Month 12 (2027-10-12) will cascade to binding-standards slip.
  • Clean-team implementation requires appointing an independent compliance officer (role, authority, conflicts policy) and establishing IT firewalls; this is a governance and technical task best completed in parallel with binding-standards development (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12).
  • Retain external counsel through Month 60 (2031-10-12) for ongoing monitoring and contingency rework planning; budget EUR 2–5M for three-year engagement.

4. Federated Inter-Carrier Clearing and Settlement Mechanism Design and Reconciliation Platform

The federated clearing layer (EUR 220M investment) is the financial backbone enabling single-payment through-tickets, refund reversals, and commission netting across 25+ carriers and independent distributors. Without a concrete, validated clearing rulebook and reconciliation platform by Month 6 (2027-04-12), carriers cannot model settlement risks and distributors cannot price integration costs. Reconciliation errors >2% will lengthen settlement cycles from the target 5 business days to 15–30 days, deterring distributor participation and threatening the 40% through-ticket goal.

Data to Collect

  • Existing bilateral and sector clearing arrangements: settlement formats used by RSC (GB), Trenitalia–ÖBB bilateral, SBB–partner operators; netting rules, dispute procedures, settlement cycle times
  • Carrier financial accounting systems: whether carriers use ISO 20022 XML or legacy formats for revenue reporting; payment processing timelines and bank reconciliation capabilities
  • Distributor settlement data requirements: what financial reporting and reconciliation information distributors need to verify carrier shares and commission allocations
  • Third-party payment processor capabilities: which processors can support multi-leg transactions, netting reversals, and refund reversals across carriers within a 5-business-day cycle
  • Current reconciliation error rates and dispute resolution procedures in existing transport clearing (RSC, airline clearing) to set realistic thresholds for the federated model

Simulation Steps

  • Build a detailed ledger model of a three-leg through-ticket (Paris–Amsterdam–Berlin) showing: passenger payment (EUR 200), carrier A leg share (EUR 60), carrier B leg share (EUR 80), carrier C leg share (EUR 50), distributor commission (3%, EUR 6), clearing transaction fee (0.5%, EUR 1), with refund reversal and stale-seat adjustment scenarios; trace the netting and payout in Excel or a specialized settlement simulator
  • Simulate the settlement data flow: passenger books through Distributor X on through-ticket, Distributor X submits transaction to clearing platform by 17:00 UTC T+0, clearing platform matches against carrier submissions (A, B, C each submit leg-level journals), reconciliation flags mismatches (amount variance >0.50%, timing variance >2 business days), escalation procedure triggered if unresolved by end of T+2, payout to Distributor X and carriers scheduled for T+5
  • Model the ISO 20022 XML mapping required to standardize journal entries across carriers; identify common data gaps (missing booking reference, conflicting amounts, timestamp variance) and design tolerance bands and automated recovery procedures
  • Simulate four reconciliation-error scenarios (missing transaction, duplicate transaction, amount variance EUR 0.50 vs. EUR 5.00, timing variance 1 day vs. 5 days); measure error detection time, manual review effort and payout delay per scenario; compare against the proposed 0.5% error target and EUR 5-business-day settlement SLA

Expert Validation Steps

  • Commission an independent clearing and settlement specialist (e.g., consultancy with fintech or banking clearing expertise: Gartner, EY, or specialized clearing-house operator) by Month 1 (2026-11-12) to review existing RSC, Trenitalia–ÖBB and airline clearing precedents; deliver findings by Month 3 (2027-01-12)
  • Establish a dedicated Clearing Design Workstream (reporting to steering group) by Month 1 (2026-11-12) to publish a Federated Clearing Rulebook by Month 6 (2027-04-12) specifying netting model (bilateral/multilateral), journal entry standard (ISO 20022), settlement cycle (5 business days), reconciliation tolerance (amount <0.50%, timing <2 days), and dispute procedure; present three worked examples (Paris–Amsterdam–Berlin, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon)
  • Engage payment service providers (e.g., SWIFT, Euroclear, or a fintech settlement platform) by Month 6 (2027-04-12) to validate that the clearing rulebook is technically feasible and that refund reversals and stale-seat adjustments can be processed within the settlement cycle; obtain binding letters of intent by Month 12 (2027-10-12)
  • Pilot the federated clearing mechanism on one priority corridor with 500–1,000 transactions (Months 18–24 = 2028-04-12 to 2028-10-12) to validate reconciliation procedures, measure actual error rates and payout times; if error rate exceeds 2%, refine tolerance bands and escalation procedures before rolling out to remaining three corridors

Responsible Parties

  • Independent clearing and settlement specialist (methodology review, existing-system analysis)
  • Clearing Design Workstream (rulebook development, worked examples, coordination with carriers and PSPs)
  • EU Agency for Railways (review and approval of rulebook by Month 9 = 2027-07-12)
  • Payment service providers (technical validation and platform procurement)
  • Programme Office (release of EUR 220M clearing budget against verified reconciliation performance; establishment of settlement operations team by Month 24 = 2028-10-12)

Assumptions

  • High: Existing clearing precedents (RSC, bilateral arrangements, airline clearing) can be adapted to the federated through-ticket model without fundamental architectural change; if the federated model requires novel netting semantics (e.g., multilateral netting across >5 carriers simultaneously), development time extends beyond Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • High: All carriers will submit settlement data in a standardized ISO 20022 XML format by Month 24 (2028-10-12); carriers with legacy financial systems may resist format migration, requiring custom adapters (EUR 10–20M estimate) and extending deployment to Month 36 (2029-10-12).
  • High: A reconciliation error rate of 0.5% by Month 30 (2029-04-12) is achievable; in reality, federated multi-carrier settlement typically experiences 2–5% error rates initially, declining with operational maturity. If actual rates exceed 1.0% for >2 consecutive months, the proposed penalty regime (5% tranche loss) will trigger carrier suspension, fragmenting the network.
  • Medium: Payment service providers can support EUR settlement netting and refund reversals within a 5-business-day cycle; if PSP latency constraints force a 10-business-day cycle, cash-flow friction for distributors increases and participation drops by 10–15% (estimate).
  • Medium: The reconciliation platform (EUR 20–40M) can be procured as a commercial offering (SaaS or managed service); if custom development is required, cost escalates to EUR 50–100M and timeline extends to Month 30–36 (2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12).

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 6 (2027-04-12), publish a Federated Clearing Rulebook specifying netting model, settlement currency (EUR), journal entry standard (ISO 20022 XML), settlement cycle (5 business days with daily netting), reconciliation tolerance bands (amount <0.50%, timing <2 days), dispute procedure and payout schedule. Include three worked examples showing journal entries, netting and payout per distributor and carrier. Obtain approval from the EU Agency for Railways and steering group. Procure a shared reconciliation platform capable of processing >10,000 transactions/day by Month 24 (2028-10-12). Pilot the clearing mechanism on one priority corridor (500–1,000 transactions) at Months 18–24 (2028-04-12 to 2028-10-12) and achieve <0.5% error rate by Month 30 (2029-04-12).

Notes

  • The clearing rulebook is a policy and technical document; it must be owned by a dedicated workstream (not delegated to a contractor) so governance authority and carrier buy-in are maintained.
  • Reconciliation tolerance thresholds (0.5% error, <2 day timing variance) are aggressive for federated multi-carrier settlement; validate against industry benchmarks (RSC, airline clearing) by Month 3 (2027-01-12) and revise if infeasible.
  • Refund and stale-seat adjustment procedures are novel in rail clearing; pilot testing (Months 18–24 = 2028-04-12 to 2028-10-12) is essential to validate that these edge cases do not cause settlement delays or disputes.
  • Settlement operations team (Clearing and Settlement Operations Lead, 1–2 FTE) must be hired and on-boarded by Month 18 (2028-04-12) to prepare for Month 30 (2029-04-12) live operations.
  • If pilot error rate exceeds 1.0% at Month 24 (2028-10-12), escalate to Programme Director and DG MOVE; consider deferring Tier 2 API exposure (Month 36 = 2029-10-12) until clearing is stable.

5. Real-Time Availability Layer Architecture, SLA Monitoring and Graceful Degradation

The availability query topology (Decision 5) determines whether distributors can reliably show through-tickets to passengers within acceptable latency. If combined three-leg queries exceed 5 seconds or fail >1% of the time due to carrier outages, passengers will prefer single-operator bookings or competitor platforms. The streamed availability shadow and graceful degradation to scheduled-only are essential to masking carrier outages and maintaining through-ticket attractiveness without centralizing inventory (which carries competition-law risk).

Data to Collect

  • Carrier booking-engine latency and availability baselines: p50, p95, p99 query response times and monthly uptime % per carrier, measured over 12-month rolling window
  • Shared event-streaming platform capabilities: can Kafka, RabbitMQ or similar support seat inventory updates from 25+ carriers with <5-second propagation delay and exactly-once or at-least-once delivery guarantees
  • Distributed cache feasibility: can a Redis or similar cache hold 24-hour seat snapshots for 100,000+ itineraries (Paris–Amsterdam–Berlin, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon corridors) with stale-data TTL <5 minutes and sub-100ms lookup latency
  • Failover and degradation thresholds: at what latency (3 sec? 5 sec?) and availability (99%? 98.5%?) should through-ticket search fall back to scheduled-only offers without real-time seats
  • Passenger preference and SLA trade-offs: do passengers accept scheduled-only (no pricing, no seat choice) fallback if real-time is unavailable, or will they abandon through-tickets for single-operator bookings

Simulation Steps

  • Model multi-leg latency: assume each carrier's booking engine operates at p95 latency of 2 seconds (proposed threshold); when a distributor queries three carriers in sequence (Paris, then Amsterdam, then Berlin), combined latency = 6 seconds + network variance (±1 second estimate) = 5–7 seconds total, already exceeding any reasonable SLA for search; model parallel queries (concurrent calls to all three carriers) and show that p95 combined latency depends on the slowest responder, reducing to ~2–3 seconds if each responder meets the SLA
  • Simulate availability: if each carrier is 95% available (industry baseline), combined three-leg availability = 0.95^3 = 0.857 (85.7%), below the proposed 99.5% SLA; model the effect of upgrading carriers to 99.5% (combined = 0.995^3 = 0.985, 98.5%, still below 99.5%); show that 99.5% combined requires each carrier to exceed 99.83% (unrealistic without redundancy). Recommend that the SLA target be revised or a cached shadow introduced to mask carrier outages.
  • Design the availability shadow cache: distributed Redis nodes hold recent search results (itinerary + prices + seat availability) keyed by origin, destination, date, class; update frequency every 5 minutes from carrier event feeds; expiration policy: if a result is >5 minutes stale, mark as 'stale' in search UI but still display it; if carrier API is unavailable, degrade to scheduled-only (no pricing, no seats) rather than showing expired prices that cause booking failures
  • Model graceful degradation: when a carrier endpoint is unavailable >30 seconds, the distributed cache switches search results to scheduled-only for routes involving that carrier; publish a user-facing message ('Real-time seat availability temporarily unavailable; scheduled services are shown below'); measure passenger impact: how many passengers abandon search vs. accept scheduled-only fallback (requires usability testing, Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12)
  • Simulate failure scenarios: (1) carrier endpoint down 2 hours during peak booking (summer season); (2) network partition between EU hub and carrier datacenter (60 second lag before failover); (3) event-stream publisher backlog (availability shadow is 2 hours stale); for each scenario, measure: detection time, user-visible fallback, recovery time and payout delay in clearing

Expert Validation Steps

  • Commission a distributed-systems architect and real-time platform specialist by Month 1 (2026-11-12) to validate the streamed availability shadow design against production requirements (sub-100ms cache lookup, <5-minute staleness, graceful degradation to scheduled-only); deliver architecture design by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • Deploy SLA monitoring synthetic probes by Month 12 (2027-10-12) that query each carrier's booking engine every 5 minutes from geographically distributed locations, measure latency percentiles and uptime, and publish monthly public scoreboard showing p50/p95/p99 latency and availability per carrier; attach automatic escalation: if p95 latency >3 seconds or availability <99% in a month, notify carrier CIO within 24 hours and escalate to steering group if unresolved in 15 business days
  • Conduct chaos-engineering tests at Months 18, 30, 42 (2028-04-12, 2029-04-12, 2030-04-12) simulating carrier endpoint failure, network partition and event-stream lag; verify that the distributed cache switches to scheduled-only within 30 seconds and that passengers are informed transparently; validate reconciliation platform recovery (no lost or duplicated transactions) when clearing system resumes operation
  • Run live pilots on one priority corridor (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) with 500–1,000 passengers; measure stale-seat booking failures (target <1%), graceful-degradation frequency (target <2% of searches fallback to scheduled-only), passenger satisfaction with fallback experience and reroute success rates; publish findings by Month 18 (2028-04-12) and adjust thresholds if needed

Responsible Parties

  • Distributed-systems architect (architecture design and validation)
  • Real-time platform team (SLA monitoring proxy, distributed cache deployment by Month 12 = 2027-10-12)
  • Carriers (achieve and maintain SLA targets: p95 latency <2 seconds, 99.5% availability)
  • Standards-working group (integrate SLA requirements and cache architecture into OSDM binding standards by Month 18 = 2028-04-12)
  • Programme Office (publish SLA scorecards, attach funding tranche penalties for SLA misses, trigger chaos-engineering tests)

Assumptions

  • High: A p95 latency of <2 seconds per carrier is achievable; legacy booking systems may not meet this target without infrastructure upgrades. If <70% of carriers achieve p95 <2 sec by Month 30 (2029-04-12), the combined three-leg SLA is unachievable and the programme must either (a) accept higher latency and lower through-ticket conversion, or (b) rely more heavily on cached shadow, which increases stale-seat failure risk.
  • High: A 99.5% combined three-leg availability is achievable with 99.83% per-carrier SLA, which is unrealistic without carrier infrastructure investment or redundancy; the actual achievable combined availability with 99.5% per-carrier SLA is ~98.5% (0.995^3), below the 99.5% target. The SLA target must be revised or passengers must accept scheduled-only fallback for ~1.5% of searches.
  • Medium: Passengers accept scheduled-only (no real-time pricing, no seat selection) as a fallback for ~1–2% of searches when a carrier is unavailable; if <50% of passengers accept scheduled-only fallback, through-ticket conversion drops by 5–10% (estimate) when fallbacks are frequent.
  • Medium: A distributed cache (Redis or equivalent) can be procured and operated at EUR 15–25M; if custom development is required, cost escalates and timeline extends beyond Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • High: Event-stream ordering and exactly-once delivery can be maintained across 25+ carriers using Kafka-like topology; if carriers experience >1% of events lost or duplicated, the availability shadow becomes unreliable and scheduled-only fallback frequency increases.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 6 (2027-04-12), publish a detailed architecture specification for the streamed availability shadow (cache architecture, stale-data TTL, fallback thresholds, event-stream ordering guarantees). By Month 12 (2027-10-12), deploy SLA monitoring synthetic probes and public scoreboard showing p50/p95/p99 latency and monthly availability per carrier. Establish p95 latency <2 seconds and 99.5% availability as binding SLA targets in conformance gate (Decision 6). Attach funding tranches to SLA performance: carriers missing SLA targets for two consecutive months lose 5% of their next funding tranche. Conduct chaos-engineering tests at Months 18, 30, 42 (2028-04-12, 2029-04-12, 2030-04-12) and validate graceful degradation to scheduled-only within 30 seconds. Run live pilots (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) achieving <1% stale-seat failure and <2% scheduled-only fallback frequency.

Notes

  • The p95 latency <2 seconds and 99.5% availability SLA targets are ambitious and may require carrier infrastructure investment beyond their private IT budget (EUR 1.5–3.0 billion estimate); confirm feasibility with carriers by Month 3 (2027-01-12) and revise targets if needed.
  • SLA monitoring is a critical lever for ensuring through-ticket reliability; public scorecards create transparency and market pressure for carrier compliance, but must be updated monthly and published without delay.
  • Graceful degradation to scheduled-only is a safety valve, not a solution; if >5% of searches trigger scheduled-only fallback, passengers will migrate to competitors and the through-ticket value proposition erodes.
  • Chaos-engineering tests at Months 18, 30, 42 (2028-04-12, 2029-04-12, 2030-04-12) are essential operational readiness gates; if tests fail (e.g., cache recovery takes >5 minutes, clearing platform loses transactions), remediation is mandatory before proceeding to the next tier or corridor.
  • Stale-seat and reconciliation errors are linked: if the availability shadow is too stale (>5 minutes), stale-seat failures cascade to clearing disputes when a passenger attempts to book a seat that was already sold by another distributor. Tolerance bands in reconciliation must account for this edge case.

6. Passenger Rights Legal Compliance and Accessibility Conformance Validation

Through-tickets must deliver passenger-rights protection equivalent to or better than single-operator services, or the programme violates Regulation 1371/2007 and exposes the Commission and carriers to enforcement actions and lawsuits. Accessibility (wheelchair spaces, assistance, multilingual information) must be designed into booking and rerouting flows early, not retrofitted post-launch. Complaints handling (target: halved distributor complaints by Month 60 = 2031-10-12) requires a professional staffed operation, not a secondary administrative task, to deliver credible passenger experience and regulatory compliance.

Data to Collect

  • Through-ticket passenger entitlements per EU Regulation 1371/2007: assistance, compensation, refunds, information rights, disability accommodation; comparison with single-carrier entitlements
  • Carrier accessibility resource inventory: wheelchair spaces available per service, assistance notice periods per carrier, bicycle spaces, accessibility of stations and vehicles
  • Baseline passenger complaints per corridor: complaint volume, categories (booking error, payment, disruption, refund, accessibility, lost luggage), resolution time, appeal outcomes per carrier
  • Multilingual user needs: passenger cohort breakdown by first language (EU member-state official languages), reading proficiency levels, sensory accessibility needs (screen reader, captions)
  • Existing passenger-rights compliance procedures in single-operator rail services to adapt for through-tickets

Simulation Steps

  • Map through-ticket passenger rights against Regulation 1371/2007 requirements in a compliance matrix: for each right (assistance, compensation, refunds, information, accessibility), specify: (1) what a single-operator passenger gets, (2) what a through-ticket passenger gets under the proposed programme design, (3) any gaps or disadvantages for through-ticket passengers. Highlight discrepancies and design adjustments needed.
  • Model accessibility scenarios: a wheelchair-using passenger books Paris–Amsterdam–Berlin through-ticket requiring assistance at station, wheelchair space on each leg, and accessible toilet facilities onboard; trace the atomic confirmation logic (Decision 10: reject itinerary if any leg lacks capacity) and show how many itineraries are rejected due to accessibility gaps; estimate accessibility availability under the proposed 80% wheelchair access and 90% assistance thresholds
  • Simulate complaints handling: baseline complaint volume (estimated 100–200 per corridor annually, sourced from CER data); segment by category (15% booking/payment, 30% disruption/rerouting, 20% refund, 20% accessibility, 15% other); model resolution time (target: 30 days for standard, 15 days for priority accessibility cases); estimate staffing (target: 40–60 FTE for complaints team serving four corridors)
  • Usability test scenarios with diverse passenger cohorts: (1) non-native speaker (test multilingual error messages, accessibility of help text at B1 CEFR reading level); (2) visually impaired (test screen-reader compatibility, high-contrast mode); (3) mobility-impaired (test assistance request flow, confirmation feedback); (4) elderly (test font size, clickability, layout clarity). Measure task completion rate and time-on-task for each cohort.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Commission an independent legal review by Month 1 (2026-11-12) from rail-passenger-rights counsel (e.g., European transport law specialists at university law clinics or transport law practices) to assess through-ticket design against Regulation 1371/2007 requirements; deliver opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-12) identifying any compliance gaps or required design adjustments
  • Engage disability-rights organisations (European Disability Forum (EDF), European Blind Union (EBU), Disability Equality Europe) and BEUC (consumer) as observers in a Passenger Rights Oversight Board starting Month 6 (2027-04-12); conduct quarterly reviews of compliance manual, accessibility audit findings, and complaints data
  • Conduct accessibility usability testing with 50+ passengers (≥15 with mobility/sensory disabilities, ≥15 non-native speakers) on wireframes of booking, assistance request and complaints flows at Months 4, 8, 14 (2027-02-12, 2027-06-12, 2027-12-12); iterate designs and test again before binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12)
  • Commission an independent accessibility audit of all four priority corridors (Month 6 = 2027-04-12) covering station and vehicle accessibility, staff training on PRM assistance, rolling-stock capacity; map gaps and develop carrier-specific remediation plans; make corridor go-live (Month 48 = 2030-10-12) conditional on meeting minimum accessibility thresholds (proposed: 80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours' notice)
  • Obtain formal approval from the EU Agency for Railways of the Passenger Rights Compliance Manual (Month 9 = 2027-07-12) and the Accessibility Audit (Month 9 = 2027-07-12); make these documents binding operational requirements for all carriers and the clearing entity

Responsible Parties

  • Independent passenger-rights legal counsel (Month 1 = 2026-11-12 to Month 6 = 2027-04-12)
  • Passenger Rights Lead role (develop compliance manual, lead accessibility audit, establish complaints handling)
  • EU Agency for Railways (approve compliance manual and accessibility audit)
  • Disability-rights and consumer organisations (quarterly oversight board participation, usability testing)
  • Carriers (implement accessibility improvements, staff training, compliance certification)
  • Clearing entity and public distributor concession (support complaints handling and accessibility features)

Assumptions

  • High: Through-ticket design can meet or exceed Regulation 1371/2007 entitlements without material cost escalation or schedule slip; if design gaps require significant rework (e.g., extending assistance notice period from 24 hours to 72 hours across all carriers), programme schedule slips 2–3 months.
  • High: Accessibility thresholds (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours) are achievable by Month 40 (2030-02-12) for the four priority corridors; carriers report that rolling-stock retrofits and staff training require 18–24 months. If <70% of services meet thresholds by Month 40 (2030-02-12), atomic confirmation (Decision 10) will reject 15–25% of itineraries, reducing through-ticket availability and passenger choice.
  • Medium: Complaints handling can be operationalised with 40–60 FTE and EUR 25–40M budget allocation; if complaints volume is 2–3x higher than baseline estimate (due to new system complexity, transition period friction), staffing scales to 80–100 FTE and cost escalates to EUR 50–75M, exceeding the EUR 100M consumer-rollout budget.
  • Medium: Disability-rights and consumer organisations will participate constructively in co-design and oversight starting Month 6 (2027-04-12); if organisations withhold endorsement due to design gaps or perceived tokenism, they may publicly oppose programme launch, triggering political and regulatory scrutiny.
  • Low: Multilingual usability testing with 50+ passengers is feasible within budget (EUR 50–100K estimate) and will yield actionable design revisions; if testing reveals widespread comprehension gaps in error messages or assistance flows, additional iteration (Month 14–18 = 2027-12-12 to 2028-04-12) may be required, compressing the final standards approval cycle.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 6 (2027-04-12), obtain independent legal opinion confirming that through-ticket passenger rights meet or exceed Regulation 1371/2007 entitlements; identify any gaps and publish required design adjustments. By Month 9 (2027-07-12), publish a Passenger Rights Compliance Manual approved by the EU Agency for Railways and an Accessibility Audit of all four priority corridors with carrier-specific remediation plans. Establish accessibility thresholds (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours) as conditions of corridor go-live (Month 48 = 2030-10-12). Conduct usability testing with 50+ passengers (≥15 disabled, ≥15 non-native speakers) at Months 4, 8, 14 (2027-02-12, 2027-06-12, 2027-12-12) and achieve >85% task completion rate for all cohorts. Establish a Passenger Rights Oversight Board (Agency, disability-rights and consumer organisations) meeting quarterly starting Month 6 (2027-04-12) to audit compliance and complaints trends.

Notes

  • The Passenger Rights Compliance Manual is a binding operational document; all carriers must certify staff training to its procedures as a precondition of conformance (Decision 6) by Month 30 (2029-04-12).
  • Atomic confirmation of accessibility and bicycle spaces (Decision 10) will visibly reduce through-ticket availability if carriers lack capacity; expect 10–20% itinerary rejection (estimate) initially. Design must include fallback options (best-effort booking with compensation, manual assistance by staff) or passengers will prefer single-operator bookings.
  • Complaints handling is a critical service-level metric; if resolution time exceeds 30 days for 30%+ of cases, the target of 'halved complaints by Month 60 (2031-10-12)' is unachievable. Staffing and systems must scale dynamically.
  • Multilingual information design requires professional translation and localization (not machine translation); budget EUR 50–100K for professional translation of key passenger information into at least 18 EU official languages and testing at B1 CEFR reading level.
  • Accessibility audit (Month 6 = 2027-04-12) must feed into corridor-specific remediation plans with cost, timeline and responsibility assigned to each carrier. Make audit results public (anonymised per GDPR) to create transparency and market pressure for compliance.

Summary

This project plan establishes six critical data-collection and validation workstreams for an EU cross-border rail through-ticketing programme targeting 40% of cross-border journeys within EUR 1.5 billion public budget by Month 60 (2031-10-12). The six most sensitive areas—carrier liability pricing (high sensitivity: determines participation), technical system integration (high sensitivity: determines schedule feasibility), competition-law clearance (high sensitivity: determines clearing design viability), clearing and settlement mechanism (high sensitivity: determines financial backbone), real-time availability architecture (high sensitivity: determines search reliability), and passenger-rights compliance (high sensitivity: determines regulatory risk)—must all proceed in parallel Months 0–6 (2026-10-12 to 2027-04-12) to unblock the Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate. The most urgent immediate actions are: (1) Commission the actuarial study by Month 1 (2026-11-12) and deliver interim carrier feedback by Month 4 (2027-02-12) to obtain carrier sign-off; (2) conduct the technical audit by Month 2 (2026-12-12) and publish tier assignments by Month 6 (2027-04-12); (3) file DG COMP pre-notification by Month 2 (2026-12-12) and secure guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12); (4) establish steering governance with 75% supermajority voting by Month 1 (2026-11-12) and hold binding votes on Decisions 1–5 by Month 6 (2027-04-12); (5) rebase the EUR 1.5 billion budget with variance triggers (EUR 100M, EUR 200M, EUR 300M) and publish monthly cash-flow forecasts starting Month 1 (2026-11-12); (6) commission passenger-rights legal review by Month 1 (2026-11-12) and obtain Agency approval of compliance manual by Month 9 (2027-07-12). If any of these workstreams slip past their gate (Month 4 = 2027-02-12 for liability, Month 6 = 2027-04-12 for audit and steering votes, Month 12 = 2027-10-12 for DG COMP guidance), the binding-standards milestone (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) is at risk and the entire timeline compresses or defers to Month 12 (2027-10-12) contingency.

Documents to Create

Create Document 1: Project Charter

ID: 7d4cb30a-54ae-41ca-bd17-9f8a314f0623

Description: Foundational governance document establishing programme authority, scope, objectives (40% through-ticket share, halved complaints by Month 60 = 2031-10-12), stakeholders, success criteria, and decision-making structure. Defines Programme Director accountability, steering group composition (75% supermajority rule) and escalation paths to Commission. Primary audience: EU institutions, carriers, distributors, national regulators.

Responsible Role Type: Programme Director

Primary Template: PMI Project Charter Template

Secondary Template: EU institutional project charter (sample from DG MOVE prior programmes)

Steps to Create:

  • Workshop with DG MOVE leadership and CER to define charter scope and success criteria by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27)
  • Draft charter covering authority, stakeholder roles, decision rights and escalation by Month 1 (2026-11-12)
  • Obtain signed approval from DG MOVE Director-General, EU Agency for Railways Director and CER President by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27)
  • Publish and distribute to all 25+ carriers and steering group members; archive with Commission

Approval Authorities: DG MOVE Director-General, EU Agency for Railways Director, CER President, European Commission Transport Commissioner (if escalated for mediation)

Essential Information:

  • Define the Programme Director's authority, delegation limits and accountability for delivery of the 40% through-ticket target and EUR 1,500M budget cap by Month 60 (2031-10-12).
  • Specify steering group composition (biweekly meetings, 75% supermajority voting rule on Decisions 1–3 and 12), member roles and escalation paths to the Commission Transport Commissioner for deadlock resolution.
  • Establish decision-making authority: which decisions require steering votes (liability backstop, clearing architecture, public distributor mandate, remuneration band), which require Commission approval, and the binding-vote deadlines (Month 6 = 2027-04-12 for Phase 1 gate).
  • Articulate the programme's scope: federated settlement, streamed availability shadow, carrier-funded guarantee pool, last-resort concession; excluded: central inventory exchange, public pay-first fund, full consumer app.
  • Define success metrics: 40% through-ticket share, distributor complaints halved, binding standards Month 18 (2028-04-12), Tier 1 API exposure Month 30 (2029-04-12), four-corridor go-live Month 48 (2030-10-12), public spend within EUR 1,500M.
  • Detail the governance model: Programme Office (80 staff, DG MOVE) and Technical Secretariat (50 staff, Agency, Valenciennes); liaison officers in Brussels, Valenciennes, Berlin, Madrid; external advisory board for oversight.
  • State the risk-escalation framework: budget variance triggers (EUR 100M/200M/300M) and remediation actions; deferral of TEN-T extension or concession funding cuts; no pool draw-downs after Month 36 (2029-10-12).
  • Clarify stakeholder roles: which parties control which decisions (carriers: liability model sign-off; DG COMP: Article 101 guidance; steering: binding votes on Decisions 1–3, 12; regulators: observer seats).
  • Specify document governance: how the charter is approved (by DG MOVE DG, Agency Director, CER President), published and archived; how amendments are handled.
  • Outline Phase 1 readiness gate (Month 6 = 2027-04-12): liability model signed by 8+ major carriers, technical audit published, steering votes held; escalation triggers for Month 9 (2027-07-12) and Month 12 (2027-10-12) if unresolved.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous Programme Director authority or steering voting rule delays critical decisions (liability, clearing, distributor role) by 1–2 months, cascading to binding-standards deadline (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) and triggering 2–4 month slip to Months 20–22 (2028-06-12 to 2028-08-12), which compresses Phase 2 conformance work.
  • Stakeholder roles unclear: carriers unsure whether they must sign liability model or can block via CER, distributors uncertain of their rights, regulators unclear on observer scope. Results in steering deadlock, withdrawal of major participants (e.g., Trainline rejecting clearing design), and loss of 15–25% of through-ticket volume (estimate).
  • Escalation path undefined: when deadlock occurs (e.g., CER refuses liability caps, BEUC demands stronger rights), no clear path to Commission mediation leaves the governance loop stuck for 3–6 months.
  • Budget variance triggers absent or loose: concession overruns or adapter acceleration (EUR 150–250M, estimate) are not met with clear corrective action, leading to ad-hoc Commission approval requests, audit findings and erosion of stakeholder confidence.
  • Phase 1 readiness gate vague: no explicit decision on what 'signed liability model' means, which carriers constitute binding supermajority, or what happens if only 5–7 carriers sign (instead of 8+). Results in false starts, rework and delay.
  • Scope ambiguity: whether the programme includes a full public consumer app, a sandbox, or a last-resort concession not clearly stated in the charter. Causes competing implementation efforts, budget conflict and competing stakeholder expectations.
  • No charter publication or distribution mechanism: if the charter is not formally signed and published by Month 1 (2026-11-12), institutional clarity is missing, carriers and distributors lack a reference document, and the programme lacks legal grounding for enforcement of milestone conditions.

Worst Case Scenario: The charter is drafted without clear decision-making authority, voting rules or escalation paths. The steering group is convened at Month 2 (2026-12-12) but within two weeks, CER and large carriers disagree on liability-model caps; BEUC and disability bodies demand stronger passenger-rights guarantees; and Trainline and Omio object to the clearing architecture, claiming competition-law risk. With no formal supermajority rule or Commission mediation clause, the steering group becomes deadlocked. The Programme Director cannot force a vote or escalate. By Month 9 (2027-07-12), no binding decisions have been made on liability, clearing or the public distributor mandate. DG MOVE escalates to the Transport Commissioner, who convenes an emergency working group. The binding-standards milestone (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) slips 4–6 months to Months 22–24 (2028-08-12 to 2028-10-12). Mandatory API exposure (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) becomes unachievable; the mandatory milestone date passes with only Tier 1 carriers (8–10 large operators) ready, leaving 15–17 smaller and regional carriers outside. The four-corridor go-live (planned Month 48 = 2030-10-12) is delayed to Month 60 (2031-10-12) at best. The 40% through-ticket target is downgraded to 20–25% (estimate). TEN-T extension is deferred beyond the five-year horizon. Member states and carriers lose confidence; regulatory appetite for mandatory API exposure weakens; the programme ends with a 'lessons learned' review and significantly reduced ambition.

Best Case Scenario: The charter is signed by the DG MOVE Director-General, EU Agency for Railways Director, CER President and Commission Transport Commissioner by Month 1 (2026-11-12). It clearly specifies Programme Director authority, the 75% supermajority steering voting rule, binding-decision deadlines and escalation paths to the Commissioner. Steering group meets for the first time Week 1 of Month 2 (2026-12-12), with biweekly cadence thereafter. An option paper for each critical decision is published by Month 2 (2026-12-12), signalling the three alternatives and trade-offs to all stakeholders. By Month 3 (2027-01-12), the technical audit is complete and tier assignments are visible. The liability actuarial study interim report is published. At the Month 4–5 (2027-02-12 to 2027-03-12) steering meetings, carriers negotiate and 10 major carriers sign the liability-model framework with agreed caps and co-insurance thresholds. DG COMP feedback on Article 101 has arrived (Month 12 = 2027-10-12), indicating clean-team clearing is acceptable. At Month 6 (2027-04-12), the steering group votes: Decisions 1–3 and 12 all pass with 8–9 of 9 core members in favour. The technical audit is published. The charter is formally filed with the European Court of Auditors. Binding standards are delivered by Month 18 (2028-04-12) on schedule. Tier 1 API exposure is achieved by Month 30 (2029-04-12). Four-corridor through-ticketing goes live by Month 48 (2030-10-12). The 40% through-ticket target is on track. Carriers and distributors cite the charter's clarity and decision rules as enabling their investment. The programme is heralded as a model for multi-stakeholder EU infrastructure coordination.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Adopt a faster charter-approval pathway: convene a single working session with the DG MOVE Director-General, Agency Director and CER President by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27); present a pre-drafted charter with decision authority, voting rule and escalation path already in place (drawn from a template of prior EU rail programmes); seek their written sign-off by email within one week; publish by Month 1 (2026-11-12). This reduces workshop time from one week to one day.
  • If CER or carriers formally object to supermajority voting, offer a consensus-plus rule: require binding decisions to pass with 75% supermajority (7 of 9 core members) for Decisions 1–3 (liability, clearing, distributor), but allow bilateral fallback agreements for individual carriers on specific terms; this preserves the binding decision for the baseline but allows opt-outs, reducing stakes and objections.
  • If stakeholder alignment is uncertain by Month 3 (2027-01-12), establish a temporary Steering Working Group (Month 3–5 = 2027-01-12 to 2027-03-12) with smaller, focused task teams on each decision (liability team, clearing team, remuneration team), feeding weekly progress to the steering group; this gives stakeholders a voice and shortens decision cycles from 1 month to 1 week per team.
  • If the Commission Transport Commissioner cannot commit time for mediation, delegate escalation to the Agency's Board of Stakeholders (a standing body with regulator and carrier representatives) and require the Agency Director to resolve any 2–2 split on a core decision within two weeks, with options papers forcing a choice rather than debate.
  • If phase-gate readiness cannot be met by Month 6 (2027-04-12), schedule a 'soft gate' at Month 6 (2027-04-12) with public go/no-go communicated, but allow a 3-month contingency phase (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-12 to 2027-07-12) for final negotiations on any decision not yet signed, deferring binding standards from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 21 (2028-07-12) (estimate) only if absolutely required.
  • If the charter cannot be formally approved by the Transport Commissioner due to political constraints, issue a Commission Decision or formal Letter from the Director-General of DG MOVE (rather than a charter) that states the same authorities, voting rule and escalation paths, with the same legal force but lower bureaucratic friction.

Create Document 2: Carrier Liability and Rights Backstop Model (Actuarial Specification)

ID: a5455000-dd85-4e1c-a8df-38ac7a07c015

Description: Technical actuarial specification defining the carrier-funded mutual guarantee pool: per-incident caps, co-insurance thresholds, contribution-weighting formula tied to trailing on-time performance, reserve adequacy analysis and quarterly pool-monitoring procedures. Based on 24-month historical missed-connection and rerouting-cost data from at least 5 major carriers. Output: binding liability terms that carriers sign off to expose inventory. Primary audience: CER, 25+ national operators, DG MOVE, Finance lead.

Responsible Role Type: Actuary / Carrier Liability Specialist

Primary Template: Actuarial valuation report (Insurance Directorate standard)

Secondary Template: Financial model template (Excel sensitivity analysis, Monte Carlo simulation for loss clustering)

Steps to Create:

  • Engage independent actuarial firm by Month 1 (2026-11-12) with 90-day delivery target
  • Collect 24-month missed-connection, rerouting-cost and incident-clustering data from SNCF, DB, SBB, Renfe, ÖBB and one smaller operator by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27)
  • Analyse data to derive baseline incident frequencies, cost distributions and carrier-specific risk profiles by Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Develop three sensitivity scenarios (conservative, base, aggressive) for cap levels (EUR 250-2,000 per passenger) and co-insurance triggers (EUR 20M-100M annual draw) by Month 2.5 (2026-12-27)
  • Produce final recommendations with worked examples for three carrier profiles (large, regional, small) and confidence intervals by Month 3 (2027-01-12)
  • Present model to CER and 10+ major carriers for written feedback by Month 4 (2027-02-12); obtain binding sign-off from at least 8 major carriers and CER by Month 4 (2027-02-12)
  • Establish quarterly pool-monitoring process (publish incident rates, contribution adjustments, drawdowns within 15 business days of quarter-end) starting Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • Revalidate model quarterly; adjust parameters if actual rates diverge >20% from forecast

Approval Authorities: CER, at least 8 major carriers (binding written letters of intent), Programme Director, DG MOVE Commissioner

Essential Information:

  • Specify the carrier-funded mutual guarantee pool structure: per-incident cap (EUR 500–1,000 per stranded passenger, proposed threshold), co-insurance trigger (EUR 50M annual draw, proposed threshold), and contribution-weighting formula tied to trailing 12-month on-time performance.
  • Quantify baseline missed-connection frequencies, rerouting costs and incident clustering from 24-month historical data from at least 5 major carriers (SNCF, DB, SBB, Renfe, ÖBB, one smaller operator).
  • Model three sensitivity scenarios (conservative, base, aggressive) for cap levels and co-insurance triggers using Monte Carlo simulation for loss clustering, with confidence intervals at p50, p75 and p95.
  • Develop worked examples showing pool contributions and drawdown profiles for three carrier profiles: large (>10% network share), regional (2–10%) and small (<2%), demonstrating predictability of exposure.
  • Establish quarterly pool-monitoring procedures: defined incident-rate reporting, contribution-adjustment triggers, reserve-drawdown approvals and publication timelines (within 15 business days of quarter-end).
  • Specify the decision rule for reserve exhaustion and escalation: what happens if actual incident rates exceed forecast by >20% in a quarter; trigger for public reinsurance or cap adjustment.
  • Calculate the reserve adequacy for the carrier-funded pool under force-majeure scenarios (single-day corridor-wide disruption affecting >5,000 passengers) and identify the ceiling beyond which public top-up occurs.
  • Define the liability recourse mechanism: how the pool recovers costs from a carrier whose delay caused a missed connection; specify the API, data requirements and dispute-resolution timeline.
  • Produce a binding liability-terms summary (2–3 pages) that carriers will sign off to expose inventory; include risk allocation, contribution calculation, payout rules and quarterly review cycle.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Vague or asymmetric caps and co-insurance rules leave carriers unable to price their participation, triggering 30–40% carrier refusal and fragmenting the through-ticket network by Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • Actuarial model based on <24 months of data or fewer than 5 major carriers understates loss clustering risk; actual pool drawdowns exceed forecast by 50–100% in year 2–3, exhausting the EUR 150M force-majeure reserve by Month 36 (2029-10-12).
  • Poorly defined quarterly monitoring procedures leave incident rates and contributions opaque; carriers dispute share calculations, delaying payouts by 30–60 days and reducing distributor confidence in the pool's creditworthiness.
  • Absence of a clear recourse mechanism allows a chronically late-running carrier to avoid contribution increases, subsidising pool payouts across all participants and creating unfair incentives.
  • Sensitivity analysis limited to point estimates (no confidence intervals) gives false certainty; actual volatility emerges at Month 30 (2029-04-12) when the pool is live, forcing emergency redesign and 6–12 month rework.
  • Missing escalation rules for reserve exhaustion leave the Commission unable to decide whether to top up the pool or trigger cap adjustments; policy deadlock delaying compensation payouts by months.

Worst Case Scenario: The actuarial study underestimates incident-clustering risk by relying on 12 months of data instead of 24, or excludes smaller carriers' higher disruption rates from the sample. At Month 30 (2029-04-12), when the pool goes live, actual missed-connection rates are 50–100% higher than forecast. Pool drawdowns climb to EUR 80–120M in the first 12 months (Months 30–42 = 2029-04-12 to 2030-04-12), rapidly exhausting the EUR 150M force-majeure reserve. By Month 42 (2030-04-12), the Commission faces a choice: top up the pool from remaining EUR 1,500M budget, which starves later-wave TEN-T corridor funding, or cut carrier caps by 40–50%, which triggers new disputes and carrier demands for contract renegotiation. Carriers who signed based on the flawed model sue for release from through-ticket obligations. The programme's credibility collapses, reducing participation from 25+ to ~12 carriers. The 40% through-ticket goal falls to 10–15%, and the four-corridor go-live slips from Month 48 (2030-10-12) to Month 60 (2031-10-12). The programme is seen as fundamentally broken.

Best Case Scenario: An independent actuarial firm completes a rigorous 24-month historical-data analysis of all major carriers plus two smaller operators by Month 3 (2027-01-12), with Monte Carlo modelling revealing realistic loss-clustering patterns and per-carrier risk profiles. The draft liability model specifies symmetric caps (EUR 750 per passenger, proposed threshold) and a co-insurance threshold (EUR 50M annual draw, proposed threshold) that carriers can price into inventory decisions. At least 8 major carriers and CER sign binding letters of intent by Month 4 (2027-02-12), confirming they will expose inventory if the model holds. Quarterly monitoring procedures are clear: incident rates published within 15 days, contributions adjusted quarterly based on trailing performance, and the reserve remains untouched through Month 48 (2030-10-12). This enables the Programme Director to take the liability decision to the steering group on schedule at Month 6 (2027-04-12), unblocking the binding-standards milestone. Carrier confidence in the pool's fairness drives 25+ participants to expose seats by Month 30 (2029-04-12). The four-corridor through-ticket network reaches 35–40% penetration by Month 48 (2030-10-12), meeting the headline target.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the independent actuarial study cannot be completed by Month 3 (2027-01-12) due to data availability or firm capacity constraints, commission a rapid Monte Carlo analysis using synthetic loss distributions calibrated to the 2019–2023 UNIFE rail incident database and regulator-published delay statistics by Month 2.5 (2026-12-27); use a conservative upper-percentile (p95) estimate for the cap and co-insurance trigger, accepting higher cost to ensure buffer headroom.
  • If fewer than 5 major carriers provide 24-month granular incident data, establish a data-sharing agreement with national regulators who hold historical disruption logs; use cross-operator aggregates to derive loss-clustering parameters, deferring carrier-specific risk profiles to the quarterly monitoring phase.
  • If carrier sign-off deadlocks at Month 4 (2027-02-12) due to divergent risk appetites (some carriers want lower caps, others higher), publish three binding liability variants in the standards (conservative, base, aggressive) and let each carrier choose its tier at Month 6 (2027-04-12); charge premium contributions for low-cap tiers and require higher-cap carriers to contribute more, so the pool remains balanced by choice.
  • If disputes over the recourse mechanism emerge (e.g., how to assign causality for a delay), establish a three-tier dispute-resolution path: (1) automated reconciliation if incident data is clear; (2) bilateral mediation between carriers within 10 business days; (3) binding arbitration by an independent transport industry arbiter, with costs split between disputing carriers, reducing the need for pre-agreed rules and allowing iterative case law to develop.
  • If the force-majeure reserve proves insufficient by Month 36 (2029-10-12), trigger an immediate policy review: establish a EUR 50–100M supplementary grant from the European Union Cohesion or Recovery budgets (if available) as a one-time top-up, conditional on carriers accepting a 5–10% contribution increase in the following year and committing to resilience investments (e.g., redundant links, faster crew repositioning).

Create Document 3: Inter-Carrier Clearing and Settlement Rulebook (Federated Netting Architecture)

ID: ddb801e9-c11f-4ed8-8d22-311cd3e64a08

Description: Definitive specification of the federated clearing layer: multilateral netting model (bilateral, multilateral, or hybrid per corridor), settlement currency (EUR), reconciliation cycle (5 business days), journal entry standard (ISO 20022 XML mapping), dispute escalation procedure, penalty regime and payout schedule. Includes worked examples of three-leg through-tickets showing revenue allocation and carrier payouts. Resolves critical ambiguities: who receives the passenger payment, how positions are netted per leg and per distributor, and how disputes over carrier share are arbitrated. Primary audience: carriers' finance teams, clearing specialist, competition-law counsel, DG COMP.

Responsible Role Type: Clearing and Settlement Systems Architect

Primary Template: Banking/payment system settlement specification (ISO 20022 messaging standard)

Secondary Template: Rail Settlement Plan (RSP) clearing rulebook (GB precedent, adapted for EU federated model)

Steps to Create:

  • Establish dedicated Clearing Design Workstream by Month 1 (2026-11-12) reporting to steering group
  • Define netting model (bilateral, multilateral, or hybrid) and prepare position papers on trade-offs (control vs. complexity, bilateral familiarity vs. multilateral efficiency) by Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Specify settlement data format (ISO 20022 XML) with full journal entry mapping, per-transaction fields and required metadata by Month 3 (2027-01-12)
  • Model worked examples (Paris-Amsterdam-Berlin, Wien-München-Zürich, Madrid-Barcelona-Lyon three-leg itineraries) showing commission splits, refund reversals and carrier payouts by Month 4 (2027-02-12)
  • Workshop with carriers' finance leads and the clearing architect to validate netting logic and payout timing by Month 5 (2027-03-12)
  • Publish final Rulebook with all appendices (reconciliation tolerance bands, dispute escalation, penalty schedule, payout SLAs) by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • Submit to DG COMP as part of binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12); obtain Agency approval by Month 12 (2027-10-12)

Approval Authorities: Clearing Design Workstream (carriers + Programme Office), Programme Director, EU Agency for Railways, DG COMP (for competition-law review)

Essential Information:

  • Definitive specification of the federated multilateral netting model: clarify whether netting is bilateral per carrier pair, multilateral across all legs, or hybrid per corridor, with explicit trade-off analysis (control vs. complexity, existing bilateral familiarity vs. efficiency gains).
  • Settlement currency (EUR confirmed), reconciliation cycle (5 business days target), and journal entry standard (ISO 20022 XML mapping with full field list and required metadata per transaction).
  • Revenue allocation formula: specify how a single through-ticket payment is split among carriers per leg, how commissions are deducted, and how refunds are reversed across carriers in real time.
  • Worked examples of three actual priority-corridor itineraries (Paris–Amsterdam–Berlin, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon) showing step-by-step netting, payout timing and commission handling for a full round-trip through-ticket with a missed connection and subsequent reroute.
  • Dispute escalation procedure: define thresholds for automatic reconciliation (tolerance bands, error types), manual review triggers, carrier-to-carrier arbitration process, and escalation to the clearing entity or regulator.
  • Penalty regime: specify financial consequences and tranche hold-backs for carriers exceeding reconciliation error thresholds (proposed: >1% monthly error rate loses 5% of next funding tranche), settlement delays (>5 business days) and data-format non-compliance.
  • Payout schedule: confirm settlement windows (T+5 business days proposed), exceptions for refunds or disputed amounts, and payment-service-provider integration requirements.
  • Reconciliation tolerance bands: quantify acceptable variance per transaction type (seat sales, refunds, commission corrections, cancellations) and aggregate monthly thresholds before escalation.
  • Competition-law risk statement: confirm that the netting model and data flows comply with Article 101 TFEU as advised by DG COMP, with reference to the clean-team protocol and segregation of commercially sensitive data.
  • Governance and change control: specify who approves changes to the rulebook post-binding standards (the Agency with carrier consensus, or the clearing entity unilaterally), and how emergency operational adjustments are handled.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous netting model leaves carriers unable to forecast their payouts from multi-leg through-tickets, causing refusal to expose inventory and blocking the mandatory API exposure milestone (Month 30 = 2029-04-12).
  • Inconsistent ISO 20022 field mapping or missing required metadata causes reconciliation mismatches of 2–5% (estimate), extending settlement cycles from 5 to 10–15 business days and deterring distributor participation by 15–20% (estimate).
  • Unclear dispute escalation thresholds and penalties result in carriers and distributors contesting every stale-seat or refund reversal, overwhelming dispute-resolution capacity and delaying payouts by 2–4 weeks (estimate), which triggers cash-flow complaints and reduces through-ticket volume.
  • Vague revenue allocation formula invites carrier disputes over fair share; without worked examples, 3–4 major carriers challenge the rulebook post-launch, requiring Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12) rework and a 3–6 month delay in full-corridor go-live.
  • Missing payout schedule or payment-service-provider integration requirements delay payouts to distributors and carriers, creating operational friction and reducing confidence in the clearing layer by 20–30% (estimate).
  • Failure to address competition-law compliance explicitly leaves the rulebook legally vulnerable to Article 101 TFEU challenge post-adoption (Month 24–36 = 2028-10-12 to 2029-10-12), forcing 3–12 month rework (estimated cost EUR 50–100M) and restructuring of data flows.
  • Unclear change-control governance allows unilateral clearing-entity modifications to netting or penalty rules without carrier consent, eroding trust and triggering legal disputes or partial carrier withdrawal.
  • Absence of force-majeure provisions (e.g., how to handle a single-day corridor-wide disruption affecting 10,000+ passengers) leaves the pool exposed to unpredictable drains and forces emergency public funding (up to EUR 50–100M estimate) not budgeted as operational cost.

Worst Case Scenario: If the rulebook is incomplete, legally opaque or operationally ambiguous at binding-standards approval (Month 18 = 2028-04-12), carriers will not commit real-time inventory to the federated clearing layer. This triggers either full network non-participation (5–10 major carriers refuse to expose seats, reducing coverage to isolated regional routes) or a 6–12 month post-binding rework, cascading the mandatory API exposure milestone from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12). Estimated outcome: the 40% through-ticket goal is unachievable; realistic through-ticket share falls to 15–25% (estimate), confined to 4–6 priority corridors instead of the full TEN-T network by Month 60 (2031-10-12). The programme loses EUR 200–400M of budget value and faces political pressure to extend the completion deadline to Month 72–84 (2032-10-12 to 2033-10-12), undermining the five-year delivery promise.

Best Case Scenario: A complete, legally vetted rulebook approved by DG COMP and signed by all steering-group carriers by Month 6 (2027-04-12) enables carriers to price their through-ticket exposure, commit inventory and finance their API adapters with confidence. Clear netting logic and worked examples allow independent distributors to integrate with the clearing layer without legal or operational uncertainty. Reconciliation standards set to <0.5% error and 5-business-day settlement create payout predictability that attracts both large and small distributors to the platform. By Month 30 (2029-04-12), all Tier 1 carriers (15–18 operators) expose live inventory; by Month 48 (2030-10-12), the four priority corridors deliver through-ticketing at 35–45% share (estimate), and the platform becomes self-reinforcing as more distributors invest in search and booking features. The programme demonstrates proof of concept on the priority corridors and achieves the full 40% through-ticket target across TEN-T by Month 60 (2031-10-12).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If consensus on a single multilateral netting model is not reached by Month 3 (2027-01-12), publish two parallel rulebooks: one for bilateral settlement (carriers pair-wise, clearing entity nets positions daily) and one for multilateral (all legs together). Allow carriers to choose their preferred method and corridor; start Tier 1 deployment with bilateral (simpler, faster) and migrate to multilateral after Month 42 (2030-04-12) once operational confidence is established.
  • If ISO 20022 full-field mapping cannot be specified by Month 4 (2027-02-12) due to carrier IT system constraints, adopt a phased standard: Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding includes a minimal subset of mandatory fields (transaction ID, carrier, leg, fare, commission, refund flag), and a 'OSDM XML+CSV fallback' for legacy systems that cannot produce full ISO 20022. Commit to full convergence by Month 36 (2029-10-12).
  • If worked examples for all three corridors cannot be completed by Month 5 (2027-03-12) due to carrier data constraints, publish one detailed end-to-end example (e.g., Paris–Amsterdam–Berlin) with step-by-step reconciliation, and defer the other two to Month 6 (2027-04-12) as annexes. Conduct a live pilot walkthrough with 10–20 transactions per corridor at Months 12–18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) to validate the logic operationally before binding.
  • If DG COMP competition-law clearance is not confirmed by Month 12 (2027-10-12), implement a clean-team protocol: the clearing entity operates behind a data firewall and releases only aggregated netting results (per-carrier payout, total throughput) to participants, not individual transaction flows. This reduces competition-law exposure and allows binding standards to proceed; detailed transaction data remains confidential within the clearing entity.
  • If carrier consensus on penalty thresholds (error rates, settlement delays) is not reached by Month 5 (2027-03-12), establish a 'learning curve' period: Months 30–36 (2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12) are operated with no penalties, only performance reporting. Activate penalty regime from Month 36 (2029-10-12) onwards once carriers have proven compliance capabilities and settled operational bugs.

Create Document 4: OSDM Binding Standards Specification (Federated Through-Ticketing Profile)

ID: 23f8ef58-1a31-4d53-93d7-8f0cb4b772e6

Description: Canonical OSDM version pinned by delegated act specifying all APIs, data structures and conformance rules required for federated through-ticketing across the four priority corridors. Includes profiles for availability query, booking, ticketing, refunds, accessibility metadata (wheelchair, assistance, bicycle spaces), multilingual support (≥18 EU languages), settlement data submission, ticket validation (barcode/credential format) and disruption event notification. Incorporates competition-law and GDPR constraints identified in binding standards workstream. Primary audience: carriers' CIOs, distributors, conformance testers, EU institutions.

Responsible Role Type: Standards & Technical Specification Custodian (at the EU Agency for Railways)

Primary Template: UIC OSDM Specification (reference implementation, versioned)

Secondary Template: W3C/OASIS API specification template (OpenAPI 3.0 or similar)

Steps to Create:

  • Commission standards writing group by Month 1 (2026-11-12) comprising OSDM community, 3-4 major carriers, 2 distributors and Agency technical staff; meet biweekly
  • Consolidate binding standards requirements from all five critical decisions (liability, clearing, public distributor, funding ladder, availability topology) into one specification by Month 9 (2027-07-12)
  • Publish option papers on critical API design points (federated vs. central inventory, netting engine format, refund reversal semantics) by Month 6 (2027-04-12); hold written consultation among carriers by Month 9 (2027-07-12)
  • Draft OSDM binding-standards profile incorporating: availability query (federated, with shadow caching), booking (carrier authority), settlement data submission (ISO 20022), ticket validation (credential format), accessibility metadata, multilingual payloads, disruption events and refund reversal; include conformance test suite by Month 15 (2028-01-12)
  • Obtain DG COMP clearance and competition-law counsel review by Month 12 (2027-10-12); incorporate any required clean-team protocols or data-minimisation constraints by Month 14 (2027-12-12)
  • Finalise binding-standards text and submit to Commission for delegated-act drafting by Month 18 (2028-04-12); target publication in Official Journal by Month 20 (2028-06-12)

Approval Authorities: EU Agency for Railways (Standards Custodian), DG MOVE, DG COMP, European Commission (delegated act), CER (stakeholder consultation)

Essential Information:

  • Specify the complete OSDM API surface required for federated through-ticketing: availability query (federated endpoints with shadow caching), booking (carrier authority), settlement data submission (ISO 20022 format or equivalent), ticket validation (barcode/credential format), accessibility metadata (wheelchair spaces, assistance notice periods, bicycle capacity), and disruption event notification.
  • Define the conformance test suite: test cases for latency (<2 seconds p95 per query), availability (≥99.5%), stale-seat error rates (<1%), multilingual payload support (≥18 EU languages), settlement data format validation, accessibility metadata completeness, and ticket validation handshake interoperability.
  • Incorporate all binding-standards requirements from the five critical decisions: liability backstop data fields (incident reporting, reroute cost attribution), clearing settlement message formats (federated netting, EUR-denominated, 5-business-day cycle), public distributor interface (query and booking API), funding-ladder verification fields (API availability attestation, booking-error rates per carrier).
  • Detail the competition-law and data-protection constraints: identify which data flows require clean-team separation, which payloads must be aggregated or anonymised per GDPR, and which API designs minimise commercially sensitive information exposure (e.g., federated inventory vs. centralised exchange implications for Article 101 TFEU).
  • Establish the versioning and change-control process: publication timeline (target Official Journal Month 20 = 2028-06-12), version numbering, deprecation policy for legacy API versions, and escalation rules for competition-law or passenger-rights changes post-binding.
  • Quantify the technical scope: count the APIs (availability, booking, refund, settlement, disruption, validation, accessibility), payloads per API, multilingual variations, test cases per API (estimate: 50–100 test cases per major API), and integration effort per carrier tier (Tier 1: 600–800 person-days, Tier 2: 800–1,200, Tier 3: 1,200–1,800, estimate).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous or incomplete API definitions leave carriers unable to implement compliant systems by Month 30 (2029-04-12) mandatory exposure; 8–15 smaller operators miss the deadline by 6–12 months, fragmenting corridor coverage and reducing through-ticket volume by 20–30% (estimate).
  • Absent or weak competition-law constraints (e.g., no data-minimisation rules for shared inventory or clearing) trigger a DG COMP challenge post-Month 18 (2028-04-12), forcing EUR 50–100M rework and 6–12 month redesign delay (estimate), and potentially unwinding carrier investments.
  • Incomplete accessibility metadata definitions (e.g., no standard for wheelchair-space representation across carriers) prevent atomic booking confirmation; itineraries without spaces are refused, lowering through-ticket availability by 10–15% (estimate) and creating legal exposure under EU Regulation 1371/2007 and the Accessibility Directive.
  • Missing or unclear settlement data formats (e.g., no standard for refund-reversal messaging) cause reconciliation errors >2%, lengthening settlement cycles from 5 to 10–15 business days; 15–20% of distributors withdraw due to cash-flow friction, reducing through-ticket volume by 10–15% (estimate).
  • Failure to specify the federated vs. central inventory architecture clearly allows carriers and distributors to interpret the standard differently; this leads to incompatible implementations and multi-quarter rework by Month 30–36 (2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12).
  • Absent test-suite rigor (e.g., no latency or availability test cases) permits carriers to claim conformance while delivering systems that fail in production; through-ticket success rates drop from 90% to 70–80% (estimate), eroding the commercial value proposition.

Worst Case Scenario: A binding-standards specification that is incomplete, ambiguous on critical APIs (availability, booking, settlement), or silent on competition-law and accessibility constraints could result in: (1) 40–50% (estimate) of smaller carriers unable to implement by Month 30 (2029-04-12), forcing the mandatory API exposure milestone to slip to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12) and reducing participating carriers from 25 to ~15; (2) A DG COMP Article 101 TFEU challenge within 6–12 months of publication, triggered by data-sharing or inventory-pooling provisions not approved in advance, forcing EUR 50–100M rework and unravelling carrier commitments; (3) Accessibility metadata gaps preventing atomic booking of assistance and wheelchair spaces, creating legal exposure under Regulation 1371/2007 and triggering regulator enforcement actions; (4) Settlement data format inconsistency causing >2% reconciliation errors, extending the clearing cycle to 10–15 business days and causing 15–20% of distributors to withdraw, reducing the through-ticket share from 40% to 15–25% (estimate) and likely programme failure to meet the binding target by Month 60 (2031-10-12). Combined impact: delivery delay of 12–24 months and unachievable goals, consuming most of the EUR 1,500M budget on rework instead of rolling out value.

Best Case Scenario: A complete, unambiguous OSDM binding-standards specification published by Month 20 (2028-06-12) enables: (1) All 25+ carriers and distributors to implement conformant systems on predictable timelines (Tier 1 by Month 30 = 2029-04-12, Tier 2 by Month 36 = 2029-10-12, Tier 3 by Month 42 = 2030-04-12); (2) A rigorous conformance test suite reducing post-go-live integration failures and allowing carriers to validate readiness 4–6 months before mandatory exposure; (3) Pre-cleared Article 101 TFEU compliance (via clean-team protocols and data-minimisation rules) documented in the specification, eliminating post-launch legal challenges and carriers' hesitation to commit inventory; (4) Atomic booking confirmation of accessibility (wheelchair, assistance, bicycle) and settlement fields, enabling the accessibility targets (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours) and reducing reconciliation errors to <0.5% by Month 30 (2029-04-12); (5) Successful pilots of 2,000–4,000 passengers per corridor (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) validating the architecture and building carrier and distributor confidence, resulting in early over-commitment of inventory and 40%+ through-ticket share achieved by Month 54 (2031-04-12) instead of Month 60 (2031-10-12).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If binding-standards drafting slips beyond Month 15 (2028-01-12): Publish an interim 'Fast-Track OSDM Profile' (Month 12 = 2027-10-12) covering only the critical path APIs (availability, booking, settlement, ticket validation) with simplified multilingual support (6–8 core languages) and deferred accessibility and disruption APIs; use the Fast-Track to unblock pilot deployment and carrier integration Months 12–18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12), then merge into the full binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12).
