  • If competition-law clearance from DG COMP is unavailable by Month 12 (2027-10-12): Adopt a maximum-separation design by Month 14 (2027-12-12) where the specification mandates clean-team arrangements for the clearing function, minimises shared inventory visibility, and requires all netting data to be aggregated per carrier pair; submit this design for expedited DG COMP guidance by Month 14 (2027-12-12), accepting a 4–6 week review cycle and targeting Month 16 (2028-02-12) approval before binding standards finalise.
  • If carrier survey by Month 3 (2027-01-12) reveals that some carriers cannot implement accessibility metadata by Month 30 (2029-04-12): Adopt a phased accessibility commitment where Tier 1 carriers expose wheelchair and assistance metadata by Month 30 (2029-04-12), and Tier 2/3 carriers provide 'best-effort' (non-atomic) accessibility data by Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12), with atomic booking deferred to Month 48 (2030-10-12) for full network; use the Phase 1 pilots to identify carriers' capability gaps by Month 18 (2028-04-12) and adjust tier assignments.
  • If settlement data-format standardisation (ISO 20022 or equivalent) is not approved by CER and carriers by Month 9 (2027-07-12): Establish an interim 'Common Settlement Gateway' (part of the clearing budget, EUR 20–40M estimate) that accepts each carrier's native settlement format, auto-translates to a canonical EUR-denominated format within the gateway, and handles reconciliation internally; this preserves compliance timelines at the cost of gateway complexity and operational risk (single point of failure) until carriers migrate to the standard by Month 42–48 (2030-04-12 to 2030-10-12).
  • If the full specification exceeds 500+ pages and becomes difficult for carriers' technical teams to implement uniformly: Decompose the binding standard into three modular profiles (Alpha: Availability & Booking, Beta: Settlement & Validation, Gamma: Accessibility & Disruption) published in sequence (Alpha Month 18 = 2028-04-12, Beta Month 20 = 2028-06-12, Gamma Month 21 = 2028-07-12); carriers implement Alpha first and commit to Beta/Gamma integration by Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12), reducing per-carrier on-boarding burden and allowing earlier go-live of basic through-ticketing.

Create Document 5: Technical Audit and Carrier Conformance Tier Assignment Report

ID: 35471efb-e283-4507-bde2-7a6b06fc740f

Description: Independent assessment of all 25+ participating carriers' booking-system readiness against binding standards, published with tier assignments (Tier 1: Month 30 = 2029-04-12; Tier 2: Month 36 = 2029-10-12; Tier 3: Month 42 = 2030-04-12) and per-carrier integration roadmaps. Covers API build effort, event-streaming capability, latency (p95 seconds current state), availability (12-month %), legacy-system dependencies, staffing availability and estimated adapter cost per operator. Identifies bottlenecks (mainframe retrofit, payment-processor integration) and recommends shared-adapter modules. Output: basis for adapter funding allocation and conformance milestones. Primary audience: carriers, Programme Office, finance lead.

Responsible Role Type: Carrier Integration & Technical Onboarding Manager

Primary Template: Technical due diligence assessment template (system architecture audit)

Secondary Template: Capacity and constraint analysis (IT resource planning template)

Steps to Create:

  • Tender independent audit firm by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27); award by Month 1 (2026-11-12)
  • Send audit questionnaire to all 25+ carriers by Month 1 (2026-11-12) covering: current API state, event-streaming capability, latency profiles, annual uptime %, legacy system details, staff FTE available
  • Conduct on-site system assessments (30+ days across four EU hubs) Months 1-2 (2026-11-12 to 2026-12-12); validate questionnaire responses
  • Analyse integration effort per carrier using established patterns (mainframe retrofit typically 9-15 months for smaller operators, 6-9 months for modern systems) by Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Publish draft tier assignments and per-carrier roadmaps by Month 3 (2027-01-12); circulate for carrier comment by Month 4 (2027-02-12)
  • Finalise tier assignment (Tier 1 = 12+ carriers with <12 months integration remaining; Tier 2 = 6-10 carriers with 12-18 months; Tier 3 = remaining) by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • Publish final audit report with all roadmaps, bottleneck assessments and shared-adapter recommendations; submit to steering group and Programme Director

Approval Authorities: Audit firm (technical opinion), Carrier Integration Manager, Programme Director, steering group (acceptance of tier assignments)

Essential Information:

  • Assess the current API readiness, event-streaming capability and on-time latency (p95 seconds, current state) for all 25+ participating carriers' booking systems.
  • Evaluate existing annual system availability (12-month %), legacy-system dependencies and integration dependencies (mainframe retrofit, payment-processor integration).
  • Quantify integration effort per carrier in months, using established patterns (mainframe retrofit: 9–15 months for smaller operators, 6–9 months for modern systems).
  • Identify staffing availability (FTE) per carrier dedicated to conformance integration during Months 1–30 (2026-11-12 to 2029-04-12).
  • Estimate adapter cost per operator and identify shared-adapter module opportunities (e.g. mainframe-to-OSDM bridges, payment-processor connectors) that can be funded centrally.
  • Assign all 25+ carriers to conformance tiers: Tier 1 (Month 30 = 2029-04-12), Tier 2 (Month 36 = 2029-10-12), Tier 3 (Month 42 = 2030-04-12), with clear, per-carrier roadmaps showing milestones, dependencies and risk flags.
  • List bottleneck carrier pairs (e.g. carriers whose integration is blocked by another's API readiness on a shared corridor) and propose sequencing to unblock critical paths.
  • Provide tier-wise funding allocation recommendations: EUR 30M shared adapters, EUR 80M Tier 1, EUR 80M Tier 2, EUR 50M Tier 3, with payment triggers tied to SLA milestones (latency, availability, error rates).
  • Detail the audit methodology, sample size of on-site visits (30+ days across four EU hubs), questionnaire design, validation approach and confidence intervals per carrier tier.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Underestimated integration effort on smaller carriers (e.g. mainframe retrofit overstated as 6 months instead of 12–15 months) causes 40–50% of Tier 2 and Tier 3 carriers to miss their assigned milestones, fragmenting corridor coverage and pushing full mandatory API exposure from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12), delaying four-corridor go-live by 6–12 months.
  • Failure to identify shared-adapter bottlenecks (e.g. mainframe or payment-processor integration needed by 8+ carriers) leaves EUR 80–150M in central adapter funding unallocated and forces carriers to self-fund, creating unequal participation and budget waste.
  • Incomplete on-site validation of questionnaire responses allows carriers to understate legacy-system complexity, leading to unrealistic roadmaps that collapse 12–18 months later when retrofits prove harder than stated, eroding steering confidence and triggering cascade delays.
  • Missing carrier interdependencies on shared corridors (e.g. Carrier A's booking-engine latency gates Carrier B's through-ticket availability) leaves integration sequencing undefined, allowing serial delays to cascade rather than being planned as concurrent workstreams.
  • Inaccurate staffing availability forecasts result in carriers lacking FTE when conformance testing begins at Month 12 (2027-10-12), causing 4–8 month slippage in API readiness and cost inflation as carriers hire contractors at premium rates.
  • Weak or absent confidence intervals per tier allow steering group to treat assignments as absolute, then challenge tier placement once integration starts, re-allocating funding mid-programme and destabilising the tranched release schedule.
  • Omission of validation gateway details (which SLAs must be met before each tier advances to the next milestone) leaves the funding release mechanism toothless: carriers have no clear incentive to hit latency/availability targets because payment is not conditional.

Worst Case Scenario: The audit is incomplete, on-site visits are superficial or omitted, and tier assignments rely on carrier self-reported questionnaire data without independent validation. Tier 2 and Tier 3 carriers (6–15 operators, 35–45% of network) are optimistically placed at Months 36 and 42 (2029-10-12 and 2030-04-12) but discover during Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12) that mainframe retrofits, legacy payment-processor integrations or understaffed IT teams require 18–24 months, not 12–15. Shared-adapter modules are not identified, leaving each carrier to fund its own bridge solution. By Month 36 (2029-10-12), only 10–12 of the 25+ target carriers are API-live, not the 18–20 forecast for Tier 1 and early Tier 2. Critical corridors (e.g. Wien–München–Zürich) are fragmented because a regional operator missed the milestone. The Programme Office burns EUR 150–200M in emergency adapter acceleration funding, exceeding the original EUR 240M allocation by 60–80% (estimate). Four-corridor through-ticketing slips from Month 48 (2030-10-12) to Month 60–66 (2031-10-12 to 2032-04-12). Through-ticket share at Month 60 (2031-10-12) is 15–20% instead of 40% (estimate). Steering group loses confidence in the programme schedule, and smaller member states and carriers withdraw or demand re-negotiation of obligations, triggering a political backlash and potential programme cancellation or major restructuring by Month 48 (2030-10-12).

Best Case Scenario: The audit is conducted by a credible, independent firm with on-site assessments of all 25+ carriers across four EU hubs (30+ days, Month 1–2 = 2026-11-12 to 2026-12-12), questionnaire responses are independently validated, and per-carrier roadmaps with clear milestones, risk flags and dependency maps are published by Month 6 (2027-04-12). Shared-adapter modules (mainframe bridges, payment-processor connectors, event-stream SDKs) serving 8–12 carriers are identified, and the Programme Office allocates EUR 30M for development by Month 12 (2027-10-12). Tier assignments are credible and include 90%-confidence intervals on integration timelines per carrier. Carriers can reliably plan internal team allocation and external contracting. The steering group and the Carrier Integration Manager accept the tier assignments and funding tranches. By Month 30 (2029-04-12), 15–18 large and corridor-critical carriers (Tier 1) go live, meeting SLA targets. By Month 42 (2030-04-12), 22–24 of the 25+ target carriers are API-live. Four-corridor through-ticketing launches on schedule at Month 48 (2030-10-12). The 40% through-ticket goal is achievable within the EUR 1,500M budget, and TEN-T extension (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) proceeds as planned. Programme credibility and carrier buy-in remain high, and the regulatory and competition-law pathway is unblocked.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If a full independent audit is not feasible within Month 2 (2026-12-12), commission a rapid (4-week) diagnostic assessment of the 10 largest carriers only, published by Month 3 (2027-01-12), while launching a self-audit questionnaire for smaller carriers due by Month 4 (2027-02-12), with spot-checks on 3–5 second-tier carriers by Month 6 (2027-04-12). Accept higher confidence-interval ranges (25–30% variance instead of 10–15%) and allow tier assignments to be provisional, with a formal re-audit gate at Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • If audit costs exceed budget (estimated EUR 2–3M), leverage existing regulatory audit data: request the EU Agency for Railways and national rail regulators to share technical compliance reports they hold on carrier systems, supplement with a focused questionnaire on integration timelines and shared-adapter needs, and hire one dedicated analyst to synthesise findings by Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • If on-site carrier visits are constrained by travel or local IT security policies, substitute remote technical deep-dives via video call and remote system-architecture walkthroughs (screen-sharing with live system demos) at Month 1–2 (2026-11-12 to 2026-12-12), supplemented by architecture-review workshops co-hosted by the Agency and CER in Brussels and Valenciennes at Month 3 (2027-01-12); accept that the audit will be less hands-on but faster to execute.
  • If tier assignments are not accepted by the full steering group by Month 6 (2027-04-12), escalate disagreements to a bilateral mediation process: the Carrier Integration Manager and one independent arbiter (appointed by the Agency) meet individually with each carrier ranked in Tier 2 or 3 to resolve contentious assumptions (staffing FTE, legacy-system complexity) by Month 9 (2027-07-12), with binding mid-point scores if disagreement persists.
  • If shared-adapter modules cannot be fully specified within the audit timeline, establish a 'best-guess' module list by Month 6 (2027-04-12) covering the most obvious shared needs (mainframe OSDM bridge, event-stream SDK, payment-processor adapter), allocate EUR 20–30M for development, and fund a separate technical workstream (Month 6–12 = 2027-04-12 to 2027-10-12) to validate the modules and identify additional ones, releasing remaining EUR 10M adaptively in Month 12 (2027-10-12).

Create Document 6: Competition Law Pre-Notification Memorandum and Article 101 TFEU Safe-Harbour Argument

ID: b05e4a09-46f7-47ac-95f9-eacfcf158f44

Description: Comprehensive legal memorandum submitted to DG COMP (pre-notification under Regulation 1/2003) describing all aspects of the inter-carrier clearing mechanism, shared availability data layer, through-fare construction, distribution remuneration band and carrier-funded guarantee pool from an Article 101 TFEU perspective. Demonstrates non-discriminatory access, proportionality of restrictions and pro-competitive benefits (lower consumer fares, improved journey connectivity). Identifies required clean-team protocols, data-access controls and governance safeguards to satisfy competition-law scrutiny. Requests formal DG COMP guidance letter confirming compatibility or identifying required modifications. Primary audience: DG COMP, Programme Director, Competition Law Counsel, carriers.

Responsible Role Type: Competition Law & Regulatory Affairs Counsel

Primary Template: EU competition-law pre-notification memorandum (format per Regulation 1/2003)

Secondary Template: Article 101 TFEU exemption argument template (using established precedents in transport and digital markets)

Steps to Create:

  • Engage external EU competition counsel by Month 1 (2026-11-12)
  • Gather technical specifications from clearing architect, standards custodian and real-time engineer Months 1-2 (2026-11-12 to 2026-12-12) describing shared mechanisms in concrete detail (data flows, participant roles, access rules)
  • Draft memorandum addressing: (1) notification of the clearing and data-sharing arrangements as potentially restrictive practices; (2) demonstration that each arrangement is necessary for through-ticketing and proportionate; (3) definition of non-discriminatory access criteria; (4) clean-team protocols isolating competitive strategy from clearing function; (5) public-authority oversight (Agency role) as safeguard by Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Circulate draft to Programme Director and DG MOVE legal counsel for review by Month 2.5 (2026-12-27)
  • File formal pre-notification with DG COMP covering letter and signed memorandum by Month 2 (2026-12-12) end of week
  • Attend initial DG COMP briefing meeting (approximately Month 3-4 = 2027-01-12 to 2027-02-12) to respond to questions and flag urgent clarifications needed
  • Obtain formal DG COMP guidance letter confirming safe-harbour or identifying required design changes by Month 9-10 (2027-07-12 to 2027-08-12)
  • If guidance identifies concerns, revise memorandum and designs (clean-team protocol, governance safeguards) and resubmit by Month 12 (2027-10-12)
  • Obtain final DG COMP approval of any clean-team protocols or safeguards by Month 14 (2027-12-12)

Approval Authorities: DG COMP (formal guidance letter), DG MOVE (substantive review), Programme Director (sign-off on safe-harbour argument)

Essential Information:

  • Demonstrate that the inter-carrier clearing mechanism, shared real-time availability data layer, through-fare construction rules and distribution remuneration band are necessary and proportionate restrictions on competition under Article 101 TFEU, with pro-competitive benefits (lower fares, improved journey connectivity, passenger rights continuity).
  • Specify all shared mechanisms in concrete technical detail: data flows, participant roles, access rules, and governance safeguards that prevent misuse for anti-competitive purposes.
  • Define non-discriminatory access criteria for independent distributors and smaller carriers to the clearing layer, real-time data feeds and OSDM-compliant APIs, with enforcement and audit mechanisms.
  • Detail clean-team protocols isolating the clearing function from participants' commercial strategies: information barriers, access controls, data aggregation and segregation of competitive information.
  • Describe the role of the EU Agency for Railways as independent public-authority oversight body, with powers to audit clearing operations, enforce non-discrimination and report suspected violations to DG COMP.
  • Cite established EU competition-law precedents in transport and digital markets (e.g. MasterCard, Clearstream, RailTeam) demonstrating that inter-carrier coordination can satisfy Article 101(3) TFEU exemption criteria when proportionate and subject to safeguards.
  • Identify specific design choices (federated vs. central clearing, quota mechanisms, sunset clauses, dispute resolution) and explain how each reduces restriction on competition or enables pro-competitive benefits.
  • Request formal guidance from DG COMP confirming compatibility of the clearing and data-sharing arrangements with Article 101 TFEU, or identifying required design modifications to secure safe-harbour status.
  • Address potential DG COMP concerns (e.g. data pooling heightening collusion risk, exclusionary rules blocking smaller distributors, capacity caps that limit passenger benefit) and demonstrate mitigation through the safeguards outlined.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete technical specification of the clearing and data-sharing mechanisms allows DG COMP to infer anti-competitive intent or unchecked potential for collusion, triggering a dawn raid or formal investigation that disrupts the programme for 12-24 months and imposes fines on participating carriers.
  • Absence of credible non-discriminatory access rules or weak clean-team protocols invites a challenge that the mechanisms are designed to foreclose independent distributors or smaller carriers, forcing redesign of the clearing layer and 6-12 month delay.
  • Vague or unsubstantiated claims about pro-competitive benefits without economic evidence (consumer surplus, journey availability) allows DG COMP to dismiss the Article 101(3) exemption argument, requiring the programme to operate without safe-harbour status, leaving carriers exposed to later enforcement action.
  • Failure to address known DG COMP precedent concerns (e.g. information pooling in RailTeam investigations, capacity allocation in air-transport cases) creates a perception of legal naïveté, reducing credibility and increasing scrutiny intensity.
  • Missing or inadequate description of the Agency's oversight role and audit powers allows DG COMP to conclude that the programme lacks meaningful external enforcement, failing the proportionality test.
  • Legally deficient memorandum (weak reasoning, poor precedent analysis, inconsistent with Regulation 1/2003 formats) prolongs DG COMP review from the target Month 12 (2027-10-12) to Month 18-24 (2028-04-12 to 2028-10-12), compressing or deferring the binding-standards milestone.
  • Absence of clear fallback or design-modification pathways leaves no negotiating room if DG COMP identifies concerns, forcing either programme retreat or unresolved legal exposure that deters carrier participation.

Worst Case Scenario: DG COMP initiates a formal investigation into the clearing and data-sharing arrangements under Article 101 TFEU on the grounds that the pre-notification memorandum is incomplete, legally unconvincing or fails to demonstrate pro-competitive benefits. A dawn raid and information request issued at Month 9-12 (2027-07-12 to 2027-10-12) paralyzes the Programme Office and participating carriers for 3-6 months. Carriers facing investigation uncertainty withdraw from inventory exposure, delaying mandatory API exposure from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 42-48 (2030-04-12 to 2030-10-12) and reducing participation from 25+ to 12-15 operators (estimate). If the investigation concludes that the clearing mechanism violates Article 101 TFEU without an effective exemption, the programme is forced to restructure the clearing and data layer, requiring 6-12 months of redesign and resubmission, pushing the binding-standards milestone to Month 24-30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12). This reduces the through-ticket share from 40% to 15-20% (estimate) and leaves EUR 200-300M of the public budget unallocated. Reputational damage to the programme and enforcement risk to carriers deters future EU infrastructure initiatives in digital rail services.

Best Case Scenario: DG COMP issues a formal guidance letter by Month 12 (2027-10-12) confirming that the inter-carrier clearing mechanism, shared real-time data layer, through-fare construction rules and distribution remuneration band are compatible with Article 101 TFEU, conditioned on the specified non-discriminatory access rules, clean-team protocols and Agency oversight. This enables carriers to commit binding inventory exposure and budget without legal hesitation. The binding-standards milestone is met on time at Month 18 (2028-04-12), mandatory API exposure milestone at Month 30 (2029-04-12), and the four priority corridors go live at Month 48 (2030-10-12) with full participation from 25+ operators. The safe-harbour status becomes a replicable model for future EU digital transport initiatives and removes legal risk from the programme's balance sheet, allowing the 40% through-ticket target and full TEN-T coverage by Month 60 (2031-10-12) without regulatory uncertainty.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If DG COMP indicates concerns with data pooling or clearing governance during Month 3-4 (2027-01-12 to 2027-02-12) briefing, immediately engage an alternative clean-team design (separate legal entities, external audit board, third-party data custodian) and resubmit a revised memorandum by Month 8 (2027-06-12) before DG COMP's review window closes, avoiding full investigation escalation.
  • If DG COMP raises exclusionary concerns about access rules, commit to a third-party dispute arbiter (designated by the Agency) to review distributor access claims and issue binding decisions within 30 days, demonstrating concrete non-discrimination enforcement independent of the Programme Office.
  • Commission an independent economic-impact study (estimate: EUR 0.5-1M) by Month 3 (2027-01-12) quantifying consumer surplus, journey availability gains and modal-shift benefits of the programme, using established econometric methods; embed findings in a revised memorandum submitted Month 9 (2027-07-12) to strengthen the Article 101(3) exemption case.
  • If uncertainty persists through Month 10 (2027-08-12), request a Phase 2 formal notice from DG COMP (Regulation 1/2003 Article 19) setting a 90-day reply deadline, converting the review to a structured formal process with defined gates and milestones that compresses uncertainty, even if it extends the guidance timeline to Month 14-15 (2027-12-12 to 2028-01-12).
  • Establish a contingency non-compliant clearing pathway (federated bilateral netting with no shared data layer, longer settlement cycles) and document its inferior competitive outcomes; present this as a fallback if DG COMP rejects the centralised mechanism, demonstrating that the proposed design is the pro-competitive alternative to fragmentation.
  • If legal certainty cannot be obtained by Month 14 (2027-12-12), launch the programme under Regulation 1/2003 Article 101(3) block exemption (rail transport services exemption, if applicable to digital services) or a Commission declaration of non-opposition, accepting residual legal risk but preserving momentum for the Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards deadline.

Create Document 7: Passenger Rights Compliance Manual and Regulation 1371/2007 Legal Opinion

ID: 66be3b09-2d41-481b-8d22-a529c38af236

Description: Comprehensive operational manual and legal opinion ensuring that through-ticket passengers retain rights equivalent to or superior to single-carrier passengers under EU Regulation 1371/2007 (railway passengers' rights). Covers assistance, rerouting, compensation, refunds, information provision, complaint handling and accessibility obligations for each participating entity (carriers, clearing layer, public distributor, independent distributors). Includes step-by-step procedures for handling missed connections, force-majeure claims, passenger assistance requests and disability accommodations. Based on independent legal review by rail-law specialist. Output: binding compliance requirement for all parties. Primary audience: carriers, distributors, the clearing entity, EU Agency for Railways, national regulators.

Responsible Role Type: Passenger Rights, Accessibility & Consumer Protection Lead

Primary Template: Legal opinion (from an EU rail-law specialist)

Secondary Template: Operations manual template (step-by-step procedures per role)

Steps to Create:

  • Commission independent legal review (from a specialist in EU passenger-rights regulation) by Month 1 (2026-11-12)
  • Provide reviewer with: binding standards drafts, liability model, clearing rulebook and public distributor specification (as they emerge Months 3-6 = 2027-01-12 to 2027-04-12) for gaps analysis against Regulation 1371/2007
  • Reviewer publishes preliminary opinion on any gaps (compensation below single-carrier levels, refund delays not justified, accessibility not addressed) by Month 3 (2027-01-12); confirm by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • If gaps are identified, revise liability model and clearing rulebook (Decisions 1, 2) by Month 9 (2027-07-12) to close them
  • Develop compliance manual specifying: who (carrier, clearing entity, distributor) is responsible for each right (assistance, compensation, information) at each journey stage (booking, travel, disruption, refund) by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • Publish worked examples of compliance scenarios (missed connection with compensation owed, passenger with mobility needs requesting assistance, refund reversal across carriers) by Month 9 (2027-07-12)
  • Submit both legal opinion and manual to EU Agency for Railways for formal approval by Month 9 (2027-07-12); obtain written approval by Month 9 (2027-07-12)
  • Publish manual as a binding operational requirement; require all carriers and distributors to certify staff training by Month 30 (2029-04-12)

Approval Authorities: Independent legal reviewer (legal opinion), EU Agency for Railways (compliance manual approval), carriers and distributors (acceptance and staff training certification)

Essential Information:

  • Provide a comprehensive legal opinion from an EU rail-law specialist confirming that all through-ticket passenger rights (assistance, compensation, refunds, information, complaint handling) under EU Regulation 1371/2007 are preserved or exceeded in the programme's liability model, clearing rulebook and public distributor specification.
  • Detail step-by-step operational procedures for each participating entity (carriers, clearing layer, public distributor, independent distributors) covering: missed-connection detection and rerouting, passenger assistance requests for persons with reduced mobility, compensation and refund claims, force-majeure handling, and information provision in at least the EU working languages.
  • Identify specific gaps between the draft programme design (liability backstop, clearing settlement timings, distributor roles) and Regulation 1371/2007 requirements; recommend design changes to close each gap.
  • Specify who bears responsibility (carrier, clearing entity, distributor) for each passenger right at each journey stage: booking, travel, disruption, rerouting, compensation and refund.
  • Provide worked examples demonstrating compliance for at least five high-risk scenarios: (1) missed connection with compensation owed across carriers; (2) mobility-assistance request with short notice; (3) refund reversal when a passenger cancels a through-ticket; (4) force-majeure disruption affecting multiple legs; (5) complaint escalation across carriers.
  • Establish training requirements and sign-off procedures for all carrier and distributor staff handling passenger claims, assistance and complaints; specify certification timelines for conformance gates.
  • Document how the manual aligns with national variations in passenger-rights enforcement and complaint-handling procedures per member state; identify any national-level regulatory conflicts.
  • Confirm that accessibility obligations under EU Regulation 1371/2007 and the Accessibility Directive are met by the Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining design, particularly atomic confirmation and best-effort fallbacks.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If the legal opinion finds material gaps between the programme design and Regulation 1371/2007 (e.g., compensation below single-carrier levels, settlement delays not justified, assistance commitments unfulfillable), redesign of the liability model and clearing rulebook is forced, delaying binding standards from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12) and consuming EUR 10–20 million in rework.
  • Unclear responsibility allocation between carriers, clearing entities and distributors leads to passengers being denied compensation or assistance because each party believes the other is liable; this triggers regulatory complaints to the EU Agency for Railways and national regulators, risking enforcement action and programme suspension.
  • Incomplete or ambiguous operational procedures for missed-connection handling and refund reversal result in inconsistent passenger outcomes across carriers and member states; distributors face unpredictable liability exposure and withdraw from the programme, reducing through-ticket volume by 10–20% (estimate).
  • Failure to obtain formal written approval from the EU Agency for Railways by Month 9 (2027-07-12) means carriers lack confidence that the programme's rights design meets regulatory standards; participation drops and mandatory API exposure milestone slips by 3–6 months.
  • Incomplete accessibility guidance in the manual means onboard staff and station agents apply inconsistent standards for mobility assistance and bicycle reservations; passengers with disabilities file complaints, forcing ad-hoc remedies and damaging programme credibility.
  • If staff training and certification requirements are not clearly specified and enforced, carriers and distributors deploy untrained personnel, leading to passenger rights violations, complaints and potential fines under Regulation 1371/2007.
  • Unaddressed national regulatory variations leave smaller member states unclear on how to align their local rules with the programme's passenger-rights baseline; regulatory conflicts delay participation or reduce network coverage.

Worst Case Scenario: The legal opinion, completed too late or with insufficient detail, identifies fundamental incompatibility between the programme's carrier-funded liability pool and Regulation 1371/2007 rights (e.g., compensation thresholds too low, settlement timelines cause traveller hardship, assistance commitments exceed carrier capacity). Remediation requires redesign of the liability model and clearing rulebook by Month 9 (2027-07-12), consuming EUR 15–25 million and delaying binding standards to Month 24 (2028-10-12). Meanwhile, carriers unable to confirm compliance with passenger rights refuse to sign the binding liability agreement by Month 4 (2027-02-12), blocking the core commercial consensus. The EU Agency for Railways issues a non-conformity notice, suspending the programme until gaps are closed. Mandatory API exposure is pushed from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12); four-corridor go-live slips from Month 48 (2030-10-12) to Month 60 (2031-10-12), and the 40% through-ticket target becomes unachievable (realistic outcome 20–25%, estimate). Operational procedures for missed connections and assistance remain undefined; staff confusion and passenger complaints spike, leading to negative media coverage and reduced consumer adoption of through-tickets. Total cost and schedule impact: EUR 30–50 million, 6–12 months delay.

Best Case Scenario: An independent legal review completed by Month 6 (2027-04-12) confirms that the liability model, clearing rulebook and public distributor specification preserve or exceed all Regulation 1371/2007 rights. The opinion identifies one minor gap (settlement timelines for refund reversal) and the remediation is trivial (adding 1 business day to the 5-day cycle). The legal opinion is published and provides carriers and distributors with binding assurance of compliance. Operational procedures are detailed, realistic and approved by the EU Agency for Railways by Month 9 (2027-07-12), allowing carriers and distributors to train staff and deploy systems with confidence. Worked examples show that the programme handles high-risk scenarios (missed connections, mobility assistance, refunds) consistently and fairly. Carriers sign the liability agreement by Month 4 (2027-02-12); the steering group votes unanimously on Decisions 1–3 by Month 6 (2027-04-12). Binding standards are published on schedule at Month 18 (2028-04-12); mandatory API exposure proceeds on Tier 1 schedule by Month 30 (2029-04-12); four-corridor through-ticketing goes live at Month 48 (2030-10-12); the 40% through-ticket target is achieved by Month 60 (2031-10-12). Accessibility thresholds (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours) are met and validated in pilots, setting a programme standard. Passenger trust in through-tickets is high; complaint rates fall below baseline, supporting the 50% reduction target. Regulatory approval is swift; no challenges under Regulation 1371/2007 or accessibility law emerge.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If an independent legal reviewer is not available by Month 2 (2026-12-12), form an internal task force from the EU Agency for Railways, DG MOVE and national regulators, supplemented by one contracted external rail-law counsel. Assign clear responsibility for each section (compensation, assistance, refunds, complaint handling). Complete a preliminary compliance assessment by Month 4 (2027-02-12); obtain external peer review by Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • If Regulation 1371/2007 gaps cannot be closed by design changes (e.g., carriers cannot guarantee assistance within the required notice period), publish a 'conditional compliance' manual that documents the gaps transparently, specifies best-effort fallbacks (e.g., 'assistance with at most 4 hours' notice on 90% of services, best-effort on remainder') and obtains explicit carrier and regulator sign-off on the conditional terms. This avoids unenforceable promises but maintains transparency.
  • If operational procedures cannot be detailed for all five high-risk scenarios by Month 6 (2027-04-12), prioritise the two highest-impact scenarios (missed-connection rerouting and compensation claims) and publish detailed procedures by Month 9 (2027-07-12). Document the remaining three as 'to be detailed by Month 12 (2027-10-12)' and defer full pilot testing by 2–3 months. Conduct live pilots at Month 15–18 (2028-01-12 to 2028-04-12) instead of Month 12–15 (2027-10-12 to 2028-01-12).
  • If the EU Agency for Railways is slow to approve the compliance manual (beyond Month 9 = 2027-07-12), secure written approval in phases: (a) liability and compensation procedures by Month 9 (2027-07-12); (b) assistance and accessibility procedures by Month 12 (2027-10-12); (c) complaint handling by Month 15 (2028-01-12). Begin carrier training on (a) immediately; defer training on (b) and (c) until those sections are approved, reducing schedule slip to 1–2 months.
  • If national regulators flag conflicts between the programme's rights baseline and local passenger-rights rules in specific member states, establish a 'national variation annex' to the manual specifying the programme requirement and the local requirement for each member state. Where they conflict, apply the higher standard and document the cost impact (longer settlement cycles, additional staffing). Obtain regulatory approval per member state by Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • If staff training and certification cannot be completed for all carriers and distributors by Month 30 (2029-04-12), tier the requirement: (a) Tier 1 (large carriers, critical staff) certified by Month 24 (2028-10-12); (b) Tier 2 (regional, front-line) by Month 30 (2029-04-12); (c) Tier 3 (all others) by Month 36 (2029-10-12). Defer full mandatory API exposure to Month 42 (2030-04-12) to allow Tier 3 completion; launch Tier 1 API pilots by Month 30 (2029-04-12).

Create Document 8: Risk Register and Mitigation Plan

ID: 1cf3e242-1219-46e5-a228-8e182514a07b

Description: Comprehensive risk register documenting all identified risks (regulatory slip, carrier refusal, legacy-system latency, stakeholder deadlock, pool overruns, competition-law challenge, accessibility compliance, etc.) with likelihood, severity, mitigation strategies and trigger-based contingency actions. Includes 20 risks from the pre-project assumptions, with residual-risk assessment post-mitigation. Updated quarterly Months 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 60 (2027-04-12, 2027-10-12, 2028-04-12, 2028-10-12, 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12). Primary audience: Programme Director, steering group, DG MOVE, carriers.

Responsible Role Type: Programme Director (with support from Financial Risk Manager and Competition Law Counsel)

Primary Template: Project risk register template (ISO 31000 risk management standard)

Secondary Template: Programme-level risk dashboard (Jira, Asana, or similar)

Steps to Create:

  • Compile initial risk register (20 risks from pre-project assumptions) by Month 1 (2026-11-12)
  • Assess each risk: likelihood (Low/Medium/High), severity (Low/Medium/High), ownership, mitigation lead and residual-risk post-mitigation by Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Establish risk-mitigation workstreams with assigned owners: actuarial study (Month 1 = 2026-11-12 start, Month 3 = 2027-01-12 delivery), technical audit (Month 1 = 2026-11-12 start, Month 6 = 2027-04-12 delivery), DG COMP pre-notification (Month 2 = 2026-12-12 filing), steering governance (Month 1 = 2026-11-12 start, Month 6 = 2027-04-12 binding votes), budget rebaselining (Month 6 = 2027-04-12 start), etc.
  • Publish risk register and mitigation roadmap to steering group by Month 3 (2027-01-12)
  • Track mitigation progress monthly; update risk register quarterly (Months 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 60 = 2027-04-12, 2027-10-12, 2028-04-12, 2028-10-12, 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12)
  • Escalate any risk where likelihood or severity changes from Medium/High to High, or where mitigation is failing, to Programme Director and steering group within 5 business days
  • At each major milestone (Months 6, 18, 30, 48, 60 = 2027-04-12, 2028-04-12, 2029-04-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12), conduct risk-rating review and adjust mitigation intensity or contingency allocations

Approval Authorities: Programme Director, steering group (quarterly risk review)

Essential Information:

  • Compile a comprehensive risk register that identifies all 20 pre-identified risks (regulatory slip, carrier refusal, legacy-system latency, stakeholder deadlock, pool overruns, competition-law challenge, Article 101 TFEU exposure, accessibility compliance, validation gaps, modal-shift shortfall, operational failures, capacity gaps, regulator blocking, commission-band disputes, specification forks, reconciliation errors, disruption-handling failures, validation interoperability, distributor withdrawal, and programme-staffing turnover) with precise likelihood (Low/Medium/High) and severity (Low/Medium/High) ratings
  • Define ownership and lead role for each risk mitigation (e.g., Programme Director owns carrier liability model; Financial Risk Manager owns pool draw-down policy; Competition Law Counsel owns Article 101 pre-notification)
  • Establish trigger-based contingency actions keyed to budget variance thresholds (EUR 100M: defer TEN-T to Months 60-72 = 2031-10-12 to 2032-10-12; EUR 200M: cut concession 20%; EUR 300M: restrict to four corridors) and schedule slip tolerances (2-4 month standards delay → Month 12 = 2027-10-12 gate; 6-12 month Regulation slip → shadow standards workstream)
  • Quantify residual risk post-mitigation for each risk, noting which risks remain Medium/High even after planned actions (e.g., carrier refusal, Article 101 challenge, legacy latency all High residual until Month 6-12 = 2027-04-12 to 2027-10-12 gates close)
  • Create a risk-monitoring dashboard showing: (1) open risk count by severity; (2) mitigation-workstream status (on-track, at-risk, overdue); (3) next escalation or decision point per risk; (4) evidence of mitigation delivery (e.g., actuarial study completion, technical audit, DG COMP guidance letter)
  • Establish a quarterly update cycle tied to major milestones (Months 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 60 = 2027-04-12 onwards) with defined escalation protocol: any risk moving from Medium to High, or mitigation failing, escalated to Programme Director and steering group within 5 business days
  • Specify the Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate: carrier liability model signed by at least 8 major carriers and CER, technical audit published, steering votes held on Decisions 1-3 and 12; if unmet by Month 9 (2027-07-12), transition to Month 12 (2027-10-12) contingency gate
  • Document the residual risk after each mitigation: e.g. 'Carrier Refusal (Risk 3): After actuarial model and carrier sign-off by Month 4 (2027-02-12), residual likelihood Medium (down from High); unresolved by Month 6 (2027-04-12) escalates to Steering and triggers deferral to Month 12 (2027-10-12)'
  • Include a sensitivity analysis showing impact of three major risk scenarios: (1) carrier participation drops to 15-20 (from 25+) → through-ticket share 20-25% vs. 40% target; (2) Regulation adoption slips to Month 30 (2029-04-12) → binding-standards gate to Month 30 (2029-04-12), mandatory API to Month 42 (2030-04-12); (3) pool draw-down exceeds EUR 150M in Months 24-36 (2028-10-12 to 2029-10-12) → triggers EUR 200M budget-variance action
  • Identify interdependencies between risks that compound programme impact: e.g. 'If both legacy latency (Risk 7) AND stakeholder deadlock (Risk 5) occur, mandatory API milestone slips 6-12 months and EUR 150-250M adapter acceleration is triggered, exhausting contingency'

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • An incomplete or outdated risk register leaves the Programme Director and steering group unaware of emerging threats (e.g., a carrier's booking-system retrofit missing its Tier 1 deadline not flagged until Month 32 = 2029-06-12, too late for contingency action), cascading the missed milestone to later corridors and stretching the schedule beyond the Month 60 (2031-10-12) target
  • Unclear ownership of risk mitigation leads to diffused accountability: if 'carrier participation' risk has no single owner, nobody drives the actuarial study and carrier sign-off by Month 4 (2027-02-12), and the Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate cannot be certified, stalling the binding-standards pathway
  • Missing or mis-stated trigger-based contingency actions result in crisis-reactive budget decisions: a pool draw-down that breaches EUR 200M in Month 32 (2029-06-12) is discovered ad-hoc instead of triggering the pre-agreed 20% concession-funding cut, forcing hasty reallocation and regulatory complaints
  • Absence of a residual-risk framework means high-likelihood risks (carrier refusal, Article 101 challenge, legacy latency) are treated equally to low-likelihood ones (location/travel delays), misallocating limited mitigation effort and leaving critical path risks unmanaged
  • A risk register that does not connect to funding tranches or milestone releases allows risks to fester unaddressed: if 'stakeholder deadlock' risk has no 'funding hold' link, the steering group can release conformance-test funding before a deadlocked decision is resolved, wasting EUR 10-20M on downstream work blocked by the unresolved choice
  • Lack of quarterly update discipline means risks drift below the Programme Director's radar until they trigger crises: a 2-month slip in the technical audit (from Month 2 = 2026-12-12 to Month 4 = 2027-02-12) is not flagged in Month 3 (2027-01-12), so the Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate is planned without knowing carrier tiers are unassigned
  • Missing escalation protocol allows low-severity risks to accumulate in silence until they compound into high-severity ones: minor reconciliation-error trends (0.7% → 0.9% → 1.2% per month) go unreported in monthly updates, and by Month 28 (2029-02-12) the settlement-error risk is breaching 2%, forcing emergency system redesign at EUR 30-50M cost
  • No sensitivity analysis means the Programme Director cannot communicate realistic downside scenarios to the steering group or the Commission: without a 'carrier participation drops to 15' scenario, the EUR 1.5 billion budget allocation assumes all 25 operators join, and a shortfall to 15 operators is met with unplanned budget reallocation that triggers EUR 200M variance and plan changes
  • Absence of risk interdependencies means the Programme Director does not see how two Medium risks can compound into a catastrophic path: e.g. if both 'legislative slip' and 'pool drain' occur, the programme loses 12 months on standards and burns EUR 250M on pool top-ups and adapter acceleration, exhausting contingency and blocking the full TEN-T rollout
  • A risk register disconnected from the decision log means decisions that mitigate risks (e.g., 'Carrier-funded guarantee pool with per-incident caps') are not tracked back to which risks they retire, leaving ambiguity about whether Decision 1 actually addresses Risk 3 or whether secondary risks remain unhandled

Worst Case Scenario: A convergence of three high-impact risks—carrier refusal due to unpriceable liability (Risk 3), legacy-system integration delays on 40% of smaller operators (Risk 2), and a 12-month slip in Regulation adoption (Risk 1)—triggers a cascade failure in the binding-standards milestone (target Month 18 = 2028-04-12). Carrier sign-off on the liability model stalls because the actuarial study (commissioned Month 1 = 2026-11-12) is incomplete by Month 6 (2027-04-12), and the technical audit reveals that 8–15 smaller operators cannot meet the Month 30 (2029-04-12) API exposure deadline without EUR 150–250 million in unbudgeted adapter acceleration. Steering deadlock on Decisions 1 and 2 persists until Month 12 (2027-10-12), and Regulation adoption is delayed to Month 30 (2029-04-12) due to parliamentary amendments. The programme loses 12 months on binding standards (slipping to Month 30 = 2029-04-12), mandatory API exposure cascades to Month 42 (2030-04-12), and four-corridor go-live extends to Month 60 (2031-10-12) or beyond. The carrier-funded guarantee pool, starved of sign-ups, drains EUR 200+ million in force-majeure top-ups and pool reinsurance by Month 36 (2029-10-12), triggering the EUR 200M budget-variance action: 20% of concession funding is cut (EUR 60M), the concession term extends to 7 years, and member-state capacity building is reduced by 30%. The through-ticket share goal drops from 40% to 15–20% because participation falls to 15–18 operators (vs. 25 target) and the extended timeline prevents full TEN-T rollout within the 60-month horizon. The programme delivers value on the four priority corridors by Month 60–72 (2031-10-12 to 2032-10-12) but fails the headline 40% and 60-month targets, facing political re-evaluation and potential phase-out of the EUR 1.5 billion commitment beyond Month 60 (2031-10-12). Estimated reputational cost: loss of stakeholder trust, potential legal challenges from excluded distributors, and EU audit findings on budget overruns and schedule slip.

Best Case Scenario: The risk register and mitigation plan are completed by Month 3 (2027-01-12) and published to the steering group, establishing clear ownership, trigger thresholds and escalation paths. By Month 6 (2027-04-12), all six critical mitigation workstreams reach their interim gates: (1) Actuarial study delivers a carrier-signed liability model with caps, co-insurance and on-time-performance-weighted contributions; (2) Technical audit classifies 25 operators into Tier 1, 2, 3 with per-operator API exposure milestones and EUR 240M tiered adapter funding; (3) Steering group votes 75% supermajority on Decisions 1–3 and 12 (liability, clearing, public distributor, commission band); (4) DG COMP pre-notification is filed and initial guidance is favorable; (5) Passenger-rights legal review confirms the Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop design is compliant with EU Regulation 1371/2007; (6) Programme governance is certified with defined voting, escalation and fallback clauses. By Month 18 (2028-04-12), Regulation is adopted with the proposed binding-standards trigger, DG COMP issues a formal guidance letter confirming Article 101 compatibility, and the binding-standards milestone is achieved with OSDM pinned in an implementing act. Risk dashboard shows all 20 risks transitioned from High/Medium (pre-mitigation) to Medium/Low (post-mitigation), with only 3 risks remaining at Medium (carrier participation, late-carrier conformance, modal-shift shortfall) requiring continued monitoring. Phase 2 proceeds (Months 18–48 = 2028-04-12 to 2030-10-12) with Tier 1 API exposure achieved at Month 30 (2029-04-12), four-corridor through-ticketing live by Month 48 (2030-10-12), and full TEN-T extension completed by Month 60 (2031-10-12). Through-ticket share reaches the 40% target by Month 60 (2031-10-12), distributor complaints are halved, and the EUR 1.5 billion budget is spent within the EUR 85M headroom (no variance-triggered cuts). The Programme Office and steering group use the quarterly risk updates to stay ahead of emerging issues, and no risk breaches its severity rating during Months 6–60 (2027-04-12 to 2031-10-12). Outcome: a well-managed programme that delivers on schedule, within budget, with stakeholder confidence and regulatory support, enabling Phase 2 TEN-T extension and future modal-shift initiatives on additional corridors.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If a comprehensive 20-risk register cannot be completed by Month 3 (2027-01-12), prioritize a 'critical-path risk register' covering the six risks with the highest cascade impact on the binding-standards and mandatory-API milestones: (1) carrier refusal (Risk 3), (2) legacy-system integration (Risk 2), (3) regulatory slip (Risk 1), (4) stakeholder deadlock (Risk 5), (5) competition-law challenge (Risk 6), (6) budget overrun (Risk 4). Document these six with full mitigation and escalation by Month 2 (2026-12-12), defer medium/low risks to Month 6 (2027-04-12) review
  • If the Programme Director lacks dedicated Financial Risk Manager support, assign risk ownership to the existing Finance Team and require weekly tracker updates to a shared dashboard (Jira, Asana, or similar) that auto-escalates when a mitigation task falls 2+ weeks behind schedule. Reduce the update cycle from quarterly to monthly for Months 0–18 (2026-10-12 to 2028-04-12) to catch slippage early
  • If stakeholder consensus on risk tolerances cannot be reached before Month 6 (2027-04-12), adopt a 'risk-decision log' where each risk's mitigation strategy is recorded with the steering group's vote and any dissenting positions, so that later cascading failures are tied to documented choices rather than ambiguous ownership
  • If DG COMP pre-notification is delayed beyond Month 2 (2026-12-12), commission an external competition-law firm (EUR 0.5–1M cost) to conduct a parallel informal guidance-seeking process with DG COMP staff while the formal pre-notification is prepared, so that high-level competition concerns are identified and the formal process includes a response to those concerns
  • If the technical audit cannot be completed by Month 2 (2026-12-12), conduct a rapid desktop assessment of the largest 10 carriers' booking systems (40% of network capacity by estimate) by Month 1 (2026-11-12) and use that to establish Tier 1 and Tier 2 timelines; defer Tier 3 (smallest operators, 20% of network by estimate) audit to Month 3 (2027-01-12) to avoid delaying the Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate
  • If the actuarial study vendor is delayed or unable to deliver by Month 3 (2027-01-12), engage a second actuarial firm in parallel by Month 1 (2026-11-12) with a fast-track EUR 0.3M contract to deliver a simplified risk model (using industry benchmarks for missed-connection rates and rerouting costs instead of carrier-specific data) by Month 3 (2027-01-12), allowing the Month 4 (2027-02-12) carrier sign-off process to proceed with good-faith estimates
  • If quarterly risk-register updates cannot be automated or tracked in a shared dashboard, assign a dedicated Risk Coordinator (1 FTE, approximately EUR 0.1M/year) to manually compile monthly risk flash reports (2-page format: 5 risks flagged for escalation, 5 risks trending toward worse, 5 risks improving) and circulate to Programme Director and Steering Group by the 5th of each month
  • If the Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate cannot certify all six mitigation workstreams, adopt a 'phased readiness' approach where critical decisions (liability model, technical tiers) are certified at Month 6 (2027-04-12), and secondary gates (steering consensus on commission band, passenger-rights approval) are certified by Month 9 (2027-07-12), deferring the binding-standards window by 1–3 months
  • If budget variance thresholds (EUR 100M, 200M, 300M) cannot be monitored in real-time due to carrier billing and clearing-system delays, establish a 'predicted variance' process where the Programme Office projects draw-downs based on monthly carrier claims and reconciliation data, and flags predicted variance 1–2 months before it occurs, allowing preventive action rather than reactive cuts
  • If the Programme Director or steering group members turn over mid-phase, immediately conduct a 'risk-transition briefing' (half-day workshop) covering the current risk dashboard, open mitigation tasks, upcoming gates and escalation paths, and secure a written sign-off from the incoming stakeholder(s) to preserve institutional memory and prevent delays

Create Document 9: Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder (Tranches and Verification Criteria)

ID: 4e5e1f6d-4c10-4898-be32-d396ab9d680e

Description: Formal funding-release framework specifying which deliverables must be verified before each funding tranche is released to carriers and member-state bodies. Tier 1 (Month 30 = 2029-04-12): EUR 80M adapter funding released to Tier 1 carriers after independent audit verifies p95 latency <2 seconds, 99.5% uptime, <1% stale-seat errors on live API for 30 consecutive days. Tier 2 (Month 36 = 2029-10-12): EUR 80M released after Tier 2 conformance verification. Tier 3 (Month 42 = 2030-04-12): EUR 50M released after Tier 3 verification. Also specifies that public-distributor concession (EUR 300M) is released in tranches tied to platform launch (Month 30 = 2029-04-12), achieving passenger-volume milestones (Months 36, 48, 60 = 2029-10-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12) and complaint-reduction targets. Output: compliance incentive, budget protection, achievement of SLA targets. Primary audience: carriers, Programme Director, Finance Lead, steering group.

Responsible Role Type: Programme Director (with support from Independent Audit & Assurance Function)

Primary Template: Contract milestone and payment schedule template

Secondary Template: SLA verification checklist (per tier, verified by independent auditor)

Steps to Create:

  • Define tier-specific deliverables and SLA targets by Month 6 (2027-04-12), based on technical audit output and binding standards
  • Specify verification procedure: independent auditor conducts live testing of each carrier's API against SLA targets; tests run for 30 consecutive days (proposed threshold) before tranche release is approved
  • Draft Tier 1 verification checklist (p95 latency <2s, 99.5% uptime, <1% stale-seat errors, booking correctness, refund reversal success rate) and acceptance criteria by Month 9 (2027-07-12)
  • Publish complete funding-release ladder (all three tiers + concession tranches) and SLA-verification schedules by Month 12 (2027-10-12); incorporate into binding standards
  • At each tier's milestone (Months 30, 36, 42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12), conduct independent audit of all carriers in that tier; publish audit results and release/hold decision within 10 business days of test completion
  • For any carrier missing SLA targets, offer remediation window (15 business days) to retest; if still failing, hold that carrier's tranche and escalate to Programme Director
  • For concession tranches, tie releases to measured passenger volumes and complaint-reduction achievements (quarterly metrics); publish progress against targets quarterly

Approval Authorities: Independent Audit & Assurance Function (verification), Programme Director (release decision), DG MOVE Controller (funding authorization)

Essential Information:

  • Specify all three tiered funding tranches with EUR amounts and release triggers: Tier 1 (EUR 80M at Month 30 = 2029-04-12), Tier 2 (EUR 80M at Month 36 = 2029-10-12), Tier 3 (EUR 50M at Month 42 = 2030-04-12), each conditioned on independent audit verification of SLA targets (p95 latency <2 seconds, 99.5% uptime, <1% stale-seat errors) over 30 consecutive days
  • Define concession tranches for the EUR 300M last-resort distributor envelope: platform launch (Month 30 = 2029-04-12), volume milestones (Months 36/48/60 = 2029-10-12/2030-10-12/2031-10-12), complaint-reduction targets, with subsidy capped at EUR 60M over five years and clawback if volumes exceed forecast >20%
  • Detail verification procedure: independent auditor conducts live SLA testing against each carrier's API endpoint; document pass/fail criteria, remediation windows (15 business days to retest), escalation to Programme Director for holdback decisions
  • Specify how tranches attach to the Conformance Gate decision: conformance certificates required before SLA testing begins; document the inter-dependency between gate outcomes and fund release
  • Quantify financial consequences of missed tranches: if Tier 1 carriers miss SLAs, EUR 80M holds; calculate cascade effect on Tier 2/3 timelines and TEN-T extension funding (which draws from post-Month 48 = 2030-10-12 capacity)
  • Document variance triggers tied to programme-wide budget headroom (EUR 85M unallocated): EUR 100M variance triggers TEN-T deferral to Months 60-72 (2031-10-12 to 2032-10-12); EUR 200M triggers 20% concession cut; EUR 300M restricts to four priority corridors only
  • Provide a worked example of a single carrier's path through the three tiers, showing how SLA performance in Month 30 (2029-04-12) gates their Tier 2 eligibility and affects fund flow to their peers
  • Outline governance approval chain: Independent Audit & Assurance Function verifies deliverables, Programme Director authorizes release, DG MOVE Controller signs fund transfer; specify authority sign-off timeline within 10 business days of audit completion

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If SLA verification criteria are vague or left to auditor discretion, carriers dispute results and escalations delay fund releases by 4–8 weeks, cascading Tier 2 and TEN-T extension timelines and straining the budget reserve
  • If tranches are released without independent audit or with self-certification by carriers, compliance incentives evaporate: carriers miss latency and availability targets, through-ticket search succeeds at only 70–80% (versus target >90%), and 15–25% fewer passengers adopt through-tickets (estimate)
  • If concession tranches are not tied to measured passenger volume and complaint reduction, the concessionaire operates at a loss with no accountability, draining the EUR 300M envelope by Month 36 (2029-10-12) and forcing re-budgeting that cuts member-state capacity building by EUR 50–100M (estimate)
  • If variance triggers are not pre-published with clear thresholds (EUR 100M/200M/300M), budget overruns accumulate silently until Month 42–48 (2030-04-12 to 2030-10-12), leaving no time to descope TEN-T or cut concession subsidy, forcing the EUR 150M force-majeure reserve to be drawn for non-force-majeure pool shortfalls
  • If remediation windows and escalation paths are not defined, a single carrier's SLA failure (e.g., 2.5-second latency) can hold EUR 80M and delay Tier 2 work at other carriers, creating perverse incentives and political friction among participants
  • If the document does not bind regulators, DG MOVE and carriers to a common acceptance criteria before audits begin, disputes over what constitutes a 'pass' can delay releases by 2–3 months per tranche

Worst Case Scenario: If the Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder is absent or insufficiently detailed by Month 9 (2027-07-12), carriers lack commitment certainty and face unpredictable funding, leading 30–40% (estimate) to reduce IT investment or withdraw from the programme entirely. This fragments corridor coverage by Month 30 (2029-04-12), leaving 8–15 smaller operators unable to expose APIs and 40–50% of planned through-ticket itineraries unavailable. Unverified fund releases allow the carrier-funded guarantee pool or public distributor concession to overspend without consequence, draining EUR 100–200M of the EUR 1,500M cap by Month 36 (2029-10-12) and eliminating headroom to launch the TEN-T extension. The 40% through-ticket goal becomes unachievable; realistic outcome is 15–25% (estimate), with full network completion pushed to Month 84 (2033-10-12) or abandoned. The programme loses credibility with carriers and independent distributors, triggering legal challenges to funding allocation and regulatory complaints to national bodies.

Best Case Scenario: A well-defined Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder with transparent SLA criteria, independent audits and published variance thresholds enables carriers to commit to integration with certainty: 90%+ of Tier 1 carriers meet latency and availability targets by Month 30 (2029-04-12), their EUR 80M releases on schedule, and Tier 2/3 work advances predictably. Monthly SLA scorecards and variance alerts keep the programme within the EUR 1,500M budget cap and the EUR 85M headroom, allowing all TEN-T corridors to launch by Month 60 (2031-10-12). The concession tranches tied to passenger volumes and complaint reduction incentivise the distributor to invest in marketing and support, achieving the 40% through-ticket target by Month 60 (2031-10-12). Predictable funding releases remove a major programme risk, accelerate carrier confidence and unlock private IT investment that multiplies the public programme's impact. Regulatory oversight is clear, disputes are rare and escalations are resolved within 10 days.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If independent auditing capacity is unavailable, establish an expedited self-certification regime: carriers submit SLA evidence (API test logs, monitoring dashboards) within 15 days of Month 30 (2029-04-12); a small in-house audit team spot-checks 20% of submissions; release 80% of tranches on submission and 20% pending verification completion, reducing cash-flow friction while maintaining compliance discipline
  • If SLA verification proves too contentious among carriers, adopt a 'learning-with-verification' approach: release 50% of Tier 1 funding unconditionally at Month 30 (2029-04-12) to accelerate deployment, tie the remaining 50% to Month 36 (2029-10-12) verification of sustained SLAs; document learnings from early deployment to set more realistic Tier 2 targets
  • If concession tranches cannot be tied to measurable volume and complaint metrics (e.g., because distributor sales data lags by 30 days), use a hybrid: release 60% on schedule based on platform launch and go-live, tie the remaining 40% to quarterly audits of transaction data and complaint records (published with a 6-week lag), capping operating subsidy at EUR 12M/year with monthly burn limits
  • If variance triggers lead to constant re-baselining and cut discussions, establish a 'fixed-variance envelope': allocate EUR 100M of the EUR 150M reserve as a dedicated variance buffer specifically for adapter overruns and concession shortfalls; any variance below EUR 100M auto-adjusts by deferring lower-priority TEN-T corridors rather than escalating for re-approval
  • If governance bottlenecks delay release decisions (e.g., Controller sign-off pending budget cycles), delegate routine releases under EUR 20M to the Programme Director with post-hoc audit reporting to DG MOVE, reserving only tranches >EUR 50M for formal Controller authorization; publish a quarterly release calendar by Month 12 (2027-10-12) so participants can plan 60-day cash-flow forecasts

Create Document 10: Stakeholder Engagement and Governance Charter

ID: b10ae9e2-2c2f-482f-bdfc-8bb038bcbe14

Description: Formal charter defining the steering-group composition, roles, decision rights and escalation processes. Comprises: (1) steering core group (9 members: DG MOVE, Agency, CER, 4 major carriers, Trainline, Omio, BEUC, disability body); (2) 75% supermajority voting rule on critical decisions (Decisions 1-5, commission band); (3) Commission mediation protocol if votes do not reach 75% by Month 5 (2027-03-12); (4) biweekly meeting schedule (Mondays 09:00 Brussels); (5) fallback technical interfaces for dissenting parties (e.g., bilateral clearing for carriers refusing pooled liability, sandbox-only role for distributors refusing mandatory API). Includes observer seats for national regulators and quarterly briefings to member-state governments. Output: transparent, inclusive governance with clear escalation paths. Primary audience: steering members, Commission, member-state governments, carriers, distributors.

Responsible Role Type: Programme Director (with support from Communications & Stakeholder Engagement Lead)

Primary Template: Governance Charter template (EU institutional model)

Secondary Template: Steering group terms of reference (meeting agendas, decision log, action tracking)

Steps to Create:

  • Draft governance charter and decision-rights matrix by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27)
  • Circulate to intended steering members (DG MOVE, CER, 4 major carriers, distributors, BEUC) for feedback Months 0.5-1 (2026-10-27 to 2026-11-12)
  • Resolve any objections to voting rules or escalation procedures by Month 1 (2026-11-12); finalize charter
  • Publish charter and call steering group's first meeting (Month 1 = 2026-11-12); establish biweekly meeting cadence (Mondays 09:00 Brussels time) and action-item tracking
  • At Month 1 (2026-11-12) meeting, set the schedule for binding votes on Decisions 1-5 (by Month 6 = 2027-04-12) and option-paper circulation (by Month 2 = 2026-12-12)
  • Publish option papers for each decision (Decisions 1-5) with explicit trade-offs (speed vs. coverage, control vs. complexity, budget risk vs. carrier autonomy) by Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Hold written consultation on option papers (Months 2-3 = 2026-12-12 to 2027-01-12); compile feedback
  • Conduct binding steering votes (75% supermajority) on all five decisions by Month 6 (2027-04-12); document voting outcomes and dissenting positions
  • If vote on any decision does not reach 75% by Month 5 (2027-03-12), invoke Commission mediation; Commission Transport Commissioner or delegated advisor conducts facilitated dialogue by Month 5.5 (2027-03-27) and recommends resolution by Month 6 (2027-04-12)
  • Maintain detailed steering decision log (biweekly) and publish anonymised summary to carriers and distributors monthly

Approval Authorities: Programme Director (charter sign-off), steering members (by participation), DG MOVE (escalation authority)

Essential Information:

  • Define the steering group's composition, roles and decision rights: 9 core members (DG MOVE, Agency, CER, 4 major carriers, Trainline, Omio, BEUC, disability body), voting threshold (75% supermajority for Decisions 1–5 and commission band), meeting cadence (biweekly Mondays 09:00 Brussels) and action-item tracking.
  • Specify the escalation protocol: if a critical decision does not reach 75% by Month 5 (2027-03-12), Commission mediation must resolve the deadlock by Month 6 (2027-04-12), with clear facilitation steps and fallback technical interfaces (e.g., bilateral clearing for dissenting carriers, sandbox-only role for dissenting distributors).
  • Publish option papers for each critical decision (Decisions 1–5: liability backstop, clearing, public distributor, funding ladder, availability topology) by Month 2 (2026-12-12), each outlining three strategic choices with explicit trade-offs (speed vs. coverage, control vs. complexity, budget risk vs. carrier autonomy).
  • Document observer seat arrangements for national railway regulators and the timing of regulatory impact assessments per member state (Month 3 = 2027-01-12 deadline).
  • Establish the quarterly briefing schedule for member-state governments, carriers and distributors, including pool contribution data, SLA scorecards and commission-band compliance.
  • Clarify the binding-vote calendar: Decisions 1–5 require votes by Month 6 (2027-04-12); if any vote is deferred to Month 12 (2027-10-12), the binding-standards milestone (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) is at risk of a 2–4 month slip (estimate).
  • Detail fallback mechanisms for actors who reject core decisions: bilateral clearing recourse for carriers refusing pooled liability, third-party settlement interface for independent distributors refusing mandatory API, sandbox-only role for distributors refusing consumer-facing mandatory sales.
  • Specify the decision log and action-tracking process: steering decisions logged within 48 hours of meeting, anonymised summary published monthly to all carriers, distributors and member states.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Undefined voting rules or escalation procedures delay binding decisions by 2–4 months (estimate), cascading the binding-standards milestone from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12), which stretches the mandatory API exposure deadline (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12) and reduces four-corridor go-live readiness.
  • Unclear fallback provisions trigger withdrawal of major stakeholders (e.g., a carrier refusing pooled liability or a distributor rejecting the clearing design), fragmenting the network and reducing through-ticket volume by 15–25% (estimate), which lowers the 40% goal to 20–30%.
  • Absent observer seats or regulator engagement lead to national regulatory veto surprises late in the standards phase (Month 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12), requiring 3–6 month rework and legal disputes, estimated cost EUR 10–20 million.
  • Inconsistent or delayed monthly briefings to carriers and distributors create information vacuums, triggering competitive jockeying, rumours about pool contributions and commission bands, and loss of confidence in programme neutrality.
  • No transparent decision log or action tracking erodes stakeholder trust and makes it difficult to trace why decisions were made or who was accountable, inviting challenges to binding votes and reopening settled issues.

Worst Case Scenario: If the steering governance charter is incomplete, ambiguous or published late (beyond Month 1 = 2026-11-12), critical decisions (liability model, clearing architecture, public distributor role, funding tranches, commission band) stall at the steering table or fragment into bilateral negotiations. A deadlocked vote on the liability backstop (Decision 1) that cannot be resolved by mediation by Month 6 (2027-04-12) leaves the programme without a signed carrier risk-allocation model and triggers 30–40% (estimate) of carriers to refuse inventory exposure. This cascades: no agreed liability model means standards cannot bind (Month 18 = 2028-04-12 slips to Month 24–30 = 2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12), API exposure is postponed (Month 30 = 2029-04-12 → Month 36–42 = 2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12), four-corridor go-live fails (Month 48 = 2030-10-12 → Month 60–72 = 2031-10-12 to 2032-10-12) and the 40% through-ticket goal drops to 15–25% (estimate). Major distributors (Trainline, Omio) may withdraw if the clearing design is rejected and no fallback interface is offered. Estimated financial impact: EUR 150–200 million in sunk costs (standards work, pilots, governance overhead) with delivery 12–18 months late and outcomes 40–50% below target.

Best Case Scenario: If the charter is published by Month 1 (2026-11-12) with clear voting rules, escalation triggers and fallback options, steering members align quickly on option papers circulated by Month 2 (2026-12-12). Binding votes on all five critical decisions reach 75% supermajority by Month 6 (2027-04-12), with any dissenting carriers or distributors offered transparent technical fallback interfaces (bilateral clearing, third-party settlement) that preserve their participation. Option papers and explicit trade-offs enable stakeholders to make informed commitments: carriers agree to the signed liability model with clear caps and co-insurance thresholds; distributors accept the federated clearing architecture and the commission band; the public distributor concession is tendered with transparent subsidy caps. Monthly SLA and pool-contribution scorecards build confidence and reduce later disputes. Regulatory observers flag issues early (by Month 3 = 2027-01-12), allowing member-state regulatory impact assessments to be resolved before binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12). Early clarity on governance enables technical and legal working groups to proceed in parallel, compress the Phase 1 schedule (Months 0–18 = 2026-10-12 to 2028-04-12) and hit Tier 1 API exposure (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) on schedule, delivering four priority corridors live by Month 48 (2030-10-12) and reaching the 40% through-ticket target by Month 60 (2031-10-12) within the EUR 1,500M budget.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If consensus on the 75% supermajority rule cannot be reached by Month 1 (2026-11-12), adopt a modified consensus rule: Decisions 1–3 (liability, clearing, public distributor) require 80% supermajority (7 of 8 voting steering members, excluding observers); Decisions 4–5 (funding, availability) require 60% supermajority (5 of 8). This reduces deadlock risk but increases the chance of downstream rework once smaller carriers or distributors implement non-consensus choices.
  • If escalation to the Commission Transport Commissioner is not available or too slow, establish a binding arbitration mechanism: appoint an independent mediator (e.g., a retired EU judge or transport economist) to hear positions from 30 days after a 75% vote is missed and issue a binding recommendation within 15 days. Implementable by Month 14 (2027-12-12) if legal authority is secured from DG MOVE.
  • If major carriers (e.g., DB, SNCF, ÖBB) reject the pooled-liability backstop, offer a phased rollout: allow Tier 1 (corridor-critical) carriers to negotiate bilateral liability caps with the clearing entity in a Phase 2 opening (Month 24 = 2028-10-12), with transparency requirements so smaller carriers can see the effective caps and propose equivalent terms. This delays full-pool consensus but allows standards to proceed with interim liability rules.
  • If independent distributors refuse the federated clearing architecture, establish a third-party settlement interface: any distributor can route settlements through an existing sector clearinghouse (e.g., Equinix or Paysafe) under an escrow and netting protocol, with the clearing entity providing only the master data dictionary and dispute-resolution procedures. This preserves distributor choice while maintaining system coherence.
  • If steering deadlock persists beyond Month 9 (2027-07-12), compress the decision scope: defer Decisions 4–5 (funding release ladder and commission band) to a Month 12 (2027-10-12) secondary vote, and proceed with binding standards based on Decisions 1–3 (liability, clearing, public distributor) alone. This allows technical standards work to advance while commercial terms are negotiated in parallel, with the caveat that binding standards cannot fully specify funding tranches or commission rules until Month 12 (2027-10-12).

Documents to Find

Find Document 1: EU Rail Ticketing Regulation Proposal Text and Legislative Status

ID: fc47eb5b-741b-4632-b918-f0dfa46efa09

Description: The formal text of the Commission's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail (proposed May 2026, status not verified as of project start October 2026). Provides the legal foundation for binding standards, mandatory API exposure, passenger-rights harmonisation and the Agency's role in conformance oversight. Essential input for the binding-standards working group and for forecasting the Regulation's adoption timeline (estimated Month 18 = 2028-04-12, but 6-12 month slip plausible). Intended audience for analysis: standards custodian, competition-law counsel, Programme Director.

Recency Requirement: Current as of project start (Month 0 = 2026-10-12); must reflect the proposal tabled in May 2026, including any amendments proposed by Parliament or Council by Month 0 (2026-10-12).

Responsible Role Type: Regulatory Affairs and Stakeholder Alignment Director

Steps to Find:

  • Search EUR-Lex (Official EU Legislation Portal) for 'Regulation Digital Booking Ticketing Services Rail' or similar keywords; confirm proposal date (May 2026) and current legislative status
  • Contact DG MOVE legislative affairs unit directly (email to DG-MOVE-REGISTRY@ec.europa.eu or via the DG MOVE website) requesting a copy of the May 2026 proposal and any amendments tabled by Parliament or Council
  • If the proposal has been tabled and is available on EUR-Lex, download full text and all explanatory memoranda
  • If proposal has not yet been tabled, request from DG MOVE: a pre-release briefing or roadmap indicating the tabling timeline (estimate currently Month 2-6 = 2026-12-12 to 2027-04-12)
