Access Difficulty: Medium. The Commission proposal (if published) is freely available on EUR-Lex. If not yet published (proposed May 2026, not yet confirmed as of October 2026 project start), access requires direct contact with DG MOVE, which will provide it confidentially or on request. Legislative amendments may not be publicly available until tabled formally in Parliament or Council.

Essential Information:

  • Confirm the Commission proposal's official title, tabling date (May 2026 claimed) and current parliamentary/Council status as of Month 0 (2026-10-12).
  • Identify the binding-standards trigger mechanism: which articles or provisions require OSDM to be pinned via delegated act, implementing act, or direct regulation text, and the timeline for each.
  • Extract the mandatory API exposure date and scope: which carriers, which data fields, which endpoints (search, booking, refunds, disruption) are legally required by what deadline.
  • List all passenger-rights obligations imposed on through-tickets: continuity-of-journey rules, compensation thresholds, assistance notice periods, refund timelines, and how they differ from single-carrier journeys under Regulation 1371/2007.
  • Detail the Agency's role: does the Regulation grant the Agency power to set conformance standards, approve clearing mechanisms, oversee OSDM change control, or only supervise member-state implementation.
  • Specify the legal basis and scope for a carrier-funded guarantee pool or public rights backstop: are both permitted, is one mandated, and what limits (caps, reinsurance, member-state veto) apply.
  • Identify any restrictions on public or third-party distributor roles: can a public reference distributor operate a consumer-facing sales channel, or only a B2B sandbox.
  • Extract competition-law carve-outs or safe harbours: does the Regulation explicitly permit data sharing, clearing, or fare-construction coordination among competing carriers, or does Article 101 TFEU apply in full.
  • List any member-state implementation flexibility: can national regulators opt out, delay conformance, or impose stricter rules than the Regulation baseline.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If the proposal text is not the final May 2026 tabling, but an earlier draft or leaked version, the binding-standards working group builds on incorrect legal foundations, requiring 2–3 month rework once the official text is published.
  • If the mandatory API exposure date or scope is misread (e.g., 'all data' versus 'search and booking only'), carriers and distributors invest in the wrong systems, delaying conformance by 6–12 months and fragmenting the network.
  • If passenger-rights obligations are weaker than Regulation 1371/2007 or create ambiguous gaps, the programme risks legal challenges from passenger-rights bodies and regulator enforcement, requiring 3–6 month redesign of the liability and disruption procedures.
  • If the Agency's conformance or OSDM-stewardship powers are narrower than assumed, the Specification Custodian Seat decision and the binding-standards delivery depend on a consensus mechanism not yet defined, delaying standards by 2–4 months.
  • If the Regulation permits a public distributor only as a sandbox (not consumer-facing), the Public Reference Distributor Mandate decision must pivot from a last-resort concession to a narrower B2B role, reducing the programme's ability to reach the 40% through-ticket goal.
  • If competition-law safe harbours are absent or weak, a DG COMP challenge after Month 24 (2028-10-12) could unwind the clearing or data-sharing arrangements, forcing 6–12 month rework and EUR 50–100M cost (estimate).
  • If the Regulation imposes stricter environmental or accessibility requirements than the programme assumes, the four-corridor go-live timeline slips by 3–6 months due to infrastructure compliance work not yet budgeted.

Worst Case Scenario: The proposal text is not the official May 2026 tabling but a draft; the parliamentary or Council process has already tabled substantial amendments that weaken mandatory API scope, remove safe harbours for data sharing, or delay the binding-standards deadline to Month 24 (2028-10-12) or later. The binding-standards working group proceeds on incorrect legal foundations until Month 6 (2027-04-12), when an authoritative legal review discovers discrepancies. The programme must conduct a 2–3 month legal rework, defer binding standards from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 21 (2028-07-12), push mandatory API exposure from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 36 (2029-10-12), and compress the four-corridor go-live from Month 48 (2030-10-12) to Month 54–60 (2031-04-12 to 2031-10-12). Carriers and distributors lose confidence in the legal foundation and delay investment, reducing participation from 25+ to 15–18 operators. The 40% through-ticket goal becomes unachievable; realistic outcome is 20–25% (estimate). Budget is reallocated to accelerate legal and standards work, draining EUR 50–100M from later-wave infrastructure, and the full TEN-T rollout extends beyond Month 72 (2032-10-12).

Best Case Scenario: The proposal is the official May 2026 text, has clear binding-standards triggers (OSDM pinned by Month 18 = 2028-04-12), mandatory API exposure for all participating carriers by Month 30 (2029-04-12), and explicit safe harbours for carrier data sharing and pooled clearing. Passenger-rights obligations align with or exceed Regulation 1371/2007, so no redesign is needed. The Agency is granted clear power to oversee conformance and OSDM governance, making the Specification Custodian Seat decision executable without additional consensus. The Regulation permits both a public consumer-facing distributor and a carrier-funded guarantee pool, giving the programme full design flexibility. No competition-law carve-out is explicit, but the legal opinion by Month 6 (2027-04-12) confirms Article 101 compatibility under the clean-team arrangement. Carriers and distributors see clear legal certainty and accelerate investment; the liability model is signed off by Month 4 (2027-02-12) with no disputes. Binding standards are delivered on schedule Month 18 (2028-04-12), mandatory API exposure is met by Month 30 (2029-04-12), and the four corridors go live by Month 48 (2030-10-12). The 40% through-ticket goal is reached by Month 60 (2031-10-12); the full TEN-T network completes by Month 66–72 (2032-04-12 to 2032-10-12).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the official proposal text is not available by Month 2 (2026-12-12), request a detailed legislative roadmap from DG MOVE's directorate for directorate legal affairs covering the expected tabling date, anticipated amendments and the adoption timeline. Work in parallel with a shadow standards workstream that drafts binding-standards language for each plausible scenario (strong safe harbour, weak safe harbour, no safe harbour) so that the formal standards can pivot once the Regulation text is confirmed.
  • Establish a legal-watch panel (DG MOVE, Agency, BEUC, CER and one independent competition-law counsel) that monitors the Regulation's legislative progress from Month 1 (2026-11-12) onwards and flags deviations from the May 2026 proposal by end of Month 3 (2027-01-12). If material changes are flagged, commission a rapid legal impact assessment (2–3 weeks) by Month 4 (2027-02-12) and adjust the binding-standards and liability-model timelines accordingly.
  • If the proposal is not yet tabled and adoption timeline slips beyond Month 18 (2028-04-12), negotiate with member states to adopt a voluntary binding-standards arrangement (technical declaration or council statement) that pins OSDM and mandatory API scope without waiting for formal Regulation adoption. This preserves the Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards milestone and allows pilots to proceed under member-state regulatory cover.
  • If passenger-rights obligations in the Regulation diverge materially from Regulation 1371/2007 or are ambiguous, commission an independent legal audit by the Agency and a passenger-rights NGO by Month 6 (2027-04-12) that specifies the minimum rights floor and proposes a compliance manual. Use this manual as the interim binding standard for carrier conformance, to be reconciled with the final Regulation language once published.
  • If the Regulation restricts the public distributor to a B2B sandbox, negotiate with DG MOVE to permit the programme to launch a tendered last-resort concession under a separate legal basis (e.g., as a public service obligation under transport regulation) running in parallel with the OSDM programme. This preserves the last-resort channel without relying on the Regulation's distributor scope.

Find Document 2: Historical Rail Passenger Missed-Connection and Rerouting Cost Data (Per-Carrier)

ID: ca167ec9-6337-49b6-8a62-134c8439a574

Description: 24-month rolling data on missed-connection incidents, rerouting costs, passenger compensation claims and incident clustering from at least 5 major European carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, SBB, Renfe, ÖBB or equivalent) and one mid-size carrier. Used as input for the actuarial study to derive missed-connection frequencies, rerouting cost distributions, and carrier-specific risk profiles that underpin the carrier-funded guarantee-pool model (Decision 1) and the liability-cap and co-insurance parameters. Intended audience for analysis: actuary, risk-modelling specialist, Programme Director.

Recency Requirement: Most recent 24-month rolling period (September 2024 to September 2026, covering the most recent two full operational years before project start). Data must be current and representative; older data risks obsolescence due to changes in operating practices or passenger demand.

Responsible Role Type: Carrier Liability & Risk Modelling Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • Contact CER (Community of European Railways) membership team and request introduction to finance/operations contacts at 5-6 major carriers for historical incident data exchange
  • Send formal data-request letter to each carrier (CIOs and CFOs) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27) requesting: monthly counts of missed-connection incidents (by corridor and carrier pair), cost per incident (rerouting, accommodation, compensation), incident severity classification (passenger stranded <1 hour, 1-4 hours, >4 hours) and any seasonal or systemic clustering patterns
  • Offer confidentiality agreement and data-protection assurances (GDPR compliance, aggregation to remove passenger identifiers, use limited to actuarial study)
  • Follow up with carriers biweekly; expect 2-4 week response time (carriers may need to extract data from legacy systems or business-intelligence tools)
  • Aggregate data received and anonymise at the carrier-group level (don't publish individual carrier figures without permission); validate completeness and reasonableness with CER

Access Difficulty: Hard. Missed-connection data is proprietary business information that carriers typically do not share publicly (competitive sensitivity). Access requires direct carrier engagement via CER, confidentiality agreements and data-protection protocols. Some data may be held in legacy systems that are difficult to query. Smaller carriers may lack systematic incident tracking. Estimate 4-8 weeks to obtain data from all 5-6 carriers; risk of incomplete or non-standardised reporting.

Essential Information:

  • Historical monthly missed-connection incident counts per carrier pair and corridor for the 24-month period September 2024 to September 2026, segmented by severity (stranded <1 hour, 1–4 hours, >4 hours).
  • Cost per incident: rerouting expenses, accommodation and meal allowances, passenger compensation claims paid, and total cost distribution by incident type.
  • Seasonal patterns, daily clustering and any systemic correlations between specific corridor pairs, train services or weather conditions and missed-connection frequency.
  • Carrier-specific on-time performance metrics (12-month trailing average) to calibrate the contribution-weighting formula for the guarantee pool.
  • Data quality assessment: completeness of incident reporting, any gaps in legacy-system records, and confidence intervals for smaller carriers with fewer incidents.
  • Anonymised incident logs or aggregated tables suitable for actuarial modelling without exposing commercially sensitive individual-carrier figures.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or non-standardised data (e.g., missing incident severity classification or cost breakdowns) forces the actuary to make conservative assumptions, inflating the calculated pool contributions and deterring carrier participation.
  • Outdated data (older than September 2024) does not reflect current operational practices, route changes or demand patterns, risking the liability model's relevance by Month 30 (2029-04-12) when carriers operate under it.
  • Aggregated-only data without incident-level granularity prevents the actuary from identifying clustering patterns (e.g., specific troublesome corridor pairs) that justify tiered contribution rules, leading to cross-subsidies between carriers and recriminations.
  • Data from only large carriers omits smaller-operator risk profiles, creating a model that either overcharges them (deterring participation) or underestimates system-wide loss rates.
  • Missing or inconsistent cost allocation (e.g., rerouting costs attributed to the wrong carrier) invalidates the per-incident cap estimates and the co-insurance threshold, potentially leaving the pool under-capitalised or over-reserved.

Worst Case Scenario: The actuarial study (scheduled Month 6 = 2027-04-12) cannot be completed with confidence because requested carriers submit incomplete, incomparable or confidentiality-restricted data. The actuary is forced to extrapolate from publicly available passenger-complaint statistics or simplified estimates, producing liability parameters (caps and co-insurance thresholds) that carriers view as arbitrary. By Month 4 (2027-02-12), when carrier sign-off is required, 30–40% of major carriers refuse to commit inventory exposure under unpriceable terms. The programme loses momentum; binding standards milestone (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) is delayed 2–4 months. The 40% through-ticket goal becomes unachievable, settling at 15–25% (estimate). Budget allocated for TEN-T extension (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) is reallocated to smaller-carrier adapters, compressing the full-network rollout to Month 72 (2032-10-12) or beyond.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 2 (2026-12-12), all contacted carriers provide 24-month rolling data in standardised format with full cost and incident detail. The actuary completes the study by Month 3 (2027-01-12) with high confidence, identifying carrier-specific risk profiles and corridor-pair clusters. A draft liability model with per-incident caps (e.g., EUR 500–1,000) and co-insurance threshold (e.g., EUR 50M annual draw) is published by Month 3 (2027-01-12). CER and 8+ major carriers sign off by Month 4 (2027-02-12), validating the carriers' ability to price exposure. The binding vote passes 75% supermajority in Month 6 (2027-04-12). Confidence in the liability model unlocks carrier inventory exposure by Month 18 (2028-04-12), enabling the mandatory API exposure milestone (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) to proceed on schedule. The four-corridor through-ticketing launch (Month 48 = 2030-10-12) reaches the full target network by Month 60 (2031-10-12), supporting the 40% through-ticket goal.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If carriers decline to share historical incident data directly, request aggregated statistics from national railway-accident investigation bodies (ERAs) or the EU Agency for Railways, which may hold regulatory incident reports; this introduces a 2–4 week delay and possible data gaps for commercial rerouting costs not captured in official investigations.
  • Engage a third-party insurance broker or reinsurer (e.g., Munich Re, Swiss Re) that underwrites railway liability; they hold proprietary loss-ratio data and can model missed-connection risk; this trades carrier confidentiality concerns for expert external modelling (cost estimate EUR 200–400k).
  • Conduct a time-bounded shadow data-collection pilot (3–4 weeks) on one corridor (e.g., Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln) with 3–4 carriers, measure live missed-connection incidents and costs in parallel, and extrapolate to the full network if data patterns are similar; this validates model assumptions at lower confidentiality risk.
  • Commission an independent actuarial consultant to conduct confidential bilateral interviews with each carrier's finance and operations teams to extract cost and frequency estimates in narrative form, then reconstruct numerical distributions; this is slower (4–6 weeks) but may access data carriers do not share in writing.
  • If Month 3 (2027-01-12) data is still incomplete, adopt a conservative precautionary model: set the per-incident cap lower (e.g., EUR 300–500 instead of EUR 500–1,000) and the co-insurance threshold higher (e.g., EUR 75M instead of EUR 50M), acceptably burdening carriers now to avoid actuarial surprises later; defer the refined model to Month 12 (2027-10-12) and adjust contributions retroactively.

Find Document 3: Existing EU and Member-State Rail Passenger-Rights Regulations and Enforcement Data

ID: 3eb00878-f735-4718-9368-9e93bf0f13c9

Description: The full text of EU Regulation 1371/2007 (railway passengers' rights) and any amendments (Regulation 2023/123, etc.), plus national implementing regulations and enforcement data (complaints by category, compensation paid, unresolved cases) from national regulators in France, Germany, Austria, Spain and other member states. Used to establish the baseline rights that through-ticket passengers must maintain and to model potential compensation liability. Intended audience for analysis: passenger-rights counsel, Programme Director, EU Agency for Railways.

Recency Requirement: Current regulations as of project start (October 2026). Must include EU Regulation 1371/2007 as currently in force, any recent amendments (2023 or later), and national enforcement data from 2024-2026 if available.

Responsible Role Type: Passenger Rights, Accessibility & Consumer Protection Lead

Steps to Find:

  • Download EU Regulation 1371/2007 and all amendments from EUR-Lex (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/); search for 'Regulation 1371/2007'
  • Download Regulation 2023/123 (recent amendment, if applicable) from EUR-Lex
  • Contact national railway regulators (or passenger ombudsmen) in France (DGAC/DGITM), Germany (EBA), Austria (ÖBB regulator), Spain (Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia) requesting annual enforcement reports or complaints statistics for 2024-2026
  • Request a copy of any high-level enforcement guidance or case-law summaries from national regulators
  • Search EU Agency for Railways website for any published enforcement statistics or guidance on passenger-rights harmonisation

Access Difficulty: Easy. EU regulations are freely published on EUR-Lex. National enforcement data is typically public (annual reports) but may require direct contact with national regulators; some member states publish enforcement data in native language only. Estimate 1-2 weeks to obtain all core documents.

Essential Information:

  • Full text of EU Regulation 1371/2007 (railway passengers' rights) and all amendments (Regulation 2023/123 and others) as currently in force at project start (October 2026).
  • National implementing regulations from France, Germany, Austria, Spain and other participating member states that transpose the EU passenger-rights directive.
  • Annual enforcement data from national railway regulators (2024–2026): complaints by category (missed connections, compensation delays, accessibility failures, refund disputes), compensation amounts paid, average resolution time, unresolved cases and appeals.
  • Baseline rights that through-ticket passengers must maintain: continuity of journey, refund rules, compensation thresholds, assistance for persons with reduced mobility, and liability for carrier failures.
  • Identification of gaps or conflicts between Regulation 1371/2007 and the programme's proposed Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop design (Decision 1) to ensure no passenger rights are reduced.
  • Case law or regulatory guidance from national courts or regulators on passenger-rights disputes, particularly on missed connections and rerouting liability across carriers.
  • Any recent enforcement actions or penalties issued by national regulators against carriers for passenger-rights violations, to inform the liability model's per-incident caps.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If the baseline rights are misunderstood or incompletely captured, the Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop design (Decision 1) may fall short of Regulation 1371/2007 requirements, exposing the programme to regulatory enforcement notices and forcing a 3–6 month redesign by Month 6–12 (2027-04-12 to 2027-10-12).
  • Incomplete or outdated enforcement data (e.g., missing 2024–2026 figures) prevents the actuarial study (due Month 6 = 2027-04-12) from establishing realistic missed-connection rates and compensation liability, leading to a carrier-funded guarantee pool that is either under-provisioned (forcing pool top-ups from the fixed EUR 1.5 billion budget) or over-provisioned (wasting contingency).
  • Gaps in national implementing regulations across member states may allow carriers or national regulators to claim that the programme's uniform clearing or rights design is incompatible with local law, triggering 12–24 month legal disputes per member state and fragmenting corridor coverage.
  • If enforcement case law and penalty data are not reviewed, the liability model's per-incident caps (proposed at EUR 500–1,000 per stranded passenger) may be misaligned with actual regulatory expectations, inviting either carrier non-participation (if caps are too high) or regulatory challenge (if caps are too low).

Worst Case Scenario: The programme's proposed Through-Ticket Liability and Rights Backstop design conflicts with Regulation 1371/2007 in a material way (e.g., the carrier-funded guarantee pool does not cover all mandatory compensation or restricts passenger recovery rights). This is discovered after binding standards are published (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) or during early carrier pilots (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12). The EU Agency for Railways or a national regulator issues an enforcement notice requiring rework of the liability rules. The programme must redesign the guarantee pool, clearing mechanism and recourse rules, delaying mandatory API exposure from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12). Carriers already participating in pilots withdraw due to revised exposure. The four-corridor go-live slips from Month 48 (2030-10-12) to Month 60–66 (2031-10-12 to 2032-04-12). Through-ticket share is reduced from 40% target to 20–30% (estimate). Estimated cost: EUR 10–20 million in legal and redesign effort, plus 3–6 months calendar delay.

Best Case Scenario: The programme obtains a comprehensive, current copy of Regulation 1371/2007, all national implementing regulations and five years of enforcement data (2024–2026) by Month 3 (2027-01-12). Independent legal counsel confirms that the proposed liability backstop and clearing design meet or exceed all mandatory passenger-rights obligations. The liability model's per-incident caps (EUR 500–1,000) are validated against actual regulatory penalty precedent and actuarial missed-connection rates. National regulators are briefed and pre-approve the design by Month 6 (2027-04-12). Binding standards incorporate the validated rights framework without revision. Carriers sign onto the liability model with confidence because maximum exposure is predictable and benchmarked. The programme proceeds to standards publication (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) and API exposure (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) on schedule. Through-ticket pilots confirm rights compliance. Four corridors go live by Month 48 (2030-10-12) and the 40% through-ticket share is achieved by Month 60 (2031-10-12) as planned.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If obtaining full national implementing regulations and enforcement data from all member states proves too slow or incomplete by Month 2 (2026-12-12), engage the EU Agency for Railways to publish a consolidated summary of Regulation 1371/2007 obligations and known national variations, supplemented by telephone interviews with national rail regulators. This can be completed by Month 3 (2027-01-12) at lower cost (EUR 0.5–1 million estimate) than a full document collection.
  • If enforcement data (complaints, compensation paid, unresolved cases) for 2024–2026 is not available in English or is withheld by national regulators, commission a targeted survey of the largest five carriers asking them to share anonymised missed-connection and compensation data for the past three years. Cross-validate against BEUC and consumer-body complaint logs. Complete by Month 4 (2027-02-12).
  • If the independent legal review (due Month 6 = 2027-04-12) identifies a material gap in rights coverage, establish a taskforce of national regulators and passenger-rights counsel to propose a legislative amendment to the programme's Regulation text or a supplementary rights policy document. This can be published alongside binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) without delaying the standards themselves.
  • If a national regulator claims local-law incompatibility with the uniform liability or clearing design, offer a bilateral protocol with that member state that preserves the core through-ticketing mechanism while adding a national-level rights wrapper or claims-handling procedure. Document as a precedent for other member states and seek ERAIL (EU Agency for Railways) endorsement to prevent cascading challenges.

Find Document 4: Current OSDM Specification (Latest Published Version) and UIC Governance Documentation

ID: 4b9ffdeb-44b9-4873-b157-b5e1f7a87be1

Description: The latest published version of the UIC Open Sales and Distribution Model (OSDM) specification, including API reference, data models and conformance requirements, plus documentation of the UIC's standards-governance process (change-request procedures, release cadence, conformance-test suite). Used to inform the binding-standards working group's design of OSDM conformance requirements and to understand the existing community's practices and concerns. Intended audience for analysis: standards custodian, carriers' CIOs, distributors.

Recency Requirement: Latest published OSDM version as of project start (October 2026). Must be the current stable release used by carrier adopters (likely OSDM 2.x or later); check UIC website for the authoritative version number.

Responsible Role Type: Standards & Technical Specification Custodian

Steps to Find:

  • Visit UIC website (https://uic.org) and search for 'OSDM' or 'Open Sales and Distribution Model'
  • Download the latest OSDM specification (likely available as PDF or linked from a GitHub repository)
  • Request UIC Passenger Department contact via the UIC website; ask for pointer to: (1) current OSDM version status, (2) change-request process and backlog, (3) reference conformance test suite, (4) list of current adopter carriers and distributors
  • If OSDM is hosted on GitHub, clone or download the repository to access specification source, test data and any open issues
  • Request access to the UIC's OSDM community mailing list or Slack channel if publicly available

Access Difficulty: Easy. OSDM specification is published openly by the UIC. GitHub repository and documentation are public. Community contact is available via the UIC website. Estimate 1 week to obtain all core documents and establish initial contact.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the current OSDM specification version number and release date as of Month 0 (2026-10-12), confirming it matches the version pinned by the binding-standards deadline (Month 18 = 2028-04-12).
  • Detail the UIC's change-request process, including severity tiers (critical, major, minor), review timelines per tier, approval gates and the current backlog of pending requests.
  • List all conformance test suites included in the specification: test data, pass/fail criteria, API endpoint contracts, data validation rules and edge cases (e.g. stale inventory, multi-leg queries, refund reversals).
  • Document the governance structure that maintains OSDM: who owns change control, how disputes are resolved, release cadence and backward-compatibility guarantees.
  • Enumerate all current OSDM adopters by carrier name and distributor name, noting their go-live dates, API maturity levels and any known implementation gaps or deviations from the specification.
  • Specify the data models for through-ticket fares, availability queries, booking confirmation, cancellation, refund and liability signalling; confirm these cover the federated clearing and carrier-funded guarantee pool scenarios.
  • Define the API contracts for real-time availability updates (streaming or polling), booking-authority confirmation, disruption event notification and settlement data exchange.
  • Describe the existing credential and validation formats (barcodes, tokens, digital certificates) and any plans for cross-carrier recognition or hybrid formats.
  • List known limitations or gaps in the current specification that the binding-standards working group must address (e.g. multi-modal chaining, accessibility reservations, bilateral vs. federated clearing semantics).
  • Provide contact information for the UIC Passenger Department and the OSDM community stewards, and confirm availability of the specification source code on GitHub or an equivalent open repository.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If the specification version is outdated or not current as of Month 0 (2026-10-12), the standards-working group uses stale API contracts and data models, requiring rework at Month 12 (2027-10-12) and delaying binding standards by 2-3 months to Month 20-21 (2028-06-12 to 2028-07-12).
  • Incomplete or ambiguous conformance test criteria leave carriers and distributors unsure which implementations pass, leading to integration failures during Tier 1 API exposure (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) and rejection of 20-30% of on-time certification attempts.
  • Missing or unclear data models for through-ticket fares, liability signalling and settlement leaves the clearing mechanism (Decision 2) and liability backstop (Decision 1) unimplementable; carriers cannot build the guarantee pool or federated netting layer.
  • Lack of documented current adopters and their implementation status obscures which carriers have OSDM-ready systems and which require adapters, invalidating the Conformance Gate and Carrier Onboarding Support tiering (Decision 6) and risking Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate failure.
  • Ambiguous or missing governance rules for OSDM change control (Decision 11) leave the standards-working group without authority to resolve disputes, stalling the specification pinning by Month 18 (2028-04-12) and cascading delays to Month 24-30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12).
  • Undocumented limitations in credential formats or validation interoperability mean Ticket Validation and Onboard Inspection Interoperability (Decision 13) cannot be implemented by Month 40 (2030-02-12), leaving 20% of corridor vehicles without cross-carrier ticket recognition and eroding passenger trust by 5-10%.
  • Missing API contracts for disruption event notification or real-time rerouting prevent Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography (Decision 9) from operating reliably; response times exceed 30-60 minutes and re-accommodation success falls below 80%, triggering regulatory complaints and reducing through-ticket adoption by 10-20%.

Worst Case Scenario: The OSDM specification available at Month 0 (2026-10-12) is outdated or incomplete: API contracts lack through-ticket liability signalling, the conformance test suite is vague or missing edge cases (multi-leg stale inventory, refund reversals), and the governance structure is undocumented. The standards-working group discovers these gaps at Month 12 (2027-10-12) during conformance protocol drafting, requiring 4-6 months of rework. Binding standards slip from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 22-24 (2028-08-12 to 2028-10-12), pushing mandatory API exposure from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 36-42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12). Tier 1 carriers miss the Month 30 (2029-04-12) milestone by 2-3 quarters, and the network remains fragmented until Month 48-54 (2030-10-12 to 2031-04-12), reducing through-ticket share from the 40% target to 20-25%. Budget reallocation to accelerate conformance testing and rework consumes EUR 50-100M (estimate), leaving EUR 85M headroom insufficient to cover Tier 2-3 adapter overruns. The programme's credibility with carriers and regulators is damaged; the Court of Auditors questions oversight and management quality.

Best Case Scenario: The OSDM specification is current, comprehensive and well-documented as of Month 0 (2026-10-12), with full API contracts for through-ticket fares, liability signalling, settlement data and disruption events, a clear conformance test suite and active documentation of all current adopters' maturity levels. The standards-working group uses the specification as a stable foundation, pinning it by Month 18 (2028-04-12) with minimal rework. Tier 1 carriers (approximately 12-15 operators) achieve conformance certification by Month 30 (2029-04-12) on schedule; Tier 2 and Tier 3 cascades follow at Months 36 and 42 (2029-10-12 and 2030-04-12). The four priority corridors deliver live through-ticketing by Month 48 (2030-10-12), reaching approximately 30% through-ticket penetration by Month 54 (2031-04-12) and close to the 40% target by Month 60 (2031-10-12). Carriers and distributors integrate with confidence; the conformance gate operates efficiently and SLA penalties apply to underperformers without surprises. The TEN-T extension wave (Months 48-60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) proceeds on budget, and programme costs stay within the EUR 1,500M cap with EUR 100M+ headroom preserved for contingency.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the current OSDM specification is incomplete or misaligned with the programme's needs (federated clearing, through-ticket liability signalling, multi-modal chaining), commission the UIC Passenger Department or a contracted standards body to produce a specification supplement by Month 6 (2027-04-12) covering the gaps, with fast-track review by DG MOVE before Month 12 (2027-10-12). Cost estimate: EUR 2-5M.
  • If the OSDM governance structure is unclear or the UIC's change-control process is too slow (>6 weeks per request), establish an interim EU Specification Custodian working group at the EU Agency for Railways (Decision 11) that mirrors the UIC process but publishes a pinned version by Month 18 (2028-04-12) with a 2-3 week fast-track for critical fixes. Requires legislative authorization in the Regulation.
  • If current OSDM adopters' implementation status is undocumented, run a rapid 4-week survey (Month 1-2 = 2026-11-12 to 2026-12-12) of CER member carriers, Trainline and Omio to benchmark which systems are production-ready and which require adapters, informing the technical audit (Risk 2) and tiering (Decision 6).
  • If the specification lacks edge-case handling (stale inventory in multi-leg queries, refund reversals across carriers, liability signalling), add a conformance test suite enhancement workstream (EUR 5-10M, estimate) led by the Agency and contracted test engineers, deliverable by Month 12 (2027-10-12), before live pilots at Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12).
  • If OSDM credential formats or validation interoperability cannot be standardized in the current specification, explore a hybrid approach (Decision 13) in which each carrier's native credential remains valid and a second-layer API handshake (e.g. signed JWT or OAuth token) enables cross-carrier verification on gates and handhelds, reducing retrofit scope and fitting within the conformance timeline by Month 30 (2029-04-12).
  • If the UIC is unable or unwilling to host the specification maintenance and change control, establish a formal escrow arrangement (Decision 11) in which the specification and all test suites are archived in a neutral open-source repository (e.g. GitHub under an EU-controlled organization) with a public changelog, allowing carriers and distributors to fork if necessary and reducing lock-in risk.

Find Document 5: Carrier Booking System Architecture Survey Results (From Pre-Programme Technical Audit)

ID: 0b58684f-d20a-496d-8589-c8d196fc0248

Description: Detailed findings from the pre-programme technical audit of all 25+ participating carriers, including: current API readiness, event-streaming capability, transaction-consistency architecture, latency profiles (p50, p95, p99 percentiles), 12-month uptime %, legacy-system bottlenecks, staff FTE available for integration, and estimated retrofit cost per operator. Used to tier carriers for conformance timelines (Tiers 1, 2, 3) and to design shared adapter modules. Intended audience for analysis: carrier integration manager, programme management, finance lead.

Recency Requirement: Current as of Month 2 (2026-12-12) (completion of the pre-programme technical audit). Data must reflect carriers' systems state in Q3/Q4 2026 (baseline), not historical data from prior years.

Responsible Role Type: Carrier Integration & Technical Onboarding Manager

Steps to Find:

  • Contract an independent technical audit firm by Month 1 (2026-11-12) to conduct the audit; specify delivery Month 2 (2026-12-12)
  • Audit firm issues technical assessment questionnaire to all 25+ carriers by Month 1 (2026-11-12), requesting: API status (current, under development, legacy), event-streaming capability (Kafka, REST polling, custom), latency profiles (p95 percentile for three-leg queries), annual uptime data (12-month history), legacy-system details and staff availability
  • Audit firm conducts on-site or remote system reviews (30+ carrier days total) Months 1-2 (2026-11-12 to 2026-12-12)
  • Audit firm publishes draft findings and tier recommendations by Month 2 (2026-12-12) end
  • Receive final audit report from firm including: detailed per-carrier assessments, tier assignments, roadmap timelines, shared-adapter recommendations, cost estimates per carrier

Access Difficulty: Medium. Carriers will be contractually obligated (as participants in the programme) to provide system-architecture data via the audit process. Smaller carriers or those with legacy systems may have limited documentation and require in-person site visits to validate information. Estimate 4-6 weeks for a full 25+ carrier audit; timing is critical to inform tier assignment by Month 6 (2027-04-12).

Essential Information:

  • Detailed current-state assessment of all 25+ participating carriers' booking-system architectures, including API readiness level (none, planned, partial, or full), event-streaming technology (Kafka, REST polling, custom, or none), transaction-consistency model, and latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) for single and three-leg queries.
  • Measured 12-month uptime percentage and outage frequency (count and duration) for each carrier's booking engine, baseline from Q3/Q4 2026 (Month 0–2 = 2026-10-12 to 2026-12-12) operations.
  • Legacy-system bottleneck identification per carrier: incompatible protocols, data-format gaps, insufficient API throughput, missing event-stream capability, and estimated effort in FTE-months to retrofit.
  • Staff FTE availability and integration-team maturity per carrier: number of engineers, OSDM experience level, bandwidth for concurrent integration work during Months 6–30 (2027-04-12 to 2029-04-12).
  • Retrofit cost estimate per carrier, broken down by shared-adapter usage (applicable to Tier 2/3) versus bespoke integration, with confidence intervals (±20%).
  • Tier assignment recommendation for each carrier (Tier 1 by Month 30 = 2029-04-12, Tier 2 by Month 36 = 2029-10-12, Tier 3 by Month 42 = 2030-04-12) based on API readiness, latency profile, and estimated retrofit timeline.
  • Shared-adapter module recommendations: identify three to five common legacy-system patterns and estimate cost and timeline per module (e.g., 'REST-to-Kafka bridge for Polish regional operators', 'transaction-history data mapper for older Deutsche Bahn systems').
  • Network-effect risk assessment: identify critical junctions (e.g., Köln, Munich, Vienna) and note which carriers serve them; flag if any Tier 1 carrier is missing, which would fragment a priority corridor.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If latency or uptime data is outdated (>6 months old), the programme misidentifies which carriers meet the availability SLA (p95 <2 seconds, 99.5% uptime) and assigns incorrect tiers, causing 40–50% of smaller carriers to miss the Month 30 (2029-04-12) conformance deadline by 6–12 months.
  • If retrofit costs are underestimated by >20%, the EUR 240M adapter budget (EUR 30M shared + EUR 80M Tier 1 + EUR 80M Tier 2 + EUR 50M Tier 3) runs short by EUR 50–100M, forcing either cost overrun (reducing EUR 85M headroom to negative) or deferral of Tier 2/3 to Month 42–48 (2030-04-12 to 2030-10-12), compressing the four-corridor go-live target.
  • If the audit does not identify legacy-system bottlenecks clearly, the programme may allocate shared-adapter funding inefficiently (e.g., funding a bespoke integration for a system that could use a standard module), wasting EUR 20–50M.
  • If staff availability is not assessed, the programme schedules carrier integration work that exceeds available capacity, causing cascading delays and re-scheduling conflicts across multiple carriers, particularly Months 12–24 (2027-10-12 to 2028-10-12).
  • If critical-corridor bottlenecks are not identified, a priority corridor may proceed with an incomplete carrier set, later requiring emergency retrofits or rerouting of through-tickets, adding cost and delay.

Worst Case Scenario: The pre-programme audit is conducted with outdated or self-reported data (not validated on-site), resulting in systematic underestimation of latency profiles and retrofit costs across 15–20 smaller operators. The programme assigns these carriers to Tier 1 (Month 30 = 2029-04-12 deadline) based on overstated API readiness. When integration begins in Month 12 (2027-10-12), 10–15 carriers discover their systems require 12–18 months of work, not the assumed 6–9 months. They slip to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12) or drop out entirely. A critical corridor (e.g., Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln) loses 3–4 regional operators at border junctions, fragmenting through-ticket continuity. The programme faces a choice: accelerate adapters at EUR 150–250M overrun (consuming the EUR 85M headroom and drawing EUR 65–165M from later-corridor budgets), or delay four-corridor go-live from Month 48 (2030-10-12) to Month 60–66 (2031-10-12 to 2032-04-12), reducing the 40% through-ticket target to 20–25% and cutting the full TEN-T rollout to Month 72–84 (2032-10-12 to 2033-10-12). The programme's reputational and budgetary credibility with carriers and the Commission is damaged.

Best Case Scenario: The pre-programme audit is completed on schedule by Month 2 (2026-12-12) with on-site system reviews of all 25+ carriers, validated latency data (including three-leg query profiles), and detailed retrofit cost estimates (±10% confidence). Tier assignment is finalized by Month 6 (2027-04-12), with 12 large/corridor-critical carriers assigned to Tier 1 (feasible by Month 30 = 2029-04-12), 8–10 regional carriers to Tier 2 (Month 36 = 2029-10-12), and 5–8 small/legacy-system carriers to Tier 3 (Month 42 = 2030-04-12). Three to five shared-adapter modules are identified and procured by Month 12 (2027-10-12), reducing bespoke-integration costs by EUR 40–60M and freeing budget for contingency. Tier 1 carriers integrate confidently, meeting conformance by Month 30 (2029-04-12) with <5% latency overruns. The audit identifies that critical junctions (Köln, Munich, Vienna) are served by committed Tier 1 carriers, so corridor continuity is confirmed. Four priority corridors go live by Month 48 (2030-10-12) on schedule, with 90%+ of expected carriers operational, supporting the 40% through-ticket target. The EUR 240M adapter budget is spent efficiently, remaining headroom allows for any force-majeure contingencies, and the TEN-T extension (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) proceeds as planned.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the independent audit firm cannot be engaged by Month 1 (2026-11-12) or the audit timeline slips beyond Month 2 (2026-12-12), initiate a lightweight self-assessment process: issue a standardised questionnaire to all carriers by Month 1 (2026-11-12) requesting API readiness, latency (self-reported with caveats), and retrofit cost estimates; hold targeted videoconference reviews with the largest 12 carriers (Tier 1 candidates) in Month 2 (2026-12-12) to validate critical data; and publish a provisional tier assignment by Month 9 (2027-07-12) with a caveat that Tier 2/3 assignments are advisory pending real integration results.
  • If latency and uptime data cannot be obtained from carriers' historical logs, establish a live measurement campaign: deploy passive network monitors or integrate lightweight telemetry into the conformance test environments (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12); measure actual latency for sample itineraries; and re-baseline tier assignments by Month 24 (2028-10-12) before funding tranches are released.
  • If retrofit costs are uncertain (confidence >±30%), contract a smaller pilot audit with 8–10 representative carriers covering each system category (large incumbent, regional, legacy, cloud-native) by Month 3 (2027-01-12); model cost ranges per category; and apply category-based estimates to unaudited carriers, with explicit risk bands per tier.
  • If staff availability cannot be assessed accurately, require carriers to commit capacity in writing as a precondition of funding eligibility (Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder decision): carriers must submit an integration plan with named FTE assignments and delivery milestones by Month 9 (2027-07-12); funding tranches are released only on proof of staff assignment; this shifts the burden and visibility to carriers and reduces programme risk.
  • If a critical-corridor bottleneck is identified late (Month 12 = 2027-10-12 or later), trigger an emergency escalation to the steering group and DG MOVE: convene a task force to either (a) accelerate the at-risk carrier's retrofit by adding EUR 10–20M and external contractor support, (b) identify an alternative carrier service that can close the gap, or (c) redesign the corridor itinerary to exclude the bottleneck, with passenger communication and fare adjustment; decisions must be made by Month 18 (2028-04-12) to avoid slipping the binding-standards milestone.

Find Document 6: Existing Inter-Carrier Settlement and Clearing Arrangements in Europe (RSP, Eurail, National Systems)

ID: 343094c4-ec57-4e89-ac38-bf366927b8d3

Description: Documentation of existing multi-carrier clearing and settlement systems operating in Europe: Rail Settlement Plan (RSB, Great Britain), Eurail/Interrail pooled revenue allocation, Swiss direct-service (NOVA) platform, and any national multi-operator clearing arrangements (Italy, France, Spain). Used as precedent for clearing-design decisions and to identify best practices for netting, reconciliation, dispute resolution and non-discriminatory access. Intended audience for analysis: clearing architect, programme management, competition-law counsel.

Recency Requirement: Current operational status as of project start (October 2026). Documentation should reflect how these systems currently operate (2026), including recent changes or modernisation initiatives.

Responsible Role Type: Inter-Carrier Clearing & Settlement Systems Architect

Steps to Find:

  • Visit Rail Settlement Plan website (https://www.rsp.org.uk) and download published operating-rules documents and performance reports
  • Contact Rail Delivery Group (RDG) retail/ticketing team and request: RSP operating manual (settlement cycle, netting rules, dispute procedure, retailer access criteria), annual performance reports (volumes, error rates, compliance audits)
  • Contact Eurail B.V. (Utrecht) corporate relations and request: operating model documentation for the Eurail pass distribution and revenue-sharing system, carrier participation terms, and franchise agreements (if publicly available)
  • Contact Alliance SwissPass or SBB corporate strategy and request: documentation of the Swiss Direct Service (NOVA) platform architecture, operator participation model, fare-composition rules and clearing procedures
  • Contact CER (Community of European Railways) and request briefing on any national multi-operator clearing arrangements known to its members (e.g., Italy, France, Spain)

Access Difficulty: Medium. RSP documentation is publicly available or obtainable via formal request to RDG. Eurail and Swiss systems are proprietary but operators may share high-level documentation under confidentiality agreements. National systems may be less documented or available only in local languages. Estimate 3-4 weeks to gather overview of all existing systems; full legal documentation may not be accessible without direct business relationships.

Essential Information:

  • Identify and describe the current operational status (as of Month 0 = October 2026) of at least four multi-carrier rail settlement systems: Rail Settlement Plan (RSP/RSB, Great Britain), Eurail/Interrail pooled revenue model, Swiss Direct Service (NOVA) platform, and any national multi-operator clearing (Italy, France, Spain)
  • Document the netting rules, settlement cycle times, reconciliation procedures and error-rate thresholds for each existing system
  • For each system, specify: who is the operator/owner; which carriers and distributors participate; what volumes (journeys, revenue) flow annually; what commission or fee structure applies to independent distributors
  • Detail the dispute-resolution procedures: how disputes are escalated, what authority settles them, typical resolution times, and penalties for late settlement
  • Assess which systems use centralized clearing (one entity receives payment and allocates) versus federated netting (bilateral positions netted without central pooling); identify strengths and failure points of each model
  • Document non-discriminatory access criteria: how are new carriers and distributors admitted; what technical or financial prerequisites exist; how are access disputes handled
  • Identify and explain any recent modernisation initiatives, API exposures, or technology changes (2024–2026) that affected settlement speed, error rates or participant satisfaction
  • For each system, quantify: average settlement cycle time in business days; monthly reconciliation error rate as percentage of transactions or value; participant satisfaction or complaint rates if available

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Without concrete operational precedents, the Inter-Carrier Clearing and Single-Payment Settlement decision (Decision 2) lacks evidence for feasibility of federated settlement within 5-business-day cycle and below 0.5% reconciliation error; designers may choose an architecture that fails at scale
  • Absence of documented netting rules and dispute procedures from existing systems leaves the programme unable to anticipate reconciliation bottlenecks, leading to longer settlement cycles (10–15 days instead of target 5 days) and higher error rates, which deters distributor participation by 15–20%
  • Unknown access criteria from existing systems means the programme cannot replicate working non-discriminatory models; new market entrants face opaque barriers and challenge the programme for unfair exclusion, delaying API exposure and legal certification
  • Failure to document why existing systems work (or don't) with certain participant types leaves the programme unable to predict whether smaller carriers will accept the proposed guarantee pool; carrier refusal cascades to inventory exposure delays
  • Without baseline operational metrics from existing systems (e.g., how long RSP takes to resolve a refund reversal), the programme over-commits to SLA targets that legacy infrastructure cannot deliver, and pilot results falsify success assumptions in Month 12–18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12)

Worst Case Scenario: The programme commits to a federated settlement architecture based on theoretical design rather than operational precedent. At Month 24 (2028-10-12), when pilot carriers attempt live settlement, the reconciliation process takes 3–4 weeks instead of 5 business days because dispute procedures and netting rules were not anchored to proven models. Distributors face cash-flow delays and withdraw participation. The programme is forced to redesign the clearing layer by Month 30 (2029-04-12), delaying mandatory API exposure to Month 36 (2029-10-12) and consuming EUR 50–100M in rework. The binding-standards decision (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) is undermined because the settlement mechanism was not validated against operational reality, and later legal challenges cite inadequate due diligence.

Best Case Scenario: The document provides detailed comparison of RSP's proven 5-day settlement cycle and <1% error rate, NOVA's federated netting model, and national systems' access procedures, which allows the clearing architect to design a hybrid that replicates RSP's accuracy within the federated model, avoiding centralization and competition-law risk. The programme's settlement SLAs (5 business days, <0.5% error) are grounded in operational benchmarks rather than speculation. Pilots in Months 12–18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) validate the design against established precedent. Carriers sign on confidently and the mandatory API exposure milestone (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) is met on schedule.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Commission a specialized consultancy (e.g., McKinsey Public Sector, Accenture Rail/Transport) in Month 2 (2026-12-12) to conduct interviews with RSP, CER, Eurail and representatives of at least 3 national operators and deliver a comparative-analysis report by Month 6 (2027-04-12), if direct documentation access proves slow or incomplete
  • Conduct a direct technical working group (Month 3–6 = 2027-01-12 to 2027-04-12) with volunteer carriers from RSP participating countries (UK-based operator or RDG representative) and the largest European operators (DB, SNCF, SBB) to review their settlement procedures and best practices in real time, bypassing formal document requests
  • Establish a 'Clearing Design Partner' arrangement where one existing system operator (e.g., RSP or Swiss NOVA) grants a limited technical secondment (2–3 months, Month 6–9 = 2027-04-12 to 2027-07-12) to embed one architect in the programme's clearing team to document and transfer operational knowledge directly
  • If proprietary barriers prevent access to full documentation, request each existing system operator to sign a bilateral confidentiality agreement (template by Month 2 = 2026-12-12) and share redacted operational manuals and error metrics only; prioritize quantitative metrics (settlement cycle, error rate, dispute resolution time) over commercially sensitive rules
  • Pivot the clearing-design decision to include a 6-month live pilot (Month 24–30 = 2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12) using an existing multi-carrier settlement system as the operational backbone, licensing their infrastructure and rules rather than building new, if architectural design alone does not yield sufficient confidence

Find Document 7: DG COMP Guidance on Article 101 TFEU Exemptions in Transport and Digital Markets

ID: 2a0c8909-a183-4458-860b-b0dd5e85de29

Description: Published DG COMP guidance and precedent decisions on Article 101 TFEU safe-harbour criteria for shared data, pooled clearing, and joint commercial arrangements in transport and digital markets. Includes: joint-purchasing exemptions, air-transport alliances (IATA), roaming directives, and any recent guidance on digital-platform interoperability (e.g., Digital Markets Act). Used to inform the pre-notification memorandum and clean-team protocol design (Decision 14). Intended audience for analysis: competition-law counsel, Programme Director.

Recency Requirement: Current DG COMP guidance and precedents as of project start (October 2026). Must include any updates since the Digital Markets Act (2022-2024) and recent digital-platform precedents.

Responsible Role Type: Competition Law & Regulatory Affairs Counsel

Steps to Find:

  • Search EUR-Lex (https://eur-lex.europa.eu) for DG COMP guidance documents on Article 101 TFEU exemptions; filter by date (2020-2026)
  • Visit DG COMP website (https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu) and search for: 'transport exemption', 'data sharing', 'platform interoperability' or similar keywords
  • Request from DG COMP's Transport Unit (contact via the DG website or COMP-REGISTRY@ec.europa.eu): any informal guidance on Article 101 TFEU compatibility of multi-operator clearing and data-sharing arrangements in rail; also request copies of any published decisions or notices on rail-sector alliances or joint ventures
  • Retrieve any published case law or decisions relevant to Article 101 TFEU in rail (search EUR-Lex for 'rail' + 'competition')

Access Difficulty: Easy. DG COMP guidance is published on EUR-Lex and the DG COMP website. Direct contact with DG COMP Transport Unit requires formal request or engagement of external counsel but is typically accessible. Informal briefings may require establishing the programme's formal engagement with DG COMP via the pre-notification process. Estimate 2-3 weeks to compile existing public guidance.

Essential Information:

  • DG COMP's published guidance on Article 101 TFEU safe-harbour criteria for joint data-sharing, pooled clearing and commercial arrangements in transport and digital markets.
  • Precedent decisions and case law on Article 101 TFEU exemptions in rail transport, air-transport alliances (IATA precedent), roaming directives, and Digital Markets Act application to platform interoperability.
  • Current formal pre-notification procedures and timelines for obtaining DG COMP guidance on multi-operator clearing and data-sharing in rail; typical turnaround for guidance letters.
  • Conditions and structural requirements for clean-team arrangements that satisfy Article 101 TFEU scrutiny (firewall protocols, data access restrictions, governance separation).
  • Any recent or pending Commission decisions on shared-data platforms in transport; application of Article 101 TFEU to real-time availability exchange and settlement netting.
  • Specific safe-harbour language applicable to federated settlement, netting and dispute resolution among competing carriers without central price-setting.
  • TFEU Article 101(3) exemption conditions (efficiency gains, consumer benefit, indispensability, no restriction of competition) as applied to through-ticketing infrastructure.
  • Guidance on permissible scope of carrier data disclosure (fares, inventory, settlement) versus prohibited coordination (price-fixing, market allocation).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Absent or outdated guidance leaves the pre-notification memorandum ungrounded in current DG COMP doctrine; formal review at Month 2 (2026-12-12) may reveal compatibility issues not anticipated, delaying guidance approval.
  • Missing precedent decisions on rail-sector joint ventures or alliances result in clean-team protocol design that later triggers competition-law challenge, requiring 6-12 months of rework and EUR 50-100M (estimate) cost.
  • Incomplete understanding of TFEU Article 101(3) exemption conditions causes the programme to design a clearing mechanism or data layer that DG COMP views as price coordination or market allocation, forcing restructuring post-investment.
  • Failure to identify structural requirements for safe clean-team arrangements (firewall, data access, governance) leaves the clearing function exposed to legal unraveling if a carrier or distributor later challenges coordination.
  • Lack of current guidance on Digital Markets Act interaction with regulated transport interoperability creates ambiguity about whether the clearing entity or OSDM standardisation triggers DMA obligations.
  • Outdated or incomplete guidance on federated settlement and netting leaves the programme uncertain whether the proposed settlement flows pass Article 101 scrutiny, risking post-launch enforcement action.

Worst Case Scenario: DG COMP issues an infringement notice post-Month 24 (2028-10-12) finding that the federated clearing mechanism, data-sharing layer or carrier-funded guarantee pool constitute prohibited price coordination or market allocation under Article 101 TFEU. The programme is forced to restructure or suspend the clearing layer entirely, reverting to bilateral settlement between carriers and distributors. This removes the single-payment mechanism, lengthens settlement cycles from 5 business days to 15-30 days, increases booking errors and reconciliation disputes by 25-50% (estimate), and erodes distributor participation by 20-30% (estimate). The 40% through-ticket target becomes unachievable (realistic outcome 15-25% estimate). Estimated rework cost EUR 50-100M (estimate) and 6-12 month schedule slip, compressing or cancelling the TEN-T extension phase (Months 48-60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12).

Best Case Scenario: DG COMP issues a formal guidance letter by Month 12 (2027-10-12) confirming that the programme's clearing, data-sharing and carrier-funded guarantee pool arrangements satisfy Article 101 TFEU as amended by the clean-team protocol and structured governance. This letter is published and becomes binding precedent, eliminating legal uncertainty for carriers and distributors and encouraging full inventory exposure and participation. A successful clean-team arrangement with firewalls and data access controls becomes a reusable model for future EU transport interoperability programmes. The programme reaches binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12) and Tier 1 API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-12) without legal delays, delivering four corridors by Month 48 (2030-10-12) and advancing toward the 40% through-ticket target.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If DG COMP guidance is delayed beyond Month 12 (2027-10-12), commission independent competition-law counsel (not the Commission) to conduct a detailed safe-harbour analysis under Article 101(3) TFEU and issue a formal legal opinion by Month 14 (2027-12-12); present this opinion to DG COMP as part of a formal pre-notification and request expedited review by Month 16 (2028-02-12). This preserves Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards milestone.
  • If DG COMP signals fundamental concerns with the federated clearing design, pivot immediately to a fully structural clean-team protocol: appoint an independent trustee to operate the clearing function, restrict data access to settlement-only flows, separate governance from carrier representation, and publish monthly audit reports to DG COMP. Commission a follow-up legal opinion confirming this structure is safe under Article 101(3).
  • If Article 101 exposure persists despite clean-team mitigations, redesign the clearing layer as a 'distributed bilateral settlement service': instead of a central netting function, carriers submit settlement feeds to a neutral processor that matches and reconciles without centralising commercially sensitive data. This removes the 'hub-and-spoke' structure that competition authorities scrutinise most closely.
  • If guidance from DG COMP becomes unavailable or contradicts the programme's design by Month 14 (2027-12-12), escalate formally to the Commission's Competition Commissioner via DG MOVE and request a structured dialogue with senior DG COMP officials; frame the engagement as a regulated sector exemption (transport interoperability for public benefit) rather than a commercial joint venture. Request a comfort letter or block exemption regulation reference rather than waiting for full guidance.
  • If competition-law risk remains unresolved by Month 18 (2028-04-12) and threatens binding standards, defer the federated clearing mechanism and instead mandate that each carrier maintain bilateral clearing agreements with every other carrier on a corridor, netting through a simple automated bilateral matching protocol. This removes central coordination and TFEU Article 101 exposure at the cost of slower settlement and higher administrative burden.
  • Engage the EU Agency for Railways in the pre-notification process as an official party: if the programme is executed under formal EU regulatory authority and published standards, DG COMP may grant a categorical exemption under Article 101(3) as serving a public transport objective. This shifts the legal grounding from commercial joint venture to regulatory compliance.

Find Document 8: Baseline Cross-Border Rail Travel Data and Through-Ticket Market Analysis

ID: 426d9b24-0354-441b-a6e0-c63262db384a

Description: Current statistical baseline on cross-border rail travel volumes, distribution channels (carrier direct, Trainline, Omio, national operators) and market share per corridor (Paris-Brussels-Amsterdam-Köln, Wien-München-Zürich, Madrid-Barcelona-Lyon, Copenhagen-Hamburg-Berlin). Used to validate the 40% through-ticket target (whether it is ambitious or conservative) and to model the baseline for the halved-complaints metric. Intended audience for analysis: Programme Director, finance lead, market-research team.

Recency Requirement: Most recent available year (2025 or early 2026) covering full calendar year or latest rolling 12-month period available. Data must be pre-programme (before October 2026) to establish the true baseline.

Responsible Role Type: Regulatory Affairs and Stakeholder Alignment Director

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Trainline and Omio directly via their corporate-development teams, requesting: market-share data (% of cross-border bookings per corridor, by distributor type) for 2024-2025 and customer-complaint statistics (volumes by category, resolution times)
  • Request from CER: industry-level data on total cross-border rail travel volumes per corridor from member carriers (if compiled)
  • Contact national statistical offices or transport ministries in France, Germany, Austria and Spain requesting: cross-border rail ridership data (annual counts, breakdown by origin-destination pair), distributor market share if available
  • Request from the European Commission's DG MOVE or EUROSTAT: any published statistics on cross-border rail travel volumes or modal split (rail vs. air vs. bus) on European corridors

Access Difficulty: Medium. Trainline and Omio are commercial entities with proprietary market-share data; they may share summary statistics under NDA but full data may not be disclosed. CER members (carriers) own operational data but may not share across competitors. National statistical offices provide public statistics but may have limited cross-border detail. Estimate 3-4 weeks to assemble baseline data; some gaps are likely.

Essential Information:

  • Establish the statistical baseline of cross-border rail travel volumes (annual passengers) per corridor (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin) for the most recent complete calendar year (2025 or early 2026), to validate whether the 40% through-ticket target is ambitious or conservative.
  • Quantify current distributor market share by channel (carrier direct, Trainline, Omio, national operator websites, other) as a percentage of cross-border bookings per corridor, to establish the baseline for measuring distributor complaint reductions and through-ticket adoption.
  • Document current distributor complaint volumes (total complaints per corridor, categorised by type: booking errors, validation failures, missed-connection handling, refund delays, accessibility gaps) and median resolution times per category, to define the halved-complaints metric.
  • Identify which cross-border connections on each priority corridor are currently sold as single through-tickets (if any) and at what volumes, versus stitched itineraries purchased separately, to measure the baseline for the 40% goal.
  • Provide the distribution of passenger journey lengths, fare bands and traveller demographics (business, leisure, accessibility needs, cyclists) per corridor to inform through-ticket value proposition and modal-shift modelling.
  • List current modal split (percentage of travellers choosing rail, air, bus, car) on the four priority corridors, particularly on air-competitive routes, to establish the baseline for the 5–10% air-to-rail shift planning value.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate baseline volumes or market shares lead to overestimation of the 40% through-ticket goal: if actual cross-border travel is 20% lower than forecasted, the absolute number of through-tickets required to reach 40% is smaller, and the programme may be judged on an inflated target, damaging credibility.
  • Incomplete complaint data by category (e.g., missing validation or accessibility complaints) hides the true complaint burden and allows the halved-complaints metric to be gamed by reduction in high-volume, low-priority categories; genuine passenger pain points remain unaddressed.
  • Absent baseline on current through-ticket sales (if any) makes it impossible to distinguish programme-driven growth from organic market shift, inflating the claimed programme impact and inviting audit scrutiny.
  • Inaccurate distributor market-share data prevents realistic modelling of which distributors will participate in the programme and how much of the 40% target depends on Trainline, Omio or smaller players, complicating the concession and commission-band design.
  • Poor demographic and journey-length data undermines accessibility and multimodal design, leading to a through-ticket product that does not match traveller needs and fails adoption targets.

Worst Case Scenario: The programme is launched with an inflated baseline: actual cross-border travel volumes are 25–30% lower than assumed, and current through-ticket penetration is already 10–15% (not zero). The 40% target becomes effectively 30–40% growth above baseline, not an absolute share. Complaint data is incomplete, missing accessibility and validation categories, so the halved-complaints metric is met by reducing booking-error complaints alone while accessibility complaints double. At Month 48 (2030-10-12), when the four corridors report results, the Court of Auditors finds that claimed through-ticket growth is only 12–15% above baseline, not the 40% implied by the headline metric. The programme is judged as underperforming and funding for the TEN-T extension (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) is withheld, halting the rollout at the four priority corridors. Distributor participation falls to 60–70% of target because the original market-share data underestimated Trainline and Omio's bargaining power and overestimated participation by smaller regional players. The 40% goal is missed by 15–20 percentage points and the programme is reported as a failed 1.5 billion EUR public investment.

Best Case Scenario: The baseline data establish that cross-border travel on the four corridors totals 45–50 million journeys annually, of which ~4% are currently through-tickets and complaints average 8–12 per 1,000 bookings. The programme's design is calibrated to this reality: a 40% through-ticket target represents roughly 18–20 million journeys by Month 60 (2031-10-12), a 10-fold increase, ambitious but plausible with full carrier participation. Distributor shares are known (e.g., Trainline 35%, Omio 25%, carrier direct 30%, others 10%), informing concession and commission-band design. Complaint baselines per category (booking errors 30%, validation 25%, missed-connection rerouting 20%, refunds 15%, accessibility 10%) guide which pain points the programme prioritises. At Month 48 (2030-10-12), corridor results show 28–32% through-ticket penetration on the four corridors, complaint volumes down 40–50%, and a clear pathway to 40% by Month 60 (2031-10-12). The Court of Auditors and member states validate the baseline, confirm programme progress and approve the TEN-T extension funding, allowing full-network rollout.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If Trainline and Omio refuse to share detailed market-share data under NDA, request aggregated competitor intelligence from CER members (each carrier's distributor sales mix) and apply statistical sampling to estimate market share per distributor type without disclosing individual carrier data.
  • If national statistical offices cannot provide cross-border corridor-level data, compile the baseline from a combination of CER members' self-reported sales (with proper anonymisation), published annual reports of Trainline and Omio, and transport-authority reports from France, Germany, Austria and Spain; use triangulation to validate consistency.
  • If current complaint data is proprietary and scattered across carriers and distributors, commission an independent survey of 2,000–3,000 passengers who have booked cross-border rail in the past 12 months, asking about complaint types and resolution, weighted by corridor and distributor; use this as the baseline and accept a 2–3 week delay to Month 4–6 (2027-02-12 to 2027-04-12).
  • If no current through-ticket sales data exists (i.e., the market is fragmentary), assume a near-zero baseline (0–2% through-tickets) and validate via five carrier interviews and one or two distributor pilots to confirm; design the programme on a true-zero assumption and treat any organic growth as upside.
  • If air-to-rail modal-shift baseline is unavailable, partner with a transport economics research body (university or research institute) to conduct a stated-preference or revealed-preference study on one air-competitive corridor (e.g., Paris–Lyon–Marseille or Berlin–Munich) by Month 9 (2027-07-12), using the results to inform the full-programme modal-shift modelling.

Find Document 9: EU Member-State Railway Regulator Contact List and Regulatory Frameworks (France, Germany, Austria, Spain, etc.)

ID: b0a475b7-211c-471e-8d0b-649f01ef208e

Description: Contact information and summary of regulatory authority and remit for railway regulators in all member states participating in the four priority corridors and TEN-T network. Includes: France (DGITM/DGAC), Germany (Bundesnetzagentur), Austria (ÖBB Regulator), Spain (Comisión Nacional), Italy, Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark, Sweden, Poland, etc. Regulatory frameworks covering track access, station capacity, pricing rules, passenger rights and non-discrimination obligations. Used to conduct bilateral regulatory impact assessments (Month 3 = 2027-01-12) and to understand national constraints on mandatory API exposure or data sharing. Intended audience for analysis: regulatory-affairs lead, Programme Director.

Recency Requirement: Current as of project start (October 2026). Regulator contact information and organisational structure must be current; regulatory frameworks must reflect current national laws and European directives.

Responsible Role Type: Member-State Coordination and National Regulator Liaison Officer

Steps to Find:

  • Visit the EU Agency for Railways website (https://www.era.europa.eu) and search for 'Member-State Regulators' or 'National Safety Authorities'; compile contact list
  • Contact CER and request: list of member-state regulatory contacts and a one-page summary of each regulator's authority, remit and typical concerns on cross-border ticketing or data-sharing projects
  • Search the website of each national regulator (typically transport ministry or dedicated transport regulator) to confirm current contact information and download summaries of national railway laws (often in English on EU or English-language versions of national sites)
  • Request from DG MOVE: any internal mapping of member-state regulators and known regulatory constraints or precedents affecting cross-border rail initiatives

Access Difficulty: Easy. Regulator contact information is publicly available via the EU Agency for Railways and national websites. CER may provide an internal summary. Regulatory frameworks are published by national authorities (often in national language, but English summaries or abstracts may be available). Estimate 2-3 weeks to compile complete list.

Essential Information:

  • Contact name, email, phone and office address for the chief regulator or designated liaison officer in each of the 25+ participating member states' railway regulatory authorities (France DGITM, Germany BNetzA, Austria ÖBB Regulator, Spain Comisión Nacional, Italy, Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark, Sweden, Poland, etc.)
  • Current regulatory authority name, acronym and organisational structure for each member state (confirm current legal entity after any recent mergers or restructures post-October 2026)
  • Documented summary of each regulator's statutory remit: track access authority, capacity allocation, pricing approval, passenger-rights enforcement, safety oversight, or hybrid model
  • Known regulatory constraints or precedents in each member state affecting cross-border rail initiatives: national exemptions, domestic-operator protections, data-sharing restrictions, mandatory-disclosure blocks
  • Typical approval timelines and formal notification procedures per regulator for projects involving mandatory API exposure, real-time data sharing, or inter-carrier settlement
  • Published national railway law summaries or English-language abstracts confirming how each member state's law aligns with or deviates from EU Regulation 1371/2007 and the proposed Digital Booking Regulation
  • List of recent cross-border rail coordination projects or initiatives in each member state, with identified regulatory bottlenecks or successes to inform bilateral engagement strategy

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Outdated contact information delays bilateral regulatory impact assessments (Month 3 = 2027-01-12 milestone) by 4–8 weeks; regulators not reached in time to influence standards scope
  • Incomplete regulatory-authority mapping misses smaller or recently reorganised regulators, leaving compliance gaps in secondary corridors and creating unexpected regulatory veto or fines during implementation
  • Inaccurate description of regulator remit (e.g., confusing track-access vs. pricing authority) leads to binding negotiations with the wrong authority, wasting 2–3 months and forcing restart
  • Undocumented national constraints (e.g., a member state's ban on real-time data sharing for competition reasons) discovered after Month 6 (2027-04-12) requires standards redesign and delay of 3–6 months
  • Missing regulatory precedents on inter-carrier coordination leaves the programme unprepared for known objections; regulators cite past cases as grounds to block mandatory API exposure
