  • Absence of translated or English-language regulatory summaries forces external legal counsel to translate full national laws, adding EUR 50–100K cost and 6–8 week delay per member state
  • No record of approval timelines per regulator causes the programme to miss informal comment windows, forcing formal appeals or re-notification cycles that add 3–6 months per member state

Worst Case Scenario: A regulator is reached too late or with incomplete information, blocks mandatory API exposure citing undocumented national law or unaddressed precedents. The programme cannot defer that regulator's compliance: binding standards require all 25+ participating member states to accept the design. Discovery of the block after Month 12 (2027-10-12) forces a 4–6 month legal and regulatory reworking cycle. One major corridor (e.g., Wien–München–Zürich) loses its Austrian or German regulator's approval, fragmenting through-ticket availability across a critical node. Estimated impact: EUR 30–50 million in legal and rework costs, 6–12 month delay to binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12 → Month 24–30 = 2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12), loss of 2–3 priority corridors from scope, and reduction of through-ticket goal from 40% to 20–25%.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 3 (2027-01-12), the programme conducts bilateral impact assessments with all 25+ regulators using a current, detailed contact list and documented regulatory frameworks. Early engagement surfaces known constraints (e.g., data-sharing restrictions in specific member states) before binding standards are drafted. The programme designs the standards with known workarounds or national carve-outs that each regulator can approve by Month 9 (2027-07-12). Binding standards are adopted on time (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) with all regulators' written consent. Mandatory API exposure proceeds without post-hoc regulatory challenges. Estimated benefit: on-time binding standards, no unexpected legal rework, reduced risk of corridor fragmentation, and preservation of the 40% through-ticket goal within the five-year horizon.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If current regulator contact list is unavailable: Contact the EU Agency for Railways directly (Valenciennes) and request their internal master list of member-state regulators, typically maintained for cross-border safety and coordination matters. Expect 2–3 week response.
  • If individual regulator websites lack English-language summaries: Engage CER (Community of European Railways) to provide one-page English regulatory briefs for each member state based on their bilateral relationships; cost estimate EUR 20–30K, timeline 4–6 weeks.
  • If regulatory-authority structures have recently changed (post-October 2026): Commission a targeted research report from a transport law firm specialising in EU rail (e.g., Freshfields, CMS, Linklaters) to audit current regulator structures and remits; cost EUR 50–75K, timeline 6–8 weeks.
  • If approval timelines and precedents are undocumented: Conduct structured interviews with 2–3 major regulators (e.g., Germany BNetzA, France DGITM) to establish typical notification windows and decision cycles; resource 1 FTE for 4 weeks to coordinate, cost EUR 30–40K in staff and travel.
  • If bilateral engagement must start before the contact list is complete: DG MOVE issues a formal regulatory notification letter (template by Month 2 = 2026-12-12) to all member states' transport ministries, with request to designate and confirm the relevant railway regulator contact within 2 weeks; this creates an official channel while the detailed list is being compiled.
  • If a regulator is unresponsive or missing from EU Agency records: Escalate through the national transport minister (DG MOVE already maintains minister contacts) or the national competition authority (many regulate rail access); this ensures no regulator is overlooked.

Find Document 10: EU Accessibility Directive and Persons with Reduced Mobility (PRM) Accessibility Standards

Description: EU Directive 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act) and any transport-specific accessibility regulations (EU Regulation 1371/2007 PRM provisions, EN 13001-1 station accessibility standards). Responsible Role Type: Passenger Rights, Accessibility & Consumer Protection Lead

  • Download EU Regulation 1371/2007 Persons with Reduced Mobility (PRM) provisions from EUR-Lex

Essential Information:

  • Identify the current provisions of EU Directive 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act) that apply to digital ticketing and booking platforms for rail transport, including WCAG 2.1 conformance levels mandated.
  • List specific PRM accessibility requirements from EU Regulation 1371/2007 Articles 20-25 covering assistance notification procedures, advance notice windows, and carrier obligations for persons with reduced mobility.
  • Detail the technical standards (EN 13001-1 or successor) for station accessibility infrastructure that affect through-ticket usability, including ramp gradients, assistance provision points and evacuation procedures.
  • Specify the notice period required for advance PRM assistance requests under current EU law and any member-state variations that create compliance gaps for the programme's atomic-confirmation model.
  • Quantify the minimum percentage of rail services that must offer wheelchair-accessible spaces and assistance capability to satisfy the Accessibility Directive on a pan-European basis (not carrier-by-carrier).
  • Define the explicit accessibility compliance checklist for the programme's Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining decision, cross-referenced to binding legal obligations and the 'best-effort' fallback threshold (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours).
  • Identify any recent European Court of Justice rulings or Agency for Railways guidance (post-2024) on accessibility in digital rail services that supersede or clarify the 2019 Directive.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete coverage of Regulation 1371/2007 PRM provisions: if the document omits notice-period requirements or exclusion rules, the programme's atomic-confirmation design may inadvertently violate passenger rights, creating legal exposure at the Month 36 (2029-10-12) conformance gate.
  • Misalignment between the programme's 'best-effort' fallback (carriers unable to meet 80%/90% thresholds) and existing EU law: if the fallback contradicts Regulation 1371/2007 or the Accessibility Directive, the Agency for Railways may reject the compliance manual at Month 9 (2027-07-12), delaying carrier conformance.
  • Outdated or partial technical standards: if EN 13001-1 has been superseded or regional accessibility standards vary per member state, the programme risks issuing non-compliant station designs, which cannot be corrected within the EUR 200M capacity-building budget.
  • Missing member-state variations: if the document does not flag differences (e.g., notice periods in Germany vs. Spain, station staffing obligations), the programme's one-size-fits-all assistance-booking workflow will fail in jurisdictions with stricter local rules, fragmenting corridor coverage.
  • Vague accessibility metrics: if the document does not define 'wheelchair accessible' or 'assistance availability' quantitatively (% of vehicles, time response), the Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining decision cannot establish measurable conformance gates, making the Month 40 (2030-02-12) audit non-verifiable.

Worst Case Scenario: The programme issues a compliance manual at Month 9 (2027-07-12) that conflicts with undisclosed EU Regulation 1371/2007 PRM provisions or member-state accessibility laws. A disability-rights body challenges the atomic-confirmation model in the European Court of Justice, alleging that 'best-effort' bookings violate the Accessibility Directive and Regulation 1371/2007. The case enters litigation by Month 24 (2028-10-12), requiring a 6-9 month redesign of the Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining decision (EUR 15-25M cost, estimate). Carriers withdraw from accessibility commitments, reducing service availability and creating political pressure for the programme to either drop the accessibility scope or extend the mandate to Months 72-84 (2032-10-12 to 2033-10-12). The programme's reputation for disability inclusion is damaged, deterring other EU transport initiatives from adopting similar standards.

Best Case Scenario: A comprehensive, current accessibility standards document provides clear technical and legal baselines for the Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining decision. The programme's compliance manual at Month 9 (2027-07-12) aligns with all PRM provisions, member-state variations and technical standards, securing sign-off from disability-rights bodies and the Agency for Railways without revision. Carriers meet the 80% wheelchair and 90% assistance thresholds by Month 40 (2030-02-12), making accessible through-ticketing a standard offering rather than a best-effort fallback. The programme becomes a model for accessible EU transport standards, earning endorsement from the European Disability Forum and integration into future TEN-T and multimodal initiatives, expanding the through-ticket goal to include dedicated accessible products and positioning the EU as a leader in inclusive transport.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Commission an independent accessibility legal opinion from a EU-accredited accessibility consultant or law firm specializing in Regulation 1371/2007 and the European Accessibility Act, to be completed by Month 3 (2027-01-12), in parallel with the planned independent passenger-rights review; cost estimate EUR 30-50K.
  • Request formal guidance from the EU Agency for Railways on the compliance status of the programme's atomic-confirmation and best-effort models against Regulation 1371/2007, with written response by Month 6 (2027-04-12); include disability-rights bodies (EBU, European Disability Forum) as co-reviewers.
  • Conduct targeted usability testing with persons with reduced mobility (wheelchair users, visually impaired, deaf-blind passengers) on the programme's prototype booking interface by Month 15 (2028-01-12), using WCAG 2.1 AA conformance as the baseline; recruit 20-30 test participants per member state of a priority corridor.
  • Establish a standing accessibility advisory panel (3-5 disability-rights representatives) to review each conformance tier (Months 30, 36, 42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12) and approve accessibility thresholds; cost estimate EUR 10-15K per review cycle.
  • If member-state PRM variations create fragmentation, publish a supplementary guidance document per member state by Month 12 (2027-10-12) showing how the programme's generic accessibility rules map to national law, with carrier sign-off per jurisdiction; cost estimate EUR 50-75K.
  • Defer full accessibility conformance to a Phase 2 rollout (Months 60-72 = 2031-10-12 to 2032-10-12) if the standards document reveals insurmountable compliance conflicts; focus Phase 1 (Months 0-48 = 2026-10-12 to 2030-10-12) on accessible information and complaint handling only, not atomic assistance/bicycle confirmation.

Find Document 11: Current Trainline and Omio Booking Platform Architecture and API Capabilities

ID: 2de78274-b57e-416f-8d33-755548246459

Description: Technical documentation of Trainline and Omio's current booking-platform architecture (APIs, inventory query methods, payment processing, refund handling), integration with existing carrier systems and compatibility with OSDM standards. Used to validate the federated integration model and to assess whether independent distributors can connect to the shared clearing and real-time layers without extensive custom work. Intended audience for analysis: clearing architect, real-time systems engineer, distributor engagement team.

Recency Requirement: Current as of project start (October 2026). Must reflect the platforms' existing technical state and any recent API modernisations or OSDM adoption.

Responsible Role Type: Inter-Carrier Clearing & Settlement Systems Architect

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Trainline and Omio directly via their corporate-development or API-partnership teams, requesting: high-level technical documentation on booking-platform architecture, API endpoints exposed to carrier partners, payment processing and settlement procedures, and any OSDM compliance work underway
  • Request test-environment access and API documentation (likely under NDA) to validate integration assumptions
  • Inquire whether each distributor has already begun OSDM integration and what technical barriers they have identified

Access Difficulty: Medium. Trainline and Omio are commercial platforms with proprietary architectures; they may share summary documentation under NDA but full technical details are business-sensitive. Initial contact likely requires formal programme engagement via the steering group. Estimate 2-4 weeks for preliminary technical briefing; full platform documentation may require formal partnership agreement.

Essential Information:

  • Trainline's current booking-platform architecture: all APIs, inventory query methods, real-time search endpoints, payment processing workflows and settlement procedures used with carrier partners
  • Omio's current booking-platform architecture: all APIs, inventory query methods, real-time search endpoints, payment processing workflows and settlement procedures used with carrier partners
  • Which OSDM-compatible APIs or interfaces each platform already exposes or has planned; any pilot or production-grade OSDM adoption
  • Current latency profiles (p50, p95, p99 query response times) for single-carrier and multi-carrier (2–3 leg) itinerary searches, measured against proposed SLA targets of p95 <2 seconds
  • Current availability/uptime of each platform's booking endpoints and any known outage patterns or seasonal degradation
  • Payment processing and currency handling: which currencies and payment methods each platform supports, and how refunds and reversals are handled across carriers
  • Settlement cycle times: how long from passenger payment through clearing to final payout to carriers; any reconciliation delays or dispute handling procedures currently in place
  • Integration complexity for each platform to connect to a federated netting and dispute-resolution layer: what APIs would need to be built or adapted, estimated effort per platform
  • Data format and quality issues: whether each platform's settlement, refund and inventory data can map directly to the shared clearing-layer schemas, or requires custom transformation
  • Distributor-carrier contractual terms: which carriers each platform is currently integrated with, any exclusive arrangements, and flexibility to add shared clearing terms
  • Commercial viability: estimated percentage of through-ticket volume (vs. single-carrier tickets) each distributor expects to handle, and whether current technology economics support the federated model or require cost changes

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated platform documentation leads to false assumptions about integration feasibility, resulting in underestimated adapter development effort and cost overruns of EUR 50–100M (estimate) during Month 12–18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) technical build-out
  • Latency and availability data not provided forces reliance on generic benchmarks, masking platform-specific bottlenecks; if either distributor's real p95 latency exceeds the proposed 2-second SLA by >1 second, the federated query model fails for multi-leg journeys and through-ticket search success drops below 70%, eroding the value proposition
  • Payment and settlement procedures not validated against the federated clearing schema means custom transformation layers are built post-pilot, consuming 4–8 additional weeks of integration time and delaying the Month 30 (2029-04-12) mandatory API exposure by 2–4 months (estimate)
  • Unknown reconciliation error rates or dispute-handling volume in either platform means the shared clearing mechanism cannot be load-tested; if actual error rates exceed 1%, settlement cycles lengthen from 5 to 10–15 business days and distributors may reduce participation by 20–30% (estimate), lowering through-ticket volume by 10–15% (estimate)
  • Missing contractual flexibility analysis means the programme cannot determine whether Trainline and Omio can accept shared clearing governance and non-discriminatory access terms; if either platform has exclusive carrier agreements or proprietary settlement rules that conflict with the federated design, the programme loses 15–25% of expected through-ticket distribution capacity (estimate)
  • Absence of commercial volume forecasts from each distributor means the programme cannot validate whether the concession or independent distributor participation is economically viable; if volumes are 30–50% lower than forecast, the public budget allocation of EUR 300M for the concession becomes unaffordable relative to other priorities
  • Outdated OSDM-integration status leaves the programme unaware whether either platform has already begun standards work; if Trainline or Omio has already committed to a competing or forked API specification, re-alignment to the shared standard becomes a contentious renegotiation delaying binding standards by 2–4 months (estimate)

Worst Case Scenario: A critical document gap: If Trainline and Omio's current platform documentation cannot be accessed or is materially outdated (e.g., reflects architecture from 2024 not 2026), the programme proceeds with false assumptions about integration feasibility. The federated clearing model assumes both distributors can accept real-time settlement feeds in a standardised format and participate in a shared dispute-resolution layer; if either platform has technical or contractual incompatibilities (e.g., proprietary settlement logic, exclusive carrier agreements, or latency >3 seconds on multi-leg queries), the programme discovers this only after Month 12 (2027-10-12) pilots, at which point adapting the clearing mechanism or switching to a central exchange model requires 6–12 months of rework and EUR 50–100M additional cost (estimate). This cascades: mandatory API exposure (Month 30 = 2029-04-12) slips to Month 36–42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12), four-corridor go-live (Month 48 = 2030-10-12) pushes to Month 54–60 (2031-04-12 to 2031-10-12), and the 40% through-ticket goal becomes unachievable, settling at 20–25% (estimate). Budget impact: EUR 100–150M of the EUR 85M free headroom is consumed, forcing the TEN-T extension (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) to be deferred to Month 72 (2032-10-12) or cancelled, breaking the five-year horizon commitment.

Best Case Scenario: Trainline and Omio provide complete, current platform documentation showing APIs compatible with OSDM standards, latency and availability data confirming p95 <2 seconds and 99.5% uptime, and settlement procedures that map directly to the federated clearing schema with <0.5% reconciliation error rates. Both distributors confirm contractual flexibility to accept shared governance terms and non-discriminatory access rules, and forecast 25–35% through-ticket volume penetration on the priority corridors by Month 48 (2030-10-12). This enables: (1) Clearing architect to finalise the federated settlement-layer design by Month 9 (2027-07-12) with high confidence; (2) Real-time systems engineer to baseline integration effort at EUR 30–50M (within the EUR 80M shared adapter budget); (3) Distributor engagement team to secure binding letters of intent by Month 6 (2027-04-12), unlocking the steering group consensus on the Inter-Carrier Clearing decision; (4) Month 12–18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) pilots to proceed on schedule with both platforms live; (5) Month 30 (2029-04-12) mandatory API exposure to be met by large distributors, increasing confidence in the 40% through-ticket goal and supporting carrier participation decisions.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If Trainline and Omio decline to provide proprietary architectural documentation under NDA, request a third-party technical audit: engage an independent systems integrator (e.g., Accenture, Capgemini, Cognizant) with existing Trainline and Omio contracts to conduct a confidential platform assessment and deliver a sanitised summary of integration points, latency profiles and settlement compatibility. Timeline: Month 3–6 (2027-01-12 to 2027-04-12); cost EUR 150–250K (estimate). Risk: summary may not capture all edge cases, requiring confirmation during Month 12–18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) pilots.
  • If either distributor's existing architecture is fundamentally incompatible with federated clearing (e.g., all settlement routed through proprietary bilateral contracts with carriers), negotiate a hybrid integration layer: allow the distributor to maintain proprietary settlement internally but expose a standardised 'clearing API' that maps their settlement to the shared layer's messages. This isolates internal architecture from the programme and preserves commercial flexibility. Timeline: Month 6–12 (2027-04-12 to 2027-10-12); cost EUR 50–80M (estimate for both platforms). Risk: introduces translation layers that may degrade settlement speed by 1–2 business days.
  • If latency or availability data from either platform indicates SLA non-compliance (p95 >2 seconds or <99.5% uptime), establish a distributed caching layer (part of the EUR 50M real-time-layer budget) that pre-caches search results and degrades gracefully to cached results for that distributor during endpoint outages. This preserves search availability at the cost of slightly stale seat data (cache refresh every 15–30 minutes, estimate). Timeline: Month 9–12 (2027-07-12 to 2027-10-12); cost EUR 10–20M (estimate). Risk: introduces consistency risk if a passenger books a cached result that has since sold.
  • If either distributor cannot commit binding-volume forecasts by Month 6 (2027-04-12), defer their full integration to Phase 2 (Months 18–48 = 2028-04-12 to 2030-10-12) and start with a subset of smaller independents (Trainline, or Omio, or both, whichever provides early commitment). This preserves the timeline and protects EUR 50–80M of clearing budget. Timeline impact: minimal (Month 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12 pilots use one distributor); volume impact: through-ticket share for Months 30–48 (2029-04-12 to 2030-10-12) is 5–10 percentage points lower (estimate).
  • If the programme cannot obtain current architectural documentation by Month 2 (2026-12-12), commission a rapid parallel workstream to design the clearing mechanism and settlement-data formats as a 'platform-agnostic schema' based on OSDM, existing CER clearing standards and ISO 20022 settlement practices. Both distributors would then commit to supporting this schema rather than exposing proprietary internals. Timeline: Month 1–6 (2026-11-12 to 2027-04-12); cost EUR 200–300K (estimate). Risk: increases distributor integration effort if they must build substantial adapters, potentially adding EUR 20–40M to the overall adapter budget.
  • If Trainline or Omio is unable to meet the Month 30 (2029-04-12) mandatory API exposure deadline due to legacy system constraints, negotiate a staged participation: Tier 2 (Month 36 = 2029-10-12) or Tier 3 (Month 42 = 2030-04-12) conformance with reduced through-ticket volume expectations for that distributor during Months 30–36 (2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12) or 30–42 (2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12 or 2030-04-12). This preserves full-network coverage while allowing slower distributors to catch up. Timeline impact: through-ticket share for the slower distributor is 5–10 percentage points lower during the gap; budget impact: EUR 10–20M additional clearing-layer maintenance during the transition (estimate).

Strengths

  • Builds on proven components: OSDM standard, existing clearing arrangements and the Commission's proposed Regulation, so the programme layers over legacy carrier systems rather than replacing them.
  • Federated design (federated settlement, streamed availability shadow, carrier booking authority) limits single-point-of-failure and competition-law exposure versus a central backbone.
  • Carrier-funded guarantee pool with caps and no public pay-first fund protects the EUR 1,500M cap (user constraint); milestone tranches give compliance leverage over carriers the Commission cannot direct.
  • Clear sequencing: Month 6 (2027-04-12) readiness gate, tiered conformance (Months 30/36/42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12), pilots at Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12), four corridors by Month 48 (2030-10-12), with a fallback if prerequisites slip.
  • Strong risk preparation: technical audit, DG COMP pre-notification, passenger-rights review, SLA scorecards and variance triggers already defined.
  • Broad stakeholder base with defined governance (75% supermajority, Commission mediation) and a neutral last-resort concession capped at EUR 60M subsidy.

Weaknesses

  • Liability model is not yet priced: caps (EUR 500-1,000 per passenger) and co-insurance (EUR 50M) are indicative, so carriers cannot yet price exposure.
  • Thin contingency: EUR 85M free headroom (5.7%) against fallback exposures of EUR 150-250M for adapter acceleration (estimate).
  • Budget line items show a gap: the EUR 300M concession envelope split and who finances validation hardware retrofits remain open decisions.
  • Legacy-system latency: three-leg queries at 95% availability each yield about 86% combined, below the 99.5% SLA, and 8-15 smaller operators risk missing Month 30 (2029-04-12) (estimate).
  • Sum-of-legs fare construction gives no price reason to prefer rail over air, limiting the modal-shift outcome.
  • Heavy dependence on scarce OSDM, clearing and actuarial expertise and on a programme office of about 80 staff (estimate) across four hubs.

Opportunities

  • Passengers gain a single through-ticket with continuous rights on busy corridors; early corridor wins (Paris-Brussels-Amsterdam-Köln, Wien-München-Zürich) can build momentum and set the network effect for later extension.
  • Distributor integration through non-discriminatory OSDM access can use Trainline and Omio reach to lift through-ticket share without public sales spend.
  • Precedents (Rail Settlement Plan, Eurail/Interrail, Swiss NOVA) supply tested apportionment, dispute and onboarding practices that cut design time.
  • Neutral, emissions-sorted display and guaranteed-rebooking products can improve rail's appeal against short-haul air at low public cost.
  • Shared adapter modules and a reference test suite can lower integration cost for smaller carriers and create reusable assets.
  • Legislative momentum around the Regulation gives political backing and a legal basis for mandatory API exposure.

Threats

  • Regulation adoption slips 6-12 months beyond Month 18 (2028-04-12) (estimate, not verified), removing the legal mandate for standards and API exposure.
  • Carrier refusal if connection liability remains unpriceable; 30-40% refusal (estimate) would fragment corridors and cut the 40% goal to 15-25%.
  • Article 101 TFEU challenge after investment could force EUR 50-100M rework and 6-12 months delay (estimate).
  • Stakeholder deadlock or withdrawal of a major distributor by Month 9 (2027-07-12) could delay standards 2-4 months and cut volume 15-25% (estimate).
  • Pool or concession overruns could drain budget needed for the TEN-T extension wave.
  • Low-fare airline responses and national regulator objections limit modal shift and corridor access.

Recommendations

  • Programme Office and actuaries: commission the actuarial study at Month 1 (2026-11-12), publish the draft liability model at Month 3 (2027-01-12), obtain written sign-off from at least 8 major carriers and CER at Month 4 (2027-02-12); use the Month 6 (2027-04-12) gate, deferring to Month 12 (2027-10-12) if unresolved.
  • EU Agency for Railways: complete the technical audit of all carriers by Month 2 (2026-12-12), publish tier timelines at Month 6 (2027-04-12), and procure shared adapter modules by Month 12 (2027-10-12); tie EUR 240M adapter funds to verified API performance.
  • DG MOVE and DG COMP liaison: file pre-notification at Month 2 (2026-12-12), obtain the guidance letter by Month 12 (2027-10-12) and clean-team protocol by Month 14 (2027-12-12); keep competition counsel engaged from Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • Programme Office: set the steering group at Month 1 (2026-11-12) with 75% supermajority, publish option papers at Month 2 (2026-12-12), and agree the fallback interfaces for dissenting parties by Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • Finance lead: ring-fence the EUR 150M reserve, run quarterly re-baselining from Month 6 (2027-04-12), and resolve the open concession split and validation-hardware financing by Month 9 (2027-07-12).
  • Technical lead: launch the SLA proxy and scorecard at Month 12 (2027-10-12) and run 2,000-4,000 passenger pilots at Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) to validate latency, reroute and loss rates before binding standards.

Strategic Objectives

  • Obtain signed carrier liability model from at least 8 major carriers and CER by Month 4 (2027-02-12), with the binding steering vote by Month 6 (2027-04-12).
  • Publish binding OSDM standards and clean-team clearing protocol by Month 18 (2028-04-12), with DG COMP guidance received by Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • Reach Tier 1 API exposure at p95 latency below 2 seconds and 99.5% availability by Month 30 (2029-04-12), with Tier 2 at Month 36 (2029-10-12) and Tier 3 at Month 42 (2030-04-12).
  • Launch through-ticketing on four priority corridors by Month 48 (2030-10-12), with reconciliation error below 0.5% by Month 30 (2029-04-12).
  • Reach 40% of cross-border journeys as through-tickets (planning range 15-30% if prerequisites slip) and halve distributor complaints by Month 60 (2031-10-12) within the EUR 1,500M cap, tracking cost per through-ticket sold.

Assumptions

  • The Regulation is adopted with amendments by about Month 18 (2028-04-12), with a 6-12 month slip plausible (not verified).
  • Carriers participate voluntarily if exposure is capped and priced; about 25 targeted, 15-20 minimum viable.
  • Private carrier IT investment of EUR 1.5-3.0 billion (estimate) is financed outside the EUR 1,500M cap.
  • Federated settlement, streamed availability shadow and tendered concession remain the chosen design.
  • Modal shift of 5-10% on benchmarked routes (estimate) is a planning value, not a success metric.

Missing Information

  • Actuarial loss data: missed-connection rates, rerouting costs and incident clustering per carrier.
  • Technical audit results: API readiness, latency and availability per carrier and tier assignment.
  • Current adoption count of OSDM operators and distributors, and verified legislative status of the Regulation.
  • Baseline through-ticket share, distributor complaint volume and air-rail ratios on the four corridors.
  • DG COMP and national regulator positions on data sharing and commission band.
  • Who finances ticket-validation retrofits, and the concession set-up versus service split.

Questions

  • Which carriers would still refuse to expose connections at the proposed caps, and what exposure level would change that?
  • If the Regulation slips 12 months, which parts can proceed on a voluntary basis and which stall?
  • Is EUR 85M of free headroom plus the reserve enough given adapter and concession overrun scenarios, and what would be cut first?
  • What evidence at the Month 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) pilots would show passengers choose through-tickets over stitched itineraries or flights?
  • How will independent distributors and smaller carriers be kept inside the network if the steering vote goes against them?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Programme Director & Executive Governance Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Programme Director is the singular executive leadership role accountable for five-year delivery, EUR 1.5 billion budget and 40% through-ticket target. Requires continuous presence, decision authority across all five phases, and direct reporting to the Commission. A 5-year multi-year appointment with continuity clause is specified; cannot be part-time, contracted or temporary without risking schedule slip and stakeholder alignment breakdown. This is a core permanent public programme role.

Explanation: Owns overall programme delivery, stakeholder alignment and decision-making across five years. Chairs the steering group, mediates deadlocks among 25+ carriers, distributors and regulators, and reports to the Commission. Critical for maintaining momentum through the Phase 1 readiness gate (Month 6 = 2027-04-12) and regulatory milestone sequence. Directly accountable for the EUR 1.5 billion budget and the 40% through-ticket target.

Consequences: Without clear executive leadership, steering-group deadlock on Decisions 1–3 (liability, clearing, public distributor) cannot be escalated to Commission mediation by Month 5 (2027-03-12). Standards milestone slips from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12); budget variance exceeds EUR 100M as carriers delay participation; 20–30% of smaller operators withdraw, reducing through-ticket goal from 40% to 15–25%. Programme credibility with member states and carriers erodes.

People Count: 1 Programme Director (senior, 5-year multi-year appointment with continuity clause). Role is singular, irreplaceable; cannot be split.

Typical Activities: Chairs biweekly steering meetings with CER, carriers, distributors, BEUC and regulators; mediates consensus on critical decisions (liability, clearing, public distributor, funding) by Month 6 (2027-04-12); escalates deadlocks to Commission mediation by Month 5 (2027-03-12); signs off binding votes by Month 6 (2027-04-12); reports monthly to DG MOVE leadership and quarterly to the Transport Commissioner; approves milestone-conditional funding releases; manages personnel and budget variance; resolves carrier participation disputes and distributor access grievances; leads programme board reviews at Months 6, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48 and 60 (2027-04-12, 2027-10-12, 2028-04-12, 2028-10-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12).

Background Story: Dr. Helena Steinberg is a Swedish transport policy executive based in Brussels, with 18 years' experience in EU rail regulation and public-sector programme management. She led the transposition of the Passenger Rights Regulation (1371/2007) across five member states and managed a EUR 800M cross-border infrastructure programme for DG MOVE from 2014–2020. Helena holds a PhD in Transport Economics from Uppsala University and has chaired industry steering groups at CER and the Commission. She is fluent in Swedish, English and German, and has established credibility with both carriers and consumer bodies. For this programme, she brings executive authority to mediate stakeholder deadlock and direct the EUR 1.5 billion budget allocation across the five-year horizon.

Equipment Needs: Secure video-conferencing system (EU institutions compliant); high-bandwidth connectivity for biweekly steering calls across four EU locations; encrypted email and document collaboration (SharePoint/Teams); financial dashboard software for EUR 1.5 billion budget tracking; CRM system for stakeholder relationship management; secure phone lines for confidential carrier and Commission dialogue; backup power and redundant internet (two carriers minimum).

Facility Needs: Office in DG MOVE (Brussels, European Quarter) with secure enclosed meeting room for steering groups and mediation sessions; proximity to the Commission Transport Commissioner's office for escalation meetings; high-speed secure network (VPN-compliant with EU institutions); co-working access in Berlin and Madrid for quarterly in-person carrier engagement; 24/7 building access for crisis management during phase milestones (Month 6, 18, 30, 48, 60 = 2027-04-12, 2028-04-12, 2029-04-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12).

2. Standards & Technical Specification Custodian

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Standards & Technical Specification Custodian anchors OSDM at the EU Agency for Railways on a permanent basis, managing change requests, versioning and conformance testing over five years. This is a specified 'permanent Agency role' (not contracted work). The supporting team (2–3 technical writers, max 3) absorbs surge during binding-standards development (Months 6–12 = 2027-04-12 to 2027-10-12), but the custodian role itself is continuous and foundational to all conformance gates and milestones. Requires institutional authority and stability that only a permanent appointment provides.

Explanation: Anchors the OSDM specification at the EU Agency for Railways, manages change-request cycles, versions releases and maintains the conformance test suite. Ensures binding standards are published by Month 18 (2028-04-12), conformance tests are available to all carriers by Month 9 (2027-07-12), and the specification remains stable yet responsive to carrier and distributor needs. Essential for the mandatory API exposure milestone and technical credibility across the ecosystem.

Consequences: Without a dedicated custodian, OSDM change requests queue for 3–6 months, delaying critical bug fixes and carrier integration feedback loops. Carriers fork the specification or request extended timelines; Tier 1 API exposure slips from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 36 (2029-10-12) (6-month delay estimate). Conformance tests are ambiguous or incomplete, raising API errors in production and eroding carrier buy-in. Standards adoption is jeopardized.

People Count: 1 specification custodian (OSDM domain expert, permanent Agency role) + 2–3 technical writers and change-control coordinators (min 2, max 3, depending on change-request volume and release cadence). Solo custodian risks single-point-of-failure if unavailable; supporting team absorbs surge in change requests during Months 6–12 (2027-04-12 to 2027-10-12) binding-standards development.

Typical Activities: Manages OSDM specification versions (3–4 releases per year); processes and prioritises carrier and distributor change requests (target: critical 2 weeks, major 6 weeks, minor 8 weeks); publishes version roadmap and quarterly release calendar; maintains conformance test suite and distributes test environments to carriers by Month 9 (2027-07-12); chairs the technical standards working group biweekly; escalates blocking issues to the Programme Director; reviews carrier API implementations and certifies compliance; provides guidance on OSDM adoption to smaller operators; archives specifications in open-source repository with version control.

Background Story: Dr. Jürgen Keller is a German rail-systems architect with 22 years' experience in OSDM standardisation and API governance. He co-led the UIC OSDM working group from 2016–2024, managing version releases and conformance testing for 15+ European operators including DB, SBB and SNCF. Jürgen holds a Diplom in Computer Science from TU Munich and has published on rail interoperability standards in peer-reviewed journals. Based at the EU Agency for Railways in Valenciennes, he chairs the technical standards group and has established trust with carriers and the Commission. For this programme, he anchors the OSDM specification, manages change requests and operates the conformance test suite.

Equipment Needs: OSDM specification repository and version-control infrastructure (GitHub Enterprise or equivalent); automated conformance test suite and CI/CD pipeline; carrier API simulation tools for testing carrier implementations; distributed test environments (cloud or on-premise) accessible by carriers in four corridors; secure data storage for test results and compliance documentation; technical writing software (Confluence, Word, LaTeX); change-request tracking system (Jira or equivalent); secure communication tools for technical working group (Slack, Teams).

Facility Needs: Office at EU Agency for Railways (Valenciennes) with access to live rail test infrastructure (Lille-Europe station, Paris–Brussels corridor trains for pilot validation); secure lab space for conformance testing equipment and carrier API integrations; high-performance network (gigabit+ to support multi-carrier test environments); meeting room for biweekly technical standards working group; archive facility for versioned specifications and test data (physical and digital); proximity to carrier IT teams via regional hubs (Berlin, Munich for Deutsche Bahn and regional operators access).

3. Carrier Liability & Risk Modelling Specialist

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: Carrier Liability & Risk Modelling Specialist is a time-bound, specialist role focused on delivering the actuarial study (Month 2–6 = 2026-12-12 to 2027-04-12) and securing carrier sign-off by Month 4 (2027-02-12). Workload is front-loaded and episodic: actuarial work, pool design and presentation. After Month 6 (2027-04-12), the role transitions to quarterly monitoring, a lighter ongoing responsibility. This is not a core institutional mandate. Independent contractors with financial-services/insurance expertise are typically engaged for discrete modelling projects. Engagement extends through Month 12 (2027-10-12) for pool monitoring, after which core staff can manage the process.

Explanation: Commissions the actuarial study by Month 2 (2026-12-12), develops the carrier-funded guarantee pool model with per-incident caps and co-insurance thresholds, and secures binding carrier sign-off by Month 4 (2027-02-12). Designs the quarterly pool-monitoring process and cash-flow forecasts. This role unblocks the single largest carrier participation risk: without a transparent, priced liability model, 30–40% of operators refuse to expose inventory, fragmenting corridors.

Consequences: Without actuarial validation and a published liability model by Month 3 (2027-01-12), carriers cannot price inventory exposure. Steering-group votes on liability bog down in unresolved risk allocations; binding vote by Month 6 (2027-04-12) fails or requires Commission mediation (additional 3–4 week delay estimate). 30–40% of carriers refuse to expose connections; network fragments into bilateral corridors. Through-ticket goal slides to 15–25%. Budget overruns on adapter costs due to reduced carrier participation incentive.

People Count: 1 risk/actuarial lead (financial services or insurance background, Month 1–12 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-10-12 focused role) + 1 financial modeller (supporting Month 1–24 = 2026-11-12 to 2028-10-12 for quarterly adjustments and pool monitoring). Lead role is specialized and time-intensive (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-04-12); support can ramp down post-Month 6 (2027-04-12) if pool stabilizes.

Typical Activities: Commissions and manages the actuarial study (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-04-12) analysing 24-month carrier data on missed connections, rerouting costs and incident clustering; designs per-incident caps (proposed: EUR 500–1,000) and co-insurance triggers (proposed: EUR 50M draw); develops contribution weighting tied to trailing 12-month on-time performance; produces worked examples for three carrier profiles (large, regional, small); presents the liability model to CER and 10 major carriers by Month 4 (2027-02-12) for binding sign-off; establishes quarterly pool-monitoring process and publishes incident rates and contribution adjustments by Month 6 (2027-04-12); models cash-flow forecasts for the first five years.

Background Story: Dr. Marcus Rossi is an Italian actuarial consultant with 19 years in transport and insurance risk modelling. He has designed revenue-sharing and liability pools for Eurail, the Italian national transport operator and several fintech insurers. Marcus holds a BSc in Mathematics from the University of Rome and is a Fellow of the Actuarial Society of Italy. He brings deep expertise in missed-connection incident clustering, rerouting cost regression and carrier risk-pricing. For this programme, he leads the actuarial study that validates the carrier-funded guarantee pool by Month 6 (2027-04-12), securing carrier buy-in through transparent, priced liability models.

Equipment Needs: Statistical analysis software (R, Python, STATA, SAS) for missed-connection modeling and incident clustering; financial modeling tools (Excel, Tableau, or bespoke actuarial software); data integration tools to extract historical carrier data (incident logs, delay records, rerouting costs); secure data-sharing agreements and encrypted file transfer (SFTP, secure portals); presentation and visualization software for carrier workshops (Tableau, PowerPoint); quarterly reporting dashboards.

Facility Needs: Secure office or virtual-first setup with encrypted communication (VPN-compliant); secure data-handling facility if working on-site (e.g., Brussels or a carrier IT centre) with restricted access; teleconference facilities for biweekly actuarial working group meetings with carriers and DG MOVE; temporary workspace (6-12 months) at a large carrier's finance centre (e.g., DB in Berlin or SNCF in Paris) for direct access to historical incident data; secure document repository with version control and audit trails.

4. Inter-Carrier Clearing & Settlement Systems Architect

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Inter-Carrier Clearing & Settlement Systems Architect is a foundational design and build role spanning Months 0–36 (2026-10-12 to 2029-10-12) (design, procurement, build and stabilization of the EUR 220M clearing and reconciliation platform). This is a core institutional capability: clearing architecture is a primary decision lever, and the clearing layer underpins all settlement and refund operations from Month 30 (2029-04-12) onwards. Requires continuous design authority, vendor management and operational handover. After Month 18 (2028-04-12), a 1–2 person operations team joins to run the live platform, but the architect role is full-time and permanent until stabilization (Month 36 = 2029-10-12). Not suitable for contracting due to institutional criticality and duration.

Explanation: Designs the federated settlement layer (EUR settlement, 5-business-day cycle, shared reconciliation platform) with netting rules, reconciliation standards and dispute-resolution procedures. Procures or builds the reconciliation platform (EUR 20–40M estimate), sets reconciliation error targets (<0.5%), and coordinates with payment-service providers and carriers' financial systems. Ensures settlement does not create cash-flow friction for distributors, which would otherwise reduce participation by 15–20%.

Consequences: Without a coherent clearing design and reconciliation platform, settlement feeds from carriers remain inconsistent (different currencies, timestamps, formats), reconciliation error rates exceed 2–3% (current baseline estimate), and settlement cycle times extend from 5 to 10–15 business days. Distributors face cash-flow delays and 15–20% reduce participation. Dispute backlog grows, burning EUR 5–10M in manual resolution staff annually. Tier 1 API exposure is delayed as carriers cannot trust settlement reliability.

People Count: 1 clearing architect (fintech/banking background, Months 0–36 = 2026-10-12 to 2029-10-12 role spanning design, build and stabilization) + 1–2 settlement operations leads (Months 18–60 = 2028-04-12 to 2031-10-12 operational management). Architect role is foundational; operations team scales up at Month 18 (2028-04-12) as carrier feeds go live.

Typical Activities: Designs federated netting and settlement architecture with detailed rules for commission splits, refund reversals and dispute handling; specifies the settlement data format (ISO 20022 XML) and requires carrier compliance by Month 12 (2027-10-12); procures or builds the shared reconciliation platform (Months 6–24 = 2027-04-12 to 2028-10-12) with automated matching and manual escalation; sets reconciliation error targets (<0.5% by Month 30 = 2029-04-12) and attaches penalties for non-compliance; manages daily netting and payout operations starting Month 30 (2029-04-12); publishes monthly scorecard of settlement performance; handles dispute escalations and models cash-flow scenarios for carriers and distributors.

Background Story: Dr. Anna Bertolini is a Belgian fintech architect with 20 years in clearing, settlement and payments systems. She designed and launched the pan-European payment hub for rail operators and distributors in 2015, handling EUR 4 billion in annual transaction volume. Anna holds an MSc in Computer Science from KU Leuven and has led settlement systems for major financial institutions and payment processors. Based near Brussels, she brings expertise in netting, reconciliation, dispute resolution and regulatory compliance. For this programme, she designs the federated settlement layer (EUR settlement, 5-business-day cycle) and builds the shared reconciliation platform (EUR 20–40M).

Equipment Needs: Cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure, or EU-regulated private cloud) for the EUR 20–40 million reconciliation platform; API gateway and message-queue systems (Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ) for handling settlement data feeds from 25+ carriers; database systems (PostgreSQL, Oracle) for transaction ledgers and netting; business intelligence and analytics tools (Tableau, Looker) for daily settlement dashboards; secure cryptographic libraries for payment integrity; load-testing and performance-monitoring tools (JMeter, New Relic); encryption and key-management systems (HSM or cloud KMS).

Facility Needs: Office at or near a major financial-services centre (Brussels, Frankfurt, or London) with 24/7 access for settlement operations starting Month 30 (2029-04-12); secure data centre (Tier 3/4, ISO 27001) for the reconciliation platform with backup and disaster-recovery sites in separate geographies (geographically distributed for resilience); high-bandwidth, low-latency network to carrier financial systems and payment processors (SLA: <10ms latency to 95% of carriers); dedicated operations centre for monitoring nightly settlement batches (Months 30–60 = 2029-04-12 to 2031-10-12); secure meeting space for carrier finance teams' quarterly reconciliation reviews.

5. Real-Time Data Layer & Availability Platform Engineer

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Real-Time Data Layer & Availability Platform Engineer is a continuous infrastructure role spanning Months 0–60 (2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12): design (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-12 to 2027-10-12), build and testing (Months 12–24 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-10-12), and operations (Months 24–60 = 2028-10-12 to 2031-10-12). The streamed availability shadow and SLA monitoring proxy are critical to search experience and through-ticket success rates; downtime or poor design directly impacts the 40% goal. Requires ongoing operational ownership and incident response. Workload is not episodic; it is continuous build-to-operate. A dedicated platform engineer (1 lead + 2–3 operations engineers at Month 12 = 2027-10-12) ensures accountability and prevents single-point-of-failure.

Explanation: Builds and operates the streamed availability shadow (cached search layer) and SLA monitoring proxy that continuously tracks carrier booking-engine latency, availability and stale-seat error rates. Ensures p95 latency stays below 2 seconds and availability above 99.5% (proposed thresholds). Operates the distributed caching fallback and public SLA scoreboard. Critical for search experience quality and distributor confidence in multi-leg through-ticketing.

Consequences: Without a dedicated availability platform, SLA monitoring relies on ad-hoc carrier data collection; latency and availability metrics are unreliable. Carriers cannot be held accountable for missing SLAs; tranches of the Milestone-Conditioned Funding Release Ladder cannot be verified, decoupling funding from conformance. Through-ticket search success rates drop to 70–80% if legacy carrier systems miss latency targets. Distributed caching is absent; single-carrier outages cascade to whole-itinerary failures. Passenger experience degrades; through-ticket adoption falls short of target.

People Count: 1 platform architect (Month 0–24 = 2026-10-12 to 2028-10-12 design and build) + 2–3 platform engineers (Months 12–60 = 2027-10-12 to 2031-10-12 for build, testing and operations). Architect role front-loads during Months 0–12 (2026-10-12 to 2027-10-12) design phase; operations team ramps at Month 12 (2027-10-12) as carrier test environments come online.

Typical Activities: Designs the streamed availability shadow (cached search layer) and distributed caching fallback (EUR 15–25M) to handle multi-leg through-ticket queries; deploys the SLA monitoring proxy (Month 12 = 2027-10-12) that probes carrier endpoints every 5 minutes and tracks p95 latency, availability and stale-seat errors; publishes monthly public scoreboard of carrier performance; establishes automated escalation when p95 latency exceeds 3 seconds or availability drops below 99%; manages graceful degradation to scheduled-only offers when a carrier endpoint is unavailable; tunes caching to balance freshness versus search latency; implements incident response for carrier outages; provides SLA dashboards to the steering group.

Background Story: Dr. Sofia Papadimitriou is a Greek cloud-infrastructure engineer with 17 years in real-time systems and distributed caching. She architected the availability monitoring and search-optimization platform for a major European flight-booking portal, handling 1.5 million queries per minute with p95 latency <200ms. Sofia holds a PhD in Distributed Systems from NTUA Athens and has led platform teams at fintech and logistics firms. Based in Berlin, she brings expertise in SLA monitoring, graceful degradation and caching strategies. For this programme, she builds the streamed availability shadow and SLA monitoring proxy that track carrier booking-engine performance.

Equipment Needs: Distributed monitoring and observability platform (Prometheus, Datadog, or equivalent) for continuous probing of 25+ carrier booking engines; cloud infrastructure for SLA monitoring proxy deployment (EUR 15–25 million); caching layer infrastructure (Redis, Memcached, CDN) for streamed availability shadow; log aggregation and analysis tools (ELK stack, Splunk) for latency and error tracking; performance-testing tools (k6, Locust) for load simulation of three-leg through-ticket queries; alerting and incident-management systems (PagerDuty, OpsGenie); public-facing dashboard technology (Grafana, Kibana) for SLA scoreboard publishing.

Facility Needs: Co-located operations centre in Berlin or Munich (proximity to German carrier IT hubs) with 24/7 staffing from Month 12 (2027-10-12) onwards; high-performance network with dedicated carriers to each major carrier's booking engine (SLA: p95 <2 seconds per query, 99.5% availability); secure cloud infrastructure (EU data residency required by Regulation 1371/2007 and GDPR) with automatic failover and distributed caching nodes across EU geographies; secure office space for real-time incident response and escalation to carriers during outages; integration lab for testing new carriers' APIs (Phase 1, Months 6–12 = 2027-04-12 to 2027-10-12).

6. Competition Law & Regulatory Affairs Counsel

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: Competition Law & Regulatory Affairs Counsel is a specialist legal engagement, typically procured externally from a retained law firm or external counsel (EUR 2–5M over three years, specified estimate). The work is time-bound: DG COMP pre-notification (Month 2 = 2026-12-12), guidance acquisition (Month 12 = 2027-10-12), clean-team protocol design (Month 14 = 2027-12-12), and then monitoring for legal challenges (Months 24–60 = 2028-10-12 to 2031-10-12). This is not a permanent in-house legal function; it is a specialized, contract-based retainer. After Month 12 (2027-10-12), the role shifts to lighter monitoring and challenge detection, suitable for quarterly advisory engagement rather than full-time employment.

Explanation: Initiates DG COMP pre-notification by Month 2 (2026-12-12), secures Article 101 TFEU guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12), and designs clean-team clearing protocols to isolate sensitive commercial data. Manages bilateral regulator impact assessments with each member state and flags regulatory risks to the steering group. Prevents post-investment legal challenges that could unwind clearing and data-sharing arrangements (EUR 50–100M rework estimate).

Consequences: Without proactive competition-law management, Article 101 risk remains unaddressed until Months 18–24 (2028-04-12 to 2028-10-12), after carriers have committed IT resources. A post-investment challenge by DG COMP or a third-party distributor could force a 6–12 month redesign of clearing and data-sharing (EUR 50–100M estimate). Carriers lose confidence and reduce inventory exposure. Regulatory uncertainty delays binding standards from Month 18 (2028-04-12) to Month 24–30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12). Programme credibility erodes.

People Count: 1 external competition-law counsel (specializing in EU transport and digital markets, Months 0–36 = 2026-10-12 to 2029-10-12 primary focus, Months 36–60 = 2029-10-12 to 2031-10-12 lighter monitoring, EUR 2–5M total). May be a retained external firm rather than internal staff. Primary counsel handles DG COMP dialogue and clean-team design; monitoring phase (Months 24+) detects early signals of challenges.

Typical Activities: Initiates formal pre-notification with DG COMP by Month 2 (2026-12-12) describing clearing, data-sharing, fare construction and commission-band arrangements; prepares comprehensive legal memoranda on Article 101 compliance; obtains formal written guidance from DG COMP by Month 12 (2027-10-12); designs clean-team arrangement (if required) with independent compliance officer and IT firewalls between clearing and competitive functions; publishes data-handling protocol approved by DG COMP by Month 14 (2027-12-12); documents guidance in binding-standards text (Month 18 = 2028-04-12); monitors for legal challenges post-launch; briefs steering group quarterly on legal risk exposure and contingency redesign options (estimated EUR 50–100M rework if challenged).

Background Story: Dr. François Lefevre is a Belgian competition lawyer with 21 years in EU transport and digital-markets law. He has advised the Commission, CER and major carriers on Article 101 TFEU compliance in shared clearing, data-pooling and alliance arrangements. François holds a doctorate in EU Law from KU Leuven and has published extensively on digital-market regulation and the Regulation on Rail Ticketing. Based in Brussels, he has strong relationships with DG COMP and national regulators. For this programme, he secures early DG COMP guidance on shared data and clearing by Month 12 (2027-10-12) and designs clean-team protocols to protect the programme from post-investment legal challenges.

Equipment Needs: Legal research and case-management software (LexisNexis, Westlaw, or EU institutional libraries); secure email and encrypted document collaboration (EU institutions-compliant); video-conferencing and secure telephony for DG COMP and national-regulator dialogue; competition-law analysis tools and precedent databases; document drafting and version control (SharePoint, Confluence); risk-assessment dashboards for tracking legal exposure across clearing, data-sharing and commission designs.

Facility Needs: Office in Brussels (proximity to DG MOVE and DG COMP, European Quarter) or co-located with the Programme Director; secure meeting rooms for confidential dialogue with DG COMP officials (Months 2, 12 = 2026-12-12, 2027-10-12 primary milestones); access to EU institutional libraries and legal databases; teleconference facilities for quarterly briefings to the steering group on competition-law risk; quiet, distraction-free office space for legal drafting (Months 0–18 = 2026-10-12 to 2028-04-12, binding-standards phase).

7. Carrier Integration & Technical Onboarding Manager

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Carrier Integration & Technical Onboarding Manager is a continuous, central coordination role spanning Months 0–60 (2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12). The manager conducts the technical audit (Month 2 = 2026-12-12), assigns carrier tiers, procures shared adapters (Month 12 = 2027-10-12), manages integration roadmaps, and liaises with each carrier's CIO to unblock integration blockers throughout the conformance phases (Months 6–42 = 2027-04-12 to 2030-04-12). This role directly controls whether 20+ of 25 operators connect on time, making it critical to the mandatory API exposure milestone and through-ticket goal. Workload is ongoing, coordination-heavy and institutional. Supporting liaisons (4–6 engineers embedded in carrier teams) start at Month 6 (2027-04-12) and continue through Month 60 (2031-10-12). The lead is a full-time permanent role; liaisons can be contractors on a per-carrier or per-corridor basis, but the lead must be institutional.

Explanation: Conducts the pre-programme technical audit of all 25+ carriers by Month 2 (2026-12-12), assigns them to conformance tiers (Tier 1/2/3: Months 30/36/42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12), procures shared adapter modules (Month 12 = 2027-10-12), and manages carrier integration roadmaps and test-environment access. Liaises with each carrier's CIO/IT lead to unblock integration blockers. Essential for meeting the mandatory API exposure milestones and ensuring 80%+ of targeted carriers (20+ of 25+) connect by Month 42 (2030-04-12).

Consequences: Without proactive carrier onboarding, technical audit is not conducted; carrier tiering is ad-hoc or delayed to Month 9–12 (2027-07-12 to 2027-10-12). Integration roadmaps are unclear; Tier 2 and Tier 3 carriers miss their conformance deadlines (Months 36/42 = 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12) by 6–12 months. 40–50% of smaller operators remain unconnected at Month 48 (2030-10-12), fragmenting corridors and reducing the through-ticket goal from 40% to 20–25%. Adapter budgets are spent inefficiently, consuming EUR 100–150M overruns. Liability backstop and clearing mechanisms have insufficient carrier volume to validate assumptions.

People Count: 1 integration manager lead (Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12, full-time) + 4–6 carrier liaison engineers (Months 6–60 = 2027-04-12 to 2031-10-12, one per corridor or per 5–6 carriers, min 4 for four priority corridors, max 6 as TEN-T extends). Lead coordinates tiering, funding releases and escalations; liaisons embed in carrier IT teams to resolve technical blockers weekly.

Typical Activities: Executes detailed technical audit of all 25+ carriers' booking systems (Month 2 = 2026-12-12) assessing API readiness, event streaming, latency, availability and staff availability; publishes tier assignments (Tier 1 Month 30 = 2029-04-12, Tier 2 Month 36 = 2029-10-12, Tier 3 Month 42 = 2030-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12) by Month 6 (2027-04-12); requires each carrier to submit a detailed integration roadmap specifying system components, dependencies and monthly milestones; procures or develops shared adapter modules for common legacy patterns (EUR 30–50M) by Month 12 (2027-10-12); embeds 4–6 carrier liaison engineers in carrier IT teams to resolve integration blockers weekly; tracks conformance readiness against SLA targets (p95 <2s latency, 99.5% availability, <1% stale-seat errors) for each tier; escalates blockers to the Programme Director; manages adapter funding releases against verified performance.

Background Story: Dipl.-Ing. Klaus Mueller is a German railway systems engineer with 23 years in carrier IT integration and legacy-modernisation projects. He has led multi-year integration programmes for DB, ÖBB and SBB, retrofitting mainframe booking systems and real-time inventory platforms. Klaus holds a diploma in Railway Engineering from TU Berlin and has extensive experience with OSDM, payment-system integration and cross-border technical coordination. Based in Berlin and embedded in the German carrier community, he brings trusted relationships and technical credibility. For this programme, he conducts the pre-programme technical audit of all 25+ carriers and manages integration roadmaps across the three conformance tiers.

Equipment Needs: Technical audit and assessment tools (system-profiling software, latency-measurement tools, network diagnostics); secure remote-access infrastructure for auditing carrier booking systems (SSH, VPN, secure file transfer); spreadsheet and project-management software (Excel, Jira, Smartsheet, Asana) for tracking 25+ carrier integration roadmaps; API testing and validation tools (Postman, SoapUI); data-migration and integration-testing tools (Talend, Informatica) for smaller carriers' legacy systems; presentation and roadmap-visualization software (Lucidchart, Miro, PowerPoint).

Facility Needs: Office in Berlin or Munich (central to German-speaking carrier IT community: DB, ÖBB, SBB) with co-working or dedicated space; secure remote-access lab for auditing legacy booking systems without exposing sensitive carrier data (Months 0–6 = 2026-10-12 to 2027-04-12); secure facilities at each of 4–6 major carriers' IT centres (temporary workspace, Months 6–42 = 2027-04-12 to 2030-04-12) for liaison engineers embedded in carrier teams; high-speed connectivity to each carrier's systems for remote integration testing and troubleshooting; meeting rooms at carrier sites for weekly integration blocker resolution (Months 6–48 = 2027-04-12 to 2030-10-12).

8. Passenger Rights, Accessibility & Consumer Protection Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Passenger Rights, Accessibility & Consumer Protection Lead is a continuous compliance and coordination role spanning Months 0–60 (2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12). Primary work (legal review, compliance manual, usability testing) concentrates Months 0–18 (2026-10-12 to 2028-04-12), but ongoing auditing, carrier staff training verification, and accessibility monitoring continue through Month 60 (2031-10-12). This role ensures the programme meets EU Regulation 1371/2007 and accessibility requirements; failure exposes the programme to regulatory enforcement and legal challenge. A 1–2 person compliance auditing team joins at Month 18 (2028-04-12) for quarterly audits. The lead is institutional; auditors can be part-time or contracted audit specialists, but the lead must be full-time to maintain continuity with the Agency and carriers.

Explanation: Commissions the independent legal review of the liability and rights backstop against EU Regulation 1371/2007 by Month 1 (2026-11-12), ensures through-ticket passengers receive equivalent rights, develops the compliance manual (Month 9 = 2027-07-12), and coordinates accessibility thresholds (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours). Works with BEUC and disability-rights bodies on usability testing (Month 18 = 2028-04-12). Prevents legal exposure and ensures the programme serves persons with reduced mobility without reducing itinerary availability.

Consequences: Without passenger-rights legal review, the liability and rights backstop design may inadvertently reduce through-ticket passengers' rights below Regulation 1371/2007 requirements. EU Agency for Railways or national regulators issue enforcement notices; design must be revised (3–6 month delay estimate, EUR 10–20M rework). If accessibility thresholds are not enforced, atomic confirmation of assistance and bicycle reservations will refuse 30–40% (estimate) of itineraries lacking capacity, and the programme fails accessibility compliance. Reputational damage and regulatory escalation follow.

People Count: 1 passenger-rights lead (rail law and accessibility expertise, Months 0–36 = 2026-10-12 to 2029-10-12 primary, Months 36–60 = 2029-10-12 to 2031-10-12 lighter compliance auditing) + 1–2 compliance auditors for usability testing and carrier training verification (Months 18–60 = 2028-04-12 to 2031-10-12). Lead handles legal review and manual; auditors conduct quarterly accessibility audits and staff training checks starting Month 30 (2029-04-12).

Typical Activities: Commissions independent legal review of liability and rights backstop against Regulation 1371/2007 by Month 1 (2026-11-12); publishes legal opinion and design adjustments by Month 6 (2027-04-12); develops passenger-rights compliance manual covering compensation, assistance, refunds and complaint handling (Month 9 = 2027-07-12); submits manual to the EU Agency for Railways for formal approval; conducts quarterly accessibility audits of carrier systems and staff training from Month 30 (2029-04-12) onwards; verifies accessibility thresholds (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours) in conformance audits; coordinates usability testing with disability bodies by Month 18 (2028-04-12); resolves passenger complaints related to rights and accessibility; reports accessibility compliance to regulators annually.

Background Story: Dr. Patricia Rodriguez is a Spanish rail-passenger-rights lawyer with 18 years in EU transport regulation and accessibility law. She led Spain's implementation of Regulation 1371/2007 and has advised the European Court of Justice on disability-rights cases in rail. Patricia holds a doctorate in Administrative Law from the University of Madrid and sits on the Spanish rail regulator's consumer board. Based in Madrid, she has strong ties to BEUC, disability-rights organisations and national regulators. For this programme, she ensures the liability and rights backstop comply with existing passenger-rights law and secures accessibility certification.

Equipment Needs: Legal research software (EU Regulation 1371/2007 and accessibility-law databases); accessible document-formatting and testing tools (WCAG 2.1 compliance checkers); usability-testing software for persons with reduced mobility (screen readers, magnification tools, adaptive input devices); survey and feedback-collection platforms (Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey) for accessibility audits; email and secure collaboration tools; video-conferencing for disability-rights bodies and carrier accessibility teams.

Facility Needs: Office in Madrid or close to a major disability-rights body hub (proximity to BEUC, European Disability Forum); accessible facilities with wheelchair access, elevator access to all floors, accessible restrooms, accessible parking; meeting rooms with loop systems and sign-language interpretation facilities for disability-body engagement; usability-testing lab equipped for persons with reduced mobility (mobility aids, sensory adaptations, accessible seating, quiet areas for focus); teleconference facilities with captions and interpretation (Months 18–60 = 2028-04-12 to 2031-10-12 for quarterly usability testing with carriers and disability bodies).

9. Public Reference Distributor Concession Manager & Procurement Lead

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: Public Reference Distributor Concession Manager is a specialized procurement and performance-management role with a discrete lifecycle: business case development (Month 9 = 2027-07-12), competitive tender (Months 9–18 = 2027-07-12 to 2028-04-12), bid evaluation and award (Month 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12), and concessionaire oversight (Months 18–60 = 2028-04-12 to 2031-10-12). After award, the role transitions to contract monitoring and quarterly financial reviews, a lighter ongoing responsibility suitable for retained consulting engagement rather than full-time employment. Concession management is not a core institutional function; it is a project-based procurement activity typically handled by external consultants with fintech/procurement expertise. A 1–2 person procurement specialist team executes the competitive process (Months 9–18 = 2027-07-12 to 2028-04-12), then the role scales down to quarterly review.

Explanation: Develops the business case for the last-resort distributor concession by Month 9 (2027-07-12), issues the competitive tender by Month 12 (2027-10-12), evaluates bids and awards the concession by Month 18 (2028-04-12), and manages the concessionaire's performance through its five-year lifecycle. Ensures the service is live by Month 30 (2029-04-12), monitors costs (capped at EUR 60M subsidy), tracks volume forecasts and triggers contract reviews if overruns occur. Protects the EUR 300M concession budget envelope and ensures a neutral last-resort sales channel.

Consequences: Without concession management, the business case is delayed or underspecified. Tender is issued late (Month 18+ instead of Month 12 = 2027-10-12) or lacks clear financial/service terms, attracting weak bids. Concessionaire is awarded based on vague criteria; service launch slips from Month 30 (2029-04-12) to Month 36 (2029-10-12) or later. Operating losses accumulate; subsidy requests exceed EUR 60M cap. Commission must choose between operating the service directly (EUR 30–50M annually estimate) or leaving the last-resort role vacant, undermining the programme's claim to provide a neutral sales channel. Independents and smaller distributors withdraw, reducing through-ticket volume by 15–20%.

People Count: 1 concession manager (procurement and transport services background, Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12 full-time contract and performance management) + 1–2 procurement specialists (Months 9–18 = 2027-07-12 to 2028-04-12 for tender development and evaluation). Manager owns the business case, tender strategy and concessionaire oversight; procurement team executes the competitive process.

Typical Activities: Develops detailed business case for the public distributor concession (Month 9 = 2027-07-12) with volume forecasts, cost benchmarks and margin assumptions; issues competitive tender by Month 12 (2027-10-12) with two-stage evaluation (technical and financial); conducts bid evaluation and awards concession by Month 18 (2028-04-12); structures subsidy cap at EUR 60M over five years with clawback clause (>20% volume upside); establishes contract-review triggers if operating costs exceed budget by >15% in any quarter; requires quarterly financial reporting from the concessionaire; monitors service-level compliance (launch by Month 30 = 2029-04-12); manages contract variations and subsidy adjustments; escalates performance issues to the Programme Director; publishes annual concession performance report.

Background Story: Jean-Michel Gauthier is a French procurement and transport-concessions specialist with 19 years managing public-private partnerships in rail, bus and mobility. He has awarded and overseen concessions for SNCF, Paris RATP and several EU-funded mobility services, managing combined contract values exceeding EUR 2 billion. Jean-Michel holds an MBA from ENA (École Nationale d'Administration) and has strong relationships with the Commission procurement directorate and major transport operators. Based in Paris, he brings expertise in competitive tender design, financial controls and concession performance management. For this programme, he develops the business case for the last-resort distributor concession and manages the EUR 300M envelope.

Equipment Needs: Procurement and contract-management software (SAP Ariba, Coupa, or EU procurement portals); financial-modeling and business-case tools (Excel, Tableau, financial-analysis platforms); bid-evaluation and scoring systems; tender-management platforms (e-procurement solutions); concessionaire performance-monitoring dashboards (KPI tracking, financial reporting); confidential communication tools (secure email, encrypted teleconference) for tender evaluation.

Facility Needs: Office in Brussels or Paris (proximity to the Commission Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport, which oversees public procurement; also close to experienced concession operators in France and Belgium); secure meeting rooms for confidential tender evaluation and concessionaire negotiations (Months 9–18 = 2027-07-12 to 2028-04-12); access to EU procurement databases and legal reference materials; dedicated facilities for managing the EUR 300 million concession contract lifecycle (Months 18–60 = 2028-04-12 to 2031-10-12); quarterly meeting space with the concessionaire's finance and operations teams (Months 30–60 = 2029-04-12 to 2031-10-12).

Omissions

1. Missing Clearing and Settlement Operations Team Lead

The Inter-Carrier Clearing & Settlement Systems Architect (Role 4) designs the EUR 220M federated settlement layer and builds the reconciliation platform by Month 24 (2028-10-12). However, no operations lead is specified to own settlement execution starting Month 30 (2029-04-12), when EUR settlement, netting and payout cycles go live across 25+ carriers and distributors. Without a dedicated operations manager, nightly settlement batches, reconciliation exceptions, and cash-flow forecasts lack clear ownership. Risk: settlement delays, reconciliation backlogs exceeding 2–3% error rates, and distributor cash-flow friction that reduces participation by 10–15% (estimate).

Recommendation: Add a full-time Clearing and Settlement Operations Lead (1 FTE, Months 18–60 = 2028-04-12 to 2031-10-12) reporting to the Programme Director and the clearing architect. Responsibilities: oversee daily EUR settlement netting and payout; manage reconciliation exceptions; run quarterly cash-flow forecasts for carriers and distributors; chair monthly settlement performance reviews with carriers; escalate disputes; and manage the reconciliation SLA targets (error rate <0.5% by Month 30 = 2029-04-12). Budget: ~EUR 0.5–1.0M over five years (included in programme management allocation).

2. Missing Stakeholder Engagement and Communications Lead

The Programme Director chairs steering meetings and manages consensus, but no dedicated communications or stakeholder engagement role is specified. The programme has 25+ carriers, CER, Trainline, Omio, BEUC, disability bodies, national regulators, and member-state governments. Without coordinated, multilingual communications on decisions, milestones, and budget/schedule changes, stakeholder alignment fractures. Risk: carriers and distributors learn of decisions second-hand; confusion over milestone timelines and conformance requirements spreads; biweekly steering group meetings consume 4+ hours per steering member, reducing engagement quality. By Month 12 (2027-10-12), stakeholder fatigue on repeated briefing requests distracts technical teams from integration work.

Recommendation: Add a full-time Communications and Stakeholder Engagement Lead (1 FTE, Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12) with multilingual capability (English, French, German minimum).
