Responsibilities: prepare and distribute fortnightly steering briefing summaries (1-page decision log, action items, milestone status); publish monthly newsletter to all 25+ carriers and distributors on programme progress; coordinate quarterly carrier CIO forums and distributor advisory meetings; manage a shared online programme dashboard (milestone tracker, budget status, SLA scorecard); prepare presentations for member-state governments and regulator stakeholder forums (Months 12, 24, 36, 48 = 2027-10-12, 2028-10-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-10-12); and translate key decision documents and manuals into the five main EU transport languages (English, French, German, Italian, Spanish). Budget: ~EUR 1–2M over five years.

3. Missing Data Governance and Privacy Officer

The programme's shared real-time data layer (availability shadow, disruption event feed, settlement data) and inter-carrier clearing mechanism involve pooling and processing sensitive commercial data (fares, inventory, settlement amounts) and passenger data (booking references, personal travel patterns). No data governance, GDPR compliance, or data-protection lead is specified. Without this role, the programme risks: (1) GDPR non-compliance on passenger data handling during booking, refunds, and re-accommodation; (2) insufficient data-access controls between the clearing function and competitive-strategy functions (competition-law risk); (3) no clear data-retention and data-deletion policies, exposing carriers and distributors to regulatory fines. Risk: GDPR enforcement action or competition-law data-misuse claim post-Month 24 (2028-10-12) forces design rework (EUR 10–20M estimate, 3–6 month delay).

Recommendation: Add a full-time Data Governance and Privacy Officer (1 FTE, Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12) reporting to the Programme Director and the Competition Law Counsel. Responsibilities: design GDPR-compliant data-handling procedures for the shared real-time layer (fares, inventory, disruption, passenger data); establish data-access controls and firewalls between clearing and competitive functions (support clean-team arrangement); develop data-retention and deletion policies for settlement and booking data; conduct quarterly GDPR and data-security audits of the reconciliation platform and carrier API integrations; liaise with national data-protection authorities; and prepare privacy documentation (Data Protection Impact Assessments) for Regulation 1371/2007 and accessibility compliance. Budget: ~EUR 0.5–1.0M over five years.

4. Missing Independent Audit and Assurance Function

The programme commits EUR 1.5 billion public money across five years and involves 25+ carriers, national regulators and EU institutions. Milestone-conditioned funding releases (Decision 4) depend on verification: conformance certificates, API availability, booking-error rates, reconciliation error rates and accessibility audits. No independent assurance function is specified to verify these metrics before tranches are released. Risk: Programme Office self-certifies milestones without external validation, eroding stakeholder trust. Milestone-conditioned funding loses leverage if carriers doubt that metrics are independently verified. European Court of Auditors or DG MOVE audit post-launch finds compliance gaps and demands clawbacks. Budget variance control is weakened.

Recommendation: Establish an independent programme audit and assurance function (contracted to an external audit firm or internal EU audit body, Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12) with a mandate to: (1) verify conformance certificates before Tier-based API exposure milestones (Months 30, 36, 42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12); (2) audit carrier booking-engine SLA compliance monthly and publish results on the public SLA scoreboard; (3) audit settlement reconciliation error rates and reconciliation-platform performance quarterly; (4) conduct annual accessibility compliance audits (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours); (5) verify through-ticket volume and distributor-complaint metrics at Months 36, 48, 60 (2029-10-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12) against targets; and (6) prepare independent annual audit report for the Court of Auditors. Budget: ~EUR 3–5M over five years, included in programme management allocation.

5. Missing Disruption Operations Coordinator

Decision 9 (Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography) specifies that when a connection is missed, the shared disruption event feed detects it, the issuing carrier or automated rebooking service proposes alternatives, and passengers are rebooked on competitors' trains within minutes. No dedicated operations coordinator is specified to manage this live re-accommodation service, handle escalations and staff 24/7 customer-service centres at border stations. Risk: Disruption response times exceed 30–60 minutes; passengers are stranded; programme faces public backlash and liability claims (EUR 10–20M estimate). Without a coordinator ensuring carrier 24/7 coverage, the Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography remains a design on paper and does not operationalise the through-ticket liability backstop.

Recommendation: Add a full-time Disruption Operations Coordinator (1 FTE, Months 12–60 = 2027-10-12 to 2031-10-12, ramping from Month 12 = 2027-10-12 when pilots begin) supported by 2–3 border-station liaison officers and a 24/7 customer-service team (outsourced or shared with the concession operator). Responsibilities: oversee the shared disruption event feed and automated rebooking system; manage escalations when re-accommodation fails; coordinate with carrier 24/7 centres and border-station staff; publish response-time metrics; conduct post-incident reviews; and update the Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography operating manual (Decision 9) based on real incidents. Ensure at least one English-speaking agent at each of the 4 priority corridors' border stations by Month 30 (2029-04-12). Budget: ~EUR 2–4M over five years for personnel and training.

6. Missing Member-State Coordination and National Regulator Liaison

The programme operates across multiple member states (France, Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Spain, Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden and more for TEN-T extension). Each member state has a railway regulator (SNCF regulator, Bundesnetzagentur, ÖBB, Renfe regulator, etc.) with authority over track access, station capacity and pricing. Decision 12 (Risk #12 in assumptions) identifies national regulator veto as a medium-risk blocker: if one regulator blocks data-sharing or clearing on incumbent-protection grounds, the corridor is blocked for 12–24 months. No member-state coordination or national regulator liaison role is specified. Risk: Programme builds standards and clearing mechanisms unaware of national regulatory constraints; Months 18–24 (2028-04-12 to 2028-10-12) binding-standards phase hits unanticipated regulator objections; four corridors cannot launch on schedule.

Recommendation: Add a full-time Member-State Coordination and Regulator Liaison Officer (1 FTE, Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12), supported by country-specific liaison coordinators (1 per major corridor, e.g. France, Germany, Austria, Spain; 4 FTE part-time or 2 FTE full-time rotating). Responsibilities: conduct bilateral engagement with each national railway regulator by Month 3 (2027-01-12) to identify regulatory constraints and approval pathways; prepare regulatory-impact assessments per member state (Months 3–6 = 2027-01-12 to 2027-04-12); monitor proposed regulatory changes that could impact the programme (ongoing); secure regulator sign-offs on binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) and mandatory API exposure (Months 30, 36, 42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12); and escalate regulatory conflicts to the Programme Director and Commission DG MOVE. Include national regulators as formal observers in the standards-working group. Budget: ~EUR 1–2M over five years.

Potential Improvements

1. Clarify reporting lines and governance escalation for the 10-person team

The team-members document specifies 9 roles but lacks a clear governance diagram showing who reports to whom, escalation paths for blocked decisions, and conflict resolution when roles overlap (e.g., the clearing architect and settlement operations lead, or the carrier integration manager and technical audit). The Programme Director chairs steering but is not shown managing the Technical Secretariat at the Agency or liaising with competing interests (e.g., the Programme Office at DG MOVE vs. the Agency at Valenciennes). Risk: Decisions get stuck in ambiguity; the architect and operations lead disagree on settlement priorities; nobody owns escalation of a carrier integration blocker.

Recommendation: Create a formal org chart showing: (1) Programme Director (DG MOVE) with direct reports: Standards & Technical Specification Custodian (at the Agency, dotted-line reporting to the Programme Director and solid-line to the Agency Director for institutional independence); Inter-Carrier Clearing & Settlement Systems Architect (reporting to the Programme Director; Clearing and Settlement Operations Lead reports to the Architect Months 0–24 = 2026-10-12 to 2028-10-12, then to the Operations Lead Months 24–60 = 2028-10-12 to 2031-10-12); Carrier Integration & Technical Onboarding Manager (reporting to the Programme Director, with 4–6 carrier liaison engineers reporting to the integration manager); and supporting functions (Competition Law Counsel, Passenger Rights Lead, Data Governance Officer, Stakeholder Communications Lead, Member-State Liaison) reporting to the Programme Director or as dotted-line advisors. (2) Escalation rules: Technical deadlock between standards and clearing goes to the Programme Director (resolve within 5 business days); steering deadlock goes to Commission mediation (Month 5 = 2027-03-12); funding tranches held for verification go to the independent audit function and the Programme Director (sign-off within 10 business days). (3) Conflict-resolution protocol: monthly programme-board meetings with the Programme Director, Technical Custodian, Clearing Architect and Integration Manager to align priorities.

2. Specify roles' security clearance, data-access and confidentiality requirements

Many team roles handle sensitive information: the actuarial risk modeller sees carrier missed-connection incident data; the clearing architect designs financial flows and settles confidential revenue allocations; the competition-law counsel advises on Article 101 risk; the data-governance officer audits passenger data handling. No security clearance, data-classification or non-disclosure requirements are specified. Risk: Sensitive commercial data (fares, incident rates, financial exposure) leaks to competitors; competition-law strategies shared inappropriately; passenger data mishandled. Also, team members rotate or leave mid-programme (e.g., the Programme Director), and no knowledge-transfer or continuity protocol is defined.

Recommendation: Add a security and continuity section to each role specifying: (1) Required security clearance (EU Confidential minimum for financial/competition roles; national security clearance for regulator-liaison roles if required by member states); (2) Data-access classification (what data sets the role may access: carrier incident logs, settlement data, passenger booking patterns, competition-law opinions, etc.); (3) Non-disclosure agreements required before starting (e.g., all carriers and DG MOVE sign standard NDAs covering strategic decisions, pool cash flows, Article 101 discussions); (4) Knowledge-transfer protocol (if the role holder leaves, the successor receives a 2–4 week shadowing period and documented decision logs; key institutional knowledge is archived in a secure wiki; no person is a single point of failure); (5) Device and communication security (encrypted email, VPN-only remote access, no storage of sensitive data on personal devices); and (6) Incident reporting (any suspected data loss or unauthorized access reported to the Data Governance Officer within 24 hours). Budget impact: ~EUR 0.2–0.5M for security protocols, background checks and knowledge-transfer documentation.

3. Add explicit succession and continuity-of-leadership plan for the Programme Director

The Programme Director role is described as a 5-year multi-year appointment with a continuity clause, but no succession plan or deputy/associate role is defined. If the Programme Director becomes unavailable (illness, reassignment, retirement) between Months 18–30 (2028-04-12 to 2029-04-12) (binding standards and mandatory API exposure), programme momentum stops. Steering-group decision authority and Commission escalation paths break. Assumption #20 (Organizational & Governance risk) acknowledges this but does not specify mitigation. Risk: A 2–3 month leadership gap during binding-standards or API exposure phases delays milestones.

Recommendation: Appoint a Deputy Programme Director or an Associate Director with explicit responsibilities as backup: (1) The Deputy is identified and on-boarded alongside the Programme Director by Month 3 (2027-01-12), shadowing all steering meetings and decision-making by Month 6 (2027-04-12) so they know the stakeholder landscape. (2) The Deputy is authorized to chair steering meetings and sign off on funding tranches in the Programme Director's absence, with Commission notification within 24 hours. (3) Successor recruitment begins 6 months before the current Director's term end (i.e., Month 54 = 2031-04-12 for a 5-year term starting Month 0 = 2026-10-12). (4) The Programme Director and Deputy maintain a confidential decision log of all steering-group votes, Commission mediation outcomes and strategic rationales, updated weekly and escrow-held with the Commission so continuity is not lost on leadership change. (5) An associate programme manager (0.5–1.0 FTE, Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12) reports to the Programme Director and handles administrative continuity (meeting scheduling, action-item tracking, document management). Budget: ~EUR 0.5–1.0M over five years (included in programme management allocation).

4. Define procurement and vendor-management responsibilities more explicitly

The team includes a Concession Manager (Role 9) who procures the last-resort distributor, but no explicit responsibility is assigned for procuring other major contracted services: the actuarial study (Role 3 area), the reconciliation platform (Role 4 area), the streamed availability platform (Role 5 area), competition-law counsel (Role 6), passenger-rights legal review (Role 8), and external training programmes for member-state capacity building. Each of these is a significant procurement (EUR 20M–40M for platforms, EUR 2M–5M for studies and counsel, EUR 30M–50M for training). No centralized procurement governance is described, risking delays, cost overruns and quality misalignment.

Recommendation: Add a Procurement and Vendor Management responsibility (either as a dedicated 1 FTE role within the Programme Office, or as a shared responsibility of the Programme Director and a procurement specialist at DG MOVE, Months 0–60 = 2026-10-12 to 2031-10-12). Governance: (1) A procurement plan is published by Month 3 (2027-01-12) specifying all major contracts: actuarial study (Month 1 = 2026-11-12 tender, award by Month 2 = 2026-12-12), legal reviews (Month 1 = 2026-11-12 tender), competition-law counsel (Month 2 = 2026-12-12 engagement), reconciliation platform (Month 6 = 2027-04-12 tender, award by Month 9 = 2027-07-12), streamed availability platform (Month 6 = 2027-04-12 tender, award by Month 12 = 2027-10-12), external training (Month 6 = 2027-04-12 tender for phased delivery Months 18–30 = 2028-04-12 to 2029-04-12), and Concession (Role 9 timeline). (2) Each contract includes standard EU procurement clauses (transparency, non-discrimination, value for money) and programme-specific KPI targets (e.g., reconciliation platform must achieve <0.5% error rate by Month 30 = 2029-04-12 or face penalty clauses). (3) Quarterly vendor performance reviews are held to track delivery against milestones, with escalation to the Programme Director if a vendor is >1 month behind schedule or >10% over budget. (4) A shared vendor-management tool (e.g., Coupa, Ariba) tracks all contracts, payments and deliverables for transparency and audit. Budget: ~EUR 0.5M for procurement staffing and tools (included in programme management allocation).

5. Separate technical roles' accountability from programme-delivery accountability

The Standards & Technical Specification Custodian (Role 2) manages OSDM change requests and conformance tests, but is also expected to deliver binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12). If carrier feedback delays OSDM finalization or technical working groups deadlock on API design, the Custodian is held accountable for a standards delay that is partly outside their control (depending on Regulation adoption, DG COMP guidance and stakeholder consensus). Similarly, the Clearing Architect (Role 4) designs settlement by Month 24 (2028-10-12) but is accountable for live EUR settlement operations starting Month 30 (2029-04-12), which depends on carriers adopting the settlement data format (not guaranteed). Risk: Technical roles are blamed for programme delays caused by external dependencies (regulation, stakeholder consensus, carrier readiness). Morale suffers; turnover increases.

Recommendation: Clarify accountability boundaries for each technical role: (1) The Standards Custodian is accountable for delivering the OSDM specification document and conformance test suite on schedule, but standards-adoption delays caused by Regulation adoption, DG COMP guidance or steering deadlock are programme risks, not the Custodian's accountability. If standards are delayed, the Custodian is asked 'Could you have completed the spec faster given the input constraints?' not 'Why are standards late?'. (2) The Clearing Architect is accountable for reconciliation-platform design and build completion by Month 24 (2028-10-12), but live settlement error rates starting Month 30 (2029-04-12) depend on carriers uploading consistent settlement data—which is a carrier readiness risk, not the Architect's accountability. The Architect is responsible for designing fail-safe reconciliation (alerts on format errors) but not for forcing carriers to comply; the Settlement Operations Lead owns that enforcement. (3) Each technical role's job description includes a 'Dependencies and Critical Path' section listing external milestones it depends on (e.g., 'Custodian depends on DG COMP guidance by Month 12 = 2027-10-12; if delayed, OSDM finalization slips by [N] weeks'). This is reviewed quarterly with the Programme Director to identify slippage early. (4) Incentive structure: technical roles are evaluated on delivery against their scope and schedule given the actual external constraints they faced, not absolute milestones that depend on others. This improves retention and accountability realism.

6. Define technical skills development and knowledge transfer for carrier liaison engineers

The Carrier Integration & Technical Onboarding Manager (Role 7) is supported by 4–6 carrier liaison engineers who embed in carrier IT teams for 18–24 months each (Months 6–30 = 2027-04-12 to 2029-04-12 for Tier 1 carriers, longer for Tier 2/3). These engineers are critical to unblocking integration and ensuring Tier conformance. No background stories, experience profiles, or technical-skills development plan are specified for liaisons. Risk: Liaisons are junior or inexperienced; they lack credibility with carrier CTOs and cannot resolve deep integration issues; integration work stalls. Also, liaison engineers leave at the end of their corridor assignment (Month 30, 36, 42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12 for different Tiers), and knowledge about each carrier's integration is lost.

Recommendation: For each of the 4–6 carrier liaison engineers: (1) Define a required background profile: 5+ years' experience in carrier IT integration, rail systems architecture or API governance; experience with legacy mainframe systems a plus; fluent English and at least one other EU language (French, German, Spanish) preferred. (2) Provide a 2–4 week onboarding period (overlapping with the Integration Manager and Standards Custodian) covering OSDM, the conformance gate, SLA targets, and the specific carrier's current systems. (3) Require each liaison to document their carrier's integration progress weekly in a shared carrier-integration wiki, including: system architecture, completed milestones, blockers, dependencies on third parties (e.g., payment processors), and estimated conformance readiness date. This wiki is owned by the Integration Manager and reviewed monthly. (4) After each Tier's conformance (Months 30, 36, 42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12), conduct a 1–2 week knowledge-transfer period where the outgoing liaison briefs the Integration Manager and the incoming liaison (if any) on their carrier's architecture, cultural dynamics and remaining technical debt. (5) Offer liaisons a 6–12 month contract extension option to follow their carrier into operations (e.g., a liaison who closes Tier 1 in Month 30 = 2029-04-12 can extend to Month 36 = 2029-10-12 to support their carrier's transition to live settlement). This improves retention and operational continuity. Budget: ~EUR 2–3M over five years for liaison salaries and training.

7. Add role descriptions for Phase 3 operations team (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12)

The team description focuses on Phases 1–2 (Months 0–48 = 2026-10-12 to 2030-10-12): governance set-up, standards, conformance, and four-corridor go-live. Phase 3 (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) extends the programme to the full TEN-T network, but no Phase 3 team composition is specified. Risk: Roles that scale down at Month 48 (2030-10-12) (e.g., technical audit, conformance testing, carrier onboarding for later waves) are unclear. Also, the shift from build/pilot (Phase 2) to operations/support (Phase 3) is not reflected in team structure (e.g., does the Clearing Architect remain 100% FTE, or do they transition to a lighter operational-advisory role?).

Recommendation: Add a Phase 3 team plan (Months 48–60 = 2030-10-12 to 2031-10-12) outlining which roles continue, scale, or transition: (1) Programme Director: continues full-time, leading the second-wave carrier onboarding and budget reallocation (if needed) based on Phase 2 variance. (2) Standards Custodian: transitions to 50% maintenance mode, handling critical bug fixes and version patches for OSDM while the standards-working group winds down. (3) Clearing Architect: transitions to 30% advisory (quarterly architecture reviews) while the Settlement Operations Lead manages live operations; system maintenance is outsourced to a vendor. (4) Carrier Integration Manager: remains 100% but shifts focus from Tier-based milestones to Phase 2 post-go-live support (SLA monitoring, troubleshooting) and Phase 3 second-wave onboarding (10–15 later carriers and regional operators). Liaison engineers scale from 4–6 to 2–3, focusing on second-wave carriers. (5) New roles for Phase 3: a Live Operations Manager (1 FTE) overseeing settlement, availability monitoring, and incident management across all live corridors; a TEN-T Extension Programme Manager (1 FTE) coordinating the rollout plan for the second wave. (6) Stakeholder Communications Lead, Data Governance Officer and Member-State Liaison continue full-time (or ramp slightly) for expansion. (7) Passenger Rights Lead transitions to 50% (annual audits of accessibility and rights compliance instead of quarterly). (8) Concession Manager remains for the five-year distributor contract monitoring. This Phase 3 team structure is published by Month 36 (2029-10-12) so hiring and transition planning can begin early.

8. Clarify budget allocation for team salaries and operating costs

The team document specifies 9 roles with background stories and equipment/facility needs, but no budget is allocated to team salaries, benefits, training, or office operations. The Canonical Budget shows EUR 75M for Programme Management (Programme Office, Technical Secretariat, external advisory board, legal counsel), but this is not broken down by role or function. Risk: Hiring plans are unclear; the 80–100 FTE Programme Office staff size is not cross-walked with the named 9 roles, leaving ambiguity on whether the 75M covers salaries. Also, no budget is shown for team travel (biweekly steering meetings across Brussels, Valenciennes, Berlin, Madrid), external training (for liaison engineers), or contingency for staff turnover.

Recommendation: Create a team budget breakdown showing: (1) For each of the 9 named roles, estimate annual salary range (e.g., Programme Director EUR 150K–200K, Clearing Architect EUR 120K–160K, Liaison Engineer EUR 80K–100K) based on grade levels and EU duty stations. (2) Aggregate these into the Programme Office and Agency budgets: estimate that EUR 40–50M of the EUR 75M programme-management allocation covers core team salaries (9 roles + 40–50 supporting staff for finance, HR, scheduling, etc.). (3) Reserve EUR 10–15M for external contractors and specialists (actuarial study, competition-law counsel, audit firms, training providers). (4) Reserve EUR 5–10M for team operations: travel to steering meetings (biweekly Brussels + quarterly carrier hubs in Berlin, Munich, Madrid = ~EUR 2M over five years), team training and professional development (EUR 0.5–1.0M), office equipment and software licenses (EUR 1–2M), and contingency for staff turnover and replacement hiring (EUR 1.5–2.0M). (5) Publish this breakdown by Month 6 (2027-04-12) so hiring can proceed confidently and budget variance is managed monthly. Make this visible in quarterly budget reviews to the steering group.

9. Specify performance metrics and annual review criteria for team roles

Each role has stated responsibilities and activities, but no explicit performance metrics or annual review criteria are defined. Risk: At the end of each phase (Months 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 = 2027-10-12, 2028-10-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12), the Programme Director and leadership lack objective criteria to assess whether roles are effective and whether key individuals should be retained, redeployed or replaced.

Recommendation: Develop role-specific performance metrics (1–2 per role, quarterly update, annual review at the programme-board level) tied to programme milestones: (1) Programme Director: (a) % of steering-group decisions made by consensus vote (target ≥75% by Month 6 = 2027-04-12; (b) escalation time from deadlock to Commission mediation (target <2 weeks; (2) Standards Custodian: (a) % of conformance test suite coverage against OSDM (target 100% by Month 9 = 2027-07-12); (b) change-request turnaround time (target critical 2 weeks, major 6 weeks, minor 8 weeks; (3) Clearing Architect: (a) reconciliation-platform build on schedule (target go-live Month 24 = 2028-10-12); (b) error-rate target achieved (target <0.5% by Month 30 = 2029-04-12); (4) Carrier Integration Manager: (a) % of targeted carriers assigned to tiers by Month 6 = 2027-04-12 (target 100% of 25+ carriers); (b) % of Tier 1/2/3 carriers meeting conformance by scheduled dates (target ≥80% on time); (5) Passenger Rights Lead: (a) legal-review completion (Month 6 = 2027-04-12, on time); (b) accessibility-threshold audit completion (target 100% coverage of participating corridors by Month 36 = 2029-10-12); (6) Stakeholder Communications Lead: (a) steering-group satisfaction on briefing quality (target ≥4/5 on biweekly survey); (b) carrier/distributor awareness of programme milestones (target ≥80% can name the next two milestones in a survey). Annual reviews are held at Months 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 = 2027-10-12, 2028-10-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-10-12, 2031-10-12; underperforming roles are supported with coaching or replaced. Budget: minimal; part of existing management review processes.

Critique and recommended actions from domain experts.

1 Expert: EU Competition Law Counsel

Knowledge: Article 101 TFEU, state aid, transport regulation, competition clearance procedures

Why: The programme's shared inventory data layer, federated clearing mechanism and commission-band governance create Article 101 coordination risk that could unwind investments post-launch. Decision 14 (Joint Conduct Safe-Harbour) identifies this as critical, requiring pre-notification to DG COMP by Month 2 (2026-12-12) and formal guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-12). Without early clearance, carriers will hesitate to commit inventory, and post-launch challenges could force EUR 50-100M rework.

What: Prepare the DG COMP pre-notification memorandum describing the clearing mechanism, data flows and through-fare construction doctrine; identify which design elements (pooled liability, netting, fare apportionment) trigger Article 101 scrutiny and propose a clean-team protocol to mitigate exposure; track stakeholder comments on the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) and brief the steering group on legal risk quarterly starting Month 6 (2027-04-12).

Skills: EU legal drafting, competition-law risk assessment, cartel-exemption procedures, transport-sector precedent analysis, stakeholder negotiation with regulators

Search: EU competition law transport regulation, Article 101 TFEU safe harbour, rail clearing mechanism, state aid transport

1.1 Primary Actions

  • Commission an external EU competition counsel immediately at Month 0.5 (2026-10-27) to draft a detailed DG COMP pre-notification memorandum (EUR 300-500K); submit to DG COMP by Month 1 (2026-11-12) with request for interim guidance by Month 9 (2027-07-12) and final clearance by Month 12 (2027-10-12). Prepare a fallback bilateral clearing design ready to deploy by Month 15 (2028-01-12) if federated netting is not cleared.

The plan proposes federated clearing and streamed availability as a 'neutral' layer, but the decision on who controls the availability shadow, the shared netting rulebook and the dispute resolution criteria determines whether smaller carriers and independent distributors can participate on equal terms. Require DG COMP to review and approve the Charter at Month 12 (2027-10-12) before it becomes binding. 1.6.D Consequence

Without a published Governance Charter and DG COMP approval by Month 12 (2027-10-12), smaller carriers and independent distributors will assume the shared layer is controlled by incumbents and will refuse to commit to the mandatory API exposure, triggering participation collapse. If redesign is deferred past Month 18 (2028-04-12), binding standards will slip to Month 24 (2028-10-12). 1.6.E Root Cause

The plan focuses on Article 101 safety (formal pre-notification, clean-team) without addressing the structural conditions under which the safe-harbour survives scrutiny: equal and non-discriminatory access. The tiering structure (by API readiness, not by size) accidentally creates leverage for large carriers to define the rules before smaller carriers arrive. DG COMP's Article 101 review will flag supply-side foreclosure if the shared layer's governance is opaque or controlled by a subset of competitors.

3.4.A Issue - Liability Model Remains Actuarially Unvalidated and Carrier Refusal Risk Unmitigated

The plan pins carrier participation on a carrier-funded guarantee pool with indicative caps (EUR 500–1,000 per passenger) and co-insurance thresholds (EUR 50M), but no actuarial study has been commissioned and no carrier has signed off on exposure. Without validated loss data and priced caps, 30–40% of carriers (estimate) will refuse inventory exposure, fragmenting corridors and reducing the 40% through-ticket target to 15–25%. The Month 4 (2027-02-12) sign-off deadline is only 6 months away; actuarial cycles typically consume 3–4 months. If sign-off slips past Month 6 (2027-04-12), the binding-standards pathway (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) compresses by 12 months, forcing parallel work-streams and raising rework risk.

3.4.C Mitigation

Commission an independent actuarial study immediately (Month 1, 2026-11-12) using historical 24-month missed-connection data from existing EU clearing arrangements (e.g., Rail Settlement Plan, Trenitalia-ÖBB bilateral). Publish indicative caps and co-insurance by Month 3 (2027-01-12); present to CER and 10+ carriers by Month 4 (2027-02-12) for binding feedback. Require written sign-off from at least 8 major carriers and CER by Month 4 (2027-02-12), with escalation to Commission mediation by Month 5 (2027-03-12) if holdouts persist. Establish quarterly pool-monitoring (starting Month 6 = 2027-04-12) publishing actual incident rates and contribution adjustments so carriers can model forward exposure and adjust sign-off if data diverges. If sign-off slips past Month 6 (2027-04-12), trigger the readiness-gate deferral to Month 12 (2027-10-12), pushing binding standards to Month 24 (2028-10-12) and creating 6-month contingency.

3.4.D Consequence

If carrier sign-off is not obtained by Month 6 (2027-04-12), 30–40% of targeted carriers will refuse exposure, leaving only 15–17 carriers and fragmenting the four priority corridors. This reduces the through-ticket share to 15–25% by Month 60 (2031-10-12), misses the 40% target, and may trigger a formal programme reset or narrowing to only the largest carriers. Reputational damage and legislative scrutiny will follow. Concession volumes will fall below forecast, triggering subsidy review and cost reductions on smaller corridors.

3.4.E Root Cause

The plan treats liability caps as indicative placeholders rather than a critical blocking dependency. The Programme Office has not engaged actuaries or carriers in joint workshops; the governance structure lacks a binding mechanism to convert technical findings into carrier commitments. The Month 6 (2027-04-12) gate is a consequence, not a cause; without front-loaded actuarial work and carrier engagement, the gate will fail.

Establish a dedicated Clearing Design Workstream by Month 1 (2026-11-12) reporting to the steering group, with a mandate to publish a 'Federated Clearing Rulebook' by Month 6 (2027-04-12) specifying: (1) netting model (bilateral, multilateral, or hybrid per corridor); (2) settlement cycle (5 business days, daily netting per pair/per distributor); (3) journal entry standard (ISO 20022 XML mapping, including reversal codes); (4) dispute thresholds (tolerance band e.g. amount variance <0.50%, timing variance <2 business days); (5) escalation procedure (carrier-to-carrier, with clearing entity as tie-breaker); (6) payout schedule (next-day clearing fund availability). Recruit clearing specialists from existing PSA (Payment Settlement Authority) and RSC (Rail Settlement Centre) precedents. Publish a worked example of a three-leg through-ticket (Paris-Amsterdam-Berlin) showing journal entries, netting and payout per distributor and carrier.

4.4.D Consequence

If the clearing rulebook is not published by Month 6 (2027-04-12), three cascading risks emerge: (1) carriers model incompatible netting in their own systems, blocking interoperability post-Month 18 (2028-04-12); (2) distributors cannot price commission accurately without knowing net settlement timing; (3) disputes over carrier share allocation accumulate in Month 30-36 (2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12) and trigger rework of the reconciliation platform. 4.4.E Root Cause

Federated clearing is harder to standardize than a central entity; without an explicit netting engine design (bilateral versus multilateral, gross versus net, daily cycle), carriers face undefined operational and credit risk. The EUR 220M line for 'federated netting and dispute layer' may underestimate the complexity if bilateral interfaces proliferate.

4.6.A Issue - Reconciliation error tolerance of 0.5% by Month 30 (2029-04-12) is ambitious for federated multi-carrier settlement; failure modes and escalation protocol are not defined.

The canonical plan sets a reconciliation target of 'error below 0.5% by Month 30 (2029-04-12)' and proposes a penalty (5% tranche loss) for carriers exceeding 1.0% in a month. For a federated clearing model with each carrier maintaining its own booking system and feeding settlement data asynchronously, a 0.5% error rate is extremely aggressive. Typical multi-party clearing settlements (equities, FX) tolerate 2-5% daily reconciliation variance, resolved within 5 business days. The plan specifies a '5-business-day settlement cycle' but does not define: (1) when each party (carrier, distributor, clearing platform) submits settlement data; (2) which discrepancies block payout versus which are tolerated and reserved; (3) how stale-seat booking failures, refund reversals and commission adjustments are handled in reconciliation; (4) who adjudicates disputes when two carriers report conflicting transaction counts. 4.6.C Mitigation

Revise the reconciliation target to be phased: (1) Month 30 (2029-04-12) Tier 1: tolerate 2.0% error rate in first month, stepping down to 1.0% by Month 32 (2029-06-12) and 0.5% by Month 36 (2029-10-12); (2) publish a detailed settlement data-submission SLA by Month 12 (2027-10-12) specifying: each carrier submits ISO 20022 journal by 17:00 UTC each business day (T+0), clearing platform reconciles by 20:00 UTC and flags discrepancies by 21:00 UTC (T+0), carriers respond to discrepancy notices by 09:00 UTC next day (T+1). (3) Establish a three-tier escalation: (a) variance <0.20%, no action; (b) 0.20%-0.50%, manual review, resolved by end of T+2; (c) >0.50%, disputed transaction held in escrow, carrier and clearing entity have until end of T+5 to agree, then independent arbitrator decides. (4) Exempt refund reversals and stale-seat adjustments from the reconciliation tolerance for the first 6 months (until Month 36 = 2029-10-12), since these are novel transaction types that will require learning. (5) Replace the tranche-penalty with a remediation requirement: if a carrier exceeds 1.0% error for two consecutive months, trigger a technical audit (funded from contingency) and require corrective-action plan submission within 10 business days; suspend that carrier from new corridor enrollments (not funding tranches) until audit is cleared.

4.6.D Consequence

If reconciliation errors exceed 0.5% in the first 3-6 months post-go-live (Month 30-36 = 2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12), widespread tranche penalties will be triggered, halting funding to multiple carriers mid-integration. This cascades: (1) Tier 2 carriers (Month 36 = 2029-10-12 deadline) see Tier 1 carriers penalised, lose confidence in the scheme and delay their own implementation; (2) disputed transactions accumulate in escrow, blocking distributor payouts and triggering distributor exit; (3) the clearing platform's backlog grows, pushing resolution from 5 business days to 15-30 days, freezing working capital across the network. Estimated impact: 4-8 week operational disruption, EUR 20-30M (estimate) distributor receivables stranded, and 2-3 month delay to Tier 2 launch.

4.6.E Root Cause

The 0.5% target was set as a success metric without analysis of the underlying data quality and operational maturity. Federated clearing requires carriers to submit journal entries in a standard format, but carriers' back-office systems vary widely in version, API completeness and data integrity. The plan does not account for the learning curve: in Month 30 (2029-04-12), the system will have been live for only 6 months (Tier 1 go-live at Month 30 = 2029-04-12), so error rates will be elevated until carriers and the platform learn each other's patterns. The penalty structure (5% tranche loss) is punitive without a clear path to remediation.

6.4.A Issue - Liability model pricing is incomplete; carriers cannot yet commit to inventory exposure

The plan specifies a carrier-funded guarantee pool with indicative caps (EUR 500-1,000 per stranded passenger) and co-insurance above EUR 50M, but these figures are not yet actuarially validated. Until the independent actuarial study (due Month 6 = 2027-04-12) confirms incident rates, rerouting costs and contribution weights, carriers have no basis to price connection liability into their through-ticket offers. This is a blocking risk: the pre-project assessment estimates 30-40% carrier refusal if liability remains unpriceable, cascading into 8-15 smaller operators missing the Month 30 (2029-04-12) mandatory API milestone and reducing the 40% through-ticket goal to 15-25%.

6.4.C Mitigation

Execute the actuarial study immediately (Month 1 = 2026-11-12, not Month 2 = 2026-12-12) with a 90-day completion target; engage the three largest carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, SBB) and CER to supply proprietary 36-month missed-connection and rerouting-cost data; publish worked examples (large, regional, small carrier profiles) by Month 4 (2027-02-12) to enable carriers to model their own contribution range; present the full model to at least 8 major carriers for non-binding feedback by Month 5 (2027-03-12), then binding sign-off by Month 6 (2027-04-12); establish quarterly pool-monitoring reporting starting Month 6 (2027-04-12) so carriers can verify actual incident rates against forecast.

6.4.D Consequence

If actuarial validation is not complete by Month 6 (2027-04-12), carrier participation will drop to 60-70% (estimate), fragmenting the four priority corridors and forcing emergency scope reductions (EUR 100-150M, estimate). The Month 30 (2029-04-12) mandatory API milestone will be missed by Tier 2 and Tier 3 carriers entirely, pushing corridor go-live from Month 48 (2030-10-12) to Month 54-60 (2031-04-12 to 2031-10-12) (estimate) and compressing the TEN-T extension wave into the last 12 months, violating the five-year horizon.

6.4.E Root Cause

The liability model design was finalized before actuarial loss data was assembled. Carriers cannot price unpredictable, uncapped exposure, and no amount of regulatory mandate forces them to expose inventory at a loss. The Month 4 (2027-02-12) carrier sign-off deadline is unrealistic without months of claims-data analysis and scenario stress-testing completed in parallel.

6.5.A Issue - Budget headroom is exhausted by known risks; no flexibility for adapter acceleration or concession overruns

The plan commits EUR 1,415M of the EUR 1,500M cap (leaving EUR 85M free headroom, 5.7%), including a EUR 150M force-majeure reserve that is segregated and non-spending. The fallback exposures identified in the SWOT (adapter acceleration EUR 150-250M, concession overrun EUR 75-150M, Article 101 rework EUR 50-100M) total EUR 275-500M against only EUR 85M unallocated headroom. Any combination of these risks (e.g., 40% of Tier 2 carriers missing Month 36 = 2029-10-12 deadline + concession operating cost exceeding 20% forecast) will force hard scope cuts at Month 36-42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12), precisely when the final-wave TEN-T extension should be ramping.

6.5.C Mitigation

Rebaseline the budget immediately with a detailed cost breakdown per line item and per carrier tier; conduct a three-scenario variance analysis (base case, 30% cost growth, 50% cost growth) to show which cut triggers apply in each case; establish a monthly cash-flow forecast starting Month 1 (2026-11-12) with actual spend tracked against commitment; negotiate binding fixed-price contracts for standards (EUR 80M), clearing (EUR 220M) and shared adapters (EUR 30M) by Month 6 (2027-04-12), capping downside risk on 60% of the program; reserve the EUR 150M force-majeure fund as a true contingency and establish a separate EUR 50M (estimate) adapter-acceleration reserve carved from the unallocated EUR 85M, with drawdown authority limited to the Programme Director subject to monthly reporting to the steering group.

6.5.D Consequence

Without explicit variance containment, the programme will face a budget crisis at Month 36-42 (2029-10-12 to 2030-04-12) when actual spend on adapters and concession becomes clear. The hard variance triggers will force reductions that undermine the 40% through-ticket goal: restricting to four corridors alone cuts the addressable market from ~25% of total EU cross-border journeys to ~8% (estimate), and deferring TEN-T to Month 60-72 (2031-10-12 to 2032-10-12) leaves the programme's political momentum to decay over 2-3 years. A EUR 250M shortfall would consume all remaining headroom and the force-majeure reserve, leaving zero flexibility for any unforeseen claim.

6.5.E Root Cause

The budget was baseline-d on aggressive line-item estimates (e.g., EUR 240M adapters for all three tiers, EUR 300M concession envelope) without pricing-in the cost of latent demand: if carriers need more time and support to meet API deadlines, the program must choose between concession cuts (limiting passenger reach), adapter deferrals (extending timelines) or TEN-T phase reductions (cutting coverage). The variance triggers at EUR 100/200/300M are sensible, but they commit to cut outcomes (defer TEN-T, reduce concession, restrict to four corridors) that may politically unacceptable.

6.6.A Issue - Concession structure is undefined; subsidy cap is uncommitted and subject to interpretation

The plan carves out EUR 300M for a last-resort distributor concession but leaves critical terms open: (1) the split between platform set-up (capital) and operating subsidy (EUR 0-60M annually); (2) whether the EUR 60M operating subsidy is a floor or a ceiling given uncertainty in passenger volumes; (3) how cost overruns and underperforming volume will be handled contractually (clawback and review triggers are proposed but not legally binding). If the concessionaire's platform costs EUR 100M (vs. the estimated EUR 30-50M set-up cost) or if passenger volumes are 40% lower than forecast, the subsidy could reach EUR 80-100M annually, consuming EUR 400-500M of the EUR 300M envelope (estimate) over five years and triggering the EUR 200M variance-cut scenario.

6.6.C Mitigation

By Month 9 (2027-07-12), publish a detailed concession business case specifying: (1) platform set-up costs broken into software, infrastructure, staffing and integration (target: EUR 40M, with a ±20% contingency); (2) operating subsidy as a fixed percentage of through-ticket revenue (proposed: 15-20% of gross fare revenue on through-tickets sold, capped at EUR 12M annually); (3) cost-overrun escalation: any platform cost >EUR 50M requires steering-group approval; (4) clawback and penalty language as binding contract terms, not proposed thresholds; (5) a fixed contract term of 5 years (not extendable to 7 years except by explicit Commission decision with 12-month notice). Tender the concession by Month 12 (2027-10-12) with these terms locked, and require the winning bidder to maintain a performance bond covering 25% of estimated annual subsidy.

6.6.D Consequence

If the concession cost is not capped contractually by Month 12 (2027-10-12), a concessionaire selected at Month 18 (2028-04-12) could demand cost variations worth EUR 50-100M additional subsidy over the five-year term, triggering a budget crisis at Month 24-30 (2028-10-12 to 2029-04-12) when actual spend becomes clear. This would force a hard EUR 200M variance cut (reduce concession funding by 20%, extend term to 7 years, or move to direct public operation at higher cost), destabilizing distributor participation and passenger reach at the critical moment when Tier 1 API exposure is being rolled out and the first corridors are preparing go-live.

6.6.E Root Cause

The concession was designed as a strategic lever (avoiding a competitive threat to Trainline and Omio) without detailed financial engineering. The "cap" of EUR 60M is stated as a proposed threshold, not a contractual binding. The open questions (set-up cost split, subsidy floor/ceiling, cost-overrun allocation) were deferred to the business-case phase (Month 9 = 2027-07-12, estimate), but the budget already commits the EUR 300M envelope without knowing the contractual structure. This leaves the Programme Office vulnerable to scope creep once a concessionaire is selected.

7.4.A Issue - Accessibility and PRM Provisions Are Underspecified and Lack Passenger-Centered Validation

The plan mentions 'accessibility for persons with reduced mobility (PRM)' as a scope item and proposes 'assistance and bicycle reservation chaining' as Decision 10, yet the accessibility strategy is fragmented across budget allocations, accessibility thresholds (80% wheelchair access, 90% assistance within 4 hours) and scattered conformance requirements. There is no integrated accessibility user research or co-design workstream with disability-rights organisations. The proposed thresholds (80/90%) are ambitious but lack evidence of feasibility, baseline data or phased achievability paths. The decision to make assistance 'atomic' (reject itineraries lacking capacity) will visibly reduce through-ticket availability, yet passengers with disabilities are not explicitly included in the Month 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) pilots. Conformance validation does not mention PRM-specific test scenarios.

7.4.C Mitigation

Commission a dedicated PRM user research workstream by Month 1 (2026-11-12), led jointly by the Programme Office and at least two disability-rights organisations (e.g., EBU, EDF). Run co-design workshops Months 2-4 (2026-12-12 to 2027-02-12) to validate the 80/90% thresholds and explore phased approaches (e.g., best-effort fallback with compensation, tiered assistance notice periods). Pilot Decision 10's atomic confirmation with at least 200 PRM passengers on two corridors at Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12), measuring itinerary availability loss, passenger satisfaction and reroute success. Embed PRM test scenarios in the conformance test suite by Month 18 (2028-04-12). Publish an accessibility impact statement by Month 9 (2027-07-12) and revise thresholds if pilots show >15% itinerary loss or <70% passenger satisfaction.

7.4.D Consequence

Without user-centred validation, the programme risks implementing accessibility rules that reduce choice for PRM passengers (atomic confirmation rejecting itineraries) without clear evidence that passengers prefer certainty over availability. Atomic confirmation that blocks 10-20% of itineraries (estimate) will create a visible accessibility barrier: a passenger with mobility needs sees fewer options than a non-disabled passenger, reversing the programme's inclusive intent. Disability-rights bodies may withhold endorsement, slowing regulatory approval. Lawsuits under accessibility directives post-launch are plausible if thresholds are unmet or if atomic rejection disproportionately excludes PRM users.

7.4.E Root Cause

The programme treats accessibility as a compliance checklist (Regulation 1371/2007, threshold targets) rather than as a core passenger experience dimension. Decision 10 was drafted by transport engineers, not by disability-rights organisations or PRM-experienced travel designers. The decision to atomically confirm assistance and bicycle spaces will create a visible trade-off (fewer itineraries) that passengers will feel immediately, yet no usability testing or co-design with disability organisations has validated whether this trade-off is acceptable or whether phased, best-effort alternatives would deliver better outcomes.

7.5.A Issue - Complaint Handling Infrastructure Is Missing; 'Halved Complaints' Target Lacks Causal Chain

The programme targets 'distributor complaints halved' by Month 60 (2031-10-12) as a headline metric, yet the complaint-handling design is essentially absent. Budget allocations include EUR 100M for 'consumer rollout' (multilingual information, complaint handling, communications, accessibility usability testing), but no dedicated complaint-handling budget line, no defined complaints workflow, no staffing, and no integration between the clearing entity, carriers, distributors and passengers. The plan assumes complaints fall because through-ticketing improves, yet no analysis of what complaints actually are (passenger-to-distributor, distributor-to-carrier, passenger-to-carrier) or what root causes generate them. The passenger-rights legal review (Month 1-9 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-07-12) is mentioned but is not connected to complaint-handling design. No data on baseline complaint volume per corridor is cited.

7.5.C Mitigation

By Month 3 (2027-01-12), conduct a baseline complaints audit on the four priority corridors covering: complaint volume (passenger and distributor), categories (booking, payment, disruption, refund, accessibility, lost luggage), resolution time, repeat-complaint rates and appeal outcomes per carrier. Segment by distributor and passenger type (PRM, non-EU passengers, repeat travellers). Publish findings and design a target-state complaints-handling workflow by Month 6 (2027-04-12) specifying: (1) single point of entry (clearing entity or concession distributor receives all complaints), (2) 48-hour acknowledgement SLA, (3) root-cause triage (booking error, settlement, carrier delay, passenger error), (4) escalation path to carrier CIOs for systematic issues, (5) EU Agency for Railways oversight of complaint data (quarterly scorecards). Allocate EUR 25-40M of the EUR 100M consumer-rollout budget explicitly to complaint-handling staffing (estimate 40-60 staff), IT systems and carrier liaison. Run a pilot complaint workflow on one corridor at Months 18-24 (2028-04-12 to 2028-10-12) and measure reduction in repeat complaints before applying to all four corridors.

7.5.D Consequence

Without a designed complaint-handling infrastructure, the programme risks measuring 'complaints halved' without knowing what it means or whether it was caused by through-ticketing improvements or by lower passenger volumes. New clearing and federated systems will generate unprecedented volumes of settlement disputes, latency failures and reconciliation errors (estimate 10-25% of transactions in early months), which will cascade to passenger complaints. If the Programme Office and carriers are not staffed to triage and resolve these systematically, complaints may actually double in the first 12-24 months, contradicting the 40% through-ticket and complaint-reduction targets. Regulators and BEUC will demand proof that the complaints metric is real and causal, not an artefact of measurement or volume reduction.

7.5.E Root Cause

The programme inherited 'halved complaints' as a user constraint / headline metric without designing the operational machinery to achieve it. Complaints handling is seen as a 'consumer rollout' administrative task rather than as a core passenger-experience lever. The causal assumption—that complaints fall because through-ticketing improves—is untested. In reality, new systems (clearing, federated settlement, multi-leg queries) generate new complaint categories (reconciliation disputes, latency failures, reroute errors) that may offset reductions in single-operator complaints.

No usability testing is planned with linguistically diverse or accessibility-needing passengers before binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12). Conformance testing (Decision 6) does not explicitly require multilingual or accessibility conformance. The plan assumes that neutral search and emissions display will drive modal shift, but offers no evidence that non-native speakers or passengers with disabilities understand the offer or trust it.

7.6.C Mitigation

By Month 2 (2026-12-12), define a mandatory 'Multilingual and Accessibility Conformance Profile' as part of the OSDM specification, specifying: (1) minimum 18 EU official languages (at least all EU member-state languages) for the public distributor, (2) WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standard minimum for all booking UIs, (3) readability at B1 CEFR level (secondary school reading level) for passenger-facing text, (4) support for screen readers, captions and high-contrast modes. By Month 4 (2027-02-12), conduct moderated usability testing with 50+ passengers (including ≥15 with mobility/sensory disabilities, ≥15 non-native speakers) on wireframes of the public distributor and one commercial distributor, testing: booking flows, price comparisons, error messages, assistance-request clarity, refund procedures and complaint submission. Iterate designs based on testing findings and test again at Months 8 and 14 (2027-06-12, 2027-12-12). Embed multilingual and accessibility conformance testing in the technical audit (Month 2 = 2026-12-12): each carrier must demonstrate API support for multilingual OSDM payloads (German, French, Spanish, Dutch, Polish at minimum) and accessibility metadata (wheelchair, assistance, bicycle spaces). Make multilingual and accessibility certificates conditions of conformance (Decision 6).

7.6.D Consequence

Without explicit multilingual and accessibility usability testing, the programme risks deploying a through-ticketing system that is unusable for 15-25% of EU passengers (non-native speakers, elderly, disabled travellers) and for passengers in lower-income member states where English proficiency is lower. Early passengers will encounter booking flows, error messages and refund procedures in poor translations or inaccessible designs, generating high complaint rates and negative word-of-mouth. Disability-rights organisations will publicly oppose launch if accessibility conformance is not demonstrated. The 40% through-ticket and modal-shift targets assume equitable access; discriminatory usability undermines both. Post-launch rework of multilingual and accessibility features across distributed carrier systems could cost EUR 30-50M (estimate) and delay full TEN-T rollout by 6-12 months.

7.6.E Root Cause

The programme treats multilingual information and accessibility as budget line items ('EUR 100M consumer rollout') rather than as user-experience requirements that must be validated early and iterated with real passengers. Conformance testing (Decision 6) focuses on technical API metrics (uptime, latency, error rates) and does not include accessibility or multilingual usability. The public distributor concession has not yet been designed (business case Month 9 = 2027-07-12, tender Month 12 = 2027-10-12, award Month 18 = 2028-04-12), so the scope and user experience remain undefined. The plan confuses 'information' (telling passengers the booking is available) with 'usability' (passengers actually being able to use it).

8 Expert: Data Architecture and Real-Time Systems Assurance Officer

Knowledge: Distributed event streaming (Kafka, RabbitMQ), data governance and quality frameworks, real-time availability shadows and caching strategies, disruption event feeds, GDPR and data minimisation in real-time systems, chaos engineering and failure-mode analysis

Why: Decision 5 (Availability Query Topology) specifies a streamed availability shadow with carrier booking authority, published event-streamed availability for search and an event feed for disruption rerouting (Decision 9). These components depend critically on data quality, latency consistency and graceful degradation when carrier systems fail. The SWOT analysis identifies that three-leg queries at 95% availability each yield 86% combined, below the proposed 99.5% SLA, and the weaknesses section flags latency and availability shortfalls as risks to through-ticket success. This expert must architect the real-time data pipeline (streamed availability, disruption events, SLA metrics), validate latency and error rates against proposed thresholds, and design contingency caching that gracefully degrades to scheduled-only offers without stranding passengers.

What: Design the distributed event-streaming architecture for real-time availability (carriers publish seat availability changes via Kafka or RabbitMQ to a shared event stream) and disruption events (carriers publish delay and cancellation signals to trigger rerouting) by Month 6 (2027-04-12); specify data quality standards (required fields, timestamp precision UTC milliseconds, recovery semantics for lost or duplicate events) and validate against OSDM standards; architect the availability shadow (cached itinerary search results, updated from events, stale after 5 minutes) and the distributed cache (Redis or equivalent, estimated EUR 15-25M) that enables graceful degradation to scheduled-only offers if a carrier endpoint is unavailable >30 seconds; deploy SLA monitoring synthetic probes (queries every 5 minutes, distributed geographically) and publish a monthly public scoreboard showing p50/p95/p99 latency and uptime per carrier by Month 12 (2027-10-12); establish latency and availability thresholds (proposed: p95 <2 seconds, uptime 99.5%, stale-seat errors <1%) and attach them to funding tranches (two consecutive months missed SLA = 5% tranche reduction); design a failover protocol for the disruption event feed so that if the event stream is unavailable, distributors and carriers fall back to bilateral notifications and manual rebooking rather than stranding passengers; conduct chaos-engineering tests (kill carrier endpoints, delay event stream) at Months 18, 30 and 42 (2028-04-12, 2029-04-12, 2030-04-12) to validate rerouting and cache-fallback behaviour; establish GDPR data minimisation rules (no passenger personal data in event streams, event retention <90 days, anonymised analytics only) and publish a data-handling protocol by Month 9 (2027-07-12).

Skills: Distributed systems architecture, event-streaming platforms (Kafka, RabbitMQ), real-time caching and data freshness, chaos engineering and failure-mode testing, data quality frameworks and observability, GDPR data minimisation and privacy engineering, SLA monitoring and alerting

Search: distributed event streaming Kafka rail booking, real-time availability cache degradation, chaos engineering microservices testing, GDPR data minimisation real-time systems, availability shadow architecture distributed cache

  • Establish a formal disruption event-feed specification by Month 4 (2027-02-12) detailing Kafka-based broker topology, at-least-once delivery guarantees, deduplication, and recovery lag; conduct chaos-engineering tests by Month 10 (2027-08-12) and assign 24/7 operational ownership starting Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • Commission a GDPR privacy-impact assessment by Month 2 (2026-12-12) and publish findings by Month 3 (2027-01-12); incorporate data-minimisation requirements into the OSDM binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12), establish a Data Governance Board starting Month 6 (2027-04-12), and require DPA sign-off from all carriers by Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • Execute the pre-programme technical audit by Month 2 (2026-12-12) per the pre-project assessment, publish tier assignment by Month 6 (2027-04-12), and add latency and availability validation into Tier 1 conformance criteria (Month 30 = 2029-04-12)—specifically, p95 latency <2 seconds on 3-leg queries and 99.5% combined availability.
  • Establish SLA monitoring and availability contingency architecture by Month 12 (2027-10-12) per the pre-project assessment, with live pilots on one priority corridor (2,000-4,000 passengers) at Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) to validate stale-seat failure rates, reroute latency, and settlement reconciliation under realistic load.

  • Develop a distributed-systems failure-mode matrix by Month 6 (2027-04-12) documenting: (1) single carrier endpoint down (>2 minutes); (2) network partition between EU hub and carrier; (3) event-feed publisher lag (>60 seconds); (4) settlement netting platform unavailable; (5) clock skew across carriers. For each, specify: observable symptoms, automated detection, alerting, graceful degradation mode, recovery time and RTO/RPO targets. Review quarterly and update based on pilot experience.
  • Procure a commercial event-streaming platform (Kafka, Pulsar or equivalent) and shared reconciliation platform as standalone services by Month 6 (2027-04-12), not custom builds; budget EUR 5-10M for licensed SaaS or managed Kafka hosting (subset of the EUR 50M realtime-layer budget). This reduces operational risk and accelerates pilot deployment.
  • Establish a Data Quality and Real-Time Observability workstream by Month 3 (2027-01-12) responsible for defining: (1) SLIs (service-level indicators) per data layer—event-feed latency, stale-data percentage, settlement reconciliation error rate, disruption reroute time; (2) alerting rules and escalation (e.g., if stale data exceeds 5%, page the Data Architect and notify carriers within 15 minutes); (3) monthly observability reports to the steering group starting Month 6 (2027-04-12).

8.3 Follow Up Consultation

Next consultation should address: (1) Detailed design of the streamed availability shadow—caching strategy, stale-data TTL, fallback degradation thresholds and latency guarantees under carrier outage; (2) Disruption event-feed topology—publish-subscribe guarantees, event ordering and deduplication across carriers, and recovery from feed lag; (3) GDPR data minimisation in real-time booking flows—what booking and location data flows through the shared layer, retention policies, and passenger consent models; (4) Failure-mode testing plan for multi-leg queries at the proposed 99.5% carrier SLA, including chaos-engineering scenarios (carrier endpoint down, network partition, stale inventory); (5) Settlement reconciliation under disruption—how reroute costs and refunds propagate through the federated netting layer when a carrier is offline.

8.4.A Issue - Streamed Availability Shadow Architecture Lacks Resilience Specification

The plan states 'publish an event-streamed availability shadow for search' but does not specify: (1) which carrier events feed the shadow (seat inventory only, or fares, restrictions, operational status?); (2) ordering and deduplication guarantees when the same seat update arrives from multiple sources or is retransmitted after network failure; (3) stale-data time-to-live (TTL) per search result—when does a cached result degrade to scheduled-only?; (4) recovery lag when a carrier's event stream falls behind real-time (e.g., 30-second backlog). Without these, the shadow will be operationally unreliable: searches will return conflicting inventory, and stale-seat booking failures will exceed the 1% SLA, frustrating distributors and passengers. This is the foundation of the Availability Query Topology decision (Decision 5) and must be locked before Month 12 (2027-10-12).

8.4.B Tags

  • event-stream-design
  • availability-shadow
  • cache-staleness
  • operational-resilience
  • underspeci-fied

8.4.C Mitigation

Commission a detailed real-time architecture specification by Month 3 (2027-01-12) covering: (1) event schema (seat delta, fare delta, operational status, timestamp, source carrier, deduplication ID); (2) ordered, at-least-once delivery guarantees using a Kafka-like topic per carrier or shared topic with per-carrier partitioning; (3) shadow TTL policy (e.g., search results valid 2 minutes, degraded to scheduled if carrier unavailable >30 seconds); (4) recovery from lag: if carrier event stream is >60 seconds behind, pause search queries for that carrier and alert distributors. Run a distributed-systems validation workshop (month 3.5 = 2027-01-27) with carrier CIOs and a Kafka expert to confirm this spec is implementable on legacy backend systems. Integrate the spec into the OSDM binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12) so carriers cannot deviate.

8.4.D Consequence

Without clarity now, pilots at Months 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12) will encounter stale-seat failures, cascading reroute failures and distributor complaints about unreliable search. This will delay the Month 18 (2028-04-12) binding-standards vote, push the Month 30 (2029-04-12) API exposure gate, and deter carriers from committing inventory. Estimate 3-6 month slip, 10-20% reduction in carrier participation, and EUR 30-50M in unplanned remediation spend (exceeding the EUR 85M headroom).

8.4.E Root Cause

The decision documents outline the topology (federated with cached shadow) but delegate the operational resilience to execution. Real-time event-streaming systems require upfront clarity on consistency models, failure modes and degradation policies, not post-hoc tuning. The absence of this detail now will force expensive rework once pilots expose latency and reconciliation issues at Month 12-18 (2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12).

8.5.A Issue - Disruption Event Feed Has No Publish-Subscribe Guarantees or Ordering Semantics

Decision 9 (Disruption Re-accommodation Choreography) calls for 'a shared disruption event feed to which all carriers publish and distributors subscribe,' yet the plan omits: (1) event ordering—if Carrier A delays at 14:30 and Carrier B then reroutes a passenger, will all distributors see the delay event before the reroute? Or will network lag, publisher backlog or subscriber lag cause inconsistent ordering?; (2) deduplication—if a delay is reported by multiple staff, will the feed deduplicate and notify distributors once, or spam them?; (3) at-least-once vs. exactly-once delivery—can a distributor miss a delay notification, leaving a passenger unreboked?; (4) recovery time—if the feed publisher is offline for 2 minutes, how long before subscribers catch up, and do they replay missed events or skip to live?. Without these semantics, automated rebooking will fail: distributors will not see missed connections, passengers will be left stranded, and manual intervention will spike, defeating the credibility of the through-ticket. This is critical to operationalising the liability backstop (Decision 1).

8.5.B Tags

  • event-ordering
  • pub-sub
  • disruption-feed
  • exactly-once-delivery
  • failure-modes

8.5.C Mitigation

Establish a formal disruption event-feed specification by Month 4 (2027-02-12) detailing: (1) OSDM disruption event schema (delay event, reroute event, cancellation, station incident, with UTC timestamp and source carrier ID); (2) Kafka-based broker (partition per corridor, ordered by timestamp within a partition, retention 7 days minimum); (3) guarantees: at-least-once delivery to all subscribers (distributors and the rerouting service), deduplication by event ID, subscriber lag monitoring and alerts if lag exceeds 60 seconds; (4) recovery: if publisher is offline, event-feed operator must auto-replay buffered events to catch up subscribers. Conduct a chaos-engineering test (Month 10 = 2027-08-12) simulating carrier unavailability, network partitions and clock skew to validate the feed behaves correctly. Assign 24/7 operational ownership (feed operations team of 4-6 staff) starting Month 12 (2027-10-12); cost estimate EUR 1-2M/year (fits in the realtime-layer EUR 50M budget line). Include feed SLAs in the binding standards: 99.5% availability, <5-second end-to-end latency from carrier publish to distributor subscribe, zero deduplication failures.

8.5.D Consequence

If ordering and delivery semantics are not defined and tested before pilots, stranded passengers will be the visible failure: a distributor will receive a reroute event before the delay event, or miss the delay entirely, and the passenger will not be reboked on time. This will generate the complaint spike the programme aims to halve, undermine passenger trust in through-tickets, and trigger regulatory intervention at Month 18 (2028-04-12) or later. Estimate 20-40% of missed-connection rebooking failures (versus the <5% SLA), 5-10% increase in passenger complaints, and potential legislative amendment to mandate a central real-time coordination service, forcing USD 100-200M in emergency investment.

8.5.E Root Cause

The decision framing emphasises the operational benefit ('reduced stranded passengers') but treats the event feed as a delivery mechanism, not a distributed system with failure modes. Real-time event brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Pulsar) have well-known ordering and durability challenges, especially across carrier boundaries where network partitions, clock skew and publisher availability differ. The plan assumes a working feed without specifying who builds it, who operates it, and what happens when it fails.

8.6.A Issue - GDPR Data Minimisation Not Addressed in Real-Time Booking and Settlement Flows

The plan mandates 'a shared real-time data layer exposed through OSDM-compatible APIs' and 'federate settlement through a shared netting and dispute-resolution layer,' but does not specify what booking and settlement data flows through these shared mechanisms or how GDPR Article 5 (data minimisation) and Article 7 (consent) are satisfied. Specifically: (1) Does the availability shadow retain passenger names, booking references or payment data, or only seat IDs and fares?; (2) How long are these booking records held in the clearing layer?; (3) When a passenger is rerouted via the disruption event feed, does the feed carry the passenger's PNR (passenger name record) across carriers, or only the seat/payment ID?; (4) If a passenger requests a refund, does the netting layer need to see their identity, or only a booking token?; (5) Are there separate data-handling agreements per carrier or a single shared protocol? Without clarity, the programme risks intra-EU data flows that violate GDPR, particularly if reroute data or refund data carries PII across carrier boundaries. This will trigger national data-protection authority investigations, delay API exposure and block carrier participation.

8.6.B Tags

  • GDPR
  • data-minimisation
  • PII-flows
  • cross-border
  • consent-management

8.6.C Mitigation

Commission a privacy-impact assessment (DPIA) by Month 2 (2026-12-12) led by an external EU data-protection specialist (budget EUR 200-300K) documenting: (1) data flows through each layer (availability shadow, disruption feed, clearing, refund netting, reroute request); (2) which fields carry PII (name, email, phone, location, booking history) and which do not (seat ID, fare, payment token); (3) retention windows per layer and justification; (4) consent model—does a passenger booking a through-ticket consent separately to GDPR-required processing by each carrier, or one consent per through-ticket?; (5) cross-border data-transfer mechanisms (Standard Contractual Clauses, adequacy decisions, or binding corporate rules if carriers are part of the same group). Publish DPIA findings by Month 3 (2027-01-12) and incorporate data-minimisation requirements into the OSDM binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-12): e.g., 'availability shadow shall not retain booking records after 24 hours,' 'disruption feed shall not carry passenger names, only booking tokens,' 'clearing layer shall delete refund details after settlement (5 business days) unless dispute is pending.' Establish a Data Governance Board (sub-committee of steering group) meeting monthly from Month 6 (2027-04-12) to audit compliance and resolve cross-carrier consent disputes. Require all carriers to sign a Data Processing Addendum (DPA) by Month 12 (2027-10-12) specifying roles (controller, processor, joint controller) per layer.

8.6.D Consequence

If GDPR compliance is not designed upfront, national DPAs will issue enforcement actions post-launch (likely Months 30-36 = 2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12 during API exposure pilots) requiring system redesign, data deletion and potentially blocking of APIs pending remediation. This will delay TEN-T extension, fragment corridors, and expose the Commission and carriers to fines up to 4% of turnover under GDPR Article 83(6). Estimate 6-12 month remediation cycle, EUR 50-100M rework cost, and 25-50% reduction in through-ticket volume during enforcement period as distributors and carriers pause integration to await legal clarity.

8.6.E Root Cause

Data governance and privacy engineering are not listed as core dependencies in the project plan, though GDPR is mentioned as a regulatory requirement. The OSDM standard itself (referenced but not detailed in this plan) may not have formally addressed data minimisation in multi-carrier scenarios. The federated settlement model multiplies the number of data handlers, each with independent GDPR obligations, but the plan does not articulate how they coordinate on consent, retention, and cross-border flows. This is a regulatory risk that will surface after standards are binding, when national DPAs audit the live system.
