Reality check: fix before go.

Summary

Level Count Explanation
🛑 High 13 Existential blocker without credible mitigation.
⚠️ Medium 6 Material risk with plausible path.
✅ Low 1 Minor/controlled risk.

Checklist

1. Violates Known Physics

Does the plan's success require breaking a known law of physics (e.g., thermodynamics, conservation of energy, speed-of-light limit, causality)?

Level: ✅ Low

Justification: This is a regulatory and systems-integration programme to coordinate rail booking, settlement, and passenger rights across EU member states. Its load-bearing mechanisms are software (APIs, databases, settlement platforms), commercial contracts (clearing arrangements, liability pools), and institutional governance (standards bodies, regulators, mediation protocols). None of these depends on violating conservation laws, causality, or the speed-of-light limit, nor does the plan assert that non-physical mechanisms (sentiment, cultural alignment, or unmeasured causal factors) produce its success outcomes. Modal shift, complaint reduction, and through-ticket uptake are attributed to improved service design and transparency — ordinary human decision-making and economic behaviour, both physical.

Mitigation: No physics-related action required — the plan does not invoke physics-incompatible mechanisms.

2. No Real-World Proof

Does success depend on a technology or system that has not been proven in real projects at this scale or in this domain?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan addresses the core dependency (actuarial study commissioned by Month 1 = 2026-11-12, priced parameters by Month 6 = 2027-04-12, carrier sign-off by Month 4 = 2027-02-12) with measurable gates and escalation protocols (Commission mediation by Month 5 = 2027-03-12). However, two material gaps remain unresolved: (1) no independent actuarial firm has been engaged yet (assumed to occur at Month 1 = 2026-11-12), so delivery is at risk from late engagement or data access delays; (2) the fallback if liability model fails to win carrier consensus by Month 6 (2027-04-12) is only the "readiness-gate deferral to Month 12 (2027-10-12)," which itself slides binding standards by 6 months and cascades throughout Phase 1 without triggering programme-level contingency decisions (e.g., pivot to a two-tier pool, bilateral liability model, or scope reduction). The 30–40% (estimate) carrier refusal risk remains the single largest threat to network viability, and mitigation stops at administrative escalation rather than pre-approved design fallbacks.

Mitigation: Actuarial Project Lead: Commission an independent actuarial firm by Month 1 (2026-11-12) with interim results at Month 3 (2027-01-12) and final study at Month 6 (2027-04-12); require carrier claims data (missed-connection rates, rerouting costs, incident clustering) from 5+ major carriers by Month 1 (2026-11-12); deliver interim results and three cap/co-insurance scenarios by Month 3 (2027-01-12); conduct bilateral validation workshops with at least 8 major carriers and CER by Month 4 (2027-02-12); secure signed letters of intent by Month 4 (2027-02-12), or escalate to Commission mediation for design revision by Month 5 (2027-03-12). Additionally, prepare a fallback two-tier pool (core carriers + optional reinsurance for smaller operators) as a pre-approved contingency ready to deploy at Month 5 (2027-03-12) if unmodified pool design fails sign-off.

12. Gold Plating

Does the plan add unnecessary features, complexity, or cost beyond the core goal?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the Assistance and Bicycle Reservation Chaining feature (Decision 10, embedded in the programme scope) adds EUR 25–40M (estimated, allocated from the EUR 100M consumer-rollout budget) and operational complexity without directly supporting the 40% through-ticket share or complaints-halving targets. The feature mandates atomic confirmation of accessibility and bicycle spaces—rejecting itineraries if any leg lacks required capacity. This is presented as "required accessibility" (per EU Regulation 1371/2007), yet the plan acknowledges that atomic confirmation will visibly reduce itinerary availability by 10–20% (estimate), creating a trade-off: passengers with disabilities see fewer options than non-disabled passengers, reversing inclusivity intent. The core through-ticketing and modal-shift objectives do not depend on atomic confirmation of accessibility; they depend on search availability, latency, and price competitiveness. A best-effort accessibility model (booking with transparent notice to passenger, separate assistance workflow) would deliver accessibility rights compliance at lower cost and complexity, without blocking itineraries. The atomic model is a design choice (arguably appropriate on equity grounds) but lacks binding legal requirement and creates measurable gold-plating: EUR 25–40M spent to reduce passenger choice.

Mitigation: Project Director: Commission a cost-benefit analysis by Month 3 (2027-01-12) comparing atomic confirmation versus best-effort accessibility booking, measuring EUR cost per itinerary preserved and passenger satisfaction per model. If atomic confirmation reduces itinerary availability >15% and satisfaction <70% in pilot testing (Months 12–18 = 2027-10-12 to 2028-04-12), move to best-effort model and reallocate EUR 15–25M from accessibility to complaints-handling staffing or modal-shift features.

Material gaps remain: no written confirmation of Regulation timetable has been obtained as of Month 0 (2026-10-12); no pre-agreed regulatory waivers or corridors-of-agreement exist; state-aid clearance for the EUR 60M concession subsidy is unmapped. The programme can proceed under Decisions 1–5 with conditional deferral to Month 12 (2027-10-12) if regulatory prerequisites are not met by Month 9 (2027-07-12), but this contingency is not explicitly linked to binding-standards authority or carrier participation commitments."

Mitigation: DG MOVE & Competition Law Counsel: File DG COMP pre-notification describing federated clearing, data flows and through-fare construction by Month 2 (2026-12-12); obtain written Regulation adoption timetable from Commission legislative affairs unit and bilateral regulatory approval pathways from each member state on the four priority corridors by Month 3 (2027-01-12); secure DG COMP interim guidance and national regulator sign-off by Month 9 (2027-07-12); if Regulation adoption is not confirmed for Month 18 (2028-04-12) or any priority-corridor regulator issues an enforcement hold, invoke the pre-approved Month 12 (2027-10-12) readiness-gate deferral and contingency authority (shadow standards or voluntary pilot).

17. External Dependencies

Does the project depend on critical external factors, third parties, suppliers, or vendors that may fail, delay, or be unavailable when needed?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the programme's core real-time data infrastructure—the streamed availability shadow, federated disruption event feed, and settlement reconciliation platform—depends entirely on external vendor delivery (EUR 50M real-time layer, EUR 220M clearing platform, EUR 30M shared adapters). No contracts have been signed, no vendor performance baselines exist, and no contingency suppliers are identified. The availability shadow must sustain sub-100ms cache lookups and <5-minute staleness; the disruption event feed must guarantee exactly-once message delivery across 25+ carriers with <5-second propagation lag; the reconciliation platform must process >10,000 transactions/day with <0.5% error rate. If the primary vendors miss SLAs (proposed: latency >2 seconds, availability <99.5%, reconciliation error >1%), fallback suppliers are not contracted, and rework cascades to Phase 2 (Months 18–48 = 2028-04-12 to 2030-10-12). The pre-project assessment identifies this as 'single points of failure with no tested fallback' for the streamed availability layer and settlement reconciliation, meeting the HIGH threshold. Contingency architecture (distributed cache failover to scheduled-only, bilateral settlement fallback to carrier netting) is described conceptually but not stress-tested or contractually locked. Three-leg query combined availability at 95% per leg = 86% combined (below the 99.5% SLA), requiring architectural mitigation that is not procurement-locked. Estimated consequence: if vendor delivery slips 6–12 months or performance misses SLAs, stale-seat failures exceed 5%, reconciliation errors spike to 2–3%, and distributors exit; Phase 2 timeline slips 3–6 months, pushing four-corridor go-live from Month 48 (2030-10-12) to Month 54–60 (2031-04-12 to 2031-10-12), compressing TEN-T extension window.

Mitigation: Procurement Lead: Issue RFPs for the three critical layers by Month 3 (2027-01-12): (1) distributed cache and event-streaming platform (EUR 15–25M real-time layer subset); (2) federated netting and reconciliation platform (EUR 20–40M clearing subset); (3) shared adapter modules (EUR 30M). Obtain proposals from at least 3 vendors per layer by Month 6 (2027-04-12), fixing only price ceilings and framework terms with conditions precedent; procure shared adapter modules by Month 12 (2027-10-12), with the clearing contract conditional on DG COMP guidance (Month 12 = 2027-10-12) and clean-team approval (Month 14 = 2027-12-12). Include contractual SLA penalties (5% of contract value per month if latency >3 seconds, availability <99%, reconciliation error >1.0%), tested failover procedures (scheduled-only fallback, bilateral clearing fallback) in all contracts, and mandatory stress-testing at Months 12, 24, 36 (2027-10-12, 2028-10-12, 2029-10-12) under production-scale load (10,000 transactions/day, 25-carrier feeds). Identify and pre-qualify a secondary vendor for the reconciliation platform by Month 12 (2027-10-12) so rework does not create a single-supplier lockdown if the primary vendor misses conformance gates.

18. Stakeholder Misalignment

Are there conflicting interests, misaligned incentives, or lack of genuine commitment from key stakeholders that could derail the project?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan identifies the fundamental conflict between Finance Department incentives (quarterly budget adherence, cost minimisation) and the R&D/Carrier Integration Team incentives (long-term capability, schedule adherence, quality outcomes) but does not establish binding shared success criteria that would align both parties. The canonical facts specify that the Programme Office (80 staff, estimate) must coordinate 25+ national operators, independent distributors, and member-state bodies under a 75% supermajority steering rule, yet no explicit mechanism locks Finance and Carrier Integration to a unified through-ticket goal (40% by Month 60 = 2031-10-12) with measurable intermediate milestones. Finance is incentivised to hold budget variance within EUR 100M (defer TEN-T) and release tranches only when conformance gates are formally verified; the Carrier Integration team is incentivised to achieve API readiness (Months 30/36/42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12) on their tier dates, which may conflict with Finance's budget-release conditions if verification audits slip 2-3 weeks past funding decision dates.

Mitigation: Steering Group Finance Committee: Design a shared OKR by Month 3 (2027-01-12) uniting Finance and Carrier Integration: Key Result 1 (Finance owner): maintain cumulative variance below EUR 100M through Month 36 (2029-10-12); Key Result 2 (Integration owner): 80% of Tier 1, 70% of Tier 2, 60% of Tier 3 carriers achieve conformance by their tier dates (Months 30, 36, 42 = 2029-04-12, 2029-10-12, 2030-04-12). Publish the OKR in the binding programme charter (Month 6 = 2027-04-12); establish monthly Joint Finance & Integration Dashboard showing variance burn, conformance progress, and contingency triggers (EUR 50M, EUR 100M, EUR 200M) visible to both teams. Schedule quarterly Executive Alignment Reviews (Months 9, 18, 27, 36 = 2027-07-12, 2028-04-12, 2029-01-12, 2029-10-12) where Programme Director, Finance Lead and Integration Manager jointly review OKR progress and agree corrective actions if either KR is at risk of miss.

19. No Adaptive Framework

Does the plan lack a clear process for monitoring progress and managing changes, treating the initial plan as final?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan specifies KPIs (40% through-ticket share, <0.5% reconciliation error, halved complaints), review cadence (biweekly steering, monthly SLA reports, quarterly budget re-baselining), owners (Programme Director, Finance Lead, Carrier Integration Manager, Clearing Operations Lead), and change-control thresholds (EUR 100M/200M/300M variance triggers with pre-defined scope cuts). However, three material gaps prevent a LOW rating: (1) no unified governance charter documents the change-control decision body, escalation protocol and authority to invoke stop/re-plan—feedback loop elements are scattered across nine role descriptions; (2) escalation timelines and decision rules for individual KPI misses are implicit, not binding (e.g., if through-ticket share <35% at Month 54 = 2031-04-12, what is the escalation path and decision deadline?); (3) the variance triggers are pre-approved scope cuts, not re-plan/stop decisions—there is no documented threshold at which the entire programme is re-scoped or halted.

Mitigation: Programme Director: Develop a unified Change-Control Governance Charter by Month 3 (2027-01-12) establishing a Change Control Board (steering core members), monthly KPI review protocol with escalation rules per KPI (if through-ticket share <35% by Month 54 = 2031-04-12, escalate to Transport Commissioner within 10 days), variance-trigger decision authority (EUR 100/200/300M triggers automatically convene the Board and require a decision within 5 business days), and a formal stop rule (e.g., if net carrier participation drops below 15 operators by Month 36 = 2029-10-12, invoke programme re-plan or halt authority).

20. Uncategorized Red Flags

Are there any other significant risks or major issues that are not covered by other items in this checklist but still threaten the project's viability?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the programme's core dependencies—liability model (FM3), technical integration (FM2), regulatory clearance (FM5), clearing mechanism (FM1) and concession funding (FM7)—form 5 distinct but tightly coupled critical-path risks. A single failure (e.g., actuarial study delay, Regulation adoption slip, DG COMP Article 101 concerns) cascades across 3+ domains: FM3 (liability failure) → FM2 (carrier refusal) → FM4 (staffing stretched) → FM5 (standards slip). Fallback cost exposures (EUR 275–500M) exceed headroom (EUR 85M) by EUR 190–415M, triggering variance-cut cascades (EUR 100M/200M/300M thresholds) that force TEN-T deferral, concession cuts, or scope restriction to four corridors, each reducing through-ticket share from 40% to 15–25% (estimate). No integrating bow-tie or FTA analysis published.

Mitigation: Risk Integration Lead: Develop a formal risk cross-impact matrix and bow-tie diagram by Month 6 (2027-04-12) showing linkages among FM1–FM9, identifying 3+ shared root causes (e.g., Programme Office capacity, Regulation adoption timeline, carrier data availability) and 5+ multi-domain failure paths (liability → participation → budget → schedule, data governance → regulatory → rework). Establish NO-GO thresholds: if any two concurrent risks from different clusters materialize (e.g., FM3 + FM5 by Month 9 = 2027-07-12, or FM2 + FM7 by Month 24 = 2028-10-12), invoke contingency re-plan or scope reduction; publish contingency triggers and pre-approved response playbooks by Month 3 (2027-01-12).

Contradictions between the core documents, after repair.

Consistency: first pass found 3 high / 6 medium / 0 low contradictions. Repair: round 1: 41 edits → 2 high / 7 medium; round 2: 42 edits → 0 high / 4 medium. Published: round 2 (fewest high-severity issues). Shown below: the final check of the repaired documents (0 high / 4 medium / 1 low).

1. Force-majeure reserve usable only 'after Month 36' vs ban on public pool draw-downs after Month 36 (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Review 5.2, Review 11.3, Review 14.3: The EUR 150M force-majeure reserve 'is escrowed for pool top-ups only after Month 36'; the pool is expected to be stressed in Months 30-42.
  • Canonical pool_draw_policy; Review 14.3 itself ('violating the Month 36 ban'); Project Plan mitigation plans: 'No public budget draw-downs on carrier pools after Month 36'; the reserve is 'drawable only for force-majeure pool top-ups'.
  • Why it conflicts: The reserve is described as available only from the date after which public pool draw-downs are banned. Either the reserve is unusable when needed or the ban is breached. The canonical text lets the reserve be drawn for force-majeure but says nothing on whether the ban covers it. 'Only after Month 36' is not a canonical condition.
  • Suggested resolution: A project decision is needed on whether the force-majeure reserve is exempt from the Month 36 ban. Options: (a) exempt, drawable for qualifying force-majeure events at any time, with the ban applying to ordinary pool deficits; (b) covered by the ban, so the reserve is released or re-allocated at Month 36; (c) post-Month 36 deficits fall entirely on carriers or recalibrated contributions. Remove the phrase 'only after Month 36' from the reviews once decided.

2. Concession envelope arithmetic: subsidy cap vs EUR 300M envelope (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Review 11.1; Review 1.3: Platform set-up EUR 30-50M, 'leaving EUR 250-270M for operating subsidy (capped at EUR 60M over five years, about EUR 12M/year)'. Subsidy overrun of EUR 75-150M is said to exceed the EUR 300M envelope.
  • Canonical budget_line_concession_eur_m, concession_subsidy_cap_eur_m, open_decisions (1); Review 3.3; Self-Audit 3: Operating subsidy is capped at EUR 60M over five years; set-up is EUR 30-50M (proposed), so roughly EUR 190-210M of the EUR 300M has no stated use. EUR 60M + EUR 150M overrun = EUR 210M, which is below EUR 300M.
  • Why it conflicts: EUR 250-270M cannot be 'operating subsidy' when the subsidy is capped at EUR 60M. The overrun cannot 'exceed the envelope' while about EUR 200M of the envelope is unassigned. The 20% concession cut (EUR 60M) equals the whole subsidy cap, so it is unclear what is being cut. Review 3.3's claim that the business case 'locks the EUR 300M envelope' rests on only about EUR 110M of defined use.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide what the remaining roughly EUR 190-210M funds ('public service-level payments' is named but unquantified), or whether the envelope should be reduced and the difference returned to headroom. Until then, show the set-up / subsidy / unallocated split explicitly and remove 'exceeding the envelope' and 'EUR 250-270M operating subsidy'.

3. EUR 85M headroom claimed several times over; no funding source for the EUR 50M reserve (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Canonical budget_unallocated_headroom_eur_m; Exec Summary Risks; Review 1.2, 2.2, 3.2: Free headroom is EUR 85M. A separate EUR 50M adapter-acceleration reserve is created, and the reserve 'preserves EUR 50M+ of headroom'.
  • Review 6.1, 6.3, 11.2, 5.1, 10.2, 15.1, 5.3, 10.1; Premortem A8: Further draws on headroom: EUR 15M concession emergency (KPI 1), EUR 5-10M complaint handling (KPI 3), EUR 30-80M validation hardware (Review 11.2), EUR 30-50M or EUR 50M shadow-standards workstream (Reviews 10.2, 5.1), EUR 5-10M per slip (Review 15.1), EUR 50-75M bilateral/reallocation (Reviews 5.3, 10.1).
  • Why it conflicts: Named claims sum to roughly EUR 130-205M against EUR 85M. A EUR 50M reserve taken from headroom leaves EUR 35M, not 'EUR 50M+'. No canonical budget line contains an adapter-acceleration reserve; the lines sum to EUR 1,415M. A8 requires validation financing 'without drawing on the EUR 85M headroom' while Review 11.2 says it comes from headroom. Financing of validation hardware is an open decision (canonical open_decisions 2).
  • Suggested resolution: Decide the funding source and priority order for contingency claims: whether the EUR 50M reserve is carved from headroom (leaving EUR 35M), from the EUR 240M adapter line, or is dropped; and who finances validation hardware (carriers, public, or split). Then cap total claims on headroom at EUR 85M and delete 'preserves EUR 50M+ of headroom'.

4. Variance triggers (EUR 100/200/300M) vs EUR 85M headroom and hard cap; inconsistent trigger set (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Review 2.2 vs Review 1.2, 3.2: Fallback exposures 'exceed unallocated headroom by EUR 190-415M', and triggers at EUR 100/200/300M are 'mathematically likely' (net of headroom basis). Elsewhere the same triggers are compared with gross EUR 275-500M exposures and 'adapter slip + concession overrun = EUR 200M+'.
  • Canonical public_budget_cap_eur_m, budget_variance_triggers; Self-Audit 18: Total public budget is a hard cap of EUR 1,500M with only EUR 85M free headroom; the first scope-cut trigger is EUR 100M. Self-Audit 18 lists contingency triggers of 'EUR 50M, EUR 100M, EUR 200M'.
  • Why it conflicts: If variance is net of headroom, spend can exceed the hard cap by EUR 100M before any cut. If it is gross, an overrun of EUR 85-100M has no funding and breaches the cap before the first trigger. The basis is not stated, and Self-Audit 18 introduces a EUR 50M trigger and a different top trigger (EUR 200M) than the canonical set.
  • Suggested resolution: Define the variance measure and base (gross cost growth against committed lines, or net of headroom) so that no trigger can fire after the hard cap is exceeded. Replace the Self-Audit 18 trigger list with the canonical EUR 100M / 200M / 300M set. If the first trigger is meant to sit at or below the headroom, that changes a canonical value and needs a deliberate decision.

5. Deferral trigger and effect on the Month 18 binding-standards milestone; pilot-authority dates (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical phase1_readiness_gate, binding_standards_milestone; Review 13.1; Project Plan: Gate at Month 6; if unresolved by Month 9, defer to Month 12; binding standards remain Month 18 (user constraint). Deferral 'compresses Phase 1 by 3-6 months'.
  • Self-Audit 5, Self-Audit 14, Review 2.3, 5.1, 8.3, 9.3, 10.2: 'If liability sign-off or audit results slip past Month 6, invoke a pre-approved deferral to Month 12 and adjust binding-standards target to Month 24.' Pilot authority is set 'by Month 3 if prerequisites slip past Month 6' (Reviews 2.3, 5.1) but 'if prerequisites slip past Month 9' (Reviews 9.3, 10.2) and 'by Month 6' (Review 8.3, Self-Audit 16, Pitch).
  • Why it conflicts: The trigger is Month 6 in some places and Month 9 in others. A pre-approved retarget of binding standards to Month 24 contradicts the Month 18 user constraint, while other documents keep Month 18 and compress Phase 1. The pilot and shadow-standards contingency carries three different readiness and trigger dates.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep the canonical rule: gate at Month 6, deferral to Month 12 if unresolved by Month 9. Keep Month 18 as the milestone and record any slip beyond it as a risk outcome (estimate), not a pre-approved re-baseline. Set one date for shadow-standards and pilot-authority readiness (Month 6) and one launch trigger (slip past Month 9).

6. Concession term and timeline vs five-year programme horizon (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Canonical concession_timeline, concession_subsidy_cap_eur_m, budget_variance_triggers: Tender issued Month 12, award about Month 18, service live about Month 30; subsidy cap EUR 60M 'over five years'; EUR 200M trigger extends the term from 5 to 7 years.
  • Review 14.1; Self-Audit 15; Premortem FM7: 'The concession term ends Month 60' and 'the five-year term (Month 60) ends'. FM7 tripwire: 'fewer than 3 compliant bids at tender close in Month 12'.
  • Why it conflicts: A five-year term starting at service launch (about Month 30) runs to about Month 90, or longer with the 7-year extension, so it cannot end at Month 60. Subsidy paid after Month 60 sits outside the five-year public funding horizon. The tender is issued at Month 12, so it cannot also close in Month 12.
  • Suggested resolution: Specify when the five-year term starts (award or service launch) and who pays subsidy beyond Month 60; the term needs a decision if it is meant to end with the programme (then it is about 2.5-3.5 years, not five). Correct the FM7 tripwire to a tender-close date after Month 12, before the award at about Month 18.

7. Regulation-slip thresholds in FM5 and their relation to the Tier 1 date (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Premortem A6, FM5 tripwires; canonical regulation_adoption_assumption: A6 failure trigger: adoption later than Month 24. FM5 tripwire: Regulation not adopted by Month 21. A 6-12 month slip beyond Month 18 is 'plausible', i.e. Month 24-30.
  • Premortem FM5 stop rule; canonical mandatory_api_exposure_milestone: FM5 stop rule: convert to a voluntary corridor-pilot model only if the Regulation is not adopted by Month 30, which is also the Tier 1 mandatory API exposure date.
  • Why it conflicts: The failure trigger (Month 24), tripwire (Month 21) and stop (Month 30) disagree. The plausible slip band reaches the failure and stop dates. By Month 30 the Tier 1 build and EUR 80M tranche release are due, so the stop point comes after the commitment has been made. Tier 1 exposure at Month 30 is described as unenforceable without a statute.
  • Suggested resolution: Set one adoption-slip tolerance and say what it triggers: for example, which month adoption must be confirmed so that Tier 1 funding (Month 30) is not released on a voluntary basis. This is a project decision (the thresholds are proposed values); the options are to stop earlier than Month 30 or to accept voluntary Tier 1 exposure.

8. Pilots (Months 12-18) test settlement and reconciliation before clearing and adapters exist (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Review 15.3; Exec Summary; canonical pilots_and_validation: Pilots at Months 12-18 with 500-1,000 passengers per corridor are the basis for 'ready for Phase 2' and check '>2% reconciliation errors' and rerouting latency.
  • Review 3.2, 16.2; Exec Summary Action Orientation; Project Plan mitigation plans: Shared adapters are procured by Month 12; the clearing contract is conditional on DG COMP guidance (Month 12) and clean-team approval (Month 14); pilots before Month 14 run 'on non-contested data flows only'; reconciliation-platform automation is piloted at Months 18-24.
  • Why it conflicts: Settlement and reconciliation are the contested data flows, and their platform is not contracted or built when the pilots start. The pilots therefore cannot verify reconciliation, settlement cycle or the Phase 2 readiness criteria that depend on them. The dependency (platform, clean-team approval) is scheduled after the activity that needs it.
  • Suggested resolution: State what the pilots cover: which flows are live, which are simulated, and which settlement mechanism is interim. Move reconciliation and settlement-cycle criteria out of the Month 18 pilot readiness test, or add an interim bilateral settlement arrangement before Month 14. Both are options for a project decision.

9. Liability gate: contracting date, data thresholds and what is validated when (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical liability_decision_timeline; Review 13.1, 8.1, 3.1; Self-Audit 2: Actuarial study commissioned Month 1 (contracted no later than Month 1.5), interim Month 3, carrier loss data from 5+ major carriers by Month 1, 36 months of claims data; trailing 12-month on-time contributions; sign-off Month 4 against interim parameters.
  • Premortem FM3, FM4; Review 8.1; Pitch Risks and Call to Action: FM4 tripwire: actuarial firm 'not contracted by Month 2' (leaving one month to the Month 3 interim). FM3 tripwire: loss data 'from fewer than 3 major carriers'. Review 8.1 asks for 24 months of data. Pitch lists 'actuarial study (Month 6)' as the mitigation for the Month 4 sign-off.
  • Why it conflicts: A Month 2 contracting deadline is later than the Month 1.5 deadline and leaves one month for the interim. A threshold of 3 carriers is below the 5+ required elsewhere. The claims-data window is 24 vs 36 months. The Pitch cites the Month 6 study as the basis for a Month 4 sign-off. The Month 4 sign-off rests only on Month 3 interim parameters.
  • Suggested resolution: Use Month 1.5 as the latest contracting date (tripwire at Month 1.5, not 2), 5+ carriers as the loss-data minimum, and one data window. State in the Pitch that Month 4 sign-off is against interim parameters, with the Month 6 final study adjustable only within the agreed band.

10. Per-incident cap vs per-stranded-passenger cap (unit mismatch) (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical liability_indicative_parameters; Review 1.1; Self-Audit 4; Premortem A1: Indicative cap is 'EUR 500-1,000 per stranded passenger'.
  • Self-Audit 3; Review 7.3: 'indicative parameters (EUR 500-1,000 per-incident caps, EUR 50M co-insurance threshold)' and 'EUR 500-1,000 per-incident caps'.
  • Why it conflicts: A per-incident cap of EUR 500-1,000 would be negligible against a EUR 50M co-insurance threshold, while a per-passenger amount of the same size would scale with incident size. The unit is per passenger. The actual per-incident aggregate cap is not specified.
  • Suggested resolution: Use 'per stranded passenger' for the EUR 500-1,000 value everywhere (proposed threshold) and add that the per-incident aggregate cap is to be set by the actuarial study.

11. Direct-operation cost: EUR 30-50M total vs EUR 30-50M per year (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical fallback_cost_exposures_vs_headroom; Premortem FM7: Concession failure fallback: direct public operation EUR 30-50M (estimate), which 'fits' within the EUR 85M headroom.
  • Self-Audit 15; Review 14.1, 14.2: 'public direct management (EUR 30-50M annual cost to the Commission)'; ongoing operations 'EUR 30-50M annually', i.e. EUR 150-250M over five years.
  • Why it conflicts: If the figure is annual, direct operation over a five-year horizon is EUR 150-250M and does not fit the EUR 85M headroom. The same range is used for a total in one place and an annual figure in another, and for the concession in one case and the whole programme in another. Review 14.1's EUR 150-300M five-year extension (30-50M x 5 = 150-250M) is also not consistent with its own annual figure.
  • Suggested resolution: State the basis (total or per year) and scope (concession only or whole-programme operations) of the EUR 30-50M figure. Keep the canonical total for the concession fallback; present post-Month 60 operating cost as a separate estimate with its own unit.

12. DG COMP pre-notification timing recommendation contradicts itself (⚪ Low)

  • Executive Summary Feedback; Review 10.3: Lock DG COMP pre-notification 'by Month 2 (2026-12-12), not Month 2 (2026-12-12), to recover 4-6 week schedule buffer'.
  • Canonical competition_law_timeline; Project Plan; Premortem A3: DG COMP pre-notification Month 2 (2026-12-12), as in the canonical competition_law_timeline and all other documents.
  • Why it conflicts: The recommendation contrasts a date with itself, so it states no change, yet claims a 4-6 week buffer gain that would require filing earlier than Month 2.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep Month 2 as the canonical filing date and delete the 'not Month 2' clause and the buffer claim, unless an earlier filing is deliberately adopted, which would change the canonical value.

Summary

The plan is largely coherent on the headline structure: canonical budget lines sum to EUR 1,415M with EUR 85M headroom, tier funding sums to EUR 240M, and the Month 4 non-binding sign-off versus the Month 6 binding vote, the audit and the clearing/DG COMP timing are now mostly consistent. The unresolved problems are mainly missing project decisions rather than typos: how the reserve relates to the Month 36 draw-down ban, what the EUR 300M concession envelope actually funds and for how long, who funds the several claims on the EUR 85M headroom (including validation hardware), and on what basis the EUR 100/200/300M triggers are measured against a hard cap. A few residual date, unit and threshold mismatches remain (deferral and pilot-authority dates, Month 24 re-baselining against the Month 18 user constraint, per-incident vs per-passenger cap, annual vs total direct-operation cost), all of which are repairable by correcting text to the canonical value.

How the canonical facts were reconciled

Budget arithmetic was recomputed: the nine lines sum to EUR 1,415M, leaving EUR 85M free headroom, with the EUR 150M reserve counted once (total contingency EUR 235M); adapter, concession-cut, fallback-gap and subsidy-per-year figures all checked out. Corrected items: the supermajority rule (75% of 9 core members is 7, not 6), the regulation-delay arithmetic (12-18 month delay on Month 18 = 2028-04-12 gives Months 30-36 = 2029-04-12 to 2029-10-12, not 24-30), and the staffing-cost check against the EUR 75M management line, which left no room for the EUR 2-5M counsel cost. The three fallback cost facts were merged into one to stay within the fact limit, and calendar dates were removed in favour of month offsets, since dates are added automatically.

Initial Prompt

Plan:
Deliver a coordinated European program to make cross-border train travel as easy to search, book, and refund, aligned with the European Commission's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail. Today, travelling by rail across two or more EU member states means stitching together itineraries from disconnected national operators (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ and roughly twenty more), each with its own fares, booking system, refund policy and disruption handling, while distributors face inconsistent access to real-time inventory and post-sale operations; passengers cannot reliably buy a single through-ticket from Lisbon to Tallinn and lose passenger-rights protection the moment a connection is missed. The objective is to stand up the technical, commercial and governance arrangements that let any compliant distributor — incumbent operator, third-party platform like Trainline or Omio, or a new public European booking service — sell through-tickets across all participating carriers with continuity-of-journey rights, single-payment settlement, harmonised refunds, reduction cards, accessibility for persons with reduced mobility, and bicycle reservations. Scope covers a shared real-time data layer exposed through OSDM-compatible APIs on non-discriminatory commercial terms, an inter-carrier clearing and settlement mechanism, a passenger-rights backstop, and integration hooks for buses, ferries and short-haul air; rollout starts with the busiest cross-border corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin) before extending to the full TEN-T network. Stakeholders are DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways, CER and national operators, independent distributors, BEUC, national regulators and disability-rights bodies. Horizon is five years: binding standards within eighteen months, mandatory API exposure within thirty, full corridor through-ticketing within sixty. Public-side coordination budget is €1.5 billion covering standards work, conformance testing, the clearing mechanism, a public reference distributor, member-state capacity building and consumer-side rollout (apps, multilingual support, complaint handling); estimate the larger private carrier IT investment separately. Success means 40% of cross-border journeys sold as single through-tickets within five years, distributor complaints halved, and the train becoming the more attractive option than flying on competitive short-haul routes so that fewer travellers choose the plane. Pick a realistic scenario, not the most aggressive one.

Rationale: The prompt describes a concrete, detailed European rail ticketing program with defined scope, stakeholders, corridors, timeline milestones, a €1.5 billion budget, and measurable success criteria. It is highly specific and plannable.

Verdict: 🟢 ALLOW

Rationale: The prompt requests a policy and program plan for EU cross-border rail ticketing interoperability, a benign public-interest governance and transport topic with no operational harm potential.

Violation Details

Detail Value
Capability Uplift No

Premise Attack

Why this fails.

Premise Attack 1 — Integrity

Forensic audit of foundational soundness across axes.

[STRATEGIC] The program spends €1.5 billion of public money to build a booking-and-clearing layer on the assumption that fragmented ticketing is what keeps travellers off cross-border trains and in planes, when timetables, capacity, track access and fares decide that, and the layer pre-empts a regulation that is still only a proposal.

Bottom Line: REJECT: The premise treats a ticket-packaging problem as the cause of low cross-border rail use, front-runs an unenacted regulation, and promises a modal shift that booking infrastructure cannot deliver.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Binding standards at Month 18 (2028-04-12) and mandatory API exposure at Month 30 (2029-04-12) presuppose an enacted regulation, yet the Commission's rail ticketing proposal is still before Parliament and Council, so an ASAP start commits public money to obligations that have no legal basis and may be rewritten or diluted.
  • The 40% target counts cross-border journeys sold as a single through-ticket, which measures how tickets are packaged, not whether anyone travels more; a distributor that bundles two existing fares into one invoice hits the metric without adding a seat or a train.
  • The goal that the train becomes more attractive than flying on competitive short-haul routes cannot be reached with ticketing software, because journey time, price, rolling-stock availability and track capacity on Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln or Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon are unaffected by a €1.5 billion data and settlement layer, so every deliverable could ship on time and the headline outcome still fail.
  • A public reference distributor funded by the programme competes directly with Trainline and Omio, the independents the plan claims to serve on non-discriminatory terms, and it is built by a coordination body that also writes the standards those rivals must comply with.
  • The €1.5 billion covers only coordination, standards, testing, clearing and consumer rollout, while the larger carrier IT bill across SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ and about twenty more is left unpriced, so the programme depends on the very incumbents it is trying to open up to fund and accept the changes.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: Carriers and national regulators hold back commitments until the legislative text settles, while standards-body and conformance-testing contracts are awarded against a specification that may change.
  • 1–3 years: Incumbents deliver minimal OSDM-compatible API exposure on the four launch corridors to meet the Month 30 (2029-04-12) deadline; independent distributors get access to inventory but not to the best fares, and complaint volumes shift from 'cannot book' to 'cannot get the through-ticket price'.
  • 5–10 years: A publicly funded clearing mechanism and reference distributor become permanent infrastructure whose upkeep competes with track and rolling-stock budgets, while short-haul flight volumes on the target routes move little and the programme is judged on ticket share alone.

Evidence

  • Law/Standard — Commission Regulation (EU) No 1305/2014, TAP TSI (2014): a binding EU technical standard for rail passenger information and booking data exchange has existed for over a decade, yet booking systems remain fragmented per operator, so mandating data layers has not by itself produced through-ticketing.
  • Law/Standard — Regulation (EU) 2021/782 (2021): the recast rail passenger-rights regulation already defines through-tickets and missed connections, so the missing protection turns on what legally counts as a through-ticket rather than on a €1.5 billion technical layer.
  • Law/Standard — French Climate and Resilience Law (2021): France restricted domestic short-haul flights where a rail alternative exists, showing that modal shift from air has been pursued through route-level regulation rather than booking tools.

Premise Attack 2 — Accountability

Rights, oversight, jurisdiction-shopping, enforceability.

[STRATEGIC] — The Ticket-Without-a-Train Fallacy: the plan spends €1.5 billion (user constraint) perfecting how seats are sold across two dozen-plus carriers while the scarce thing is the train itself, so a 'train beats plane' outcome cannot follow from a better checkout.

Bottom Line: REJECT: The Ticket-Without-a-Train Fallacy is fatal: selling through-tickets more smoothly does not create trains, paths or seats, so the plan cannot deliver the modal shift it is justified by. A public machine of clearing, standards and apps is built to optimise a sales channel, not to get anyone out of an aircraft.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Pooling real-time inventory, accessibility-assistance needs, bicycle reservations and single-payment data across more than two dozen national operators and third-party platforms puts travellers' health-related and movement data into a shared layer they never chose and cannot practically opt out of.
  • A clearing mechanism, a public reference distributor that competes with Trainline and Omio while its own rules are being written, and a split of duties among DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways and national regulators leaves no single party answerable when a missed connection is disputed, and invites carriers to push disputes toward the most lenient regulator.
  • A mandatory Europe-wide inventory and settlement layer becomes one failure and attack point for ticket sales across the continent, and once carriers retire their parallel channels and align fare and refund rules to it, it cannot be unwound; other regions would copy the model.
  • The success metric (40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets, a user constraint) measures the sales channel rather than whether anyone left the plane, and the money funds apps, multilingual support and complaint handling rather than the timetables, rolling stock and track capacity that decide whether rail wins on short-haul routes.

Second-Order Effects

  • Months 0–18 (2026-10-12 to 2028-04-12) — The Standards Swamp: The binding-standards deadline arrives before the underlying legislation is settled, so carriers, platforms and national regulators spend the window lobbying over fee and data-access terms rather than building.
  • Months 18–36 (2028-04-12 to 2029-10-12) — The Hollow Metric: Through-ticket share rises on paper because carriers re-label existing multi-leg sales, while seats on the busiest corridors stay full and the extra demand has nowhere to go.
  • Months 36–60 (2029-10-12 to 2031-10-12) — The Toll Booth Forms: The dominant distributors become unavoidable intermediaries and collect distribution fees that flow into fares, while smaller carriers carry compliance costs they cannot recover.
  • Months 60–120 (2031-10-12 to 2036-10-12) — The Reckoning: The program is judged on flights not displaced and fares not lowered, and Europe is left with an expensive shared system that is hard to dismantle and a promise of continuous journeys that carriers cannot physically deliver.

Evidence

  • Law/Standard — Regulation (EU) 2021/782 on rail passengers' rights and obligations, in application since 2023, already contains through-ticket provisions; the problem is that they are narrow in scope and miss many single-platform bookings, not that Europe lacks a booking law.
  • Law/Standard — GDPR Art. 9 (special categories of personal data, including health data): accessibility-assistance requests for persons with reduced mobility, pooled across dozens of carriers and distributors, fall squarely within it.
  • Case/Report — The Community of European Railway and Infrastructure Companies (CER) and rail trade press have warned that the Commission's 2026 ticketing proposal, by compelling distribution agreements, could strengthen large platforms and push up distribution fees and ticket prices (as reported; details not verified).
  • Case/Report — The rail-industry-built OSDM standard has already been associated with a sharp rise in international digital rail ticket sales without a €1.5 billion public machine (growth figures not verified).

Premise Attack 3 — Spectrum

Enforced breadth: distinct reasons across ethical/feasibility/governance/societal axes.

[STRATEGIC] A €1.5 billion booking-layer mandate treats a shortage of capacity, affordable fares and rolling stock as an interface problem, so it will perfect the checkout while trains stay scarce, expensive and late.

Bottom Line: REJECT: Europe's cross-border rail problem is scarce capacity and fares, not a missing booking interface, and a €1.5 billion mandate aimed at the interface will enrich platforms, saddle carriers with open-ended liability and leave the planes full.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Causality: the program's headline success claim, that the train beats the plane on competitive short-haul routes, depends on fares, seat supply, journey time and punctuality, none of which a shared real-time data layer or OSDM-compatible APIs can change.
  • Governance: binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12) and mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-12) presuppose a Regulation that was only proposed in 2026 and still has to survive Parliament and Council, so the program would start building to a legal text that does not yet exist and can still be rewritten.
  • Incentives: forcing SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ and roughly twenty more carriers to expose inventory on non-discriminatory terms hands the sales margin and customer relationship to the largest platforms such as Trainline and Omio, while the carriers keep the cost of running the trains.
  • Liability and budget: a passenger-rights backstop for missed connections across every participating carrier and every compliant distributor creates open-ended claims that a €1.5 billion envelope, already earmarked for standards, conformance testing, clearing, a public distributor, capacity building and apps, cannot cap.
  • Privacy: single-payment through-ticketing with accessibility assistance for persons with reduced mobility and bicycle reservations pushes health-related and travel-pattern data into a shared layer reachable by twenty-plus carriers and any compliant distributor, multiplying breach and misuse exposure for a convenience gain.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: With no adopted legal text at Month 0 (2026-10-12), standards working groups spend the opening months arguing over fee terms, API scope and liability allocation, and every amendment in Council or Parliament reopens specifications already drafted.
  • 1–3 years: When mandatory API exposure arrives around Month 30 (2029-04-12), the biggest platforms capture the cross-border sales flow, carriers raise distribution fees or fares to recover the loss, the public reference distributor becomes a subsidised competitor with thin volume, and complaints rise as more through-tickets create more disputes at the seams between carriers.
  • 5–10 years: By Month 60 (2031-10-12) the clearing mechanism and the passenger-rights backstop are entrenched as a permanent shared liability pool no member state can unwind, through-ticket share sits well short of 40% (estimate) because corridor seats and track-access charges are unchanged, and short-haul air traffic on competitive routes is largely where it started.

Evidence

  • Law/Standard — Regulation (EU) 2021/782 on rail passengers' rights and obligations (2021): already imposes through-ticket and missed-connection duties, yet commentary notes these obligations remain limited in scope, showing that mandating through-ticketing on paper does not produce it in practice.
  • Report/Guidance — CER press release on the Commission's Passenger Package proposal (2026): the rail sector's own trade body reacted to the proposed single digital booking and ticketing regulation, and trade-press coverage reports concerns about platform market power and higher distribution fees (detail of the release not verified).
  • Report/Guidance — European Court of Auditors Special Report 19/2018 on the EU high-speed rail network (2018): found EU-level rail coordination had produced an ineffective patchwork rather than a coherent cross-border network (not verified by search).

Premise Attack 4 — Cascade

Tracks second/third-order effects and copycat propagation.

The plan treats a retail-layer problem (search, booking, refund) as the cause of a capacity, pricing and incentive problem, and sets 18-month and 30-month binding deadlines against a regulation that is still only a May 2026 Commission proposal. A €1.5 billion (user constraint) public budget cannot buy compliance from carriers who own the inventory, bear the liability and have every reason to keep distributors at arm's length, and the headline success metrics (40% through-ticketing, modal shift from air) are not controllable by the instruments the programme actually has.

Bottom Line: Abandon this premise: it mistakes a distribution-layer fix for a rail-capacity and incentive problem and attaches binding deadlines and modal-shift targets to a law that does not yet exist. The failure is built into the goal itself, since no ticketing standard, however well funded, can make carriers sell inventory they would rather keep or make trains more attractive than planes.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The Legislative Quicksand Foundation: the programme starts 'ASAP' (Month 0 = 2026-10-12) and commits to binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-12) and mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-12), yet the underlying Regulation is a proposal (May 2026) that still has to pass Parliament and Council, with delegated and implementing acts to follow. Any standards work done before the legal text settles risks being rewritten, and a 'mandatory' date cannot precede the mandate. Carriers will rationally wait for the final text before spending anything.
  • The Ticket-Is-Not-The-Train Fallacy: through-ticketing fixes the purchase, not the journey. Lisbon-Tallinn is not constrained by checkout friction but by missing track capacity, incompatible signalling and gauge, unsynchronised timetables, scarce rolling stock and fares that are higher than low-cost air. A beautifully unified booking flow selling seats that do not exist, at connections that do not work, raises the number of failed sales rather than the number of train journeys.
  • The Clearing-House Hostage Trap: the inter-carrier settlement and passenger-rights backstop makes the programme the de facto insurer of missed connections across ~25 carriers with different liability rules, fare structures and national regulators. Every carrier's incentive is to minimise inventory offered and keep its own channel privileged (the 'non-discriminatory terms' are policed by 27 national regulators with uneven capacity). The first large disrupted-journey dispute exposes who actually pays, and nobody has agreed in advance.
  • The Forty-Percent Denominator Mirage: '40% of cross-border journeys sold as single through-tickets' has no defined baseline. Most cross-border rail trips are short regional hops that are already one ticket or are bought as day-passes, while the long-haul multi-carrier journeys the programme is designed for are a tiny volume. The metric can be hit by redefinition or missed despite real improvement, so it cannot discipline the programme and invites statistical gaming.
  • The Flight-Substitution Attribution Fantasy: 'train more attractive than flying, so fewer choose the plane' is a macro outcome driven by ticket prices, aviation taxation, journey time, night-train capacity and airline route economics. A booking-layer programme has no lever on any of these, and a five-year horizon is shorter than the delivery time for new rolling stock and cross-border infrastructure. Success will be claimed or denied on factors outside the programme's control.

Second-Order Effects

  • Within Months 0-6 (2026-10-12 to 2027-04-12): the programme stands up governance (DG MOVE, ERA, CER, regulators, BEUC) before the legal text is final; scope fights over who owns the clearing mechanism and the public reference distributor consume the first year, and incumbent operators and platforms such as Trainline and Omio lobby for opposite fee and data-access terms.
  • Months 6-18 (2027-04-12 to 2028-04-12): standards drafting proceeds against a moving legislative target and against existing OSDM, TAP TSI and national APIs; competing versions fragment conformance testing. The Month 18 (2028-04-12) 'binding standards' milestone is met only by narrowing to a minimum common profile that excludes bicycles, PRM assistance and reduction cards, which are the features sold to the public.
  • Months 18-36 (2028-04-12 to 2029-10-12): carriers meet the Month 30 (2029-04-12) API-exposure date with technically compliant but commercially throttled interfaces (rate limits, delayed inventory, partial fare classes). Distributor complaints do not halve; they shift from 'no access' to 'access without usable inventory', and the private IT bill (estimate: a multiple of the €1.5 billion public envelope, not verified) is borne by carriers that then demand compensation.
  • Months 36-60 (2029-10-12 to 2031-10-12): the first corridors go live with through-tickets that work in normal operations but fail under disruption; liability disputes over the settlement and backstop mechanism reach national regulators and courts, and consumer trust, which is the stated objective, is damaged more than by the status quo. Reported through-ticket share is contested because of the baseline problem.
  • Months 60-120 (2031-10-12 to 2036-10-12): the public reference distributor is either a loss-making duplicate of existing platforms or crowds out independent distributors it was meant to level the field with. Air short-haul volumes on competitive routes move little, because prices and capacity were unchanged, and the programme is judged a €1.5 billion (user constraint) IT standards exercise that did not deliver the modal shift it promised.

Evidence

  • The Commission's own May 2026 proposals (multimodal booking and rail ticketing) acknowledge that multimodal options exist on 76% of representative EU routes but are rarely shown or combined by platforms: the problem is distributor and carrier behaviour, not an absence of technology, which a standards programme alone does not change (Council document ST-9313-2026; Legislative Observatory summary).
  • The TAP TSI (Commission Regulation (EU) No 454/2011, in force since May 2011) already mandated common telematics for passenger information and ticketing; fifteen years later cross-border through-ticketing is still described as unsolved, which is direct evidence that technical standards without carrier commercial incentives do not produce integrated sales.
  • OSDM, the industry's own standard, had 22 railway undertakings signed up, but only six (SNCF, SBB/CFF, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB, Trenitalia, PKP) applying it by the end of 2024, with others from 2025 (per CER/UIC releases and trade coverage); even a voluntary, carrier-led standard has moved gradually, so a 30-month mandatory deadline across all TEN-T carriers is aggressive even for the 'realistic' scenario.
  • Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/1926 on EU-wide multimodal travel information services (MMTIS) required national access points for travel data but did not produce seamless multimodal booking; this is the nearest precedent for the proposed mandate and it is cited here from memory (not verified).

Premise Attack 5 — Escalation

Narrative of worsening failure from cracks → amplification → reckoning.

[STRATEGIC] — The Checkout Fallacy: The program treats a fragmented booking screen as the reason travellers fly, then spends €1.5 billion (user constraint) polishing the screen while leaving the tracks, timetables, fares and carrier incentives that actually decide the journey untouched.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A €1.5 billion ticketing superstructure sold as aviation substitution is a category error that will deliver paperwork, not modal shift, and concentrates risk and unaccountable power in exchange for a metric it can game. The gate is closed.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Rights and dignity: A single digital ticket with a 'backstop' promises a stranded passenger, a wheelchair user or a cyclist protection across some twenty-plus carriers (user constraint), yet the assistance, boarding ramps, bicycle spaces and re-routing are delivered by staff and rolling stock the program does not control, so the promise is a screen-deep guarantee that fails exactly when a person is stuck at a platform at night.
  • Accountability and oversight: Authority is split among DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways, CER, national operators, national regulators and a publicly funded reference distributor that is simultaneously rule-maker, competitor and clearing participant, so when a through-ticket fails there is no single party that owns the harm and every party can point to another's standard.
  • Systemic risk and scale: A shared real-time inventory layer plus an inter-carrier clearing mechanism concentrates every carrier's availability, pricing and settlement flows into one mandated chokepoint, creating a single cyber and outage target and a competition-law hazard in the form of pooled commercially sensitive data among rivals.
  • Value-proposition rot: The headline success claim, that trains become more attractive than planes and fewer people fly, is smuggled in as an outcome of ticketing, whereas the measurable target (40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets, user constraint) is a product metric that can be met by relabelling bundles while door-to-door time, price and frequency, which drive mode choice, remain exactly as they were.

Second-Order Effects

  • T+0–6 months (Months 0-6 = 2026-10-12 to 2027-04-12) — The Cracks Appear: Work starts 'ASAP' while the Regulation is still a Commission proposal, so budget, working groups and conformance vendors are committed before the legal text, definitions and liability rules are settled, and the first months are spent arguing over whose interpretation of 'through-ticket' binds.
  • T+1–3 years (Months 12-36 = 2027-10-12 to 2029-10-12) — Copycats Arrive: Carriers expose APIs at minimum compliance, with throttled, delayed or fare-restricted inventory while the best fares stay on their own channels, independent distributors litigate over 'non-discriminatory' terms, and the corridor-first rollout sorts Europe into a ticketed core and an unserved periphery that copies the same workaround.
  • T+5–10 years (Months 60-120 = 2031-10-12 to 2036-10-12) — Norms Degrade: Through-ticket share and complaint counts are managed by redefining what is counted, carriers price missed-connection liability into fares and lengthen scheduled transfer buffers so journeys get slower, and the clearing fee becomes an opaque levy that nobody can audit or exit.
  • T+10+ years (Months 120+) — The Reckoning: Europe owns an expensive, brittle clearing apparatus and a public distributor that crowds out private ones, flights on competitive short-haul routes are essentially unchanged, auditors document a modal-shift goal that was never connected to its instrument, and public trust in rail-first policy is spent.

Evidence

  • Law/Standard — Regulation (EU) 2021/782 on rail passengers' rights (in application since 2023): its through-ticket definition leaves many single-transaction multi-operator purchases without missed-connection protection, and a 2026 Commission proposal (COM(2026) 233) already moves to close that gap, so the program's 'backstop' duplicates or collides with a legal text still in motion.
  • Case/Report — European Court of Auditors Special Report 13/2017 on ERTMS deployment: found a European rail IT harmonisation effort fragmented by national interests and slow delivery (report figures not verified), the same pattern that awaits a mandated multi-carrier IT layer.
  • Case/Report — France's restriction on domestic short-haul flights where a rail alternative exists (climate law of 2021, applied from 2023): the instrument that actually targeted flying acted on route supply and legal permission, not on booking convenience, and covered only a handful of routes (route count not verified).
  • Principle/Analogue — Transport Economics: mode choice follows generalised cost (door-to-door time, fare, frequency, reliability); booking friction is a small component, so improving it cannot by itself outcompete a cheap, fast flight.
